# Archiepiscopal Censure

<insert>S Ran</insert> <note>Likely a signature or archival mark.</note>

Not only have I myself carefully read these **Vindications** prepared by the **Noble and Most Illustrious Mr. Wolfgang Ernst Heidel** on behalf of the **Steganography** <note>A treatise on secret writing, often misunderstood as magic.</note> of the late **Abbot Johannes Trithemius of Sponheim**, but I also handed them over to three **Theologians** to be read. These men constantly asserted with one voice that they found nothing at all in those **Vindications** which opposes the **Catholic faith and good morals** even in the slightest degree. Since, therefore, the memory of **Trithemius**—to whom the holy **Church of Mainz** owes a good portion of its **Ecclesiastical History**—rightly ought to be pleasing to us, the permission for printing and circulating the present **Treatise** was obtained here all the more easily. This is especially true since its author, by the excellence of his talent and erudition, not only gives hope for more hidden knowledge, but even provides clear evidence of it. Thus I gave my judgment on the eve of the **Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary.** <note>February 1st.</note>
In the year **1675.**

->**ADOLPH GOTTFRIED VOLUSIUS,**<-
->*Doctor of Sacred Theology, Apostolic Protonotary,*<-
->*and Archiepiscopal Censor of books at*<-
->*Mainz.*<-

### MOST EMINENT PRINCE,

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter 'J' featuring a classical serif style, set within a square frame decorated with intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc> Johannes Trithemius, formerly Abbot of Sponheim <note>original: "Spanheimensis"</note> of the Order of Saint Benedict in the Diocese of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinæ"</note>, was a man of incomparable genius. Even in his own age, which was most fertile with highly learned men, he was a radiant light of all erudition. Among the countless and admirable volumes that he wrote, he began to compose a certain great and exceedingly difficult work titled *Steganographia* <note>A title derived from Greek meaning "hidden writing," the foundation of modern cryptography.</note>, a marvelous invention intended to be divided into eight books. He continued this work into the third book; however, he veiled these three books under the likeness and principles of magical instructions, using the figures of spirits and incantations <note>original: "conjurationum"</note> and riddles. He did this so effectively that, until now, no one has been found—no one, I say—who has reached his true meaning or penetrated the doctrine handed down in them by any reasoning. 

To this was added the fact that his letters to Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite of Ghent, which contained the subject matter and arrangement of this future work, were opened and read by the Prior of the Convent of Ghent. These letters were spread everywhere as if they were a miracle, and in a short space of time, they were published throughout France <note>original: "Galliam"</note> and Germany <note>original: "Alemanniam"</note> before many Princes and most learned men. They were transcribed and read with the greatest admiration by all, held to be a new and unheard-of miracle. Since no one, however learned, was able to understand either the principles or the reasons for those things promised therein, diverse judgments were stirred up in the minds of men. Some proclaimed Trithemius a divine man, others the most learned of men, while some—whose intellect <note>The text cuts off here, following the catchword 'tellectus' to the next page.</note>

...understanding was slower and whose will was more prone to rashness, they confirmed that he was a magician and performed those deeds through the service of spirits. Thus it happened that, until now, he has been publicly regarded and proclaimed as a Magician and Necromancer <note>A practitioner of "black magic" involving communication with the dead.</note>, and even dragged before the Inquisition. Turning these things over in my mind, **MOST EMINENT PRINCE**, after I had become acquainted with the life of Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous Benedictine abbot, scholar, and cryptographer.</note> and found nothing in the perusal of his volumes except that which most fully breathed the highest piety, devotion, and the other virtues of a Christian man, a Monk, a Priest, and an Abbot, I saw how unjust, rash, empty, and frivolous this common opinion was. I firmly resolved to apply whatever talent nature has bestowed upon me, or whatever erudition study has added, entirely toward vindicating the name of such a great man from such great slanders. 

Nor was the effort in vain; for within the space of six weeks, I discovered not only the genuine key to the *Steganographia* <note>Trithemius's most famous work, which appeared to be about magic but was actually about secret writing.</note> but also the solution to those things which Trithemius—to the admiration and suspicion of all—proposed and promised in his letters to Arnold Bostius <note>A fellow monk and correspondent of Trithemius.</note> and in many passages of his *Polygraphia* <note>Another foundational work on cryptography.</note>. While I was joyful and congratulating myself on such a happy success in a matter I had deemed impossible, I was nevertheless deeply anxious about the method of making this discovery of mine public. I wished for the innocence of Trithemius to be established throughout the entire world as quickly as possible, without fear that it might be suppressed at its very birth by the cruelty of the malevolent, or hidden away through contempt for an unlearned writer. At last, **MOST EMINENT PRINCE**, I took heart on that day when, by the unanimous votes of the Capitulars of Mainz <note>The high-ranking clergy of the Cathedral of Mainz.</note>, you were elevated to the Holy See of Mainz...

...of Mainz, you were elected Archbishop, and Arch-Chancellor <note>The highest administrative official of the Holy Roman Empire, a position traditionally held by the Archbishop of Mainz.</note> of the Holy Roman Empire, and Prince-Elector <note>One of the elite group of princes who had the right to elect the Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. On that day, as you flew on your family wings closest to the Eagle <note>The Eagle was the heraldic symbol of the Holy Roman Empire; Heidel is using poetic language to describe the Archbishop's rise to power alongside the Emperor.</note>, and strengthened the sacred nest of the Eagle with another column; on that day, I say, I believed that what I had so long desired with such great prayers for the innocence of Trithemius would come to pass. 

For I know, and all know with me, how you are the most merciful among the merciful, the mildest among the mild, and how much you are accustomed to show gentleness to the humble and those subject to you. Thus, although this work of mine does not deserve to appear in the sight of Your Eminence, I trust nevertheless—since you are usually mild and merciful to all—that you will not be cruel to me alone. This is especially true when I have inscribed this submitted work, *Steganography Vindicated, Unlocked, and Explained* <note>original: "Steganographiæ Vindicatæ, Referatæ & Illustratæ"</note>, with all the subjection and humility I can and must, to your Most Eminent Name, so that it may be defended from then on against the arrows of the envious. 

But I was also greatly encouraged by the consideration that I undertook this bold task because I claim no right for myself in this work, nor do I look for any honor; rather, I wish for everything to redound to the innocence, fame, and name of Trithemius. You will therefore undertake his defense all the more willingly, as it will be more acceptable to the Catholic Church, the Order of Saint Benedict, and the Holy See of Mainz itself, especially for preserving the authority of historical records <note>Heidel argues that if Trithemius is proven to be a scholar rather than a wizard, his historical writings will be seen as more reliable.</note>. If you do this, I shall have reached the goal of happiness and attained the richest fruit of my labor. 

Receive, therefore, this smallest work of mine, cherish it, and fare well in safety for a very long time for the sake of the Church, the Empire, and the Fatherland.

Thus I made my vow at Mainz on the first day of the year 1676.

# THE LIFE
# OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS
### FIRST OF SPONHEIM, THEN OF SAINT JAMES AT WÜRZBURG <note>original: "Peapolitani." This is a Latinized reference to Herbipolis, the Latin name for the city of Würzburg.</note>
### ABBOT <note>The head of an abbey or monastery. Trithemius was a famous Benedictine monk and polymath.</note>.

### PREFACE TO THE READER.

I have described the life of Trithemius from Trithemius's own *Chronicles of Hirsau* <note>A massive historical work documenting the history of the Benedictine monastery at Hirsau.</note> and *Sponheim* <note>The monastery where Trithemius served as Abbot for over twenty years and built one of the greatest libraries of his time.</note>, as well as from his personal letters; I have added scarcely anything of my own, except where the logic of the sequence and the necessity of connecting parts required it. Nor should I be judged to have inserted my own thoughts simply because I have not cited the specific locations of the source texts everywhere. You should know that I have done this for the sake of brevity, and so that an abundance of citations would not interrupt the curious reader. Meanwhile, I have often combined several pages into a single chapter, collecting meanings and phrases from here and there, so that the natural splendor of history might remain, and the unsullied truth of the narrative might be preserved.

## THE LIFE
# OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS
### ABBOT.

#### CHAPTER I.
#### THE BIRTH AND EDUCATION OF TRITHEMIUS.

In that year when Golden Mainz <note>original: "Aurea Moguntia"</note>—a free city of the German Empire and once the capital and metropolis of the Frankish kingdom—lost its liberty and fell into servitude, having been captured, plundered, and set on fire during the conflict between the two bishops Diether von Isenburg and Adolf von Nassau, with many citizens cruelly killed and driven into exile; in the year, I say, of human salvation 1462, in the tenth Roman Indiction <note>A fifteen-year cycle used in the Roman Empire and the Church for dating documents</note>, in the fourth year of Pope Pius II, and the twenty-second year of Emperor Frederick III, on the very night of the Purification of the Virgin <note>The feast of Candlemas, celebrated on February 2nd</note>, that is, on the Calends of February <note>February 1st</note>, at eleven o’clock at night and nearly the thirtieth minute, JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS was born in Trittenheim. He took his surname from this place, which is a village in the Diocese of Trier, located about four miles from that metropolitan city on the left bank of the Moselle River as it flows downstream. He was born to honorable parents of modest fortune, who provided the necessities of life through the cultivation of grapes for wine. They were, however, free citizens. His father was from the "pagan mountain," commonly called *Heidenberg*, and his mother was Elisabeth, known as being "of the long village" <note>original: "de longo vico"</note>. When the boy was only one year old, his father died. His mother, out of love for the infant and fearing that the tender child might be exposed to the mistreatment of a stepfather, remained a widow for seven years. When that time had finally passed, she took a second husband, with whom she bore several other children. All of these, however, died in their youth, except for one son named Jacob...

[sur-]name, to whom two books of *Familiar Letters* <note>original: "Epistolarum familiarium"</note> survive, written at the Abbey of Saint James near Würzburg <note>The OCR reads "Peapolim," likely a variant or error for Herbipolis, the Latin name for Würzburg, where Trithemius later lived and where the Scottish Abbey of St. James was located.</note>. Our Johannes, however, when he was fifteen years old—against the wishes of his parents and all his relatives—was touched by a love of letters. Having been assured in a way by a certain miraculous vision of his future knowledge, he began to learn his letters secretly. When this became known to his stepfather, he was met with harsh words and even harsher beatings from him, and he was pulled away with all possible force from the literary pursuit he held. 

Truly, the more he was daily afflicted by these prohibitions, the more he was inflamed with a fervent desire for learning. For at night (since he was not allowed during the day, except on holidays, and then only secretly), while everyone else was sleeping, he would leave the house and go to a certain neighboring friend who had formerly applied himself to letters. From this friend, he learned the first principles of elementary instruction in a very short time; so much so that even the teacher himself, being greatly amazed, said that he had never seen a more teachable talent or a more lively memory in any man. Johannes also described this vision which he had, which we have come to know from his own revelation as follows:

### CHAPTER II.
## THE VISION GRANTED TO TRITHEMIUS AND HIS STUDIES.

For the space of one year, with continuous fasting and prayers, he asked two very great things from the Lord God with the highest intention: one was the knowledge of the scriptures; the other, he said, he never revealed to anyone. Behold, one night as the youth was sleeping, a figure in bright clothing appeared to stand before him, holding two tablets in his hands. One of these was written with letters, and the other was depicted with certain images. He said to him: *“Choose one of these two tablets, whichever you wish.”* 

Immediately Trithemius—burning with a love of letters (of which he was still entirely ignorant at that time) even while dreaming—chose the tablet that appeared to be written. To him, the youth who had appeared said: *“Behold, God has heard your prayers, and he will give you both what you have asked for, and indeed more than you could have requested.”* Soon, on the following day, while he was thinking nothing of the vision, a miraculous opportunity was given to him to begin the letters he so desired. 

For some time, therefore, he devoted himself to letters in secret in that same village, because he did not dare do so publicly for fear of his parents. In seven days, he perfectly learned the Alphabet, the Lord’s Prayer, the Angelic Salutation <note>The Hail Mary</note>, the Apostles’ Creed, the confession of the altar <note>The Confiteor</note>, and the blessing of food and drink <note>Grace before meals</note>, and he committed them most tenaciously to memory. Furthermore, after this, he became accustomed to reading books in the German language <note>original: "Teutonicæ"</note> perfectly by himself within one month. 

When his friends, and especially the priests, saw such talent in the youth and such a love for letters, they persuaded his uncle, Peter of Heidenberg <note>original: "de monte gentili," meaning "of the pagan mountain"</note>—a mature and stern man—to see for himself what such a vehement desire for letters portended in the boy. He agreed, and as his uncle, he presented himself as the youth’s guardian despite the stepfather’s objections, and thereafter began to manage his inheritance. But how many beatings, how many insults, how [many...]

How many insults did the innocent youth suffer from his stepfather? How many showers of tears did he pour out in his distress before he could escape a yoke more cruel than any slavery? At last, he fled his step-family’s house <note>original: "domum novercam," literally "stepmother's house," though context emphasizes his stepfather's cruelty.</note>, just as the Israelite multitude fled Egypt, and for the love of letters, he completed a three-day journey through the wilderness. He traveled first to Trier, then to the lower regions, and finally to the town of Heidelberg. Thus, having completed his three-day journey in a foreign land, he finally offered himself at the Monastery of Sponheim as a perpetual burnt offering <note>original: "holocaustum;" here used metaphorically to mean a total, living sacrifice of himself to God's service.</note> to the Lord God.

---

### CHAPTER III.

## THE ENTRANCE OF TRITHEMIUS INTO THE MONASTERY OF SPONHEIM.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1482, Johannes Trithemius became a monk of the Monastery of Sponheim quite miraculously and against his own original intention. It happened in this way: when he had set out on a journey from Heidelberg with a fellow student toward his homeland, he entered the Monastery of Sponheim (because it was on his way) merely to visit. This occurred on the eighth day before the Calends of February <note>January 25th.</note> in the morning around the ninth hour. After they had finished their midday meal, thinking of nothing less than joining a religious order, he departed to continue his planned journey. 

However, being ignorant of the roads, when they both reached the mountain adjacent to the small village of Bockenaw, a massive heap of snow and a thick storm of clouds suddenly began to rise. This not only covered the path of the roads but, blowing directly against them, nearly blinded their eyes. When his traveling companion urged him to return to the monastery since they could not go forward, Trithemius replied: "It is too shameful to turn back; let us rather go forward as far as we can." But as they waited three times under the shelter of trees for the storm to end, and it only grew worse, Trithemius said to his companion again: "We must return to the Monastery; behold, you will see me staying there." He said this under the inspiration of some Divine power—though he knew it not—for even as he spoke those words, he was still not considering entering the religious life. 

Thus, having returned to this place unwillingly but by necessity, he was destined to remain according to the words he had unknowingly spoken. Led by the persuasion of Henry of Holtzhausen, who was the Prior <term>Prior: the deputy head of a monastery, or the head of a smaller religious house</term> at that time, he changed his mind. On the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary <note>February 2nd; also known as Candlemas.</note>, he cast off his secular clothing at exactly twenty years of age. Later, on the day of our Holy Father Benedict <note>March 21st, the feast of the founder of the Benedictine Order.</note>, he became a novice, and in that same year, on the Feast of the Presentation of the Virgin <note>November 21st.</note>, he made his profession <term>profession: the formal act of taking religious vows to live according to a monastic rule</term> according to the Rule along with three others. Having become a monk, he lived among the brothers without cause for complaint; he preferred the study of letters and the solitude of the cell to all the delights of this world, and he seemed to thirst for nothing more in this life than the knowledge of the scriptures.

<summary>This page recounts how Trithemius fled his abusive household to study in Heidelberg and was later "miraculously" forced by a snowstorm to take refuge at Sponheim Abbey, where he eventually took his vows.</summary>

VITA TRITHEMII
<meta>catchword: §. 4. Con-</meta>

## CAP. IV.
### DESCRIPTION OF THE SPONHEIM MONASTERY.

#### *§. 1. The Location of the Sponheim Monastery.*

The Sponheim Monastery is situated in the Rhenish Palatinate, within the County of Sponheim <note>specifically the "Anterior" or Front County of Sponheim</note>, in the region of the Hundsrück <note>original: "Cynonotorum," a Latinized name for the Hundsrück mountains, literally "dog's back."</note>. It is located one mile from Stauronesus, which is now called Kreuznach; one mile from Sobernheim, a town belonging to the Electorate of Mainz; and two miles from Bingen, a town of the Metropolitan Chapter of Mainz situated at the confluence of the Rhine and Nahe rivers. Its latitude is 50 degrees 23 minutes, and its longitude is 26 degrees 53 minutes, based on a prime meridian where Mainz is at 27 degrees 30 minutes. The monastery recognizes the Count of Sponheim as the lord of the land and territory, and the Archbishop of Mainz for its ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

#### *§. 2. The Foundation of the Church of Sponheim.*

In the year 1044 from the Incarnation of the Lord—in the fifth year of the reign of Emperor Henry III, the tenth of Pope Benedict IX, and the fourteenth of the Blessed Bardo, Archbishop and Elector of Mainz—the illustrious Count Eberhard, Count of Sponheim, founded a church in a place anciently called the <term>Mountain of the Field</term> <note>original: "mons campi."</note>. He endowed it with many goods and revenues and placed certain clerics there to read the Masses. However, he reserved for himself and his heirs the right to appoint clerics to these benefits <note>this refers to the right of "advowson," or the power to nominate a priest to a church office.</note>, just as the four altars that were within it were conferred upon succeeding priests by the senior Count of Sponheim. The most holy Blessed Bardo consecrated this church on the eighth day before the Calends of July <note>June 24th</note> in the year of our Lord 1047, in honor of the Most Blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, and he confirmed the donation of the church made by the Count.

#### *§. 3. The Elevation of the Sponheim Church into a Monastery.*

In the year of our Lord 1101, in the ninth Indiction, while Emperor Henry IV held the Roman Empire and the venerable Archbishop and Elector Ruthard governed the Church of Mainz, the illustrious Count Stephan of Sponheim, moved by divine inspiration, took care to elevate his church on the "mountain of the field" (founded by his ancestors) into a monastery. He began to build quarters and dwellings suitable for monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. However, hindered by various pressing occupations, he did not complete the work he had begun. When he finally saw that he was near death, he called his son Megenhard, the heir to his father’s estate, and charged him to finish the building started for the monastery. Thus, he fell asleep in the Lord on the fifth day before the Calends of March <note>February 25th</note> in the year of our Lord 1118. Megenhard, the noble Count, having taken up the long-interrupted work after his father's death, completed it within a few years. Count Rudolph, Megenhard's brother, along with his wife Richarde, also contributed no small expense toward the completion of the project.

OF THE ABBOT.

### §. 4. The Consecration of the Sponheim Monastery.

The building was finally completed—that is, the church built in the shape of a cross, the cloister, and the necessary houses, with the refectory and the dormitory adjacent to the cloister on the western side. Before the magnificent Count Megenhard handed over the monastery to the monks for habitation, he wished the church, which he had renovated in many ways, to be consecrated once again (as is the custom). Therefore, having removed the clerics and provided for them elsewhere, he went to Adelbert, Archbishop of Mainz, to arrange the consecration of the church, and revealed to him the desire of his heart regarding the introduction of monks to Sponheim. This most Reverend Prelate highly commended the Count's good plan, but because he himself could not come to the consecration as requested, he sent in his place the Venerable Buggo, Prelate of the Church of Worms, who at that time had been expelled from his own see for many years and was being held honorably by the Archbishop.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, on *Quasimodogeniti* Sunday <note>The first Sunday after Easter, also known as Low Sunday; the name comes from the first words of the Latin Introit for that day.</note>, the Venerable Buggo, Bishop of Worms, acting on behalf of Archbishop Adelbert of Mainz, dedicated the church and monastery in Sponheim in honor of the Blessed Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of God, and Saint Martin, formerly Bishop of Tours in Gaul. This was done with three altars: the high altar, as we have said, was consecrated to the memory of the Mother of God and Saint Martin; another in the apse facing south in memory of Saint John the Evangelist; and the third in the apse facing north at the entrance of the cloister in honor of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul. The remaining altars were erected later in the course of time.

### §. 5. The Introduction of Monks into the Sponheim Cloister.

In the eightieth year from the foundation of the church in the place called the *Mountain of the Field* <note>original: "mons campi."</note>, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1124, in the second indiction under Emperor Henry V, the illustrious Count Megenhard handed over the monastery itself, along with the church and all its belongings, into the perpetual possession of the Order of the most holy Father Benedict, and gave it to the monks to inhabit. The first monks who initially began to inhabit this very place were twelve in number; by the command of Archbishop Adelbert and at the instance of Count Megenhard, they came from the monasteries of Saint Alban and Saint James near Mainz on the Wednesday after Passion Sunday. Eight of them were priests and four were <term>lay brothers</term> <note>original: "conversi." In a Benedictine context, these were members who focused on the manual labor and external affairs of the monastery rather than the full liturgical choir duties.</note>—illustrious and distinguished men, some of whom had served as soldiers in the world for a long time before entering the religious life. When they arrived at the site of the monastery, they were received quite honorably by Count Megenhard and his wife, and they began to inhabit the cloister solemnly handed over to them. Thus, having gained possession in the name of God, the aforementioned monks unanimously elected Bernhelm—a monk of the aforementioned cloister of Saint Alban—as their Abbot and Pastor according to the monastic rule.

### §. 7. *The Reformation of the Monastery of Spanheim and the Incorporation of the Bursfelde Union.*

Since the foundations of the <term>Reformation and the Bursfelde Union</term> <note>A significant 15th-century reform movement within the Benedictine Order aimed at restoring strict monastic discipline</note>, as well as the <term>Provincial Chapters</term> <note>Regular regional meetings of monastic leaders to ensure adherence to rules</note>, were laid in the year of Christ 1417 at the Council of Constance; and since that reformation reached its completion around the year of Christ 1429 in the Monastery of Bursfelde in the Diocese of Mainz in Saxony; Seeing the devout and holy conduct <note>original: "conversationem"</note> of the Bursfelde monks, the Princes and the Bishops of the Churches desired the individual monasteries subject to them to be reformed by them. To that end, many Provincial Chapters were celebrated, just as a certain Bull was issued in the Council of Basel, and Visitors and Reformers were appointed for all Monasteries of this Order

throughout Germany and especially through the Province of Mainz <note>original: "Provinciam Moguntinam"</note>, among which was also the Sponheim Monastery to be reformed. Thus, Johannes, Abbot of St. Matthias near Trier <note>original: "Treverim"</note>, in the year 1439—supported by the authority of the aforementioned council and appointed as a visitor—visited Sponheim for the third time. However, since the monks had been born and raised in "deformity" (if I may call it that) <note>referring to a lack of proper monastic form or discipline</note> and did not wish to live otherwise than they had learned, he made little progress. In the year 1467, Otto the Abbot and the brothers of this community, fearing that they would be expelled by the Fathers of the Bursfelde Observance <note>The Bursfelde Union was a major reform movement within the Benedictine Order</note> in favor of reformation at the urging of the Princes (which was then often threatened against them), took counsel and decided to reform themselves. They sent messengers and letters of petition to the Abbots of Trier, who at that time (except for the Monastery of St. Martin) had been reformed, and especially to the Abbot of St. Maximin. They were not members of the Bursfelde Union, which was too hateful to them. They urgently petitioned for two monks who might instruct the monks and novices of this monastery in the manners and ceremonies agreeable to regular observance. However, they were unable to obtain anyone from the men of Trier. After this, they sent to Cologne, and from there two brothers from St. Pantaleon came. Upon arrival, they were gratefully received and were appointed by the Abbot as Masters to instruct the monks of this community. However, they were harassed, mocked, and sometimes even affected by beatings due to the excessive persistence and malice of the monks—especially the younger ones. When they perceived that they could accomplish nothing, they returned to Cologne, from whence they had come.

Finally, in the Year of our Lord 1469, in the second indiction, when this monastery had reached extreme poverty due to the bad governance of the Abbots and the dissolute life of the monks, and was utterly deprived of all its beauty in both spiritual and temporal matters, the most illustrious Prince Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine in Simmern and Count in Sponheim, decided to subject it to reform for the honor of

With their counsel and direction, he would lead such a necessary and holy work to its desired end. These commissioners, having received the authority for visiting and reforming from the Archbishop, arrived on the 19th day of the month of August. An hour before their arrival, the counselors of the aforementioned Prince Frederick had entered the monastery in the morning after Prime <note>The first hour of prayer after sunrise</note> with an armed hand, taking precautions so that none of the monks might escape, nor anything be carried out of the monastery. <meta>catchword: council</meta>

[The monks argued] that they could not live otherwise than they had learned, and that the Bursfelde reform <note>original: "reformationem Burſfeldenſem"</note> was too austere and unbearable for them to undergo to any degree. The commissioners, having heard these and many other objections raised against the reform, and wishing to condemn no one hastily, warned them to deliberate further; they then began their official visitation. On the following day, which was August 20th, after the inquiry was completed, the visitors found that Otto, the Abbot of that place, was for certain reasons not fit for the pastoral care required to introduce the reform. After some pious admonitions, they finally persuaded him to resign his abbatial dignity. Thus, Otto resigned the Abbey that same day. The visitors continued their inquiry on that day and the next. Finally, on the morning of August 21st at eight o’clock, they entered the chapter house again and summoned all the monks found there. When they had come and were seated in the designated place, the visitors tried to advise and persuade them in a pious and fatherly way to cast off their "deformity" <note>a term used in monastic records to describe a lack of proper discipline or "form"</note> and submit their necks to the holy reform. However, since they were in no way willing to comply with the pious warnings of the Fathers, the visitors—by the authority granted to them by the Ordinary <note>a high-ranking church official with jurisdiction, likely the Archbishop</note>—expelled them all from the monastery, stripping them by sentence of all rights to this community, regarding elections or any other matters.

Then, they turned their attention to the appointment of a new Abbot. Since no members of the original community remained, the right of election had passed to the Archbishop. Using their delegated authority, and with the advice and consent of the brothers present to introduce the reform, they named, appointed, and installed Johannes Kolenhauſen—a monk and cellarer <note>the officer in charge of a monastery's food and stores</note> of St. James near Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiam"</note>—who was present at the time. The first brothers who came for the reform of this monastery from the community of St. James were four in number; but these men, having been raised in the relative comforts <note>original: "deliciis"</note> of St. James, looked down on staying here for long because of the lack and poverty of this monastery. When those monks returned to St. James, others were sent in their place and stayed for a time, and when they also left, others were sent again. For many years, none of the monks coming from St. James showed steady perseverance in this place except for one; until finally, young men coming from the schools were gathered, and having been instructed and professed according to the custom of the order, they brought a necessary end to these frequent departures. Then in the following year, on the 2nd day of September, the annual chapter of the Bursfelde Union and Observance <note>a influential Benedictine reform movement focused on strict adherence to the Rule of St. Benedict</note> was held in the Monastery of St. Matthias near Trier <note>original: "Trevirim"</note>. At this meeting, Johannes, the Abbot of this monastery, and the monastery itself, earned the right to be incorporated into the union and the sharing of all indults, privileges, and graces in the usual form, after the necessary and customary letters were presented.

In the year of the Lord's Incarnation 1417, all the Abbots and Prelates of this order throughout the entire province of Mainz <note>original: "provinciam Moguntinam"</note> were called and summoned to the council—

<meta>This page transitions from the specific events at Sponheim (described on the previous page) to the broader history of the Bursfelde Reform's origins. It focuses on the figure of John of Reinhausen and his efforts to establish a disciplined monastic life at Clus and later Bursfelde.</meta>

### OF THE ABBOT.

...[the Council] of Constance <note>The Council of Constance (1414–1418) was a major ecumenical council that ended the Western Schism and attempted to reform church life "in head and members."</note>, for the establishment of a <term>provincial chapter</term> <note>A periodic meeting of the heads of monasteries within a specific region to ensure discipline and unity.</note> and for the beginning of the reform of the order in all monasteries. Therefore, the Abbots gathered at Constance in great numbers and, on the final day of February, they began the provincial chapter and laudably established many decrees for the reform of the order. Among others, John, a monk of Reinhausen <note>original: "Reinhaufen"</note>, was present at this chapter, sent in the name of his Abbot as a proxy. When he saw the zeal and diligence of the Fathers for the reform of the order, and heard how dangerous it is for a monk to live in "deformity" <note>original: "deformitate"; a technical term meaning a lack of adherence to the monastic Rule</note>, he was struck with compunction. He thought entirely of fulfilling the oath he had made to the Presidents in his Abbot’s name. Returning to the monastery of Reinhausen, he revealed the entire matter to his Abbot and his brothers, who were at that time most undisciplined; he recounted what he had seen, heard, done, and concluded, as well as the promises made under oath for the reform of the order. He earnestly exhorted them to amend their lives and to accept the promised reform, which had been commanded under threat of punishment. 

However, they began first to mock him, and later even to hold him in hatred and treat him with contempt. Therefore, seeing that he was despised and making no progress, and desiring to provide for his own soul's health, John went to Agnes—the wife of Otto of Brunswick and sister of the Landgrave of Thuringia, a most devout woman in Christ who was then staying in Gandersheim <note>original: "Gamundia"</note> not far from Reinhausen. He reported the acts and conclusions reached by the Fathers in the council and asked for help so that he might fulfill his oath. When that holy woman recognized his holy purpose, she promised she would bestow both help and counsel. It happened meanwhile that the Abbot of the monastery of Clus <note>original: "Clusensis"</note> died. When the Duchess learned of this, she pleaded with the Duke, her husband, that the aforementioned monk John of Reinhausen should succeed to the place of the deceased Abbot, and so it was done.

Thus ordained as Abbot in Clus, he applied every effort toward reform and began to precede his subjects in all holiness and religion according to the Rule. When the monks, who were accustomed to wicked habits, saw this, they all fled from him. But he, having gathered a few novices, instructed them in the purity of the Rule and, living in great poverty, began to serve GOD in all humility. At that time, the Monastery of Bursfelde in the Diocese of Mainz in Saxony—which Henry, formerly Count of Northeim, had founded around the year of our Lord 1097—had come to such misery and desolation that for many years only a single monk lived there, who had no income for his sustenance except for a single cow. The church, covered in straw, served as a stable for wandering cattle, though it had once been a choir of singing monks. Although the place was established in extreme poverty, it nevertheless pleased the aforementioned John, Abbot of Clus, because of its solitude and quiet. Therefore, with the consent of the previously mentioned Duke and Duchess, he left the monastery of Clus (which had also been very poor) and moved with his poor followers to Bursfelde. There he continued the reform he had begun, as best he could, in great poverty. Later, hearing of the fame and religious devotion of Johannes Rode, Abbot of Saint...

# THE LIFE OF TRITHEMIUS
<meta>catchword: men-</meta>

He <note>Referring to John of Reinhausen, the first reformer of Bursfelde.</note> came on foot to John Rode, the Abbot of St. Matthias near Trier, who had most excellently reformed his own monastery and established the necessary constitutions for preserving that reform. Because Rode was a learned and mature man, and uniquely zealous for the observance of the religious rule, John visited him, saw the praiseworthy institution, learned by experience of the holy life of the monks, and praised the constitutions Rode had published as most holy. Thus, one Abbot asked the other to grant him some of his brothers, by whose counsel and help he might complete the desired reform in Saxony. Abbot John Rode, consenting to this pious desire, provided certain monks of proven conduct from his own community and sent them back to Bursfelde with joy. And from that time—which was around the year of our Lord 1429—the holy reform of the monasteries of the Order of St. Benedict, originally poured from the men of Trier into Bursfelde, began to flourish again and was increased within a few years. Therefore, from the monastery of Bursfelde, certain monasteries in Saxony and beyond began gradually to be reformed, and from those, others still. Their Abbots, forming a union and confederation among themselves, met once every year, celebrating a <term>Synod</term> <note>A formal assembly for church administration.</note> (which we call by the customary, though foreign and improper name, a "Chapter"), in which they held discussions on those things pertaining to the utility of the reform. 

Pope Pius II confirmed this union of reformed Abbots under the name of the Bursfelde Congregation, along with the annual chapter, in the first year of his pontificate, the year of our Lord 1458. Along with many privileges which he gave, he also extended to this union the privileges of the <term>Congregation of St. Justina of Padua</term> <note>A highly influential Italian monastic reform movement known for its strict discipline and centralized structure.</note>, which are many and great. Later, in the year 1468, Adolph, the Archbishop of Mainz, by his own <term>ordinary authority</term> <note>The formal power held by a bishop to govern his own diocese.</note>, graciously admitted the observance, the union, and the annual chapter of the Fathers of the Bursfelde reform (because Bursfelde is in the Diocese of Mainz), as well as the privileges of the union and chapter as heard from the Apostolic See. Over time, the number of monasteries subject to this union grew so much that by the year of our Lord 1502, seventy-five had been reformed.

When the votes of all were scrutinized, the greater and more sound part elected Johannes Trithemius as Abbot. He had been in the order for only 8 months and 7 days since his profession, and was the most junior of all the professed monks; indeed, from the time he first took the novice’s habit, he had lived in the monastery for only 1 year, 4 months, and 7 days until the day of his election. Once the election was published, all unanimously consented to him and each signed the decree of election with their own hand. In that same year, on the day of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, he was confirmed by Albert, Administrator of the See of Mainz, in the castle of Steinheim, in the presence of Hermann of St. James, John of Seligenstadt, and Melchior of Schönau, Abbots of our order, and many others. Afterward, in the same year on November 9 <note>original: "5. Idus Novembris"</note>, which was the Sunday before the feast of Saint Martin, he received the blessing from Berthold, Bishop of Pariada and Vicar in Pontificals to the aforementioned Lord Administrator, in the Church of Saint James near Mainz. He was assisted, as is custom, by the Abbots Hermann of that place and Anselm of Limpurg, whom he had invited, both wearing their pontifical vestments.

At that time, however, he was somewhat weak in body, suffering from tertian fevers <note>A fever that recurs every third day, typically associated with malaria.</note>. Therefore, while he was remaining thus ill at Heidelberg, on the fifth day after his departure from the monastery—at the devil’s instigation—a grave disturbance occurred. This act, which was presumed far too rashly and without counsel, became the cause of many tribulations and persecutions for the Abbot, and provoked many rivals against him. But he, being cautious in his foresight and endowed with singular patience, committed the resolution of the entire matter to divine mercy.

In the midst of these events, a great assembly of Princes was held in Cologne. Joachim, the Elector of Brandenburg, who was traveling there from the March of Brandenburg, sent a mounted messenger with letters to Trithemius (who was then staying, ill, at Spires <note>Speyer; original: "Spirae"</note> in the house of the Abbot of Limburg), asking that he come down to join him in Cologne. However, because he could not yet fully identify the authors of the injuries done to him, he decided to delay his return to the monastery for a short while until he could see where the intentions of his rivals were leading. When this became known to the aforementioned Prince Margrave, he asked Trithemius to travel with him to the March of Brandenburg once the assembly of Princes had dissolved. Trithemius agreed to this, but promised he would only come after he had provided the necessary report concerning the monastery to the Prior.

Accordingly, on August 6th, the Abbot left Cologne and traveled by boat up to Mainz, and from there to Spires. Having summoned the Prior, Nicholas of Reinig, he entrusted the entire management of the monastery to him. This done, he entered the March via Thuringia and stayed with the Margrave for nine months. When these months had passed and he had obtained leave to depart, he set out on a journey toward the Rhine regions and arrived at the city of Spires on the second day of June. He had, however, sent Brother Theodoric, his chaplain, ahead from Frankfurt to Sponheim so that he might diligently inquire into the state of the monastery's affairs, investigate whether the unrest of his rivals had settled, and summon his Prior to Heidelberg; for he did not wish to return unless he first understood the feelings of the brothers toward him.

...to call. <note>The word "care" likely completes a word like "vocare" (to call) or "applicare" (to apply/arrive) from the preceding page.</note> In the meantime, it happened that the annual chapter of this order <note>The Benedictine Order</note> was celebrated at Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiam"</note> at the end of the month of August according to custom. The two presiding officers sent two prelates to Heidelberg to meet Johannes Trithemius, intending to ask him to return to the monastery of Sponheim. However, Trithemius could in no way be moved from his purpose, but is said to have given this response:

*“From the time I began to be a monk, I have always been both voluntary and prompt in spirit to obey the commands of my Fathers in all things, and I have never rashly turned away from their institutions. Only on this occasion can I, for no reason, provide my consent to their commands that I return to Sponheim to stay there once again, for the reason that I have very little confidence that I will have peace with them thereafter. For it is manifest how wickedly certain men among them have plotted against me, who (whether by malice or the simplicity of ignorance, I do not judge, but commit to the judgment of almighty GOD) have stirred up many rivals against me. Whence, if I were to return to the monastery, I would not be able to have faith in them, nor do I know for certain that their minds would trust me. It is better, therefore, that we be separated from one another than that we live in perpetual dissension; for the salvation of souls must always be placed before the comfort of bodies. And a shepherd, who considers that he cannot make the sheep committed to him any better, consults healthily for both himself and for them if he resigns his office. Today, the twenty-third year has been fully completed since I, though unworthy, was ordained Abbot of Sponheim—always being refined in the furnace of extreme poverty <note>original: "camino paupertatis nimiæ"</note>, continuous in misery and labor, and (what has usually weighed on me more than all else) never relieved by the necessary help of my brothers in so many cares. Nor was the least of the causes moving me to withdraw the fact that one of my monks—and not the lowest among them—whom I always sincerely loved as an intimate son, and whom I defended everywhere against any molesters as the apple of my own eye <note>original: "pupillam oculi mei proprii"</note>, being unmindful of all benefits, recently stationed at Mainz, by the counsel and help of a certain other 'good brother,' published a letter against me full of insults and injuries in the name of the whole convent, although it is clearly evident to me that he had no commission or consent from the convent in this matter. If this man—the man of my peace in whom I trusted, who walked with me before the poor little flock in the pastures of the Lord—has done this, or was able to do it, what will those do who are weaker, whom I have not heaped with such great benefits? If my right hand, forgotten of me, could so rashly deny me, what will the hands of strangers do? If my friend, indeed my dearest friend, has presumed such things against me, what will an enemy do? Finally, I will add this: that I (to speak the truth), a man born more for the study of the Scriptures <note>original: "studium Scripturarum"</note> than for excessive or continuous cares of secular business, desire quiet more than useless labors. The time has now come, therefore, which I have always hoped for; the occasion of resigning has been given to me, though I do not deserve it, which I have decided to accept no differently than if almighty GOD has decreed to liberate me from such great calamities with manifest piety for the honor of His name. I will therefore resign willingly, and commit myself to divine providence, lest, if I should consent to stay longer with the ungrateful, I should incur both danger to my body and detriment to my soul. Nevertheless, before I do that, it will be necessary for me to provide a place for my future dwelling. The Lord GOD, who does not despise the prayers of the poor, but sends help to those asking in an opportune time, will Himself provide a place for me (I do not doubt) in which I may more freely and quietly serve Him and work out my own salvation in silence.”*

### CHAPTER VII.

## THE TRANSFER OF TRITHEMIUS TO THE ABBACY OF ST. JAMES OF WÜRZBURG AND HIS RESIGNATION FROM SPONHEIM.
<note>The transcription "PEAPOLITANI" is likely a clerical error for *Herbipolitani* (Würzburg) or *Neapolitani* (New City), as the text consistently identifies the location as Herbipolis.</note>

Therefore, many Princes, hearing that Trithemius had departed from Sponheim and did not wish to return there, sought to have him with them. They promised him great salaries, gifts, abbacies, provostships, and most excellent provisions. However, since Trithemius had been received into the monastery of Sponheim at the age of twenty and had been laudably trained in the observance of monastic discipline from the start, he did not think it healthy or proper for himself to live in the courts of Princes. Nor did he think it honorable to break away from the holy union of [monastic] observance. Therefore, he sought a place suitable for his studies and his way of life.

Thus, Conrad, the Abbot of Saint Stephen’s in Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolensis"</note>—who had been sent to Trithemius at Heidelberg by the chapter—was moved by no small amount of compassion for him once he heard the many and reasonable causes that moved him to resign, for he was his friend. For this reason, he promised that he would work to ensure that Trithemius might obtain the Abbacy of Saint James in Würzburg. At that time, the Abbot of the mentioned monastery was a certain Kilian <note>original: "Cilianus"</note> of Ochsenfurt, who had decided to resign that abbacy for certain reasons. When he heard it was possible that Trithemius might succeed to his place, he rejoiced greatly and said, *"To no one in the world would I more gladly resign than to such a great man,"* and he asked that the matter reach its desired conclusion as soon as possible.

Because of this, Abbot Conrad of Saint Stephen brought the matter to the Most Reverend Bishop of Würzburg, Lorenz <note>Lorenz von Bibra, Bishop from 1495–1519</note>, who had previously heard many proclamations of praise regarding Abbot Trithemius. The Bishop had seen him long ago in Heidelberg at the table of the Prince Palatine and had spoken with him with great respect. Indeed, he would have gladly promoted him long ago to the Abbacy in Schwarzach, if Trithemius had answered the call on two occasions after the deaths of Abbots Michael and Paul. The Bishop responded: it not only pleased him, but he greatly desired to have Trithemius as an Abbot in his diocese.

Therefore, having heard the Bishop’s will, Trithemius was summoned by messenger and letters. He proposed the cause to the Most Serene Prince Philip, Elector Palatine, and with his consent, he went up to Würzburg. On the third day of the month of October, he came to Würzburg, and after the voluntary resignation of Abbot Kilian on the 12th day of the said month—the brothers having entrusted the choice <note>original: "compromissione," a legal procedure where the monks delegate their voting rights to a small committee</note> to the Lord Bishop and two Abbots—he was appointed as the elected Abbot of the often-mentioned monastery. On the 14th day of the same month, after the tenth hour, he was confirmed by the same Most Reverend Prelate, and he was introduced into real possession of the Abbacy of Saint James on the following day, which was the solemn feast of Saint Burchard <note>October 14th; Burchard was the first Bishop of Würzburg</note>. And so, in the Year of our Lord’s birth 1506, in the 9th Roman Indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used in the Middle Ages for dating documents</note>, on the 15th day of the month of October, Johannes Trithemius, having been elected and confirmed as Abbot of St. James in Würzburg, took real [possession]...

### CHAPTER VIII.
## DESCRIPTION OF THE MONASTERY OF ST. JAMES OF WÜRZBURG.
<note>The OCR "PEAPOLITANI" is a printing or transcription error for *Herbipolitani*, the Latin name for Würzburg.</note>

Around the year of Christ 1139, when Embricho, the 31st Bishop of the Church of Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolensis"</note>, was traveling to Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiam"</note> to conduct certain business, he encountered a certain monk named Christian on the road. He was Scottish <note>In the 12th century, the term "Scotus" often referred to Irish or Scottish monks who established "Schottenklöster" (Scots' Monasteries) across Germany.</note> by birth, and on bended knees, he asked the Prelate that, for the love of Saint Kilian—the Martyr and Apostle of Eastern Franconia who had himself been a Scot—he might grant the monks traveling from Scotland for the sake of Christ a place or hospital to stay within the city. Following the advice of his counselors, the Bishop sent the aforementioned monk to Würzburg. Not long after, the Bishop himself returned and, with the consent of all the clergy and people, assigned a location to the Scots for the construction of a monastery under the Rule of our Holy Father Benedict. This site was in the suburb of that same city across the Main River <note>original: "Mœnum"</note> in a place called Girberg. Establishing a community there, he dedicated a new chapel in honor of Saint James the Apostle on July 10 <note>original: "6. Iduum Julii"</note> in the year of our Lord 1140, in the third Indiction, during the second year of the reign of King Conrad.

The first Abbot of this same monastery was Macarius, a Scot by nation and a man of the holiest life. Bishop Embricho provided testimony of his holiness through letters strengthened by his own seal, which Trithemius asserts he himself saw whole and intact. Among other miracles he performed in this life, since he entirely abstained from wine for the love of God, one day while sitting at the table in the midst of noblemen and being unable to have water, he made the sign of the Holy Cross over a vessel of wine placed on the table for everyone, and he changed the wine into water. And so, in that monastery founded for the Scottish nation, the monks of that nation lived laudably for many years according to the Rule of the Most Holy Father Benedict. However, gradually over time, falling away from the fervor of their original institution, they finally brought the monastery itself into extreme poverty, and the monks themselves completely failed. For in the year of our Lord 1497, Philip, the last of the Scottish Abbots, died and left not a single monk in the monastery. After his death, the Most Reverend Lord Prelate of Würzburg, Lorenz <note>Lorenz von Bibra, Bishop of Würzburg from 1495 to 1519.</note>, acting by Apostolic commission and his own ordinary authority, laudably resolved to reform the vacant place in both its spiritual and temporal state. For its restoration, he introduced monks of good reformation from the Monastery of Saint Stephen in the same city, provided them with the necessities of life, and paid off almost all the debts contracted by the Scots in full. He restored the church, which had been darkened by age, making it look almost new and very beautiful; he added ornaments, chalices, and many books to the library—

### CHAPTER IX.
## THE DEATH OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS.

At last, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1516, on the 16th of December—the feast day of the Sainted Lucia, Virgin and Martyr—Johannes Trithemius passed away. He was in his 55th year, or to be exact, having completed 54 years, 10 months, and 15 days. This was the 34th year since he became Abbot of Sponheim <note>original: "Spanheimensi"</note> (specifically 33 years, 4 months, and 19 days completed), and the 11th year since he took up the Abbacy of Würzburg <note>original: "Peapolitana," a variant of the Latin name for the city</note> (specifically 10 years, 2 months, and 1 day completed). He was buried in the church of the monastery of Saint James, which is also known as the "Monastery of the Scots." His tombstone carries this inscription:

This stone with its epitaph was erected by Master Georg Flach, the Auxiliary Bishop <note>original: "in Pontificalibus Vicario"</note> to the Bishop of Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolensis"</note>. He was the fourth successor in the Abbey of St. James after the passing of Trithemius. As the monument across from Trithemius’s stone indicates, he was a Doctor of Theology of the Order of St. Benedict, a man distinguished in piety and learning. He was famously sent by the Most Reverend Conrad von Bibra, the elected Prelate of Würzburg, to the Holy Council of Trent <note>A major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church held between 1545 and 1563</note> which had been initiated by Pope Paul III. After ruling this Monastery of St. James of the Scots for sixteen years, he departed from among the living on the first of January, in the year of our Lord 1564.

### CHAPTER X.
## THE SPONHEIM LIBRARY GATHERED BY TRITHEMIO.

From the beginning of the Monastery’s foundation, the library was quite wealthy and filled with various volumes. However, during the time of Abbot Henry XII, around the year 1340, when the discipline of regular observance began to fail excessively and the monks again seized personal property for themselves, a division of revenues was made between the Abbot and the Community. The library was shamefully destroyed by the monks, who sold precious volumes at a low price so that they could satisfy their lusts and gluttony. Then, around the year of Christ 1432, when Abbot Gobelin was intruded by force, he secretly carried away all the privileges, letters, and monuments of the Monastery’s liberty without the knowledge or will of the community. He also took many precious volumes of the library which those earlier gluttons had left untouched. Thus, at the time of Trithemius’s appointment in the Monastery of Sponheim <note>original: "Spanheimensi"</note>, after everything was counted, only 48 volumes were found, and those were of little value and of even less use for true learning.

However, after he obtained the rule of this monastery, he began gradually to collect many and varied books in every faculty—both Greek and Latin—so many and so great that today in all of Germany, no library is said to have been like the Sponheim library. In it were held so many rare, so many secret, so many varied volumes known to few. For this reason, it was praised in every land to such an extent that many Princes, Bishops, Doctors, Masters, Nobles, and most distinguished men—not only from nearby but even from distant regions—were stirred by the name and fame of Johannes Trithemius and his volumes. They desired to visit, and did visit, the Sponheim monastery, to whom previously the very name of the monastery was unknown. It was truly increased by Trithemius to such a degree that when he took a census of the library’s books in the year 1502, he found one thousand six hundred and forty-six volumes. Elsewhere, Trithemius himself says that in the Monastery of Sponheim he [spent] more than two...

If any grief from their loss began to strike my soul, I formed for myself an image of death, through which I persuaded myself not only of the forgetting of books (without which I once could not live), but even of their contempt (if I may put it so). I confess I was once held by a great love for the library, and I preferred my books to all the riches of the world; but after I considered that a change in my affairs was at hand, I looked upon everything I had previously loved as no more than dung, and I commanded my soul to believe nothing thereafter to be its own except itself; and those things which it would necessarily leave behind at death, it should learn much more not to love while living in the flesh.”* This letter was written from Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipoli"</note> in the year 1500.

### CHAPTER XI.

## THE CARE OF TRITHEMIUS FOR THE GROWTH OF THE MONASTERY OF SPONHEIM 
## IN TEMPORAL MATTERS.

Even though the Monastery of Sponheim was provided for and endowed with the greatest revenues by its founder at the time of its establishment, and was also increased over time by various donations from pious men—so much so that by the time of *Crafto*, the second Abbot, the number of monks rose to over twenty—nevertheless, as time passed, through the "injury of the times," the negligence of the Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note>, the lack of discipline of the monks, the division of revenues between the community and the Abbot, the secret selling off of monastery goods, and the unnecessary contraction of debts, it gradually fell into extreme want and poverty. 

This reached such a point that Abbot *Ulrich of Zeiskeim*, the 22nd in order and the third before *Trithemius*, no longer having the means to live, was compelled by necessity to resign the Abbacy. He left behind debts of more than two thousand five hundred florins <note>A significant sum of gold coins in the 16th century</note>, in addition to the hidden damages he had brought upon the monastery by selling various goods, rents, and incomes without the knowledge of his brothers and entirely alienating them from the monastery. 

And although his two successors before *Trithemius*, *Otto Havvisen* and *Johannes Colnhausen*—especially this latter one—tried with all their might to help and reform the monastery in temporal <note>earthly or financial</note> matters, the desired progress could not follow according to their wishes. Therefore, after *Trithemius* had undertaken the government of the monastery, he directed all his care and concern toward this end. He ensured that the brothers suffered no lack of those things which seemed necessary; as much as was possible for him, he renewed the census <note>records of land ownership and taxes</note> and wrote out the renewals most elegantly. He redeemed and reclaimed pledged property, paid the debts, and finally attempted whatever could in any way lead to the growth of the monastery. 

Furthermore, when he came to the attention of Princes and Nobles and was often honored by them with great gifts, he applied those things which had been granted to him with such magnificence to the benefit of the monastery. He did not reserve them for himself, as he rightly could have; thus, in twelve years, he turned more than a thousand florins—which he had acquired as gifts from various Princes, Prelates, and other friends in exchange for his labor, study, counsel, or the publication of his writings—to the common use of the monastery and the brothers. 

He was so far from alienating, neglecting, or uselessly consuming the monastery's goods in the manner of some of his predecessors; for nothing was special to him, nothing was his own property, but all things were held in common with the brothers. There was absolutely no partiality toward him in food, drink, or clothing. Moreover, in addition to the incomparable library described above, he [repaired] many old buildings...

...which he renewed, rebuilt what had collapsed, restored what was in ruins, and made the monastery of Sponheim <note>original: "Spanheimense"</note> almost entirely new.

In the **third year of his Rule** <note>1485</note>, he recovered the farmstead in Nosbach, which Kraft II <note>Count Kraft II of Sponheim</note> had pawned to a certain soldier, his relative, for a fixed sum of money a hundred years earlier. After much labor and expense, he returned half of it to the monastery’s possession; the other half could not be obtained due to a legal dispute over the right of redemption. In the same year, he also built a new guest parlor <note>original: "stubam hospitum"</note> next to the cloister and likewise renovated the chambers. He also began the casting of a new bell.

In the **eighth year of his Rule**, he began to build from the foundations a stone barn to replace the wooden one that had previously collapsed, consumed by extreme age, and he completed it.

In the **eleventh year of his Rule**, he constructed a new Abbot’s residence <note>original: "Abbatiam." In this context, it refers specifically to the house or private quarters of the Abbot.</note>, partly from the old structure and partly from the foundations, which was quite costly and ornate. Previously, the dwelling had been too narrow, inconvenient, and dangerous due to the risk of fire, and there was nothing in it except for a tiny, bare, and empty room. Indeed, on the day Trithemius entered the Abbot’s residence, nothing was found in the house except for one loaf of bread, a biretta <note>original: "byretum," a square clerical cap</note>, and a bed with its necessary linens. For Johannes Kolnhaufen, the previous Abbot, being a lover of simplicity, was always accustomed to building dwellings that were cramped and very lowly. When he resigned, there were no storehouses in the Abbey, no chests, no tables, nor any other closed or secure containers in which anything could be stored. Trithemius, therefore, compelled by necessity, constructed the Abbey with works that were magnificent considering his poverty; he created storehouses, arranged chambers, fitted locks, established the necessary chests, and acquired many other things at no small expense.

In the **nineteenth year of his Rule**, he had the summer refectory <note>the monks' dining hall</note> painted with the figures and names of the Abbots of this monastery in order from its first founding until the present year, along with their coats of arms.

In the **twentieth year of his Rule**, he built a new conventual room from the foundation to serve as the brothers' winter refectory. He also built a new mill with stone walls from the foundation, as the old one had completely collapsed from extreme age. Also this year, due to the neglect of the cattle, one house fell completely to ruin; because it was needed, he immediately rebuilt it from the foundations with a new wooden wall and four chambers.

...it had fallen into extreme poverty and had been utterly stripped of all dignity in both spiritual and temporal matters; how the Bursfeld Reform <note>A movement focused on renewing monastic discipline and strict adherence to the Rule of St. Benedict in the 15th century.</note> had been twice attempted in vain; how finally in the year 1469, through the resignation of the Abbot, the expulsion of the wayward <note>original: "deformatorum," referring to monks who lived outside the strict rules of the order</note> monks, the election of Johannes Colnhausen as Abbot, and the introduction of new monks from the monasteries of St. Alban and St. Jacob near Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiam"</note>, the reform was introduced; and how gradually, in the observance of the holy union, the monastery began to flourish again.

Therefore, Trithemius lived in a holy and praiseworthy manner, conforming to the reform and monastic discipline, not only from the time of his entry into the monastery until his election as Abbot, but once he was made Abbot, he focused all his concern on nothing more than the most exact preservation of the holy reform that had been recently established, making it flourish as much as possible in his monastery. For as far as his own life was concerned: all the time that he could find for leisure, he devoted not to any pleasures of the flesh, but always entirely to the study of the scriptures, intent on reading day and night, always writing or learning something. No one ever found him idle; no one saw or heard of him being given to the comforts of the flesh, nor uselessly occupied in wandering talk or strolling about within or outside the monastery; nor was he intent on gluttony, drinking, or unnecessary banquets, nor toiling over any other frivolities or vanities.

Nothing was ever sweeter to him than to search the holy scriptures and to be occupied with them at every opportune time, day and night, and always to read or write something good. Furthermore, he kept his monks in the same observance and regular discipline; he wrote, he spoke, and he continually preached the word of God to them. He exhorted them both publicly and privately, in season and out of season, toward the cultivation of true wisdom—although, as he himself laments, he achieved nothing. His sacred studies always displeased them; they returned mocking laughter <note>original: "cachinnos"</note> instead of reverence for his writings, and to no one did his night-labors <note>original: "lucubrationes," referring to scholarly work done by candlelight</note> ever give less pleasure than to his own "sons" (as he called them). This was also the reason why, having abandoned the monastery of Sponheim <note>original: "Spanheimensi"</note>, he fled elsewhere; and because the monks of Sponheim made themselves unworthy of his exhortation, he was transplanted by divine providence, lest a tree be pricked by thorns any longer without fruit.

Nevertheless, although the Sponheimers were always opposed to his exhortations, often hatching many conspiracies against him and fashioning lies, and although no one wished to relieve him or sympathize with his labors while he was heavily oppressed by the care and concern for both temporal and spiritual governance throughout the entire time of his rule, he nonetheless always remained constant. He bore the full burden of pastoral care with many groans and sighs. By the splendor of his own piety and name, he covered the unseemliness <note>original: "deformitatem"</note> of his monks and preserved the dignity of the cloister, such that the monastery of Sponheim became a school of erudition and piety. But what was the appearance of the Sponheim monastery after the departure of Trithemius? As when opposites are [placed] side by side...

Johannes Gotfridi, Pastor in Mandel, exclaims on this matter in a letter to Trithemius, which is the 17th in the 2nd book of personal letters: <note>original: "Epist. fam." refers to the "Epistolae Familiares," a collection of personal correspondence.</note>

> Your very successor as Abbot, a companion of the traitor Judas, an inexperienced, lazy, and foolish man, pleases none of the neighbors, is held in contempt by the officials of the Princes, and is regarded with scorn by all.

The glory of the entire fatherland, the light of Christians, the Teacher of those in cloisters and religious life, the defender of rural priests, their instructor and advocate, also the father of the poor and the physician of the sick! Shall we say that Trithemius was lazy or idle? Let us hear his disciple Johannes Centurianus of Klüsserath <note>original: "Clusardia"</note>, Pastor in Trittenheim, in a letter to Trithemius, which is the 16th in the 2nd book of personal letters:
> Many of your enemies, giving credit to these words, believed you had perished, saying: "Alas, that splendid light, which used to illuminate the whole world with its learning, how has it been obscured by the fog of darkness? Who would have believed that Abbot Trithemius, glorious throughout almost the entire Christian world for the fame of his learning and holiness, would come to such dejection of spirit that he would so rashly desert his fatherland and friends?" I, however, who knew your teaching, prudence, and the sanctity of your life very well, always resisted these blasphemies and curses of the wicked with all my strength, and showed by many open arguments how much of an injury they had done to your most holy name. For during the two years I stayed in your monastery under your instruction to learn Greek and Hebrew letters <note>Trithemius was famous for promoting the study of "trilingual" learning (Latin, Greek, and Hebrew) among monks.</note> and to drink from the saving knowledge of the Scriptures, I could never see or hear anything of you but what was holy, upright, and religious; indeed, we saw you living in such great purity at all times that we marveled. While others were sleeping, you kept watch in the sacred study of the Scriptures, always either reading or writing something for the common benefit of many. No one ever found you idle; no one heard of you being free for feasting or drinking; no one saw you dissolved in laughter or any levity; no one ever found you speaking or associating with women, from which suspicion of evil might arise.

Thus, from these things it clearly shines forth what care Trithemius had for internal perfection, both for himself and for the entire monastery; but he was not lacking in external matters either. He adorned the Church, built chapels, erected altars, acquired relics of the Saints, and omitted nothing of those things which seemed beneficial for the internal perfection of the soul.

In the first year of his governance, he had an altar in the Sacristy consecrated in honor of St. Anne, Mother of the Blessed Virgin Mary; St. Jerome the Priest; St. Benedict the Abbot; St. Servatius, Bishop of Tongeren; and St. Barbara, Virgin and Martyr; in which many relics of the Saints were hidden away according to custom.

In the 19th year of his rule <note>circa 1502</note>, he had the great bell, which had been broken ten years earlier, recast—larger than it was before—weighing fifteen hundredweight of the finest bronze <note>original: "quindecim centenaria æris"</note>, and afterward he solemnly blessed it himself.

### CHAPTER XIII.

## THE FAME OF THE SPONHEIM MONASTERY ACQUIRED THROUGH TRITHEMIUS.

The Sponheim monastery was once distinguished and illustrious, both because of the fame of its founder and the dignity of its Abbots, as well as for the holy life of the monks. As a result, it earned excellent donations from pious men, exemptions, liberties, privileges, Apostolic and Archiepiscopal confirmations, the special protection of the Apostolic See, brotherhood with many illustrious monasteries, and finally many benefits. However, as the fervor of religion withered, the respect for the Abbots failed, and the lack of discipline <note>original: "licentia"</note> among the monks increased, it fell into such a lowly state that before Trithemius, the name of the cloister was hardly known. For as Johannes Gotfridi, Pastor in Mandel, says in a letter to Trithemius (the 17th in the 2nd book of personal letters): *“What was Sponheim before Trithemius was in it? Or who heard its name from afar?”* Certainly no-

# THE LIFE OF TRITHEMIUS

...it was insignificant, and its name was obscure, cast away in darkness, hidden and unknown. *Trithemius, through his learning and scholarly labors <note>original: "lucubrationibus"—literally "work done by lamplight," implying intense late-night study</note>, brought fame to the name of Sponheim <note>The text uses the Latin "Spanheimense"; Sponheim was a Benedictine monastery in Germany</note>, making it renowned throughout the whole world with great glory, whereas before it was entirely unknown. Trithemius himself suggests as much in a letter to the Convent of Sponheim, which is the second letter of the second book of his "Familiar Letters": It would be superfluous to recount our scholarly labors, which we wrote at intervals in the midst of pastoral care and the anxiety of worldly affairs; through these, the name of the Sponheim Monastery, previously unknown and obscure, has become sufficiently famous.* This is confirmed by Theodoric, a monk of Fulda, in the 54th letter of the second book of "Familiar Letters" addressed to Trithemius. *I was indeed saddened that the envy of your rivals was permitted to prevail so much that it gave you reason to leave your monastery—the very place you made known, bright, famous, and distinguished throughout almost the entire world by your talent, writings, and books. For what was the Sponheim monastery before your reverend fatherhood was placed in charge of it? It lay hidden in obscurity and darkness, so that for more than ten miles around there was no estimation or knowledge of its name. You made it glorious and known far and wide through your scholarly labors, as I saw for myself when I served as a student under your instruction for over three years: how many most learned men, including Princes and Bishops, stirred by the fame of your name, flocked eagerly to Sponheim from the University <note>original: "Gymnasio"</note> of Paris in France, Louvain in Brabant, Tübingen in Swabia, and also from Italy and Germany, and other more remote parts of the earth.*

There were three reasons why such a celebrated name was acquired for this monastery. The first was the fame and lifestyle of Trithemius himself, which attracted many celebrated men and even powerful Princes to come to the Sponheim Monastery, such as Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Prince-Elector, and Christopher, Margrave of Baden. The second cause was the **Library of Sponheim**, which was celebrated throughout the whole world, as was discussed at length above in Chapter 10; consequently, most excellent men came to Sponheim out of a desire to see it. For on July 4, 1496 <note>original: "quarto nonas Julii"</note>, the following men were in the Monastery to see the Library, which fame had proclaimed everywhere as a treasure: **Johannes, Bishop of Worms**, a man most learned in Greek and Latin; **Johannes Reuchlin**, also known as **Capnion** <note>A Greek translation of his German name, meaning "little smoke"</note>, a Doctor of Law and most eloquent in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, and Secretary to the Duke of Württemberg; **Franciscus Bononius Tergestinus**, a poet and orator skilled in Greek and Latin, and Secretary to the Queen of the Romans; **Heinrich von Bunau**, a knight learned in every faculty and Secretary to the Dukes of Saxony, Frederick and John; and **Johannes Vigilius**, an interpreter of both Civil and Canon law <note>original: "utriusque Juris"</note>, Secretary to Philip the Count Palatine, and a patron of all philosophers. All these most learned men, seeing such a great multitude of rare volumes in this poor monastery, were utterly astonished, praising the order and the value of the books, and the study and industry of Father Trithemius. I pass over the rest, whom the *Sponheim Chronicle* lists at length. The third cause was that the Sponheim Monastery was held at that time as a model of learning, and as the *Sponheim Chronicle* says, its walls contained more...
