...instruction, more than the dusty libraries of others. For in Trithemius’s study <note>original: "conclavi"—a private room or inner chamber</note>, which can still be seen intact (according to a certain friend), many poems and maxims of various ancient and modern authors are read on every side, inscribed in elegant letters of red and black. These are written in both Greek and Latin, and include especially the works of Sedulius, Juvencus, Fortunatus, Bishop Hildebert, Peter of Riga, and Walter of Lille <note>These were prominent Christian poets and theologians from Late Antiquity and the Middle Ages; Trithemius prized them as examples of sacred letters</note>. To these, Conrad Celtis, a contemporary and friend of Trithemius, added the following verses.

## Conrad Celtis, also called Protucius, the Poet.

> *Behold these little verses, venerable guest,*
> *Which Trithemius set down, look, with three marks.*
> *How great a cultivator of antiquity, or how great a lover*
> *Of languages he is, the inscribed wall teaches both.*

A life-sized portrait of this same Celtis, painted in colors, is seen on the wall with these words added: *Conrad Celtis Protucius, Poet Laureate, sang these things in the Year of our Lord 1494, while he was here.*

### To the future Abbot.

> *Whoever you shall be as the future Abbot, these songs of ours*
> *I ask that you wish to turn over often in a mindful heart.*
> *Be pious, merciful, and a lover of religion,*
> *And I advise you: learn to follow my Trithemius.*

## Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, to his Successor.

> *Behold, I have set down the monuments of learned men*
> *And whatever is able to greatly adorn you.*
> *I urge and admonish you to follow in our footsteps,*
> *You who will come after me to rule my house.*

### CHAPTER XIV.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE ORDER OF ST. BENEDICT, OVER WHICH TRITHEMIUS PRESIDED OR WHICH HE ATTENDED.

As was stated above in chapter 4, section 8, all Abbots and Prelates of the Order of St. Benedict throughout the entire province of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinam"</note> had been summoned to the Council of Constance <note>A major 15th-century ecumenical council held in Germany to resolve the Papal Schism and reform the Church</note> for the purpose of establishing the celebration of a Provincial Chapter and beginning the reformation of the Order in all monasteries. After the Fathers and Prelates had gathered in great number, celebrated the Chapter, and laudably established many things for the reform of the Order, from that time Provincial Chapters began to be celebrated every three years in the Province of Mainz. Accordingly, the second was celebrated at Mainz on September 1, 1418. The third was in the Monastery of Fulda on May 5, 1420. The fourth in Seligenstadt on May 3, 1422. The fifth in the Monastery of Saint Stephen at Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipoli"</note> on May 14, 1424. The sixth in Erfurt <note>original: "Erphordia"</note> on April 21, 1426. The seventh in the monastery of the mountain...

->OF THE ABBOT.<-

He himself says in a letter to the Convent of Sponheim, which is the second in the second book of his *Familiar Letters*: "We, however, who have been many times compelled to obey the command of the Fathers of the Order, have for twenty years spent nearly whole summers visiting all the neighboring provinces, etc." Likewise, in letter 68 of the first book of *Familiar Letters* to the Presidents celebrating the annual Council: "For twenty years and more (as you yourselves know), I have worked continuously for the community of the Order and the chapter—writing, speaking, and visiting; handling countless legal cases and commissions for our union before Bishops, Princes, and various others. Nor does anyone live in the Order today who has endured such great labors for the common good as you know I have sustained. Through Swabia, all of Franconia, Alsace, and through the Dioceses of Trier, Cologne, Mainz, Speyer, Bamberg, Würzburg <note>original: *Herbipolensem*</note>, and Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentinensem*</note>, I have visited at your command not once or twice, but many times. Being absent from my monastery for much time at your orders, I neglected my own affairs while caring for those of others."

## CHAPTER XV.
## BOOKS WRITTEN BY TRITHEMIUS.

In the twenty-third year of his age, as recorded in a letter to Rogerius Sycambrus, Johannes Trithemius—who was otherwise always intent on study as much as was permitted—began to commit his thoughts and discoveries to writing. He asserted a twofold reason for doing this. First, that while he was doing this, his mind seemed to be closed off from vain, useless, or even harmful thoughts. Second: even if the things he wrote benefited no one else, they would nevertheless perfect his own understanding over time and exercise his mind toward a certain facility through practice. Nor did this opinion fail him, because through the daily and continuous practice of writing, he became so adept at dictating on any subject that arose that everyone, even the most learned, marveled at the ease of his speech; and those who saw him writing at any time without prior preparation confirmed that his speech seemed to flow rather than be merely written.

Thus, from that time until the day of his death, he wrote almost innumerable small works, of which I find five catalogs written by himself. The first is at the end of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* <note>original: *de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*</note>, completed in the year 1494, in the second indiction <note>The "indiction" was a fifteen-year cycle used in the Middle Ages for dating documents</note>. The second is at the end of the *Catalog of the Illustrious Men of Germany* <note>original: *catalogi illustrium virorum Germaniæ*</note>, completed on the last day of July in the year 1495, in the thirteenth indiction. There, he explains the reason why he himself writes the catalog of books published by him, showing great humility in these words:

"I do not consider myself worthy to occupy a place among the writers and illustrious men of Germany because of the poverty of my intellect; but I do this lest there happen to me what we read has happened to many, who, hiding the titles of their own works out of humility, were also thought to be the authors of books they perhaps had never seen. But to whom do we write an apology? In these matters, the testimony of conscience should suffice for everyone; let no one seek further outside himself. Let others hide the small works they have forged out of humility; I have decided that the things I have written should be brought to light more out of humility and charity. For I prefer (if any error should occur) to be corrected while alive rather than when dead, since just as confession perishes from the dead, so correction benefits the living. Nor am I so insolent as to demand a memory of my name, which is subject to vanity, as the reward for my labor. Lest..."

These are nearly all the works of Trithemius which he is found to have written over the course of thirty-three years. If indeed any of them should have escaped this catalog, or are found listed twice due to a variation in the title, the kind reader will not be burdened to fill the deficiency and to trim the excess. 

Whether all these were published and still exist has not been certain to me up to this point; I certainly believe this: that none of these exists in name alone, but at the very least, for the most part, all were begun, even if not completed. He then either left them imperfect in Sponheim <note>original: "Spanheim"</note> after his departure, as he himself confesses in several places, or he could not finish them, being prevented by death. His death was surely too premature for the whole Christian world, the republic of letters, the Province of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinæ"</note>, and his own order. 

For if, in the space of thirty-three years—amidst continuous anxieties and cares for his monastery of Sponheim (a life full of "useless cares," as he himself says), amidst continuous journeys to the provincial and annual Chapters of the Order; and finally, among the greatest labors which he expended on the common causes and business of the Chapter, the Order, and the Union, by visiting, writing, speaking, and performing embassies before Princes, Bishops, and many others on numerous occasions...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Johannes Trithemius, transitioning from a list of his works to an evaluation of his immense productivity, his humility, and the specific fields of study he mastered. THE LIFE OF TRITHEMIUS

...is weighed, he is found to have written so many and such great things, as no one wrote for a long time before him, nor from his time until now; indeed, many have not even read as much in a much longer span of years. What might he have written in the poor, care-free, quiet Abbey of Saint James <note>The Schottenklöster or "Scottish Monastery" in Würzburg, where Trithemius spent his final years.</note>, a place so suitable and fitting for his studies, which he took up out of a love for peace and tranquility, resigning from the overly tumultuous Sponheim? But his great output is not as much to be admired as the humility with which he values his own late-night labors as nothing when compared to the works of the Church Fathers. Thus he says in a letter to Rogerius Sycambrus <note>A fellow monk and humanist scholar from the Deventer school.</note>, which is the 12th in Book 1 of his *Familiar Letters*:

> *What are our studies, Roger, compared to the nighttime labors of those great men? They devoted every moment of their lives to literature, always reading or writing something, both to raise their own intellect toward the knowledge of the highest truth and to provide useful things for posterity. What, finally, are our own labors—by which we are thought to be something above the rest—if they are compared to the short works of the aforementioned Fathers, but chaff compared to wheat <note>original: "paleæ relatæ ad triticum"</note>, and certain unripe fruits, for which there was neither time nor place, nor even a suitable climate granted for them to grow into the desired food? We write (as Horace says) poems everywhere, both the unlearned and the learned <note>original: "Scribimus... indocti doctique poëmata passim," a quote from Horace's Epistles II.1.117.</note>, and being too greedy for empty reputation, our works are far too childish; for, to be honest, we do not even keep them back until the ninth year <note>original: "nec in alterum quidem premimus annum." Trithemius is alluding to Horace’s advice in Ars Poetica to set a work aside for nine years before publishing it to ensure its quality.</note>. Even if all these things are so, we still rightly praise the talents of our people, since each person does what he can out of a love for wisdom.*

### CHAPTER XVI.

## TO WHICH STUDIES TRITHEMIUS WAS CHIEFLY DEVOTED.

I shall seem redundant in reviewing the catalog of studies of this man, whom the entire world knows was the leader of all erudition and science in his own age—though it was an age most fertile with highly learned men. He was the glory of Germany and a virtual ark of all wisdom, so that Nicolaus Gerbellius of Pforzheim <note>A noted German humanist and lawyer.</note> rightly addressed him in the 32nd letter of Book 2 of the *Familiar Letters* as follows:

> *I congratulate myself quite often, Most Reverend Father, that I was born in this most happy century, in which so many illustrious men of no small fame have appeared everywhere in Germany. Among them, you are the one who, along with Latin and Hebrew literature, also made Greek studies more enriched among the Germans. You are so powerful and shine so brightly among them that I am at a crossroads <note>original: "in trivio sim"</note> and waver like Chremes in Terence’s play <note>A reference to a character from Roman comedy known for being overwhelmed or indecisive.</note>, whether to compare you to anyone or to prefer you above all others. Truly, I do not doubt without reason, since we see in you not just a "trivium" <note>The "three ways" of basic medieval education: grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</note> but a spacious, overflowing, and most polished theater of all disciplines. We do not see in you just one or three virtues, but all of them held together firmly and in a great troop, just as if we were watching a most fitting spectacle.*

However, lest it be said that he was a practitioner of those studies from which Christian Philosophy and the monastic state of religion shrink, I have persuaded myself that this narrative is not established without reason. Our Trithemius was, therefore, first a most celebrated Poet; of this fact, besides the many poems he composed, there is clear evidence in that he loved not only poetry itself but all Poets, and treated them with the highest honor, for no other reason than the similarity of their studies—

<meta>This page continues the defense and eulogy of Johannes Trithemius’s intellectual character, categorizing his mastery across six primary fields of study: poetry, oratory, philosophy, mathematics, history, and theology. It then transitions into Chapter 17 to address and refute accusations that he was a practitioner of the occult.</meta>

-> OF THE ABBOT. <-

...which alone is the foundation for friendship among learned men. Nor does it stand in the way that in his letters to Roger Sycambrus <note>A humanist scholar and monk who was a close friend and correspondent of Trithemius.</note>—specifically the 40th in Book 2 of his *Familiar Letters*, and the 12th in Book 2 to the same man—he frequently calls the study of poetry "childish." For he says this with respect to the elderly: namely, that poems are not becoming of them, and that they should proceed in prose for the sake of the honor of old age; let immature youth play with twisted little verses, for the elderly love a level path.

Secondly, he was a most eloquent Orator. This is demonstrated by the many orations which he delivered in provincial and annual chapters and elsewhere, and sometimes even extemporaneously. All his writings testify to this, being composed in such an elegant and fluid style that nothing in them feels labored or forced, but all his expressions follow one another in the sweetest harmony.

Thirdly, he was a most subtle Philosopher. For a clear demonstration of this, let his *Familiar Letters* to his brother Jacob be read, as well as the *Eight Questions* addressed to the Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor, who consulted Trithemius on various intellectual and theological matters.</note>. Nothing will be found in them except that which is philosophical and worthy of a supreme philosopher.

Fourthly, he was a most ingenious Mathematician. A clear proof of this is exhibited in his most subtle work, the *Polygraphia* <note>Trithemius's famous work on cryptography and steganography, which he framed as a mathematical and linguistic science.</note>, and his book on the *Ecclesiastical Computus* <note>A technical term for the science of calculating the calendar, particularly the date of Easter.</note>.

Fifthly, he was a perfect Historian. His many historical works show this, as does his commendation and praise of history itself placed at the beginning of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*.

Sixthly, he was a distinguished Theologian, and he loved and thirsted for nothing except the knowledge of the Scriptures, just as he commends it in infinite places and impresses it upon his disciples. Let us hear one passage from his *Letter to his brother Jacob*, the first in Book 2 of his *Familiar Letters*:

> *Sacred Scripture, however, which we rightly call divine, far exceeds all science and learning of this world, because it proclaims truths without ambiguity. It calls the mind of the peaceful reader from earthly things to the celestial, and for the love of God, it renders that mind humble in prosperity, and strong and constant in adversity. This is the rush of the sacred river that gladdens the city of God; it is both shallow and deep, in which the simple and small lamb may walk, and the great elephant may swim. <note>original: "in quo & agnus ſimplex ac parvus ambulet, & elephas maximus natet." This famous metaphor for the Bible's accessibility and depth is often attributed to St. Gregory the Great.</note> This is a wonderful river, in which the simple Christian without literature can, with dry feet so to speak, cross securely to salvation; yet the great and subtly lettered man can also swim there with sober wisdom—though if he searches too deeply, he may be submerged.* etc.

Thus our Trithemius was a celebrated Poet, a most eloquent Orator, a subtle Philosopher, an ingenious Mathematician, a perfect Historian, and finally a distinguished Theologian, just as André Thevet <note>A French Franciscan priest and royal cosmographer to King Henry III.</note>, the Royal Cosmographer of Angoulême, calls him in his eulogy.

### CHAPTER XVII.

## IT IS SHOWN THAT TRITHEMIUS WAS NOT AN ALCHEMIST, ASTROLOGER, OR MAGICIAN.

Many people try to prove that Trithemius was an Alchemist. Firstly, because in many places, especially in his letter to Count Johannes of Westenburg etc., he makes mention of Alchemy and its principles, saying among other things: "By this single means, the secret of nature is opened to Alchemists, without...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Johannes Trithemius against accusations of engaging in the forbidden arts. ...without which no understanding of the art is acquired, nor is the effect of the operation found. Likewise, without the knowledge of this middle, this end, and this beginning through numbers, degrees, and orders, neither could a Magician give power to images without crime—or even with wickedness—nor could an Alchemist imitate nature, nor a man compel spirits, nor a prophet predict the future, nor any seeker of experiments grasp their underlying reason. 

II. That Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous occult philosopher who studied under Trithemius and dedicated his *De Occulta Philosophia* to him.</note>, in letters sent to Trithemius, boasts that he discussed many things with him concerning magic, chemistry, Kabbalah, and other secret sciences and arts that still lie hidden in obscurity. But despite these points, I am not unwilling to conclude the opposite, and I demonstrate my opinion from the very texts of Trithemius in which he mocks and rejects Alchemists. 

The first is in Letter 34 of Book 1 of the *Familiar Letters* to Germain de Ganay <note>Germain de Ganay (d. 1520), a high-ranking French clergyman and patron of scholars who corresponded with Trithemius about philosophy and the occult.</note>:

> This is the most beautiful virtue of all strength, which conquers all worldly things and penetrates every solid body, tinting each one with a desirable beauty, just as the Alchemists indeed promise in composite bodies; but they err, they are deceived, and they deceive all who have willingly listened to them. They wish to imitate nature and perform in parts that which belongs only to the universal whole, since they do not understand the root of nature's power. Do not acquiesce to those foolish Alchemists, for they are fatuous and the disciples of apes <note>original: "simiarum discipuli"; a common Renaissance insult for those who mindlessly and poorly imitate nature or true masters.</note>, enemies of nature, and contemners of the heavens, without whose intelligible knowledge Alchemy is nothing.

The second is in Book 6 of the *Polygraphia* <note>Trithemius's 1518 work on cryptography, which he framed as a system of "hidden writing" using angelic names, leading to further accusations of magic.</note>:

> Alchemy has many domestic familiars who guard their mistress with perpetual vigilance and substitute themselves in her name so that they may keep her untouched by the commerce of so many opportunistic lovers for all eternity. Vanity, fraud, deceit, deception, sophistication, greed, falsehood, lying confidence, folly, want, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the handmaidens of Alchemy; by pretending to be their beloved mistress, they keep her inviolate and willingly prostitute themselves to her wealthy, avaricious, greedy, and foolish seekers.

Nor do the arguments of the opposing side carry any weight. Not the first, for in the same letter he calls Alchemists "envious persecutors of nature." Not the second, because they could have conferred about chemistry in order to elude and refute it, and to uncover its frauds.

Neither can Trithemius be said to have been an Astrologer (I speak of Judicial Astrology <note>The practice of predicting specific human events and fates based on the stars, which was often viewed as heretical, unlike "natural" astrology/astronomy.</note>), for in many places he refutes and condemns Astrology, as in Letter 34 of Book 1 of the *Familiar Letters* to Germain de Ganay:

> The stars understand nothing, nor do they even feel; therefore they neither confer wisdom upon our minds, nor do they have any dominion over us who walk in the Spirit, confessing the Lord Jesus Christ who has all things in His power, to whose likeness we must faithfully conform ourselves according to our strength. For He Himself is the wisdom of GOD the Father; He is the fountain and origin of knowledge; He is the center of the soul, through whom all things were made. Away with reckless men, vain men, and lying Astrologers, deceivers of minds, who babble in trivialities. For the disposition of the stars contributes nothing to the immortal mind, nothing to natural science, and nothing to supercelestial wisdom; rather, a body has empire only over another body. The mind is free and is neither subjected to the stars, nor conceives their influences, nor follows their motion, but [depends] upon the supercelestial principle from which it was also made...

...is and is made fruitful, communicates such great [power]. Likewise, in Letter 50, Book 2, to Jodocus Beiselius <note>Jodocus Beiselius was a humanist and lawyer from Aachen who was a close friend of Trithemius.</note>:

I believe it has been announced to you, Jodocus, through our common friends—Roger, Herber, and Kymolanus, and others—that the state of my affairs has shifted according to my birth-chart, so that the prediction of the stars might be fulfilled, which the astronomer of King Philip <note>Likely referring to Philip I of Castile, also known as Philip the Handsome.</note> prophesied twenty years ago. I confess that I myself, having performed calculations in the meantime, often found threatening figures, but persuaded by the counsel of Saint Augustine, I regarded the prophecies of the stars as a joke. At last, that which they seemed to promise has happened to me, and an occasion is given to me by which experience must henceforth make me more cautious. The envy of rivals provided the occasion for the prophecy, which—lest the Mathematician's <note>In the Renaissance, the term "Mathematicus" (Mathematician) was frequently used to mean an astrologer.</note> prediction should waver—some malignant demon stirred up against me; for demons, if God permits, willingly cooperate with human prophecies, and through these vanities, they capture minds that are too credulous in the wandering path of error.

Finally, it cannot be said that Trithemius was a Magician—I speak of superstitious and diabolical magic, not of natural magic, by which Trithemius wishes nothing else to be understood than wisdom: namely, the understanding of physical and metaphysical things, which consists of the knowledge of divine and natural virtues. And as an argument for this opinion of mine, let Trithemius himself be heard distinguishing natural magic from the forbidden, along with his own protestation in the above-cited letter to Count Joannes Westenburgh:

> I cannot say that I am entirely ignorant of natural magic, through which wonders are performed naturally; there is nothing in me above nature, except for the Christian faith, which nature did not give, but grace. That most learned and, among the saints, truly most holy Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and "Doctor Universalis" of the Church, was famously a scientist and philosopher who was often wrongly accused of being a wizard by later writers.</note>, by reason of his most profound intellect—great and worthy of eternal memory—searched the depths of the philosophy of nature and learned wonderful things unheard of by others, so much so that among the ignorant he is injuriously held to be a magician and superstitious even to this day. He was not ignorant of the magic of nature, and he read and understood many superstitious books of the wicked without blame: nor was he therefore wicked or superstitious. For the knowledge of evil is not evil, but the use of it is. I shall therefore bear patiently what so great a man endured without sin. Nor do I deny that I know mystical things, although I am far inferior to Albert in knowledge and in no way to be compared in holiness. I confess that I have read many volumes of magicians and have examined not a few arrangements of illusions; nor have I entirely rejected from my reading those volumes which teach the "bindings" of spirits <note>original: "ligamenta spirituum" — a technical term in medieval magic for spells or talismans used to constrain or command spiritual entities.</note> and similar things, and in all these I confess I always emerged firmer in the holy faith of Christians, because by a divine gift, I understood for the most part what I had read. O most bright, O good God, how many vain, invented, and ridiculous things—to say nothing of the deceitful and abominable things—are hidden in books of superstitious magic, and in those written about the conjurations of demons, which no one can better comprehend, discern, and refute than one who understands them.

Natural magic, which at one time, relying on the principles of nature, stood pure in its simplicity, has been confused with so many lies, so many impurities, and so many deceptions, that no one, unless he be most learned in both, can distinguish one from the other. Likewise in a letter to the Margrave of Brandenburg, Lord Joachim <note>Joachim I Nestor, Elector of Brandenburg (1484–1535), who was deeply interested in the sciences and the occult.</note>:

> Would that the distance between us were shorter, and that either no care for my household affairs detained me, or an easier condition relieved me; I would fly to you at once, and gladly and trustfully approach your Serenity, and I would open the deepest and most secret things of Natural Magic, which either no one, or very few today [know...]

<meta>This page continues the defense of Johannes Trithemius, specifically clarifying his definition of "natural magic" as opposed to "superstitious magic." It addresses why the reputation of magic has suffered and asserts that Trithemius’s work was entirely compatible with his Christian faith.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF TRITHEMIUS #

...to know and understand. For all those I have known, seen, and heard who labor in natural magic itself—in the crafting of <term>images, rings, and seals</term><note>In the Renaissance, "images, rings, and seals" referred to talismans believed to capture the hidden influences of the stars and planets (astrological magic).</note>, and in the hidden operations of nature—achieve nothing, nor do they obtain any result from their operations. Instead, after long and useless work, they often fall into despair and slide toward frivolous and superstitious practices. 

But <term>natural magic</term><note>original: "Magia naturalis". During this period, this was considered a branch of science or "natural philosophy" that explored the hidden (occult) powers of the natural world, such as magnetism or the medicinal properties of plants, without involving demons.</note> is pure, solid, stable, and lawful; it is most fitting for and adorns Princes, and it has never been prohibited by the Church, nor should it be prohibited by law, since it rests upon the principles of nature and admits no superstition. 

And a little later: For natural magic not only works visible effects, but it also wonderfully illuminates the intellect of the man skilled in it toward the knowledge of divinity, and provides invisible fruits for the soul. But we see that the name of "magic" is hateful and loathed by almost all men today, so that they condemn everyone studying it with a single judgment, and they consider its every use to be utterly adverse and contrary to the Christian religion. 

And as for this unjust condemnation of the good and holy science of natural magic—from where do you think it took its beginning, Most Serene Prince? Hear my opinion. After those ancient wise Philosophers, Princes, and Kings—who were perfectly imbued with the science of natural magic—departed from this light, they left the science itself shrouded in hidden and most secret mysteries through their studies, so that access would not be open to the unworthy. 

Those men who wished to read their writings and work with them proceeded in two ways: for some of them, when they had read the wonderful experiments of the wise in magical matters, were drawn by desire and curiosity—as people are still unwillingly doing today—and began to work according to the surface meaning of the text, not understanding the things they read. When these men achieved no effect from the promised operation because of their utter ignorance, they condemned the best books—which had been proven by the experience of great minds—casting them aside with disgrace as if they were empty, false, deceitful, and frivolous. 

Others, however, laboring fruitlessly in the prescribed manner and achieving nothing in the composition of magical things, thought themselves deceived by the promises of the Authors. Lest they appear to be the only ones led astray, and so that they might have many companions in their error, they promised greater things than they had found. They knowingly mixed vain, frivolous, and fabricated things into the books of the wise, introducing various characters and unknown names in which they claimed great secrets lay hidden, and through which knowledge they said wonderful things could be done. 

Others, not content with mocking men in the aforementioned way, further confounded the natural magic they did not understand by adding <term>diabolical institutions</term><note>original: "diabolicas institutiones". These are rituals or instructions specifically intended to summon or bargain with demons, which Trithemius's defender argues were later forgeries added to ancient texts.</note>. By these, the volumes of the wise were so defiled and confused that they cannot be understood or corrected by scholars at this time. What is more serious is that they are condemned by almost all good men—who cannot distinguish the truth since they have not learned it—as evil, reprobate, superstitious, diabolical, and contrary to our most holy faith. 

Thus, the holy and good Magic, which was once written by the Authors in a right and pure (though hidden) manner, has been so confused, defiled, and infected that even hearing its name seems horrendous to Christians—and it is indeed horrendous to all, and not so much hated as it is impenetrable. 

Therefore, I would indeed concede that Trithemius was a Magician, but a **natural** one, who knew and performed everything he ever professed to know with GOD and without injury to our Christian faith. Although out of many men, very few can be found who understand the mysteries of hidden natural inventions. He was a mortal man; he was knowledgeable; he was a Christian of constant faith, a faithful...

It concludes that Trithemius was a practitioner of this pure, natural magic, which is entirely compatible with Christian piety.</summary>

### CHAPTER XVIII.

## THE VIRTUES OF TRITHEMIUS.

Trithemius was of such an elegant appearance, such calm eloquence, and a countenance so composed toward all humanity, sweetness, and modesty, that he drew the minds of all who looked upon him into admiration and love. This external physical beauty was accompanied in an indissoluble bond by internal goodness of soul, wisdom, gentleness, mercy, and humility; these natural gifts elevated him to such perfection that nothing shone forth in him except what was lofty, majestic, and worthy of a supreme <term>Prelate</term><note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as an abbot or bishop.</note>. The maturity of his words and deeds expressed an internal severity of mind that was revered and feared not only by the religious but also by secular people, to such an extent that in his presence, men who were otherwise dissolute and frivolous—as if some divine power were violently restraining them from within—could display nothing but honesty and maturity. He was pleasant at times, but never dissolute; he knew how to moderate his cheerfulness with his usual gravity, so that when he "laughed with holy Job," no one would believe it was a mere laugh. <note>This is a reference to Job 29:24: "If I laughed on them, they believed it not," implying his dignity was so great that his smile was treated with profound respect rather than casualness.</note> A clear testimony of this matter is provided by Rogerius Sycamber, a cloistered Canon in Hegen and a very close friend of Trithemius, in his 11th Letter of Book 2:

> I recently wrote a certain forecast full of jokes and witticisms, which pleases many; but since your censorial severity spurns all jokes, I did not judge it right to send it to you, who are accustomed to being far too formidable toward trifles because of your maturity of life and words. <note>original: "Scripsi nuper quoddam prognosticon jocis & facetiis plenum... tua censoria severitas jocos aspernatur universos..."</note>

This maturity was followed by a majesty and authority in ruling, so that not only by divine appointment but also by human disposition and natural affinity, he could not have been a monk without also being an Abbot—one to whom the supreme government of a monastery ought to be granted. 

But these are the external virtues of a wise man; I shall now ascend to his internal ones. In this task, however, I am confident I shall find neither beginning nor end, for he was so perfect in every kind of virtue that from whichever I begin, I will either say less than his dignity deserves, or by wandering too far, I must pass over the others in silence. Therefore, with a short pen, I will touch upon the more important ones, inviting the reader to the source itself. First among these is his love and devotion to the monastic life, his observance of the <term>Bursfelde Reform and Union</term><note>The Bursfelde Congregation was a 15th-century reform movement aimed at restoring strict discipline, prayer, and scholarship to Benedictine monasteries in Germany.</note>, and his contempt for riches and wealthy Abbeys. These virtues shine out especially from the fact that, although he was known and dear to the highest Princes and could have obtained a most desirable living condition among them, and although many powerful Abbots of the order wanted to have him with them, and although he could have been provided with the finest Abbeys, he did not wish to dwell in the courts of Princes, nor to depart from the holy union of observance, as he himself says in Letter 35 of Book 2 of his *Familiar Letters*:

> For if I had wanted to live on the salaries of Princes, it would certainly not have been necessary to live here in poverty. For there are many who would take me in with a generous provision... <note>original: "Nam si Principum vivere stipendiis voluissem, non utique conversari isthic in paupertate fuisset necessarium."</note>

-># THE LIFE OF TRITHEMIUS<-

...to be provided for with honor; but I could never be induced to allow myself to be joined with **courtly butterflies** <note>original: *aulicis me papilionibus*; a dismissive metaphor for flighty, superficial courtiers.</note>, for philosophy no less than religion forbids it—a religion which I do not know how to keep unharmed amidst courtly tumult, if indeed anyone ever could. Truly, as he says in Letter 50, Book 2:

> *Life is not for fish on dry land, nor is a monk’s way of life safe without the <term>cloister</term><note>The enclosed, private living quarters of a monastery, symbolizing separation from the secular world.</note>; therefore, lest I make myself a liar, I have chosen to live poor and cast down in a monastery, rather than to appear wealthy and glorious with Princes in the secular world.*

Likewise in Letter 58, Book 2:

> *For it is not becoming for men—indeed, it is not even permitted—who have once surrendered themselves to divine service, to return to secular acts, nor to live in cities, those who are devoted to monasteries. A fish in the kitchen and a monk in the court of a Prince appear to differ not at all from extreme danger, since each is close to death: one of the life and the flesh, the other of the spirit and the mind. For just as it seems impossible for a fish in a kitchen to be long delayed from death, since it was brought there to be eaten by men, so it is not possible that a monk in the court of a Prince or in the tumult of worldly action can keep his monastic purpose inviolate, especially if the desire for ambition or greed draws him outside the monastery.*

Thus, Trithemius chose to live poor in a monastery rather than to live as a wealthy man in the world against the monastic rule; for, as he says in Letter 50, Book 2:

> *Having food and clothing, a Christian is commanded to be content; for those who desire to become rich fall into various temptations of demons. A monk, however, who loves riches, is neither a monk nor a Christian, but rather an <term>apostate</term><note>One who abandons their religious vows or faith.</note> and an infidel, because he both transgresses the Gospel and, as a despiser of his monastic vow, lies to his Lord.*

But Trithemius did not only flee the courts of Princes; he also looked with contempt upon wealthier Abbeys, as he himself says in Letter 77, Book 1:

> *This place [the Abbey of Sponheim] has truly held me for many years by my excessive love for it, and it always pulled me back from consenting to 'fatter' <note>Meaning wealthier or more resource-rich.</note> Abbeys which were offered to me, as you know.*

And this is also confirmed by the *Chronicle of Sponheim*, continued to the year 1506. Secondly, among the virtues of Trithemius, there presents itself gentleness, patience, and the contempt for revenge. In demonstration of this, Trithemius speaks elegantly in Letter 32, Book 1:

> *I myself am prepared, the Lord Jesus knows, and I am not troubled, for the glory of His name, for my own sins, and for the love of the heavenly kingdom, not only to freely leave behind the Abbey and all favor of this world, but even to subject myself to extreme want and devote myself to beggary. I have endured unmerited injuries and insults from the Prince of the Cynonotorans <note>original: *Cynonotorum*; likely a Latinized wordplay referring to a specific group or person, potentially "dog-like" critics.</note>, which, though I could have thrown back upon his own head, I preferred to embrace patience rather than to stir up vengeance against the will of God. There is a God in heaven who sees the injuries I suffer without cause; He, I do not doubt, will avenge them. For as he says in Letter 75, Book 1: it belongs to Christians, and especially to those in the cloister, to conquer injuries by being silent and fleeing rather than by responding or struggling; and the more our profession of the monastic institution binds us to perfection, the less is it permitted for us to repel force with force, but rather it is necessary to sustain whatever adversities more patiently. We are Christians, and those of the cloister are bound even more strictly to humility, because of which all heavy and bitter things must be borne patiently by us for the love of Christ. I, so that I might prove myself a servant of Christ, however useless, look at how much I have sustained without my own desert—things which I could have turned back upon my rivals—but I never wished to bring evil upon those who harm me, hoping...*

This one thing I add: Trithemius was a most devoted servant of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and a most fierce defender of her <term>Immaculate Conception</term><note>The theological belief that Mary was preserved from original sin from the moment of her conception; Trithemius was a prominent advocate for this doctrine before it was officially defined by the Church.</note>, for a clear proof of which one should see, among other things, the *Chronicle of Spanheim* <note>original: *Chronicon Spanheimense*</note> for the year 1494.

## CHAPTER XIX.

### CONCERNING THE FAVOR OF PRINCES TOWARD TRITHEMIUS AND HIS FAMILIARITY WITH THE MOST LEARNED MEN.

I would be tedious if I wished to enumerate those highest Princes who pursued Trithemius with the greatest honor and honored him with most precious gifts; longer still, if I attempted to insert into this treatise a catalog of those most famous men—not only of Germany, but of all Europe—who, for the sake of seeing and hearing Trithemius, came to <term>Spanheim</term><note>Modern Sponheim, the site of the Benedictine abbey where Trithemius served as Abbot and built one of the greatest libraries of the age.</note> after completing the longest journeys, sought his friendship, and spread the fame of his name everywhere. Spanheim knows this; let it speak of how many Princes, Bishops, Prelates, and men most celebrated for their doctrine and erudition from the whole world it saw during the 23 years under Abbot Trithemius. And certainly they did not come there because of Spanheim itself, *for what was Spanheim before Trithemius was in it? Or who had heard its name?* I would be longest of all if I thought to recall the fame of Trithemius which he attained in the whole world because of the insight of his almost divine genius and his incomparable learning in all the sciences, and to repeat anew what the world said, wrote, and thought of him. Let it suffice, therefore, to enumerate only the principal Princes of Germany with whom Trithemius was in favor and high esteem. Among them, the first is the Holy Roman Emperor himself, **Maximilian I**, who was exceedingly delighted by Trithemius’s company; he not only frequently had him summoned by letters so that he might stay with him for some time, but he even plainly desired to enroll him into his own household. Especially when Trithemius had left Spanheim, never to return, the Emperor solicited him many times both by himself and through **Matthew of Gurk**, the Bishop. The second is **Philip**, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria and Prince Elector, to whom...

Trithemius was most intimate [with the Prince] and stayed with him for many days at Budoras <note>Likely Büderich, near Wesel.</note>; this was the reason he fell out of favor with the Duke of the Cynonoti <note>original: *Cynonotorum*; likely referring to the Hunsrück region ("Dog’s Back") where Trithemius’s former monastery, Sponheim, was located.</note>, which stirred up the envy of his rivals, and finally forced him, though innocent, to endure so many injuries and plots. He was held in such high esteem by this last-mentioned Cardinal that, when the said Cardinal and Trithemius were together at the table of the Elector of Brandenburg at the Diet of Princes in Frankfurt in the year 1503, the Cardinal said to Trithemius as he was about to depart: *O, how lately known, how quickly you leave us:* <note>original: *O quam tardè notus quam citò recedis*</note> and afterward he presented him with extraordinary gifts and promised great things if he would travel with him to Rome. He also confirmed, by Apostolic authority, the *Course*, *Rosary*, *Treatise*, and *Orations* written by Trithemius in praise of St. Anne, and graced them with <term>indulgences</term><note>In the Catholic Church, a remission of the temporal punishment due to sin; here, the Cardinal is granting spiritual benefits to those who use Trithemius's devotional writings.</note>. Even from the furthest reaches of Gaul <note>France</note>, the Bishop of Cahors invited Trithemius to him with offers of large donations; for that prelate, moved by Trithemius's fame, desired to have him in France either permanently or for a time, and promised much for that purpose.

As I am about to enter the arena to defend the *Steganography* <note>Trithemius’s famous work on cryptography and "angel magic," the title literally means "hidden writing."</note> of Trithemius, I notice that I must struggle against three kinds of Adversaries. First, there are those who reject the present edition of *Steganography* as a forgery, contending either that Trithemius never intended to publish his *Steganography* to such a curious world—and therefore everything he promised in many places is frivolous, lies, and for the sake of empty glory—and that he imprudently scattered these ideas among the common people just to sell a sham <note>original: *fucum venderet*; a Latin idiom for "to deceive" or "to sell a pretense."</note> to great Princes. Or, they argue that he did indeed possess inventions of the rarest subtlety in this art, but (as he says himself) he did not bring them to light because he was deterred by the malice of scoundrels, the ingratitude of the world, or the sheer magnitude of the labor, and so he buried them forever in his mind. Or perhaps, they say, some "true" *Steganography* of Trithemius wanders or hides in the depths of libraries, and that the present edition is nothing like his genuine and legitimate offspring. Second, there are those who do grant the book to its Author (whose name it proudly bears), yet they attack it with censures more harsh than is just. They claim it contains traces of a counterfeit birth; that it teaches things that should not be found in a religious and learned man; and that it betrays destructive dogmas relating to Magic—not natural magic, but the forbidden kind. Finally, third, there are those who accuse and condemn both the book and the Author of forbidden magic, necromancy <note>the practice of communicating with the dead.</note>, and superstition. The entire assault of the Adversaries is divided into two main parts: one concerns the Author, and the other concerns the book. Therefore, I believe the opposing defense must likewise be divided into the same number of parts, one of which concerns the Author and the other the book. As far as concerns

# PREFACE.

I believe that for the defense of this author, one would more easily find a beginning than an end; for the man's monastic life, his religious zeal, and his fervor of piety speak for him. He is defended by his close friendship with Emperors, Kings, Princes, and the most learned men; he is further testified to by the almost infinite multitude of small works which he composed with the highest devotion in praise of the Immaculate Virgin, St. Anne, St. Joseph, and various other Saints. Finally, the glory of illustrious Ecclesiastical writers and the luminaries of Germany will fight for him. As for the defense of the book itself, I shall easily elude all the arrows of the adversaries; for they are aimed from the darkness, and the adversaries themselves do not know what they are targeting, but only guess, and have so often missed the mark until now that they have finally been forced to admit their own ignorance. Indeed, it would be easy to put an end to this entire dispute—and the reader would no doubt judge the present discussion superfluous—if, omitting this *Steganography Vindicated* <note>The "Vindicated" refers to the current defensive text the reader is holding.</note>, I hurried immediately to the *Steganography Unlocked* <note>original: *Steganographia Referata*; this refers to the decoded version of the text where the secrets are explained.</note>. For in that work, the obscure uses of metaphors, the intricate circumlocutions of riddles and enigmas, and the "horrendous conjurations of spirits" <note>Trithemius used the names of angels and spirits as part of his cryptographic keys, which led many to believe he was practicing black magic rather than simple coding.</note> are brought out of the shadows and into the light, from resemblance to truth, and from a barbaric appearance to the gentleness of common language. They are revealed in such a way that even a moderately learned person can solve the entire difficulty of the *Steganography* at a single glance, making Trithemius’s innocence and the injury done by his antagonists manifest without any further defense. 

However, since the purity of the book and the author's reputation for innocence can be restored even without knowledge of the genuine key, I judged it would not be entirely out of place to place the *Vindicated* before the *Unlocked*, so that what is missing in one may receive perfection and clarity from the other. Thus, those who do not happen to penetrate the key of the *Steganography* may learn from this *Vindication* not to show themselves as rash judges who pronounce a sentence upon a cause before they have recognized its truth. In this work, I must primarily establish the following:

1.) That Trithemius, by the subtlety of his talent, truly possessed most ingenious steganographic inventions. 

2.) That he did not merely conceive them in his mind and bury them there, but also wrote them down, at least in part. 

3.) That those inventions which he inserted into the book he calls *Steganography* are still in existence, and that this work is none other than the present edition, which others call the *Darmstadt edition* <note>A specific manuscript or printed version of the text associated with the city of Darmstadt.</note>. 

4.) That nothing is contained in that *Steganography* which could not be written by a religious and learned man; there are no destructive dogmas or matters pertaining to magic, and nothing contrary to Gospel teaching or the faith. 

5.) That nothing necromantic, nothing magical, and nothing superstitious is taught there, but that all things taught therein are supported by true, lawful, and natural principles. 

So let it be.

## CHAPTER I.

### WHAT IS STEGANOGRAPHY?

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter N at the start of the chapter, featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

The definition of the name, derived from the Greek words *steganós* <note>original: "στεγανὸς"; meaning covered, secret, or hidden</note> and *graphō* <note>original: "γράφω"; meaning I write</note>, describes the thing itself: Steganography is "hidden writing," or the art of revealing the intentions of one's mind to those who are absent through a secret script. Truly, since Kings and Princes encounter many affairs which they do not trust to communicate safely via ordinary letters to their deputies who are far away, it is worthwhile for any of them to possess several special modes of writing and messaging. By these, they may most safely convey their secrets to friends; especially in these times, in which—with a license for sin prevailing—no safe trust is found anywhere in the world. 

Hence, we read that many of the wise men of old—Philosophers, Kings, and Princes—once devised various and manifold methods by which they might safely entrust the secrets of their counsel and whatever hidden mystery had to be confided to their messengers sent to distant places. These methods were designed so that the messengers would be fit to carry them and remain secure from every attack of the wicked. In this way, neither would the simplicity of those practicing the <term>Cabala</term> <note>The author refers here to the Cabala not just as Jewish mysticism, but as a system of symbolic or encoded interpretation used in cryptography.</note> strip the mystery bare, nor would the innate curiosity of the <term>bacucei</term> <note>original: "bacuceorum"; a term used in this context for "fools" or "know-nothings" who pry into things they cannot understand.</note> cause harm to official matters. 

Some, in the mystery of this proposed art, kept familiar <term>Light-loving owls</term> <note>original: "bubones Philophotos"; Trithemius often used the names of spirits or birds as metaphors for specific cryptographic keys or methods.</note>; others kept <term>Light-hating owls</term> <note>original: "Misophotos"</note>; and others called both into practice through the art. Again, some transposed the known letters of the common alphabet, while others fashioned their own unique <term>Characters</term> under the guise of Barbarian scripts. Furthermore, others used the service of visible letters, writing with red lead or common ink; while others formed characters that were invisible at their own discretion. And who could express all the modes of secret writing used by the ancients? 

Such was the state of antiquity; but today's more unruly world has forced the invention of other and far more subtle modes of secret writing. These have been illustrated with the most ingenious inventions by Giambattista della Porta, Gerolamo Cardano, Blaise de Vigenère, Erycius Puteanus, Herman Hugo, Father Athanasius Kircher, Gustavus Selenus, and finally Father Caspar Schott, of the Society of Jesus. Yet, how much they have excelled in this most subtle art, it is not within my power to examine, nor—

nor of will; it only pleased me to apply a touchstone <note>original: "lapidem lydium"; a reference to a Lydian stone used to test the purity of gold, here meaning a standard of judgment</note>, against which the ingenious reader may himself test all their steganographic inventions. Truly, three things are required for a perfect Steganography. First: That the modes of secret writing are entirely free from suspicion. ### CHAPTER II.

## DID TRITHEMIUS INTEND TO WRITE A WORK ON STEGANOGRAPHY?

The *Chronicle of Sponheim* <note>original: "Chronicon Spanheimense"; Trithemius's own history of the abbey where he served as Abbot</note> for the year of Christ 1499 writes about the Steganography conceived in the mind of Trithemius in these words: In the aforementioned year, on the Monday after Palm Sunday, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of this Monastery, wrote back to Arnold Bostius—a Carmelite living in Ghent and a most learned and religious man—who had inquired by letter what he was writing. Responding as to a true friend, he wrote that he had in his hands a great work on Steganography at the request of a certain Prince. This work treated certain secret and wonderful things and arts newly invented by him, which had been known to no man before this time, just as the work itself proves. However, before the letter had reached Ghent, Bostius himself, to whom it had been written, passed away to the Lord on the fourth of April <note>original: "pridie nonas Aprileis"</note>, which is the Thursday after the feast of Easter (on the anniversary of Trithemius’s birth). Therefore, the Prior of the Convent of Ghent opened the letter sent to Bostius, read it, and spread it everywhere as if it were a miracle. In a short space of time, it was published throughout France <note>original: "Gallia"</note> and Germany <note>original: "Alemannia"</note> before many Princes and most learned men; it was copied and read with the greatest admiration by all, and held to be a new and unheard-of miracle. But in truth, since no one, however erudite, was able to understand either the principles or the reasons for those things promised therein, they put forth ambiguous opinions. Some proclaimed Trithemius a divine man, others a most learned one. Some, whose intellect was slower and whose will was readier for rashness, claimed he was a magician <note>original: "magum"</note> and performed these things through the service of spirits...

...they confirmed, but how pure all the natural things are that are reported in that same letter is clear from the beginning of the book *Steganography*. Moved by this novelty, many most learned men from the furthest borders of *Gaul* <note>original: "Gallia"; here referring to modern-day France</note> came here to see and speak with *Trithemius*. Nor is this a conjecture made by guessing, but the multitude and excellence of his works provide infallible proof, by which he creates amazement and admiration for the world. Whether you look at the elegance of the style in them, or weigh the subtlety of the subject matter, you will stand astonished; nor will you be able to agree with yourself which quality to admire more among such a great number of works.

And what is the reward for such labor, except perhaps a small weight of gold, which is transitory, and for that reason rather to be despised by a Christian Monk? It was never my intention to labor for temporal reward, for I see myself called into the vineyard of the eternal King.”*

### CHAPTER III.

## WHAT DID TRITHEMIUS PROMISE HE WOULD WRITE IN THE STEGANOGRAPHIA?

There will be four books, each with at least one hundred chapters..."

...will be extinguished. I began this work at the urging of a certain great Prince, whom there is no need to name. You ask, what does this work teach? It teaches the greatest things, amazing and incredible to all who are ignorant of them, things which have never been heard of throughout the ages.

For the **first book** contains more than a hundred ways of <term>writing secretly</term> <note>original: "occultè scribendi" — this is the basis of cryptography and steganography</note> whatever you wish, without any suspicion, without the transposition of letters, and without any fear. The words used are plain and familiar, lacking all suspicion, but no one will ever be able to perceive my intention without the art, no matter how learned he may be; it is a truly amazing thing.

The **second book** will contain much more wonderful things. Specifically, through this art, I can make the concept of my mind known to one who knows my art at any distance—even at a hundred miles or more—securely, without words, without writings, and without signs. I can do this through any messenger <note>original: "nuntium"</note>; if that messenger were captured on the way, or even interrogated through the harshest tortures, he could confess nothing about my message because he knows absolutely nothing about it. Furthermore, I can even do this without a messenger whenever I wish. I can also indicate my will to someone sitting in prison who knows the art, even if I am far away and no matter how well he is guarded—even if he sat three miles underground. And I can do all these things most extensively and universally, whenever and as often as I wish, naturally, without any superstition or the aid of any spirits whatsoever <note>Trithemius emphasizes "naturally" to insist his methods are scientific/mathematical rather than demonic, as he was often accused of summoning spirits to carry messages</note>. These are wonders, I confess, but hear of things even more wonderful.

The **third book** teaches an art by which I can take an unlearned man <note>original: "idiotam," meaning a layman or someone lacking formal education</note> who knows only his mother tongue and has never known a word of the Latin language, and in two hours teach him to write, read, and understand Latin quite elegantly and eloquently. He will be able to do this as much as he wishes, so that whoever sees his letters will praise his words and understand his Latin compositions.

The **fourth book** contains many amazing <term>experiments</term> <note>original: "experimenta" — here meaning practical demonstrations or methods</note>, but purely natural ones. For instance, I can indicate my mind to one who knows my art while eating, or while sitting with others, without words or nods, as broadly as I wish—even while speaking, preaching, playing the organ, or...

To these men, and to you, I respond as I have responded to many: that many natural things are possible which seem impossible, or even supernatural, to those ignorant of the forces of nature. And behold, I speak before my **GOD**, who knows all things: those wonderful things I have predicted are much more excellent, deeper, and greater than I could write or you could believe, and yet they are all purely natural, without any deception, without superstition, without magic art, and without the invocation or service of any spirits whatsoever.

I have said these things so that if a rumor ever reaches you that I either know or can do wonderful things, you would not consider me a **Magician**, but a **Philosopher**. For just as it happened to *Albertus Magnus* <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a polymath and theologian whose deep interest in the natural sciences led to legends that he was a sorcerer.</note>, that most profound investigator of natural things—who was held to be a *Magician* by the common people because of the wonders he performed through the hidden power of nature—I am certain the same could happen to me. If you ask, "Where did I get these things, which no one else knows?" Listen. I did not learn these from man, nor through man, but through revelation—I know not from whom. 

For when, on a certain occasion during the present year, I was thinking what new thing I could find that was hidden from all, I began to consider if I could devise those wonderful things I have mentioned. When, after long imagining, I despaired entirely as if of an impossible thing, I lay down to sleep that night, laughing at my own folly for having attempted impossibilities. That same night, someone stood by me, saying:

> "Those things you have thought, O *Trithemius*, are not in vain, though you thought them impossible for you or anyone else to find." And I said to him: "If therefore they are possible, tell me, I pray, how they are done." And opening his mouth, he taught me about each thing in order, showing how those things I had thought about in vain for many days could easily be done.

Behold, before **GOD**, for I do not lie, but speak the truth: I have taught these things to no one yet—although many promising great things have often asked—except for one Prince to whom I am writing. I have made him certain of the possibility of this art by a clear demonstration; nor is it fitting [to teach] these...

He was the first of all to commit <term>Arthrology</term> <note>Communication using the joints of the fingers.</note> and <term>Dactylogy</term> <note>Communication using the fingers themselves, similar to modern sign language or finger-spelling.</note> to writing. By using these, one person reveals to another most securely whatever secret he wishes, which no one else sitting nearby will notice, much less understand. Bedanus himself taught that this very thing could be done in many other ways; however, since we have written nothing of these in the <term>Polygraphia</term> <note>Trithemius's first published work on cryptography (1518).</note>, we rightly refuse to say more here. We long ago assigned a proper place for these difficult matters in the <term>Steganographia</term>, which we do not yet intend to publish. And who could express all the ancient modes of secret writing? For some practitioners of the art used <term>Philophotos</term> <note>Greek for "light-loving." In Trithemius's cryptic systems, these likely refer to methods or "spirits" that operate in the open or through visible means.</note> owls in the service of their craft, others used <term>Misophotos</term> <note>Greek for "light-hating." These likely refer to methods involving darkness or invisible inks.</note>, and others called both into practice. Again, some transposed the known letters of the common alphabet; others fashioned their own characters under the guise of "Barbarian" scripts. Others still made use of visible letters by writing with cinnabar <note>A bright red mineral (mercury sulfide) used for ink.</note> or common ink, while others formed characters that were invisible at their whim. The modes of visible characters for secret writing are truly too many to count, and utterly innumerable...

# STEGANOGRAPHY

...to mention all of these is neither our wish nor within our power. Of invisible methods, however, there are three types more commonly used among mortals today:

The first is called **Dermatic** <note>original: "Dermaticum"; from the Greek 'derma', meaning skin.</note>, by which a certain artificial writing is produced on the backs of messengers using a wash of a specific fluid; it remains visible only to those who know the secret of the art, and no one else is able to discern it. 

The second is called **Hyphasmatic** <note>original: "Hyphasmaticum"; from the Greek 'hyphasma', meaning woven fabric.</note>, by which one writes on cloth with specific substances. Once dried, the writing cannot be seen at all, until it is perceived after being soaked in cold water. 

The third type is named **Aleotic** <note>original: "Aleoticum"; likely referring to a "wandering" or varied method.</note>, which is multifaceted and varied, both in form and material, and possesses almost innumerable modes of secret writing. This writing is done on paper or without paper, using <term>alum and gall</term> <note>The original Latin uses the anagrams "nemilua & cala" for "alumine & galla"—common ingredients for invisible ink.</note>, with <term>vinegar</term> <note>original: "rapho," an anagram for "opha" or "sapho" (soap/vinegar derivatives).</note>, with <term>onion juice</term> <note>original: "lapolce," likely "cepolla" or onion.</note>, and various other things. 

Likewise, letters are written and hidden in various ways and places, such as "under a thin plank" <note>original: "sub rare tabulata"</note>, "under a redder dew-thread" <note>original: "sub rorifila rubior"</note>, "in a scale" <note>original: "in leopi"</note>, "in a dead bottle" <note>original: "in neco flas"</note>, "in a hollow gourd" <note>original: "in ceocali"</note>, "in a place of rest" <note>original: "locubat"</note>, "in a crate" <note>original: "ratera"</note>, "in a lily" <note>original: "in lispilie"</note>, and in other similar, nearly infinite ways. <note>These strange Latin phrases are examples of Trithemius’s "steganograms"—sentences that look like nonsense or poetic descriptions but serve as containers for hidden messages.</note> Truly, because none of these serves our present purpose, it is appropriate that we hasten to those things which reason demands. 

There is also another type called **dactyletron** <note>From the Greek 'daktylos', meaning finger.</note>; this is not for writing, but a method using the most subtle signs by which one person can intimate the concept of their mind to another. This is varied by so many differences that there is no one in the world who can count all the species of such a great mystery. By the principal method, as well as many others descending from it, you—sitting at a table or in any other place—can artificially and securely communicate whatever you wish to one who knows the art, most safely and without anyone's suspicion. Finally, it remains recorded in the inventions of <term>Steganography</term> how you may announce the secret of your mind to one who is absent without using letters, even while the messenger themselves remains unaware of what they are conveying.

**Fourth.** Trithemius in his *Polygraphia*, page 64 (beginning with the word "propterea"): We shall therefore give, in the four following books, easier modes of writing; although they may not be entirely free from the suspicion of onlookers, they nonetheless elude the understanding of most people. In *Steganography*, however, there are more abundant modes of writing most secretly and without any suspicion, where a single word does not represent a letter, but rather each word represents another entire word suitable to the mystery. 

Let us provide an example of this; as if you wished to forewarn a friend of some imminent danger under such a narrative of words: *They have conspired for death...*

...your [house] Malancius, Tiberius, John & Peter, servants of the Count of Asoto, and on the fourth day after St. Lawrence’s Day <note>St. Lawrence’s feast day is August 10; the "fourth day after" would be August 14.</note> at night they will surround your house; decide what you will do. Steganography cloaks this secret thus:

> I pray you, dearest friend, that you send me ten florins <note>A gold coin used across Europe.</note> by the bearer of these presents, because they are very necessary to me for the construction of a certain building; I will faithfully restore them to you. <note>original: "Oro te amice charissime, ut mutuo mihi transmittas decem florenos..."</note>

Who would believe or suspect a secret to lie hidden in the speech written above? Let us place that same secret under another narrative:

> Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who willed to become man, to suffer and die for us, have mercy on me, an unworthy sinner, now and in the terrible hour of my death. <note>original: "Domine Jesu Christe, fili DEI vivi..."</note>

Behold, you now have one hidden meaning of your heart veiled by a double narrative within the boundaries of Steganography, in speech both brief and faithful, which the whole world could not even suspect—nor, if they searched for a hundred years, could they find it by any means, even if all the learned men were to convene. Finally, this Steganography teaches how to hide this same secret intention of your heart not only in one or two of the prescribed narratives, but in almost infinite ways, and to announce it most safely, most secretly, and most securely to whomever you wish. All methods of this kind of invention can also be changed through <term>metathesis</term> <note>A method of rearranging letters or sounds to create new meanings; essentially a transposition cipher.</note> in infinite turns, and through them, everything can be written and announced.

### CHAPTER IV.
## WHETHER TRITHEMIUS ONLY CONCEIVED HIS STEGANOGRAPHY IN HIS MIND, OR ALSO WROTE IT DOWN?

Father Caspar Schott <note>A 17th-century German Jesuit physicist and mathematician who published extensively on Trithemius's work.</note> proposes this very question in his *Steganographic School*, Class 7, Inquiry 2, and reports that Father Athanasius Kircher <note>A famous Jesuit polymath; he was skeptical of the "magic" in Trithemius’s work and sought to explain it through natural means.</note> is of the opinion: That the *Steganographia* of Trithemius, which he himself mentions in the letter to Bostius cited a little while ago, was not actually written by the Author, but only conceived in his mind; and he thinks he can prove this from Trithemius’s own words. 1. Because in the aforementioned letter to Bostius, when dividing the work into parts, he uses a verb in the future tense:

> There will be, however, four books; each will be distinguished by at least one hundred chapters. <note>original: "Erunt autem quatuor libri..."</note>

From this, it clearly appears that it was only conceived in his mind. Secondly: Because Trithemius himself says in countless places that his *Steganographia* is never to be published; as at the beginning of the same letter:

> I have in my hands now a great work, which if it should ever be published—which God forbid—the whole world will wonder. <note>original: "In manibus jam habeo grande opus..."</note>

Second, that the texts say Steganography ought not be published; ought to remain buried; ought to lie hidden in darkness; ought not be given to the public; this does not fail our purpose: for even written things can lie hidden in darkness, remain buried, and not be given to the public; and if we more accurately unravel the specific meaning of those words, they apply more to those things which have already been committed to writing than to those which are only conceived in the mind.*

The third cause, indeed, is the judgment of the unlearned common people, who attribute everything they do not understand to the evil arts <note>Meaning magic or witchcraft</note>. Nor, from the time it is probable that it was published, can any steganographer be found who does not make mention of it. What of the fact that many most learned men have, until now, attempted—not entirely unsuccessfully—to vindicate it from its censors, while others, on the contrary, have afflicted it with unjust slanders, laughed at it, and condemned it? Thus, it must be that some version of the *Steganography*, which the glory of Trithemius’s name has made famous, has circulated through the bookshops.

### CHAPTER VI.

### DOES TRITHEMIUS’S STEGANOGRAPHY STILL EXIST?

We are brought into the present doubt by the variety, so it seems, of the small works which are said to boast the title of Trithemius’s *Steganography*. Father Gaspar Schott <note>A famous Jesuit polymath and student of Athanasius Kircher</note> says in his *Schola Steganographica*, Class 7, Question 3, that he has seen two versions. One, as they call it, was published in Quarto <note>A book size where the printed sheet is folded twice to form four leaves</note> in Cologne, with the commentaries of Juan Caramuel <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682), a Spanish philosopher and mathematician</note>, written by him while still quite a young man in Spain. The other was similarly published in Quarto in Darmstadt in the year 1621, with this title: *Steganography: that is, the sure art of revealing the will of one's mind to those who are absent through secret writing. By the most Reverend and Distinguished Man Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim and most perfect Master of Natural Magic; prefixed to this work is its key, or true introduction, composed by the author himself, hitherto greatly desired by many but seen by very few, now made public for the sake of students of the more secret Philosophy.* And he thinks in the following question that the other—

Thirdly, it is no obstacle that he says many things are contained in it which cannot be attributed to a religious and learned man. For Trithemius himself confesses that his *Steganography* was composed in such a way that, to readers—especially the unlearned masses—it would create a sinister impression at first glance. Hence he protests in so many places: *nothing is held in it that is frivolous, nothing contrary to the Evangelical tradition or the Catholic faith, nothing superstitious is taught at all, but all things are supported by natural, lawful, and honorable principles, and the ministry, veiled in strange instructions <note>original: "peregrinis institutionibus"</note>, requires an erudite reader.* This was intended precisely so that these great secrets would not reach the ears of common, ignorant, or wicked people, and so that no one from the ranks of the unlearned—no one, unless they are most studious—could by their own power perfectly penetrate the secret of his science and his full intention. Just as the wicked and the reprobate hunt for opportunities to become worse not only from evil things but even from good and most holy institutions, he wished to ensure the same did not happen to his own most secret and otherwise useful (to the State <note>original: "Reip." or "Res publica," meaning the common good</note>) and most honorable invention, so that the wicked might not use it for evil as much as the good use it for good. 

And this is the very reason why I believe that the small work—not only what Kircher read, but also those which Bellarmine and Possevino describe—coincides with the Darmstadt edition. There are things that do not sit well with a religious and learned man, as Caramuel <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz, a Spanish Cistercian monk and polymath who defended Trithemius</note> testifies in *Steganographia Vindicated*, in the dispute:

### Whether Trithemius’s Steganography and the *Little Key* <note>original: *Clavicula*</note> could have been justly forbidden.

At first glance and on the surface, they appear to be dogmas veiled under the guise of magic, according to the testimony of Charles de Bovelles and Johann Weyer in his *Treatise on the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: *De Præstigiis Dæmonum*</note>, book 2, chapter 6.

Having established these points, let us approach the question: **Does the true Steganography of Trithemius still exist?** Certainly, if we consider Trithemius’s own words, in which he speaks of his *Steganography* in many places; if we combine so many and such precise protestations <note>formal declarations of innocence or intent</note> with which he tries to remove and uproot all unfavorable opinions and suspicion from his *Steganography*; if we weigh the *Apology* which he published against Charles de Bovelles and his followers; if, finally, we read through the assessment of Charles de Bovelles and his successors—though it may be unjust and reckless, coming as it does from a man otherwise most learned who judged only the surface of the *Steganography*—we will find a certain extraordinary method of <term>Steganography</term> <note>The art of "hidden writing" or cryptography</note>. It was elaborated in the manner of a foreign instruction in imitation of and similarity to magical foundations, to which surely all the small works described thus far correspond exactly. Therefore, whatever the case may be—whether they coincide or differ—one of those will be the true *Steganography* of Trithemius.

---

### CHAPTER VII.
### THE FORM OF THE STEGANOGRAPHY IN THE DARMSTADT EDITION IS DESCRIBED.

In the previous chapter, I believed—and I suspect I did not err—that all the small works cited and brought forward there, which boast the title of Trithemius’s *Steganography*, coincide into one; and that it was no other than the Darmstadt edition of the *Steganography* that was seen, read, and subjected to censure by all those authors. Therefore, I judge that its method and form should be outlined in this chapter in a proper order. That book is indeed *Steganography*—that is, as I defined it at the beginning, the art of opening the will of one's mind to those who are absent through hidden writing. Its method, then, is this: When you are about to announce some secret to a friend, you call upon a spirit with the proper <term>conjuration</term> <note>In this context, a ritualistic calling, though Trithemius used these "spirits" as metaphors for cryptographic keys</note>, designated for that business, time, or place; to this spirit you commit your secret to be carried—which otherwise is safely trusted neither to man nor to letters. Then, you write letters that are in no way suspicious, and which he himself <note>the messenger or the spirit</note> would not even be thought to understand,

This is a great secret, which none of the sages before dared to commit to writing. Moreover, if that friend of yours wishes you to know anything regarding his own business, he can inform you with the same spirit within the same space of twenty-four hours, provided he is well-perfected in this art.
