### CHAPTER VIII.

## IS THE DARMSTADT EDITION THE TRUE STEGANOGRAPHY OF TRITHEMIUS?

Following the general reasoning by which I affirmed above in Chapter 6 that all the small works mentioned—which boast the title of Trithemius’s *Steganography*, especially the <term>Darmstadt edition<note>The "Editio Darmstadiana" refers to the 1606 publication of the Steganographia in Darmstadt. It was the first time this controversial text, which had circulated in manuscript for a century, was printed.</note></term> since it coincides with the others—agree with the form and method of the true *Steganography*, I now descend to specific reasoning and assert: The Darmstadt edition is the true and genuine *Steganography* of Trithemius, and nothing less than his own legitimate offspring, regardless of what <term>Father Caspar Schott<note>Caspar Schott (1608–1666) was a Jesuit mathematician and student of Athanasius Kircher. He wrote the "Schola Steganographica," which analyzed Trithemius's work.</note></term> may persuade himself based on a false hypothesis in his *Schola Steganographica* (Class 7, Error 4, number 9). I establish this opinion of mine with the following arguments.

First: Because, according to Father Schott in the aforementioned place, the Darmstadt edition entirely reflects the genius and style of Trithemius, which he displayed in his <term>*Polygraphia*<note>Trithemius's more "straightforward" work on cryptography, published after the Steganographia caused a scandal, though it still used complex systems of word substitution.</note></term>. In that work, the author veils the teaching he delivers under the names of various spirits and the obscurities of exotic words. For this reason, Father Schott also surmises that Trithemius's *Steganography* was not written in plain and clear words, but was intentionally shrouded in wondrous and ingenious riddles, <term>enigmas<note>original: "gryphis"; this refers to "gryphoi," a Greek term for difficult or knotted word-puzzles.</note></term>, metaphors, allusions, and obscurities—partly so it would not be understood by the common crowd, and partly so that the intellect of the curious would be tested if they ever stumbled upon it. Just as he entangled the *Polygraphia* in such obscure (yet very fitting and ingenious) circumlocutions while pretending to explain the individual books, it could scarcely have been understood by even the most gifted mind if he had not afterwards added a key to each book for the sake of <term>Emperor Maximilian<note>original: "Maximilianus Caesar"; Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I, who was Trithemius's patron and recipient of his cryptographic secrets.</note></term>. Therefore, Father Schott also concludes: if there exists a *Steganography* published under Trithemius’s name which mentions various spirits—diurnal, nocturnal, wandering alone, stubborn, benevolent, etc.—and their various companions and ministers, as well as various conjurations composed of foreign and meaningless words by which said spirits are called, sent away, or constrained, it does not immediately follow that the work is a forgery.

Second: Because in the said edition, there are precisely as many books as Trithemius himself admits to having written; for he says he wrote two completed ones and a third that was unfinished. 1. In the Preface of the *Polygraphia* to Maximilian—

Nor, **thirdly**, does the objection stand that if **Trithemius’s** *Steganography* were true, the person who published it would have deserved great merit from the <term>republic of letters<note>The 'Respublica literaria' was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars in the late 17th and 18th centuries who shared ideas through letters and publications.</note></term>, and therefore would not have withheld his name, but would have diligently explained from where, from whom, and on what occasion it came to him. **Response**: besides the fact that this argument is very weak, the Author—that is, the one who sent this edition to the press—did not do so intentionally for several reasons: 

1. Because the book is very small, and he did not consider it particularly honorable to place his name upon it. 
2. Or because he added nothing of his own at all, but only gave **Trithemius’s** text to the public exactly as he found it. 
3. Or because he himself did not understand the matter, and thus thought it inglorious to boast of the title of an unknown science. 
4. Or because the sinister reputation of **Trithemius** was already known to him, and since this edition (found perhaps in a hidden library) corresponded to that reputation, he did not want to reveal his name lest he fall under suspicion of **Magic** along with **Trithemius**. 

And finally, how many books—even good and useful ones—are published without an Author’s name, to say nothing of those that suffer suspicion and the judgment of the <term>Inquisition<note>The Roman Inquisition, which censored or banned books deemed heretical or dangerous, including those involving the occult or "natural magic."</note></term>?

Nor, **fourthly**, does the objection stand that according to the letters to **Arnold Bostius**, the methods ought to be such that there is no man in the world who, by natural industry, could know or even suspect what is contained in the letters, except him who knows the art from the man himself—namely **Trithemius**—or from someone he taught; yet today, through the author of the *Steganography Vindicated* <note>original: "Steganographiæ Vindicatæ"</note>, all are explained precisely. **Response**: **Trithemius** rightly says that no one can suspect or know what is contained in the letters. For I confess the weakness of my own intellect; I confess that I could never have found the secret meaning of any letter by any art, unless I had first devoted all my study to the reading and solution of the <term>conjurations<note>In Trithemius's system, the "conjurations" were lists of names of spirits or strange incantations that actually functioned as the cryptographic keys. To the uninitiated, they looked like black magic; to the initiated, they were merely data.</note></term>, which are the key and rule for reading the letters. Once these were known and explained, I confess that the explanation of the letters was easy enough for me; and certainly, unless I had found the key for the individual letters contained in the *Steganography* through the explanation of the conjurations, I would never have wished to discover their secret sense. 

Let the clever reader prove the truth by experiment when, in the *Steganography Illustrated* <note>original: "Steganographia Illuſtrata"</note>, I shall have added some letters without a key; let him discover how much work it is to find the secret meaning of a letter for which the general key is known—to say nothing of a letter for which no key is provided.

### CHAPTER IX.

## WHETHER THE DARMSTADT EDITION OR TRITHEMIUS'S STEGANOGRAPHY SHOULD BE UNDERSTOOD LITERALLY.

Since the Darmstadt Edition is, at last, the true *Steganography* of **Trithemius**, I shall now use those terms interchangeably. Having outlined the form of the Darmstadt Edition above in Chapter 7, the form of **Trithemius’s** *Steganography* will be the same. The question now arises: are those things said there regarding spirits and conjurations to be understood according to the letter? That is, are spirits called forth by true adjurations, do they truly fly to the caller, receive a secret, carry it to one who is absent, bring back a response, and perform similar tasks as are suggested therein? Or are they instead to be taken in some tropical <note>figurative or metaphorical</note> sense, through a translation of truth into a likeness?

The first view—that it is literal magic—was fully adopted by **Carolus Bovillus** <note>Charles de Bovelles (1479–1567), a French philosopher who famously denounced Trithemius after a brief visit</note> and his follower **Joannes Weierus** <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician and occultist</note>, the most unjust slanderer of **Trithemius** in his treatise *On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: "De Praestigiis Daemonum"</note> book 2, chapter 6. Although his words deserve eternal darkness rather than the light of this *Steganography Vindicated*, yet because opposites shine more clearly when placed side by side, and so that the whole world may see how great an injury he inflicts upon **Trithemius**, and how all his followers and successors must eventually recant their song, I have judged it not inappropriate to insert his words here word-for-word into this vindication. Thus he speaks in the aforementioned place:

> Into this number (namely, of magic books) belongs also the book of **Joannes Trithemius**, the Abbot of Sponheim, described as the *Steganographia*, of which **Carolus Bovillus** makes mention with these words: "I betook myself (he writes) to **Trithemius**, whom I found to be a remarkable sorcerer, but otherwise grasped in no part of philosophy; he has forged a book and given it the name *Steganographia*, which I took by surprise <note>original: "überrumpelt," suggesting he examined it without the author's full permission</note> and read no more than the beginnings of several chapters, but held it in my hands for barely two hours and immediately threw it from me; for a horror and dread seized me because of such conjurations, and such barbaric and unusual names of spirits—I had almost said devils—which in my opinion are for the most part taken from foreign languages: Arabic, Chaldean, Hebrew, Greek (for there are none or very few in Latin). However, a multitude of strange signs, with which the conjurations are marked, are found there; and although **Trithemius** writes in a letter to **Bostius** that it is all bright, clear words, without any transposition of letters and words, so that everyone may read and understand..."

For throughout his entire *Steganographia* <note>The art of "hidden writing," Trithemius's famous work on cryptography disguised as magic</note>, he occasionally allows splendid little godly prayers to flow in, which might be sent to a good friend instead of an ordinary *Letter* <note>original: "Send-Brieffs"</note>. For it seems to me he handles the matter just as *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite</note> judges *Apollophanes* in an *Epistle to Sosipater*: "He uses divine things (he says) against God, and goes about trying to diminish and bring to nothing the true wisdom of God through useless worldly wisdom." 

However, when he lets himself be heard and boasts that he wishes to bring all things to pass without the help and assistance of spirits, in that he lies (as *Daniel* said in chapter 13 <note>A reference to the story of Susanna in the Book of Daniel, where Daniel exposes the lies of two elders</note>) upon his own head. It is also (unless my senses deceive me) the good Angel of God who is still present to cut him in two, and to sever the unlucky, unjust covenant he has entered into and established with the harmful angels (as far as one can gather from his work). But let that pass for now. Yet, as far as the often-cited *Steganography* of our *Joannis Trithemius* <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and polymath</note> is concerned, he maintains—as far as I still have it in fresh memory—this order:

First of all, he divides the names of the spirits; then he arranges their conjurations in order and attaches to each their own particular *Character* <note>a magical sign or symbol used as a cryptographic key</note> or sign. Finally, he distinguishes the *Figures*, from which the names of the spirits belonging to each conjuration are drawn, wherever necessity requires. In these figures, he also separates the spirits into four quarters: into *Imperiales* <note>Imperial</note>, *Duces* <note>Dukes</note>, *Comites* <note>Counts</note>, and *Servos* <note>Servants</note>—that is, into Emperors or supreme commanders, Dukes, Counts, and Servants. He assigns 12 *Imperatorum* <note>Emperors</note>, according to the twelve winds of which the *Philosophers* write, among which four are the most prominent: namely, those of the East, the West, the South, and the North, which he calls the Great *Imperatores*. Under each *Imperatore*, he appoints about 30 or 40 Dukes, and under each of those many more Counts, who in turn each have a number of Servants under them. Now, after all things he needs to use are so orderly divided, he begins the matter in such a way:

When he intends to discover and make known to one of his good friends—who is far away—his counsels, which he calls *Secreta* <note>secrets</note>, he writes a prayer instead of a *Letter* <note>original: "Send-Brieffs"</note>, which he masterfully colors with a veneer of great holiness and devotion. After he has printed one of the 12 *Imperatorum* *Characteren* <note>Emperors' symbols</note> upon it, he sends it to his friend, who also understands the "coinage" <note>likely referring to the system of code</note>. As soon as the friend has received and opened it, he pays particularly good attention to the end of the *Missive* <note>letter</note> to see with which *Imperatoris* *Character* <note>Emperor's symbol</note> it is sealed and protected. If it is one from the East, he proceeds, turns, and stretches the letter toward...

In my opinion, however, these conjurations are not a complete, perfect speech that possesses a full sentence or meaning, but rather a gathering-together of the names of many spirits, arranged in a wondrous manner according to the fashion and way of the magical art. Such names, as mentioned before, are for the most part unknown, being Arabic, Chaldean, or Hebrew. I also remember reading these words in his book, among others: "These spirits," he says, "are exceedingly harmful and mischievous; they are sworn enemies of the light and love darkness; therefore, a powerful conjuration is indeed required so that they may be forced to provide what is necessary."

It is also required that the conjurer be composed and have a man's heart <note>meaning great courage</note>; for should he become terrified in the middle of the conjuration and, out of fear, either tremble a little or fail in the pronunciation of the conjuration—whether by omitting several words or displacing them—the Devil will immediately wring his neck and blow out the light <note>a metaphor for ending his life</note>. Now, if this is so, who would be so childish as to hold these spirits to be anything but vengeful?

I have also seen in the often-mentioned work several conjurations which he calls <term>Potentes</term> <note>Latin for "powerful ones"</note>, that is, powerful and strong conjurations. These, as he claims, are intended to be useful when someone constantly desires the service of the spirits, so that he may at all times keep one with him and under his roof, forcing it to wait untiringly upon his service. Such a spirit, however, should be lodged in a place far from people, so that he does not happen to kill those who pass by.

# STEGANOGRAPHIA

Up to this point, he has been a slanderous babbler <note>original: "maledicus blaterator"</note> without foundation and without reason, driven only by a lust for calumny. But truly, Weyer <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued that many "witches" were actually suffering from mental illness, but who also criticized Trithemius for what he perceived as demonic magic.</note>, you must have been simple-minded, lazy, of dull wit, and someone immersed in carnal pleasures and worldly cares. It is not permitted for everyone to reach Corinth <note>A classical proverb meaning that not everyone has the means or talent to achieve difficult or expensive goals.</note>; believe me, this most high science does not suit your humble and unrefined mind. Rather, you are among that number who find it more familiar to despise wisdom than to learn it, and whom Trithemius neither desires nor wishes to penetrate these mysteries of his. Listen to what he says to his followers and those he invites to the contemplation of this science:

> *The great mysteries of this art cannot be penetrated except by the most studious men—those, specifically, whom a love of secrets and nature itself drive toward investigation, and who, out of a desire to attain knowledge, refuse to undergo no honest and possible labor. Lazy men, dull of wit, whom neither love incites to the study of wisdom's secrets nor nature assists, should understand that if they are unable to understand this most secret art of our invention, it is not to be blamed on us. Instead, it should be ascribed to their own sluggishness, laziness, and malice. Indeed, because they possess minds immersed in carnal pleasures and worldly cares, they cannot find the leisure to devote themselves to these matters with diligence; or, perhaps thinking themselves already wise or most learned, they despise our compositions as if they were unworthy of their reading. There will also be some so accustomed to standing by ancient and foreign traditions that they judge whatever they have not learned therein to be either impossible or superstitious. Nothing is more unfit for the knowledge of this profound art than such people, who either will not or cannot contemplate its highest points.*

Again, in the Preface to *Steganographia*:
> *Lest this great secret reach the ears of common, ignorant, or wicked men, I have considered it a primary part of my duty to wrap it in mysteries—since it teaches how to understand mysteries without knowing them—so that no one from the ranks of the ignorant, no one unless most studious, may be able to perfectly and fully penetrate the secret of this science by his own virtue and according to our intention, unless through reception from a teacher, which the Hebrews call Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabulam." While referring to Jewish mysticism, Trithemius often used the term to mean a "received" oral tradition or secret key passed from master to student.</note>, which is set over the most hidden mysteries.*

Again, in the preface to Book 3 of *Steganographia*:
> *But I, fearing that such a wonderful work might be despised by the ignorant due to its excessive obscurity, or eventually burned by fire—since I have long been experienced in it through many proofs—wished to commit it to clearer letters,*

so that to both learned men and those most studious in the magical arts, with **GOD’S** help, it might in some measure become accessible; yet, it shall at all times remain hidden from the ignorant "turnip-eaters" <note>original: "Rapophagis," a derogatory term for the uneducated or those of low status who eat peasant food.</note> and in no way be understood by their dull intellect. For certainly, he must be of the most simple wit (says Father Caspar Schott <note>Caspar Schott (1608–1666) was a Jesuit mathematician and student of Athanasius Kircher who sought to explain Trithemius's work through natural science rather than sorcery.</note> in his *Scholia on Steganography*, class 7, question 4, number 5) or surely of the narrowest conscience, who believes that Trithemius speaks of true spirits, or teaches that true conjurations should be employed, and that truly summoned spirits fly to him, accept his commands, carry responses to absent parties, and perform similar tasks suggested there. 

The **Prince Spirits**, whom he mentions, are the signs <note>In modern terms, these are the "keys" or "indicators" that tell the recipient which cipher is being used.</note> by which various modes of operation are distinguished from one another and are sent in letters written to those initiated in the art, so that they may know how the steganographic method of hiding a secret was used, and which method they must use to uncover it. The **Minister Spirits** and **Companions** are the letters of the Alphabet, by whose various transposition or order the secret is hidden and revealed. **Diurnal Spirits** are the letters with which letters or narratives are written openly, containing no secret; **Nocturnal Spirits** are the letters with which the secret concept is drafted. **Adjurations** are the rules and precepts to be observed in each mode of operation. Other obscure formulas of speech, which seem to present some hint of superstition, are employed to torment the minds of the curious.

Behold the clearest and most accurate figurative <note>original: "tropicam," referring to a trope or metaphor.</note> explanation and reduction; which Trithemius himself also suggests in the Preface to Book 2 of his *Steganographia*:

> Since I am to mention spirits again, I think I must preface this: nothing in this art of ours is to be considered frivolous, nothing contrary to the Evangelical tradition or the Catholic faith, and I shall hand down nothing superstitious at all. For everything which we have said in the preceding volume, or are about to say in the following ones, is supported by natural, licit, and honorable principles; it is a mystery veiled only by strange instructions and words wrapped in the names of spirits. They require a learned Reader: for we use the service of a spirit <note>Here, "spirit" refers to the breath or the "hidden soul" of the message—the cipher itself.</note> to veil a secret that would harm the wicked if it were made public.

Father Schott says in the same place that Trithemius uses similar forms of speech in his *Polygraphia* <note>Trithemius's other major work on cryptography, published in 1518, which was less controversial because it was more clearly technical.</note>, which could not have been understood by anyone, nor read without forming a sinister opinion of the Author, unless he had explained them through an attached key; even though it is most certain and confessed by all that the work contains nothing evil or destructive. 

Therefore, you followers of Weyer, sing your recantation <note>original: "palinodiam cantare," to take back what was said.</note>! Restore the purity, innocence, and fame of this book; acknowledge your error and ignorance, and come into *Steganographia Reserata* <note>meaning "Steganography Unlocked."</note> to see how these allegories are reduced to truth by most fitting reason.

## CHAPTER X.

# WHETHER THE STEGANOGRAPHY OF TRITHEMIUS IS PERFORMED BY THE POWER AND MINISTRY OF SPIRITS.

**I**t was shown in the preceding chapter that the *Steganography* <term>Steganographia: literally "hidden writing," the title of Trithemius's most famous and controversial work</term> of Trithemius, as it stands, can be reduced and explained in a most fitting manner and according to the Author’s own intention, in the same sense which I likewise recounted in full from Father Caspar Schott. The question now arises again: notwithstanding those explanations, is Steganography nevertheless performed by the ministry of spirits? This is not the place for me to wander too far into the essence, nature, properties, power, office, and ministry of spirits, whether good or evil; I shall say it in a single word: this is what is disputed—whether Trithemius's *Steganography* is performed by an express or tacit pact with a demon <note>original: "pacto cum dæmone." In the early modern period, a "pact" was a formal agreement with a supernatural entity, the legal basis for a charge of witchcraft.</note>, by virtue of which the demon is bound to obey the will of the person practicing Steganography according to its terms. 

Immediately, another general question—or rather a slander—entangles itself here, which was already stirred up in the time of Trithemius himself and was resolved, rejected, and eluded by him through so many apologies and protestations: was Trithemius a Magician <term>Magus: a practitioner of magic; here used in the derogatory sense of a sorcerer</term> and did he have a pact with demons? Far be it from me to call Trithemius’s reputation, innocence, and piety into doubt, or even to raise such an opinion or question about him; in this present chapter, I intend only to defend, protect, and vindicate his innocence, asserting from the very threshold: Trithemius was never a Magician, never a Necromancer; but if he wrote or did anything that exceeded the grasp of the unlearned masses, or even otherwise learned men, all those things were supported by the forces of nature and drew their origin from the foundations of true and Christian Philosophy. He had no pact with demons or spirits; he had no commerce with Magicians and Necromancers; and therefore his *Steganography* does not operate by any ministry of spirits, but rather the mystery of the Steganography is veiled under their names and offices.

There appear to be two distinct and preliminary questions here (to use this name for the time being), one of which consumes the other. One is specific and concerns only the *Steganography*, agreeing with the title of this chapter; the other is general and attacks the Author himself. They appear so joined together that he who concedes the first is also bound to concede the second, and he who denies the second is also compelled to deny the first; but if we look more deeply into... <meta>catchword: trospi- (likely "introspiciamus" or "introspiciantur," meaning "if we look into")</meta>

If we look closely, there is really only one point of contention: that by which the purity of the book is disputed. For if you succeed in staining the book with the mark of magic, you will triumph in the other matter as well; but if you defend the purity of the book, you will have vindicated the author himself from every blot. For it was *Steganography*—*Steganography*, I say, alone—that gave birth to this sinister judgment and opinion concerning Trithemius. It does not matter that even in his own time, before he had ever written *Steganography*, he suffered the opinion and suspicion of the common people, as he himself confesses in various places, and especially in the often-cited letters to Capellerius, the Mathematician of Paris:

> I have written nothing yet for which anyone could deservedly wonder; I have done nothing stupendous. And yet I endure the opinion of the common folk, while many think me a Magus <term>Magus: a magician or sorcerer; here used as a legal and religious accusation</term>, asserting that I have raised the dead, summoned demons from the underworld, predicted the future, brought back thieves with incantations, and bound robbers. All of these things are fabrications and lies; I have never done them nor even thought of doing them. I confess I have read many books of the Magicians—not to imitate them, but so that I might eventually refute and confound their most wicked superstitions, which I trust I shall shortly do with the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ. What do you think the foolish and rash ignorance of unlearned men will think of me in the future when I bring *Steganography* to light <note>original: "in lucem produxero," referring to the publication or public revelation of the work</note>—the very work that has already conjured such lies about me, even though no one has yet seen its secrets? However, I do not make much of these babblings, being content with the testimony of my own unburdened conscience. Nevertheless, I do not intend to give occasion for bad suspicion as much as is possible, etc.

From this it clearly appears that he did not intend to publish *Steganography* lest he should confirm the opinion of the common folk by a manifest proof. It does not matter, I say, because it was only the estimation of the unlearned commoners, without reason or foundation—without reason indeed, by which they attribute everything they do not understand to evil arts. He confesses he read the books of magicians, not to imitate them, but to refute and confound their wicked superstitions by arguing against them. This he clearly confirms in the letters to Roger Sicamber <note>original: "Rogerium Sycambrum." Roger of Venray, a fellow monk and close friend of Trithemius</note>, often cited at the end:

> I have decided for the future, if the Most High (who alone can do all things) wills it, to labor upon a work—the greatest of all mine—which will be divided into twelve books. Their subject matter will be: concerning demons, profane arts, and their evil deeds by which they wretchedly deceive the human race. It is my intention to explode and refute all superstitious arts of demons and men with all my strength, and to demonstrate from the very books of the fools who handed them down how exceedingly vain, pernicious, and detestable they are. For such a work seems necessary to me...

He was a man endowed not only with singular genius, sharp judgment, and every kind of learning, but was also exceptionally religious, most tenacious of his regular order <note>Referring to his status as a Benedictine monk and abbot</note>, and most pious toward God and the Saints, as all who have written about his life and deeds confess. Who then, unless they possess either no judgment or a perverse one, would think that he either did not know how to distinguish lawful from unlawful, or natural from superstitious things, or that he wished to thrust perverse and harmful dogmas upon his readers, especially upon princes and his particular friends? Certainly, it is clear from his "Antipalus" <note>Referring to "Antipalus Maleficiorum" (The Enemy of Witchcraft), a work in which Trithemius attacked sorcery</note>, from the "Eight Questions" addressed to Emperor Maximilian I, and from his other works, that he was the sharpest enemy and strongest pursuer of the evil arts. They say he was curious and a lover of new arts and sciences; but he was pious, he was ingenious, he was prudent, and he was most learned. In short, he was held in high esteem by the Princes and all the learned men of his age, who were able to discern good from evil, lawful from unlawful, and natural from superstitious, and who could have detected his perverse doctrines—if he had poured out any—and not only abandoned their high opinion of him, but...*

Thus far Father Schott: <note>Referring to Caspar Schott, the Jesuit scientist who defended Trithemius in the 17th century.</note> and to this judgment of a most learned man, nearly countless apologies and protestations conform—those which Trithemius inserted into his *Steganography*, <term>Steganography: From the Greek for "hidden writing," Trithemius’s system of codes that appeared to many like magic spells.</term> those in various places where he mentions it, and those in his *Eight Questions* to Emperor Maximilian. > "Of all those rashly judging my unknown works, finally the most reckless and unfair estimator of you has burst forth into the open: Charles de Bovelles, a Picard <note>A native of Picardy, France.</note> by nation. When he had traveled through the upper parts of Alsace and come to me at Sponheim <note>Spanheim: The Benedictine abbey where Trithemius served as Abbot.</note> for the sake of hospitality, intending to return to France by way of Trier, I treated him with whatever kindness I could. I provided all the benefits of hospitality with a cheerful face for as long as he was with me. And since, as is common among friends most devoted to literature, I had shown my guest all my things worth seeing, the mentioned work *Steganography* (not yet finished at that time) also presented itself among others. Bovelles saw it, and read it in passing with his mind occupied elsewhere; he said he marveled at the invention and praised it, but he did not care to understand the method. Hence, when he asked for the key to understanding it, he deserved to hear or perceive nothing of those things contained in that study of ours. Having returned to France after this, he returned evil to us for good, and shamefully violated the bond of Christian friendship. For when asked by Lord Germain de Ganay, <note>A high-ranking French cleric and friend to both men.</note> a mutual friend and later Bishop of Orléans, what he had found and seen with me at Sponheim, he wrote back falsehoods instead of truths and lies instead of gratitude, condemning and rashly judging those things which he was not at all able to grasp with his intellect. For believing that the prize of learning should be won through envy and lying, he wrote a letter back to the aforementioned most learned man, full of many falsehoods, lies, injuries, and insults. In this letter, making mention of the *Steganography* which he did not understand, he falsely, lyingly, and most injuriously [claimed] that I was devoted to wicked arts, a Magician <note>original: "Magum"</note>, and a Necromancer <note>original: "Necromanticum"; one who communicates with the dead, a charge of dark magic.</note>..."

# STEGANOGRAPHY

> ,, proclaims with rash presumption. # DEFENSE

<header>->DEFENDED<-</header>
<meta>catchword: None [original: Nullus]</meta>

...[forbidden] <note>original: "titæ," continuing "vetitæ" from the previous page</note> art, but they instead directed it toward a most pure meaning, far removed from any stain of wrongdoing. They defended its innocence and integrity with formal apologies, even if they themselves were not yet able to penetrate the true meaning and the genuine nature of the allegory.

It is proved, thirdly, because no reason can be brought forward by adversaries as to why *Steganography* <term>Steganography: Here referring to Trithemius’s book, which used the names of spirits as a code for secret writing; critics mistook these for actual demonic conjurations.</term> ought to be interpreted in the literal sense which the letter suggests. In fact, it is most appropriately directed toward a tropical <term>Tropical sense: A figurative or metaphorical interpretation of a text.</term> meaning, and this interpretation is expressed by the Author himself in the clearest words, commanded by him, and excused with a formal protestation of his intent. Even the slanderer **Weyer** <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician famous for opposing the burning of witches, who nonetheless initially struggled with Trithemius’s reputation.</note>, cited in the previous chapter, finally noticed this and sang a "palinodia" <note>original: "palinodiam," a poem or statement retracting a previous sentiment; a recantation.</note> in his apology against the slanders of *Leonis Suavius* <note>The pseudonym of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), a French alchemist and scholar.</note>, in these words:

> "You offer me no further testimony to throw in my face / except that of **Agrippa** <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a student of Trithemius who defended his teacher’s occult reputation.</note> in his defense of **Trithemius**. You falsely claim that I raged against him / and that I supposedly scolded and cursed his memory. Because you have written all this against the truth / I shall shove your own words back into your 'lion-throat' <note>original: "Löwen-Hals," likely a pun on the name of his opponent, Leonis Suavius.</note> / and thus make you blush with shame. For otherwise I have not even thought of **Trithemius**; for thus it stands in my other book / Chapter 6: '*Steganography* by **Johannes Trithemius**, Abbot of Sponheim, is mentioned by **Carolus** [Bovillus] with these words,' etc. And later, after the words of **Bovillus** <note>Charles de Bovelles, the original accuser who labeled Trithemius a magician.</note> were recounted / I added: 'Whom **Trithemius** nonetheless accuses of lies and godlessness / as he excuses himself in the preface of the book *Polygraphia* to Emperor **Maximilian**.' If I only added this much / that the matter will be understood differently by those who read it with diligence: does that constitute 'raging,' 'scolding,' and 'cursing' another’s memory?"

Thus indeed **Weyer** acknowledges his error, yet he still tries to twist the opinion he previously declared concerning **Trithemius** against the manifest meaning of the words.

Nor does it stand in the way of this assertion that many very subtle and conscientious men (whom I decline to name) did not admit this explanation of Trithemian *Steganography*, but nonetheless pursued it with the sharpest censures. For I respond that just as blind men are ridiculous when judging colors, so those should be rejected who have dared to judge things they have not understood. For as **Caramuel** <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682), a polymath who was among the first to successfully demonstrate the cryptographic keys to Trithemius’s work.</note> says in the *Conclusion of Steganography Defended*:

### CHAPTER XI.

### SHOULD THE METHOD BY WHICH TRITHEMIUS WROTE *STEGANOGRAPHY* BE CONDEMNED?

I have shown, I believe, that Trithemius’s *Steganography* <term>Steganography: From the Greek "steganos" (hidden) and "graphein" (to write). While today it means hiding data, here it refers specifically to Trithemius’s 1499 book which disguised a system of cryptography as a book of black magic.</term> actually contains nothing of magic or superstition, and that everything presented there under the figures of spirits and conjurations can be reduced to a most exact interpretation. However, because that style of writing—at least—since it was adopted in the likeness and imitation of magical instructions, still suffers great criticism even from the most learned men, I have judged it necessary to undertake this form of defense. Certainly, the already cited **André Thevet** <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a French Franciscan priest and explorer.</note> in his *Eulogy of Johannes Trithemius*, although he otherwise praises Trithemius with the highest honors and regards his incomparable genius, admirable erudition, and the excellence of his writings with the greatest veneration, nevertheless could not restrain himself from breaking out into these words:

> *It would be a superfluous thing to recite here the catalogue of his other books: I only wish to say that he is to be blamed in this, that being too curious about the black and occult sciences of Magic, he wrote in his book, entitled "The Steganography," several superstitious things unworthy of an ecclesiastical man. By this means, he provided material for many—who were looking for any excuse—to mock the Monks, saying that the status of a religious person did not consist of recounting such superstitions and astrological movements. Furthermore, it is thought that he penetrated deeper and had communication with familiar spirits, which I would not wish to approve.* <note>original French: "Seroit chose superflue reciter en ce lieu le catalogue de ses autres livres... ce que je ne voudrois approuver."</note>

And **Caramuel’s** <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682), a Spanish scholastic philosopher and mathematician who studied Trithemius’s codes.</note> address to Trithemius seems to agree with this and possess some weight and foundation; it is found in the commentary on the Prologue of the *Steganography* under the phrase *not without cause*, where he says:

> *Not without cause, my Trithemius, do you place your protestation before this most hidden work, but it is without effect, without fruit, and without utility. For the audacity of ignorant men has reached such a point that, even before your protestation, they would say you were a Necromancer and a Mage, entangled in the miseries of some express or at least implied pact,* <note>A "pact" refers to a diabolical agreement with the devil, a common accusation against Trithemius.</note>

They believed it was teeming with superstitions; leaning on their prior opinion after your protest, they further assert that you are not only a <term>Graphomanticum</term> <note>From the Greek roots for "writing" and "divination"; someone who uses writing for magical or prophetic purposes.</note>, but also a perjurer, and completely alienated from God. In this way, no suspicion of superstition would remain to make your name—otherwise illustrious—hateful. Nor would you have so greatly diminished the authority of your Order <note>The Benedictine Order, to which Trithemius belonged as Abbot of Sponheim.</note>, which is common to you and me at least in substance and appearance, and which was acquired with the greatest labor and praise by so many Martyrs, Confessors, and Virgins over so many years. So that you may know this to be true, you must remember your enemies, who, even while you were alive, sowed the most bitter judgments and injurious opinions against you. Remember the *Apology* which you wrote with great care against **Bovillus** <note>Carolus Bovillus (Charles de Bovelles, c. 1479–1567), a French scholar who visited Trithemius in 1503 and later denounced him as a sorcerer.</note>, who, by your own testimony (in your letter which **Adolphus à Clauburg** published in the <term>Polygraphia</term> <note>Trithemius’s other major work on cryptography, published posthumously in 1518.</note>), saw and read your work in passing. Being occupied with other thoughts, he said he marveled at the invention and praised it, not caring how it might be understood; yet, having returned to France, he returned evil to you for good and basely violated the bond of Christian friendship. When asked by Lord **Germanus de Ganay** <note>Germain de Ganay (d. 1520), a high-ranking French cleric and patron of letters.</note>, a mutual friend and later Bishop of Orléans, what he had found and seen at Sponheim, he wrote back falsehoods for truths and lies instead of love—labeling as a sorcerer the man he should have honored as a benefactor, condemning and rashly judging things he was not capable of comprehending. Nor would I wish you to be unmindful of **Cardano** <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath who criticized Trithemius for being "full of vanity."</note>, who, contradicting himself three times, proclaimed you and your works to be magical, false, and necromantic.

Turn your eyes to the most pious Doctors so that, when you see what the holiest men have written about you, you may not wonder that your name and works are ill-spoken of among men who were either born with fewer titles of modesty or followed a less pious way of speaking.

First among these should be the primary definition, serving as a rule and norm for all others: the edict of the Spanish Inquisition. As it is most pious in all matters (and thus also in its work), it refused to grant that the <term>Steganographic Work</term> was composed by you; instead, judging it a forgery, it prohibited it with these (or similar) words: 

> The *Steganography* which is falsely attributed to **Johannes Trithemius**, a man otherwise [learned], etc., is commanded in its entirety to be committed to the flames.

...they judged; **Pereira**, **Aloysius**, and others believe it was falsely attributed to the holy author. <note>The author is referring to Benedict Pereira (1535–1610) and other theologians who tried to protect Trithemius’s reputation by suggesting he didn't actually write the more "magical" parts of the book.</note>

*“I saw, with his Polygraphia and Stenografia (had he said Steganography, he would have spoken more correctly), the Abbot Trithemius, finally nauseated by the demons for whom, while alive, he seemed to have a constant hunger; he was very angry with **Cardano**, who was across from him, because Cardano had spoken ill of him alone.”* <note>original Spanish: "Vî con su polygraphia, y Estenografia... al Abad Tritemio, harto de demonios, y a que en vida parve, que siempre tubo ambre dellos, muy inojado con Cardano..." Girolamo Cardano was a famous polymath who had criticized Trithemius for vanity.</note>

This means: I saw (I suppose in hell, where Quevedo was at that time) with his *Polygraphia* and *Steganographia* the Abbot Trithemius, finally sickened by the demons for whom, in life, it seems he was plagued by a hunger; he was extremely angry against **Cardano**, who was also there in that region, because Cardano had uniquely attacked him, etc.

Thus **Caramuel** <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682), the likely author of this defense.</note> addresses Trithemius, but he himself in the *Conclusion of the Steganographia* finally responds to this objection, which he also places there in these very terms:

> I confess, nothing is found in the *Steganographia* that is superstitious in reality, but the method appears as such; for he uses the names of spirit-conjurations, as well as names of ruling spirits and their ministers; he even uses nomenclatures which all sound evil, and thus should be deleted rather than corrected.

He responds, however:

> The explanation is evident, because to determine classes and species of spirits and to distribute their locations is not unusual for <term>Glottosophists</term> <note>From the Greek roots for "language wisdom"; scholars who study the hidden structures of speech.</note>. For the Greeks—as the learned know, and if the ignorant do not, how are they to be convinced?—recognize "spirits" even in writing; they distinguish them into classes of "closed" and "soft," and they "conjure" them in determining their placements. <note>In Greek grammar, the marks for breath sounds are called "spirits" (pneumata). The author is cleverly arguing that Trithemius’s "spirits" are just linguistic marks, not actual demons.</note> But neither is the distinction of "spirits" into Kings and ministers unusual in <term>Glottography</term> <note>The study of written language.</note>; because our Trithemius, a scholar of Hebrew <term>Hebræologus</term>, imitating the accents (which are themselves called "spirits" in Hebrew study), distinguished them into "rulers" and "ministers." Thus you may see that the Trithemian way of speaking is neither new nor rare, but is common enough to all grammarians and lovers of language.

# VINDICATA
<note>Latin: "The Vindicated." This refers to the ongoing defense of Trithemius’s reputation.</note>

### L 2

He demonstrated such an obscure, though vastly different, manner of writing—to the wonder of everyone and beyond their understanding—in many places of his **Polygraphia** <note>Trithemius’s 1518 work on cryptography; the title literally means "Many-Writing."</note>, as seen in the Preface of the **Polygraphia** to the Emperor Maximilian near the beginning:

> *That famous Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the prince of mathematicians, according to his own principles, attached a white bird—naked about the head and feet—to a staff cut into the shape of a quadrangle <term>tetrogonus</term>, in a circular fashion. Having arranged his assistants in due proportion, he entrusted the work to the flying instrument, until the image of the white bird appeared changed into a magpie <note>original: "pica"</note>. When this was duly accomplished, he detached it with his own hand; but when he had allowed it to fly away, a great dispute suddenly arose among his inner circle, and soon there arose a first-of-its-kind, overly wandering monster of a twisted monastic image, at the sight of which no one could think what it truly was. Nor did the disagreement of the owls <note>original: "bubonum"</note> rest until the image of the master skillfully banished the magpie with a similar quadrangle.*

Who, even the most ingenious, would have succeeded in seeking out the explanation of this speech, unless he himself had published the key for the sake of Emperor Maximilian? Who would not suspect that something superstitious lay hidden? Yet it is certain that there is none; conversely, no one will be able to apply the key to this obscure speech without the greatest admiration and pleasure.

In many other similar places in the **Polygraphia**, and in others more suited to the **Steganographia** <note>literally "Secret Writing"; this was Trithemius's most controversial work, often accused of being a book of black magic due to its use of "angel" names as keys.</note>, he uses formulas of speech which he afterwards explained most appropriately at a whim: as in the cited place on formerly page 20:

> *There were also those whom celestial harmony taught to compose foreign voices, of which there was a double use for those who understand: while one suspended the sense, the other lifted the mind to the heavens. God can do all things. Many have tried to seek light in the shadow without light, yet they were least able, because the fire lies buried in the ashes. Some practiced painters of masks distinguished one wind into two at a point, one of whom—a hater of wisdom <term>misophos</term>—always hides in the shadows; the other—a lover of wisdom <term>philophos</term>—hates the darkness, loves the light, and guards the secret <term>arcanum</term> with an owl.*

Again, in the index of those things contained in the first book, on page 30:

> *Consequently, we likewise advise the seeker that, as often as a leaf is moved by the wind, he should discern the property of each nature, and compare the night itself to the day by degrees and minutes, and conform the darkness to the light. But if Phoebus <note>A poetic name for the Sun.</note> prejudices the night, or the night prejudices the sun, whereby a confusion of eclipse would arise, either let unity resume the binary which it sent away in the light, or let the shadow of night be reduced to the first line of the sun, etc.*

What else is the wind than the spirit? What are the light and the sun, the shadow and the night, but the secret...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Johannes Trithemius, arguing that his use of demonic imagery was a deliberate psychological barrier designed to protect his cryptographic secrets from the unworthy and the superstitious.</meta>

->STEGANOGRAPHIA<-

...and open? That is, that which is hidden in the **shell** <note>original: "cortice"; literally "bark" or "husk," a common metaphor for the outer, literal meaning of a text hiding a deeper truth</note>, and this, which is found in the common operation of signs.

Therefore, I firmly hold that the manner in which Trithemius wrote his *Steganographia* <note>Trithemius’s most controversial work, which used the names of angels and spirits as a cover for a sophisticated system of cryptography</note> cannot be criticized for any reason. I maintain that all those who have attempted to disprove and carp at it have neither read nor understood the common method of writing used by the most ancient philosophers and wise men, nor have they understood Trithemius’s style, which he demonstrates everywhere in concealing the mysteries of his secrets.

I am also entirely convinced that although Trithemius possessed countless ways of hiding secrets, he chose this one above all others for a specific purpose: just as the horrendous names of spirits, the portentous words of conjurations, and the formidable danger of "erring" usually terrify at first glance, he intended to distinguish the fearful from the steadfast. He wished to separate those worthy of understanding his highest concepts from the unworthy. Those of such scrupulous conscience—who would believe that nothing lay hidden beyond the external sense of the letter—he intended to drive away and repel from the very threshold of this science.

And certainly, such a strategy did not fail him. For I know—indeed, I have known many—for whom the mere name of "spirits" and "conjurations" at first hearing struck such horror that they trembled in their whole body, protected themselves with the sign of the holy cross, and condemned the book to the flames. Nothing is more ridiculous to me than those who attribute no power to words, signs, names, and figures, yet suffer a trembling in all their actions at the mere sound of words like "spirits" and "incantations." 

Let them not, therefore, allow themselves to be driven away at the very threshold by such empty fear. Let them enter further; let them read the preface; let them read the whole *Steganographia*. Let them read it **without irritation** <note>original: "sine stomacho"; literally "without a stomach," meaning without bitterness or anger</note>, and let them be judges without envy. I know they will judge differently; I know they will say that something lies hidden, veiled under the names of spirits and conjurations, even if they cannot immediately penetrate the substance of the matter itself. 

This is excellently stated by **Father Schott** <note>Kaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit mathematician and student of Athanasius Kircher, who worked to "clear" Trithemius's name by explaining the mechanics of his codes</note> in his *Schola Steganographica*, Class 7, Question 4, numbers 4 and 6. Although he admits that the specific contents of each book and chapter in the **Darmstadt edition** <note>A 1606 edition of Trithemius's work</note>—specifically the "conjurations" of spirits composed of barbaric and meaningless words—eluded all his diligence and study in understanding and interpreting them, he nevertheless hit the mark and defended the Author through a general explanation of all the mysteries.

**Objection 1:** You will object that although a certain explanation can be detected and divined from a reading of the general *Steganography* <note>Johannes Trithemius’s 1499 work, which masked cryptographic methods under the guise of spirit summoning</note>, many people have nonetheless not attained it. Instead, they understood everything according to the literal sense and truly believed that by the recitation of conjurations, spirits are forced to appear, receive commands, and execute all tasks, just as they are so splendidly described in that book. Thus, they took the opportunity—driven by a superstitious opinion and the hope of the promised effect—to read these conjurations and wait for spirits to appear.

**I respond:** A sword is a good tool; it is also put to good use whenever it is carried for defense without injury to one’s neighbor. But if it is wrongly used to cause injury to anyone through abuse, a good thing is turned into an evil one. He who is good does not abuse a good thing for evil; rather, if he is able, he converts evil into good. And there is nothing in the world so good and holy that the wicked <note>original: "reprobi"</note> do not frequently abuse it for evil purposes.

**But you insist:** A sword is a neutral <note>original: "indifferens"; in philosophy, a thing that is neither inherently good nor evil but depends on its use</note> instrument and was invented more for protection and one's own defense than for the injury of another; just as war was introduced by the <term>Law of Nations</term> <note>original: "Jure Gentium"; the legal concepts common to all humanity</note> for the defense of the fatherland. However, the method of *Steganography*—using spirits and their conjurations—is plainly based on magical and forbidden principles which cannot be adopted for good. Even if they could, one must not do evil so that good may result. Therefore, there is a great difference, and it is no wonder if *Steganography* is interpreted as evil at first glance.

**Response 1:** Regarding the comparison: by its very nature and use, a sword is intended to cause injury. If it did not intend this, it would not be so sharp; it would be blunt, like the practice swords used in fencing schools. Thus, a sword is a "worse" instrument in its essence than the method of *Steganography*. **Response 2:** All those terms—*Spirits*, *conjuration*, etc.—are in themselves neutral. The fact that they have been adopted by many into magical teachings does not prevent them from also being adopted into a good system of learning.

**Objection 2:** This is the objection Trithemius himself raises at the end of the Preface to the *Clavis Steganographiae* <note>The "Key to Steganography," Trithemius's explanatory manual</note>: *“But someone might object to me, saying: If you wanted this science of yours to be hidden, why did you wish to commit it to writing?”* But continue reading Trithemius’s own response: *“To this man, if I must respond, I say: Because I neither ought to, nor* <insert>could</insert> *hide this science from the best of Princes...”* <note>Trithemius dedicated his work to Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine; he argues that knowledge must be preserved for worthy rulers even if it remains hidden from the public</note>

### CHAPTER XII.

## WHETHER TRITHEMIUS’S STEGANOGRAPHY COULD HAVE BEEN JUSTLY FORBIDDEN.

Caramuel <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682), a Spanish bishop and mathematician who defended Trithemius.</note> also proposes this question in specific terms in his *Steganography Vindicated* <note>original: "Steganogr. For some argue in this way: A work that is falsely attributed to Trithemius was forbidden; but, as we have seen, the Darmstadt edition <note>The 1606 edition published in Darmstadt, which Caramuel defended as the authentic text.</note> is not falsely attributed to him, but is his true *Steganography*; therefore, that edition was not forbidden.

**Response 1.** It is not necessary to concede the premise: that it was ever forbidden. For the words only suggest the question of whether, before the publication of the present *Steganography Vindicated and Revealed*, it *could* have been forbidden by anyone. For I am certain and confident that after the publication of this work, it will no longer be subject to any censure.

**Response 2.** Even conceding the premise, and that it was forbidden by the Spanish Inquisition <note>original: "Inquisitione Hispanica"</note> (which is Caramuel’s view), I say that it does not matter to me whether this or another edition, true or spurious, suffered the sentence of the Inquisition.

I. That the book is condemned because it is evil, and consequently it is believed to be spurious.
II. That the book is forbidden because it is spurious, and consequently, with other appearances joined in judgment—

### P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' within a square frame featuring ornate floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>Until now, I have kept the curious reader waiting, and I have delayed the world’s eager expectation—though perhaps not entirely necessarily. Therefore, I am glad to have reached this point, where I can and will assert Trithemius’s innocence and the purity of his *Steganography*, not only with probable arguments and presumptions drawn from Trithemius’s piety; not by testimonies so recent that they might suffer from a lack of understanding of the *Steganography* or be accused of bias; but by the thing itself, by the *Steganography* itself—I mean its explanation—which is so clear and easy that even to one moderately learned, or indeed even to one who knows only how to read Latin letters besides his mother tongue, German <note>original: "Teutonicam"</note>, the whole difficulty will be revealed to the eye at first glance. ### CARAMUEL’S *STEGANOGRAPHY VINDICATED* IS EXAMINED.

Juan de Caramuel, <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682) was a Spanish Cistercian monk and polymath. He was one of the first to attempt a public mathematical and logical defense of Trithemius.</note> a Cistercian Monk and public Professor of Sacred Theology, published a book in Cologne forty years ago, to which he prefixed the following title: *A genuine, easy, and clear declaration of the Steganography, as well as the Little Key of Solomon, by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim of the Order of Saint Benedict (which, understood by no one until now, have been condemned by many and branded with the mark of necromancy).* This is surely a work believed impossible by the ungodly until now; much desired by the more saintly, who venerate the character, life, and writings of Trithemius; most rich in secrets for theorists of the Cabala <note>In this context, "Cabalea doctrina" refers to the Christian interpretation of Jewish mystical traditions, often associated with hidden meanings in text.</note>; and eternally necessary for Doctors, Theologians, Commentators, experts in Hebrew wisdom, Latinists, students of human curiosity, Kings, Princes, and all who occupy positions of literary or fortunate eminence. A grand title! If the result matches it, I will bid farewell to my own labor (whatever it may be) right at the threshold, and it would be necessary for me to pour myself out fully in praise of Caramuel instead of my own *Steganography Unlocked*. Therefore, I judged it necessary to place this present examination at the beginning of this work so that, if it appears that Caramuel's key is true and genuine, I may be permitted to escape the great difficulty of this work by simply admiring his; or, if it happens that Caramuel's key is not legitimate, and does not unlock Trithemius’s *Steganography* as desired, I too may deserve an excuse if the result [of my proposal]...

For this first book, he assigns two general keys: the first for the first 16 chapters, and the remaining one for the rest. I understand the first key as follows:

*First:* He increases the ordinary letters of the Latin Alphabet to 32, which is specifically double the number of the chapters, winds, and spirits. He does this by adding various signs, abbreviations, and ancient, German, and Spanish letters in this manner:
A b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z
& æ œ ę ç † or 9.

*Second:* To each wind, of which there are 16, he attributes two letters in order; he begins from the east, and assigns to it † and a. To the <term>subsolanus</term> <note>The Latin name for the wind blowing from the direction of the rising sun; the east wind.</note> he assigns b and c, and so on consecutively.

*Third:* In place of the 16 spirits, he sets down sixteen different alphabets, produced by an ordered <term>metathesis</term> <note>A mathematical shifting or transposition of letters in an alphabet, a common technique in cryptography.</note> of the letters placed above. Thus, the power of the letters is varied just as many times; and since there are 32 letters and 16 spirits, each individual alphabet skips two letters in order and value. Three examples demonstrate the matter:

Fourth: Therefore, when one intends to announce a secret to some friend, which might be, for example: *I wish to besiege Strasburg, be in the said woods* <note>original: *Volo obsidere Strasburg sis in dicta sylvâ*</note>, he transforms all these letters of the secret into others according to the arrangement of the Pamerficlis Alphabet <note>A specific cipher method named by Caramuel; this is a simple Caesar shift where 'A' represents 'e'.</note>; the said sentence will thus stand animated as: *U n k n narhcdqd rsqtratqf rhr hm rxkut chbst.*

Fifth: On the occasion of the number 36—the square corresponding precisely to the number of letters of the Holy Cross <note>The "Holy Cross" likely refers to a specific 36-letter prayer or a 6x6 cryptographic grid used as a master key.</note>—he makes yet another transformation of the letters of the secret to be announced in many places. For he arranges the letters of the mystical sense into a square, and commits them to the four Universal Ministers; Ebra, Sotheani, Abrulcha, and Rasbiel. The first of these is interpreted as "the one passing or leading through," that is, **direction** [reading forward]; the second, "the slope of the camps," that is, **descent** [reading downwards]; the third, "the passing and ascending arrow," that is, **ascent** [reading upwards]; the fourth, "the runner retreating in fear," that is, **regression** [reading backwards]. The matter will be made clear by an example, using this sentence: *May Claudia and Leopold live, may they conquer and triumph* <note>original: *Vivat Claudia Leopoldus, vincat triumphet*</note>. Since it contains exactly 36 letters, it is arranged into a square in this manner:

| V | I | V | A | T | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L | A | V | D | I | A |
| L | E | O | P | O | L |
| D | U | S | V | I | N |
| C | A | T | T | R | I |
| U | M | P | H | E | T |

This sentence, thus arranged, can be read and written in four ways:
1. By **Ebra**, that is, directly from V towards C, and thus it is read: *Vivat Claudia Leopoldus vincat triumphet.*
2. By **Sothean**, that is, by descending from V towards U, and thus it is read: *Vlldcu iaeuam Vvostpadp vthtio irecalnit.* <note>This is read by following the columns from top to bottom, starting with the first column: V-L-L-D-C-U, then I-A-E-U-A-M, etc.</note>
3. By **Abrulcha**, that is, by ascent, and thus it will stand:

**Seventhly:** To make the reading even more difficult, he does not begin to accent the letters from the first word, but according to an intricate, yet regulated system. This varies based on the diversity of <term>pilorums</term> <note>These are technical time-units or intervals specific to Trithemius's system, used to determine the spacing of the hidden message.</note>, half-pilorums, double-pilorums, triple-pilorums, quadruple-pilorums, and those categorized as daily, midday, evening, or midnight intervals, etc., as he explains at length in the final chapter. In the first chapter, he sets out a fourfold difference: for he begins either from the ten-thousandth word of the Letter (understanding that the letter is repeated several times), or from the thousandth, the hundredth, or the very last. In the current example, he began from the hundredth word.

**Eighthly:** At the end of the "open" Letter <note>The visible message, such as the prayer above.</note>, he places certain signs: the first for the **Principal Spirit**, the second for the **Universal Minister** to whom the Letter is entrusted, and the third to mark the specific word from which the accenting began. Then, he transmits the letters to his friend without danger of discovery. Then—

**Ninthly:** The person receiving the letter looks at the sign for the starting word, identifies the accented letters, and places those noted letters into a square according to the sign of the Universal Minister. Once arranged in this way, he applies them to the alphabet of the Principal Spirit and understands the secret.

Up to this point, I have explained the key of Caramuel <note>Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz (1606–1682), a Spanish polymath who defended the monk Johannes Trithemius against charges of magic by claiming his "demonic" spells were actually complex ciphers.</note>; now I will say briefly what should be thought of it. I state first: Caramuel’s defended <term>Steganography<note>The practice of concealing a secret message within an ordinary-looking text or physical object.</note></term> is most ingenious and subtle, and letters written in that manner can be understood by no mortal, nor can the secret lying hidden under them be extracted. Let the reader explore the truth by experiment, but let him first see how great the difficulty is—even when the key is known—to come to a knowledge of the hidden secret of any letter, and then let him judge what he might find if the key were unknown. But, since nothing is blessed in every part, it suffers from two defects: first, that the methods of writing secretly are too intricate and difficult, and it is not right to entangle Kings and Princes (whom the immense care of a kingdom sufficiently fatigues) in such great obscurities when far easier methods are available. Second, these methods are not without suspicion; for it is not customary for those writing in Latin to mark vowels with an accent; therefore, since it is something new, it generates suspicion immediately, and the letter will not reach its intended destination.

I state second: Caramuel can persuade no one based on any foundation that this Steganography of his is the true key to Trithemius. 1. For he cannot know whether the explanation he provides for certain <term>incantations<note>The original text uses "conjurationum," referring to the passages in Trithemius’s book that look like spells to summon demons but which Caramuel claims are ciphers.</note></term> is legitimate, for he brings forward no reason, no derivation, and no principle for understanding and explaining them; instead, he only twists some of their words into a Latin sense by distorting <note>original: "corrumpendo"</note> them from Hebrew or Greek. 2. Caramuel cannot know that the incantations of chapter eight and following are without a key, as he says in that same place—namely, because, as he says, they are unexplainable and placed there only for the sake of ornament. I can indeed easily admit that they are unexplainable to *him*, but that they were placed there only for ornament ought to be proven, not merely asserted; for it is not probable that they were placed there by Trithemius in vain. 3. He can provide no reason why the letters or prayer formulas ought to be explained according to his meaning, since he assumed the secret sense and the starting point of the signaling at his own whim, and those same letters could be twisted into infinite other such meanings. 4. He can bring forward no consistent reason why Trithemius would have assumed 32 letters of the alphabet, especially since they are so...

**I state III:** Caramuel’s *Steganography Defended* <note>referring to *Steganographia vindicata* (1670) by Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz.</note> is in no way the key to Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Benedictine abbot whose work on steganography was long suspected of being black magic.</note>, nor does it reach the mind of Trithemius even from afar. Father **Caspar Schott** <note>A Jesuit mathematician (1608–1666) who published extensively on cryptography and technology.</note> feels the same as I do; although he did not know the true key himself, he clearly recognized that Caramuel’s key was anything but genuine. I prove my opinion thus:

1.) The methods of writing secretly, which Trithemius promised he would hand down, must be without any suspicion; but Caramuel's methods are by no means so, as we have seen; therefore they are not the <term>Steganography<note>The art of hidden writing. Trithemius’s book appeared to be a grimoire of spirit conjuration, but was actually a system for hiding messages.</note></term> of Trithemius, nor the key. 

**I prove it II:** Trithemius’s Steganography applies only one simple sign to the letters, by which, once known, the recipient can come to the knowledge of the spirit <note>In this context, the "spirit" refers to the hidden meaning or the governing rule of the cipher.</note>; but Caramuel assumes three, therefore they do not agree with each other, nor can the key be genuine. 

**I prove it III:** Caramuel explains no conjuration, in which, however, the whole force of Steganography consists, and which alone branded the Author and the book with the mark of superstition; and thus he does not fulfill what he so splendidly promises both in the title and in the letters to **Lord Andreas de Herrera** in *Steganography Defended*, page 104; therefore he satisfies neither himself, nor Trithemius, nor us.

But why have I been so long? I could have hurried to the *Steganography Revealed* <note>original: "Steganographiam Referatam." This is likely the title of the author's own work or section.</note>, and by the actual entry into the Steganography—hitherto held to be inaccessible—demonstrate both the truth of my key and exclude the vanity of Caramuel’s. Therefore, I invite you, benevolent Reader: please take up the general key in the following chapters; please attempt the entrance; if an obstacle is found, the special key will remove it. I only ask that, once the entrance into Steganography is opened, you regard this labor of mine, such as it is, with fairness and kindness, and not believe that you would have entered before me.

### CHAPTER II.

# THE KEY TO THE FIRST BOOK OF TRITHEMIUS'S STEGANOGRAPHY IS REVEALED.

Father Schott <note>Caspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and mathematician who was fascinated by Trithemius's work.</note> painted a shadow in the darkness excellently, and did not stray far from the truth, when he explained the principal Trithemian "spirits" as general steganographic modes, the "inferior spirits" as leaders and counts representing special modes, and the "conjurations" as rules, and so forth. For indeed, the matter stands thus. Therefore, the thirty-one chapters of the first book contain just as many general modes of secret writing, exactly as Trithemius promised in his letters to Arnold Bostius <note>A Carmelite monk and friend to whom Trithemius revealed that his book was not about magic, but secret communication.</note>. All of these modes consist in this: that a letter or a prayer formula is so constructed that the initial letters of all or of certain specific words, when joined together according to a regular prescribed order, yield the secret meaning <note>original: *arcanum*</note> which I intend to signify to a friend. The matter is clear, yet it is pleasing to make it clearer with an example: The following prayer formula is so arranged that the first letters of the first, third, fifth, and so on—every alternating word from the beginning to the end—when joined together (with the punctuation marks separated), reveal the secret sense to the reader.

> *Lover of human salvation, greatest Creator of all, imposes upon us obedience to his commandments, to whom we are all bound to obey out of love; indeed, he has promised the tabernacle of eternal happiness to those who are obedient; let us look upon the obedience of Christ, which let us strive to imitate, so that we may deserve to enter into the eternal happiness promised to us, and to be joined to the eternal dwellings of the angels: let us perform penance while we can, spending our precious time fruitfully; let us beware lest death snatch us unawares, which refuses to grant delay to anyone. Therefore, brothers, do not delay to perform penance, for quickly death will come to you, which none of you can long evade. Therefore, look upon your passing days, beginning penance while you have time; the hour of departing hence approaches; O death, most terrible of terrible things, how quickly you consume us wretches, and make our shortest sojourn, full of many injuries, cruel to the wretched. Let us wretches wake up, with Christ Jesus our most pious Savior exhorting and attesting to us that we should rebuke shameful negligences and, with good works, solicitously guard the ways of justice. Nourishing Redeemer of the human race, hear us and grant us pardon for our sins. O Father of mercy, be favorable to us in all our adversities.*

> Heal, O Lord, our weak souls, for we are Yours; grant to us afflicted worms the rest of eternal pleasantness, so that, by always looking upon You, we may praise You. If, in this prayer formula, the initial letters of the alternating words are written separately and divided into words, this sentence will emerge: **"Tonight after 12:00 I will come to you near the door that leads to the garden; wait for me there; see to it that all things are prepared."** <note>original: "Hac nocte post XII. veniam ad te circa januam quæ ducit ad ortum, ibi me expectabis, age ut omnia sint parata." The prayer provided above actually spells out the final two words: S-I-N-T P-A-R-A-T-A.</note> The logic is the same for all other modes in this first book, at least regarding the general principle of initial letters. However, alternating letters are not used in every case; rather, their variations can diverge into almost infinite types. Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Benedictine abbot and polymath whose work on "Steganography" was long feared as a manual of black magic.</note> describes thirty variations in this book, leaving the rest to the diligence and curiosity of the ingenious reader. I set before your eyes the Trithemian modes in the order of the chapters.

The **First Mode** uses the initial letters of every word as significant. It should be noted—so that it is not necessary to constantly repeat "initial letters" in this description—that I shall call words either "significant" or "idle" <note>original: "significativas aut otiosas"</note> depending on whether their initial letters serve the secret <term>arcanum|A hidden or secret mystery; in this context, the encrypted message.</term> or are empty of it. 

The **Second Mode** uses the first word as significant and the second as idle throughout. 

The **Third Mode** uses the first word as idle and the second as significant. 

The **Fourth Mode** uses the first word as idle and follows it with two significant words. 

The **Fifth Mode**, similar to the fourth, uses one vacant word and follows it with two functioning ones; it concludes each word of the secret message with as many idle words as there are letters remaining at the end of that word. 

The **Sixth Mode** follows two idle words with two significant ones. 

The **Seventh Mode**, similar to the sixth, proceeds by two vacant and two functioning words, and concludes each word with as many idle ones as are found at the end of the letter. 

The **Eighth Mode** proceeds by alternating three vacant and three significant words. 

The **Ninth Mode** is similar to the eighth, but concludes each mystical word with as many idle ones as there are letters at the end. 

The **Tenth Mode** begins with four idle words and proceeds by alternating with four significant ones. 

The **Eleventh Mode** is similar to the tenth, but concludes each mystical word according to the custom of the ninth. 

The **Twelfth Mode** first takes five vacant words and follows them with five significant ones. 

The **Thirteenth Mode** is similar to the twelfth, but concludes the mystical words as in the eleventh. 

The **Fourteenth Mode** begins with a vacant word and proceeds through the significant—

The **Fifteenth Mode** places one significant word at the beginning, follows it with one idle word, then two alternating words, then three, and so on up to eight; furthermore, from eight it descends again through seven, six, etc., down to one, and then ascends and descends again as long as necessary. The **Sixteenth Mode** is entirely similar to the previous one, except that it begins with an idle word just as the other began with a significant one. The **Seventeenth Mode** makes the entire first line idle, then one word is empty and three are significant. The **Eighteenth Mode** receives two idle lines, then two words are empty and four words are significant, alternating.
