### STEGANOGRAPHY

*Let us form for ourselves, for the sake of example, a secret of the kind that must be entrusted to no one.*

I have a certain secret for my Prince which is to be shared with absolutely no one. I do not dare to commit it to writing in the usual way, lest through negligence or forgetfulness the discarded pages be read; much less do I wish to announce it through a human messenger, lest it happens that it be revealed to others by him in some manner. Therefore, I choose to attempt the mystery of this art, through which my secret will remain hidden for all time. Let us write a letter, of whatever kind we please, which fears no man’s gaze <note>The strategy here is "hiding in plain sight"—writing a message that looks like an innocent, albeit formal, letter of greeting.</note>.

->To the Most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine,<-
->Duke of Bavaria, Arch-Steward <note>original: "Archidapifero," a high ceremonial office held by the Electors of the Palatinate.</note> of the Holy Roman Empire, Prince Elector,<-
->*Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, with prayers and service.*<-

*Most Illustrious Prince, with humble submission and service. The kindness of your Renowned Duchy has commanded me to commit to writing certain most occult matters expressed in words. I would rejoice, not without devout exultation, if strengths equal to my will were to be added, to assign a most honorable and suitable place for the benefits shown, and to humbly offer the service due to your grace. The novelty of the work to be undertaken—without a preceding path—detains the weakness of my heart, a task for which I know I am far from equal. For it will involve immense and great labor, and it strikes much sluggishness into my attempts; nevertheless, I shall try my strength, being about to obey your grace. I shall approach a most kind judge, no doubt, if the desired possibility of completing it is not present for my good will, where, with the most abundant humanity, the Glorious and Most Magnificent Prince, lover and defender of letters, gives his judgment. Under his most humane protection, the University of Heidelberg, adorned with many most learned and erudite men of the most recent genius, transcends all the schools throughout Germany <note>original: "Alemanniam"</note>. Therefore, Most Illustrious and Most Humane Prince, if I have anything or am anything, I know I owe it all to your kindness, which I shall always take care to show most promptly with humble submission. And although there may be others wiser who could have rendered this work better or more usefully or more elegantly in no small measure, I nevertheless wished to show my most devoted, upright, and joyful mind toward your grace in some way, and to experiment with newly discovered great things, which I believe no other has found. Given on the 16th day before the Kalends of April <note>March 17th</note> in the year of our Lord one thousand five hundred, etc.*

Upon receiving this letter, or any other like it, the person to whom it is sent—provided he is skilled in the art—understands it to be within the "character of Armadiel." Once this is known, let him turn himself to wherever the art commands him to turn, and speak the charm <note>In the context of Trithemius’s "magic," the "charm" or "carmen" is often a mnemonic key or a specific instruction for extracting the hidden letters from the text.</note>.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->THE CHIEF AND SUPREME SPIRIT OF THIS CHAPTER IS CALLED CARNESIEL, WHO DWELLS IN THE EAST, HAVING UNDER HIM MANY DUKES AND PRINCES WITH THEIR SERVANTS, WHOSE OFFICE IT IS TO REPORT ALL THINGS THAT ARE SENT TOWARD THE EAST.<-

Since there are so many human affairs, and even more may arise, for which no prince or spirit has been specifically assigned in the previously mentioned ranks <note>referring to the "mansions" or levels of the spiritual hierarchy described in earlier chapters</note> to communicate secrets to distant friends, we do not want those practicing this art of <term>Steganography</term> <note>Hidden writing or cryptography</note> to encounter any difficulty in perfecting their work. Therefore, after having mentioned certain specific spirits who preside over specific secrets, we also wish to describe certain general princes of spirits for announcing general matters. 

Thus, if something happens to occur that someone needs to report, for which no specific assignment is found in the previously mentioned ranks, it may be referred to these spirits, who in their own way have authority over all things. However, this is done so that the general nature of their office does not take away from the specific spirits, nor should a specific secret that is not clearly defined refuse the service of the general office. 

There are, therefore, four great princes who, with their dukes and under-servants, preside over all secrets to be reported that were not mentioned above. The first of these, **Carnesiel**, presides over all things that we wish to send toward the East; **Caspiel** toward the South, **Amenadiel** toward the West, and **Demoriel** over those things sent generally toward the North. When, therefore, you wish to report some secret through a spirit to a friend far away in the East, call one or more—as many as you wish—from the princes of Carnesiel, turning yourself during the whole operation toward the eastern region, as you have learned according to the art. I shall describe for you the names of the princes with the number of servants, as many as suffice for the present business: and take care that you do not err in anything.

### *The Key.*

In the 17th mode, the entire first line of letters or narrative is void of secret intent; then, after one word is skipped, three words are significant; then again one word is idle and three others contribute to the secret, and so it proceeds to the end. This can be easily gathered from the numbers you see attached to the spirits. <note>Trithemius is explaining a cryptographic "grille" or pattern. To the casual observer, the text looks like magic; to the initiated, it is a code where only specific words are read to reveal the true message.</note>

### Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, Theologian, Poet, and most eloquent Orator

->Greetings.<-

*I would greatly desire, Jakob Wimpfeling, that you would finally satisfy, even if late, your promise and my expectation of you; you are not ignorant of what you promised and what I expect. I do not desire you to be a monk, but to live with monks;*
hurry, let us live together likewise. Behold, the Hour of Our Passing Draws Near, Greatly to be Feared. Why then do we delay? Why do we unhappy ones neglect the Brief and Sorrowful State of Our Dwelling here? Why do we Refuse to perform penance for our Faults and Excesses in this Time of Salvation? Let us prepare ourselves for death, since it Hastens Quite Terribly, it Calls All the Reprobate, it spares no one, it respects no one, it Denies an Audience to those who Pray, it Despises the Tears of the Exiles, and it looks down upon the threats of princes; it Wipes Out the Names and Glory of kings and the Pride of Tyrants. O how it empties out the weak; therefore, brother, let us repay the Benefits of the Redeemer Shown to us, which are Very Useful, by sedulously thinking on them. By Amending our Guilt and Continually Shining with Good Morals, so that we may be able to appease the Strict Examination of the Judge as he Hastens to the Seat of judgment, who will Show Himself Terribly to the Rejected, but Joyfully to the Elect. Farewell. From Sponheim, the fifteenth of the Kalends of April <note>March 18th</note>, in the year of our Lord 1500. <meta>τ-like mark</meta>

## CHAPTER XXI.

### WHOSE SUPREME EMPEROR AND PRINCE IS CALLED GERADIEL, WHO DWELLS IN NO SPECIFIC REGION OF THE WORLD, BUT IS ACCUSTOMED TO BE PRESENT EVERYWHERE AS A WANDERER.

Beyond those Emperors, Princes, and Dukes of the spirits whom we have named in the previous chapters—those who reside in fixed places throughout the visible world—there are also many others assigned who are wandering, unstable, and staying in no fixed place. The ancient sages and <term>magi</term> <note>Wise men or practitioners of high magic.</note> called these *astatos*, <note>original Greek: ἀστάτους</note> that is, "the unstable ones," because they fly through the air like flies, without order, without a fixed home, and without restriction. 

Among these are several who are not useless to us for Steganography, because they do not require the observation of specific locations; rather, they can be summoned by conjuration in any place. The first of these is called **Geradiel**. He does not have any duke or prince under him, but only many and nearly innumerable servants. He takes these into his service according to the orders they hold among themselves and according to the 24 hours of the day and night. Their general duty is to announce whatever secrets you wish, to whichever region you desire.

In this table, you have the 18,150 ministers and servants of the great prince Geradiel, numbered and arranged in their proper order according to the hours. You should recognize that their arrangement and accounting are entirely necessary for the operation of <term>Steganography</term> <note>literally "hidden writing"; Trithemius's system of using spirit names as a cover for cryptography</note>, so that you may know with how many servants they are accustomed to come at any given hour, or how the prince himself is not accustomed to come, but rather the servants assigned to that hour. I advise you, however, that in your operations, you should take care to observe the hour in which the prince himself comes personally with the servants of that same hour; otherwise, in the absence of their commander, they are not always willing to obey the practitioner in all things. Therefore, when you wish to operate through this prince, after performing the necessary preliminaries, speak the conjuration.

### Key.

In the 21st mode, the letters of each mystical word are arranged so that the second is placed first, then the first, followed by the fourth, then the third, then the sixth, then the fifth, and so on. For example, the word **Peter** <note>original: "petrus"</note> would be arranged as **eprt su**. Once this is done, the individual words of the narrative or Letter are ordered so that their first letters yield the letters of the mystical words arranged in this manner. This is clearly seen from the numbers of the servant spirits, all of whom you will find arranged in that way.

### Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, offers this work to all the learned and curious who read this art without a teacher.

*Amend your lives fundamentally. ### CHAPTER XXII.

After Geradiel follows Buriel, a great prince indeed, but perverse and wicked, who hates, pursues, and detests all other spirits—and especially the princes. He has under him dukes and princes whom he is accustomed to send into service with their servants and attendants, the multitude of whom is nearly innumerable. ## CHAPTER XXIII.

### WHOSE SPIRIT AND SUPREME PRINCE IS CALLED HYDRIEL, AND HE DWELLS IN THE WATERS: HAVING UNDER HIM 100 DUKES, 200 COUNTS, AND NEARLY INNUMERABLE SERVANTS.

There is another among the principal spirits, a prince who is called Hydriel, and he dwells in waters, pools, lakes, marshes, and the sea, and around springs, cisterns, and rivers; having under his dominion at least 100 dukes or princes, 200 counts or sub-princes, and many servants. The duty of these spirits is generally to report all things, whether through water or through land, whether it be by day or by night. And you should know that these princes are quite benevolent and willing in all matters, but they do not appear as such when they are summoned by oath <note>Latin: *conjurati*; referring to spirits compelled by ritual magic</note>. For they frequently appear in the form of a serpent—sometimes a small one—having a very beautiful maiden’s head with flowing hair. None of them travels alone, but every prince brings with him at least two counts and 80 servants; however, so that you do not fall into error during the operation, I will list the names of some of the dukes for you.

# CHAPTER 24.

## WHOSE PRINCE IS CALLED PYRICHIEL, HAVING UNDER HIM MANY COUNTS AND SERVANTS, THE NUMBER OF WHOM IS UNCERTAIN.

Pyrichiel, a certain supreme prince of spirits, does not seem to us, according to our art, to be entirely rejected, because he is considered to be quite benevolent. He does not have dukes or princes under him in the manner of the others, but only counts and servants, whose number is uncertain. There are those who say that he has dukes and princes under him, but they seem to us not to sufficiently understand his nature and custom, as they have dreamed up counts and servants to be dukes. The name of Pyrichiel is derived from the word for "fire" <note>The name stems from the Greek "pyr" (fire), as noted by the author's reference to the spirit's affinity for the element.</note>; because he is frequently accustomed to dwell around fire.

### CHAPTER XXV.

### Key.

**Method 25.** This method receives one idle letter at the end and places two signifying letters alternatively; this is easily gathered from the number added to the spirits. <note>Trithemius is explaining a cryptographic rule where certain letters in a sequence are "nulls" (idle) while others carry the actual message.</note>

aPrOySiThUlNeArMeVeArCrAlNoTiElMaVyArLiElNeTy

## CHAPTER 29.

### WHOSE SUPREME PRINCE IS CALLED MACARIEL, HAVING UNDER HIS COMMAND LEADERS, PRINCES, COUNTS, AND NUMEROUS SERVANTS ASSIGNED TO VARIOUS MINISTRIES.

Macariel is also one of the supreme spirits who preside over the operations of <term>Steganography</term><note>Trithemius’s term for "hidden writing," which we now call cryptography. He frames these methods as the work of "spirits" to add an air of mystery or to provide a mnemonic structure.</note>; we must not omit him along with his princes and servants, because he is sufficiently useful, prompt, and faithful for all things whatsoever we may desire. He has 40 princes, of whom no fewer than four are ever sent into service: specifically, three leaders and one count with many servants. They observe this order among themselves: by turns, one of the leaders always performs the office of count, according to the four parts of the year. It is necessary for the operator to have full knowledge of all these. But now, let us name some of these princes who will be abundantly sufficient for the operation of our Steganography.

->Key.<-

Just as in the method immediately preceding, the path is run three times from the end toward the beginning; here, however, four runs are made. Always after one "valid" word <note>A "valid" word is one containing a letter of the secret message.</note>, three "vacant" <note>A "vacant" word is a filler word used to disguise the message.</note> ones follow (just as there were two there). And just as in that method one begins from the first word, so here the first run begins from the fourth, the second from the third, and so on.

**Macariel myrno chamerosy purmy maresyn ameos peanam olradu chabor ianoes fabelron dearsy chadon vlyses ; Almos rutiel pedaron deabry madero neas**

The Governor of a King or Prince, stationed in a land or province, has understood through a most secret report that enemies intend to break into the province shortly. He wishes to advise the Prince, but cannot do so through messengers, because they would be tortured by the adversaries on the road to make them surrender the secret; nor can he send letters, because they are all opened by the enemy. He wrote, however, explaining our faith in volumes to be honored. Moreover, he had a wife, a jealous lover of our religion, noble in humility and innocence, a glory in her chastity. ## *Let the letters be as you please, fearing nothing.*

Begin, most beloved brothers, to amend your negligence, wiping away past sins with constant tears, praying to the Savior of all living things in the time that remains. <note>original: "Incipite Fratres Dilectissimi..." This entire paragraph is a "carrier text." Give life to those who mourn, O glorious Life-giver. You will not despise men in exile. Hear us, most weak and humble, in the terrible hour of death; grant pleasant light, Consoler of all and Guide of the humble. In the year 1500, on the 7th of the Calends of April [March 26], I, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, wrote this. ☿. ☿. <note>The symbol ☿ represents Mercury, often used in this context to signal communication or the "spirit" of the message.</note>

### WHOSE SUPREME PRINCE IS CALLED BYDIEL, HAVING UNDER HIS DOMAIN 20 DUKES, AND 200 COUNTS; THE NUMBER OF HIS SERVANTS IS UNCERTAIN, BUT THEY ARE VERY MANY.

There still remains one of the supreme spirits assigned to us for the work of Steganography <note>Steganography here refers to "secret writing," the title and subject of the book.</note>: the last indeed in order, but equal to the first in dignity: whose name, by reason of his office, is called **Bydiel**, having under his command 20 dukes, 200 counts or sub-dukes, and many attendants and servants. When, therefore, you wish to work through these spirits in this art, having first performed the necessary preliminaries, say the conjuration.

->The Key.<-

Finally, the 31st and last method of the present book takes two vacant [letters] <note>meaning "null" or "filler" letters that carry no meaning</note> from the beginning and receives two significant [letters] alternately; when the end is reached, starting again from the beginning toward the end, those letters which were previously idle now serve in secret. <note>Trithemius is describing a transposition or skip-cipher where the message is hidden by alternating between meaningful and meaningless letters, then reversing or repeating the process.</note>

->Conjuration 1.<-

> Bydiel marchan chamerosi philtres maduse vear casmyron eralnoti pean deuoon fabelros eltida camean ueor, oniel vear thyrso liernoti ianos prolsato chanos elasry peanon elsathas melros notiél pen foes probys chyras lasbroy mauear iothan liernoti chrymarson. <note>While this looks like a magical incantation, it is actually the "carrier text" for the cipher described in the Key above. To the uninitiated, it appears to be a list of "barbarous names" used in ritual magic.</note>

### Key & Meaning.

mArcHAnPhItTrEsVeArCrAlNoTiDeUoOnElTiDaVeOr VeArLiErNoTiPrOlSaToElAsRyElSaThAsNoTiElSoEsChYrAs MaVeArLiErNoTi. *Meaning.* From the beginning, two are discarded and two are valid; thereafter, those remaining are also valid. <note>original: "A capite vacant duo & duo valent postea restantes etiam valent." This is a cryptographic instruction: ignore the first two letters of a word, take the next two, and so on.</note>

Once the song has been recited as required, the summoned spirits will immediately appear in visible form, walking gracefully and leading one another by the hand like friends; they will be well-disposed toward you and obedient in all things.

->*Let my secret be of whatever kind it may be.*<-

My secret is that I desire to know of a friend far absent, which is a matter of great secrecy: it concerns a hidden substance which must be lost if the mystery should happen to be made public in any way. Wherefore I commit this to be carried not to man, nor to letters, but to the spirits alone, whom I know to be both secure and faithful.

## *Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Rutgerus Sicamber*
## *Sends greetings and dedicates this present short prayer of Basil the Great.* <note>Rutgerus Sicamber (c. 1452–1514) was a fellow monk and friend of Trithemius. Basil the Great was a 4th-century church father; his name is used here to give the secret message the appearance of a harmless religious text.</note>

> *The glory of ineffable eternal blessedness is acquired through good exercises and humility. Now, mortals, wipe away your errors with diligent tears; love God, adoring His holy name. Learn to always humbly imitate the path of the humble crucified Jesus Christ, rendering honor to Him, sweetly burning with the love of our most kind Savior. Glorify and exalt His laudable goodness; bless His holy name, being zealous for the fire of His goodness; despise vain honors. In adversity, learn to give praise; love the exercise of devotion; cultivate humility, the most noble virtue; exult in Jesus, who snatches us from death and saves us. Farewell. The 7th of the Kalends of April, in the year of the Nativity of our Lord 1500.* <note>The first letters of the Latin words in this prayer form the secret message to be delivered to the recipient.</note>

The friend receiving the letters, being already skilled in the art of Steganography <term>Steganography: here meaning the art of hidden writing or "secret spirit communication"</term> and having recognized the character of Bydiel, shall, after performing those things which are customarily performed, say the conjuration generally.

### STEGANOGRAPHY

...or thinking themselves most learned, do they despise our compositions as if they were unworthy of their reading? There will also be some so accustomed to ancient and foreign traditions that they consider whatever they have not learned in those sources to be either impossible or superstitious. Nothing is more foolish for the knowledge of this profound art <note>Trithemius uses the term "art" (ars) to refer to his system of secret communication, which he masks as a system of angel magic.</note> than those people who either will not or cannot look into its deepest mysteries. 

However, for those who are both fit and willing to study, I have decided to briefly warn them at the end of this book so that they may be able to profit in this art (should any such people exist in the future). First and foremost, they must be warned to keep the art itself always hidden, lest it fall into the hands and knowledge of the wicked, who might perform many execrable crimes through it. For even if the art is truly good in its own right, its practice could be turned to evil by the impious just as much as to good by the virtuous. Let it remain, therefore, a secret among the good, for it would be harmful if made public among the wicked. Nor, however, should they despise the knowledge of the good for this reason—that it benefits the wicked for evil ends—just as one does not scorn the sword that strikes down a man. 

Next, students of this art are warned not to presume to proceed to operation in it unless they have first been perfectly instructed in everything required for the practical science. For it does not escape me how many dangers <note>Trithemius frequently suggests that "magic" is dangerous to the unskilled, a common trope to ensure only careful, dedicated students used his cryptographic methods.</note> those who are less skilled subject themselves to whenever they attempt to operate in this matter.

Likewise, he who is well-instructed and wishes to work through this science must remember to observe diligently (according to what we have said, both regarding the circle and in the individual tables and chapters) the difference, locations, names, orders, and offices of the supreme spirits <note>In the context of the Steganographia, "spirits" are metaphors for specific cryptographic systems, keys, or alphabets.</note>, as well as their leaders, and how many counts there are in their number. He must observe what order they follow and how many subordinates they preside over, so that he knows how to express these things in the conjuration <note>The "conjuration" is the act of encoding the secret message into a seemingly innocent cover text.</note>. For unless the operator of the art guards all these things diligently, he will not be able to succeed or reach the desired effect of his intention. Furthermore, let him attend carefully to when and for what duties or secrets each spirit is to be called, and in which part of the world it dwells, lest he err in the locations or in any of the particulars of those he wishes to call.

Likewise, let everyone intending to work in this science be advised to attend most diligently to pronouncing the words of the conjurations correctly, in which the great power of our operation consists. For when an error is committed in the conjurations, the spirits called and to be called not only...

# BOOK ONE.

...<note>The text continues from the previous page: "...perils that [pericu]lum..."</note> they not only do not obey, but even completely resist. Consequently, let the operator be forewarned not to call one spirit in place of another, but each in his own order, time, and office, as has been sufficiently stated by us in almost all chapters of this book. For if, either by error or any other negligence, he calls one for another, he will profit nothing in his operation, but rather provoke danger for himself.

Also in conjurations, let the spirit who is called be expressed by name along with his subordinates, and let the cause of the calling be established beforehand in one's intention. Nor should the act of operation be performed for trivial and profane matters, which one could otherwise safely communicate to another without danger through ordinary letters or messengers. For this art is not to be used except for announcing great and arduous things, which, if made public, would bring either loss or danger to the operator.

Also, it is necessary for every operator in this art to know the natures of the spirits: which are good, which are evil, which are prompt and benevolent in obedience, and which are harsh and rebellious; furthermore, which preside over nocturnal operations and which over diurnal. For unless he knows the natures of the spirits before he begins to work, he will proceed with the greatest difficulty and will easily be driven into a state of stupor <note>Original: "stuporem." In this context, it refers to a state of being mentally overwhelmed or paralyzed by the supernatural forces one is attempting to command.</note>.

Also, when the called spirits appear visible before the operator, once the secret word has been sent, he should commit the secret of his mind to the leader or count of the spirits with appropriate and fitting words in silence. For there is no need to speak to the spirit with a raised voice; rather, use a low whisper. Great care must also be taken by both the operator and the recipient not to perform anything pertaining to <term>Steganography</term> <note>Literally "secret writing." Trithemius uses this term to describe his system of encrypted communication, which he masks behind the language of angel summoning.</note> in the presence of other men who are ignorant of this art, provided they can have access to a secret place. If they are unable to be alone, but happen to be forced to operate among others, let them act so secretly, so prudently, and with such industry that none of those present understands anything regarding the presence of the spirits. For all spirits assigned to the service of this art are of such a nature and condition that they utterly detest and flee the noise of men, and they hate public gatherings.

Also, the operator must be careful not to direct a spirit without a letter, or at least the character <note>A "character" refers to a specific sigil or occult symbol representing a spirit's authority.</note> of its emperor; because, where the spirit does not see that character impressed, it [refuses] to obey the caller and...

# STEGANOGRAPHY

...<note>The text continues from the previous page: "[the spirit]... utterly disdains to carry se</note>crets to anyone. However, we send letters for a twofold reason, even though we could announce a secret without letters through the spirit alone: namely, to protect the men carrying the symbol from suspicion, and to constrain the spirit, bound to the symbol itself, to obey our friend. <note>Trithemius uses the term "spirit" as a metaphor for the encoded message itself, and the "character" or symbol as the physical key that unlocks it.</note>

## *The Key.*

After the author has described thirty-one modes of Steganography under the names, offices, and conjurations of spirits in as many chapters up to this point, he now briefly encompasses them all together in the present chapter. He sets before the reader’s eyes the names and properties of each in order, so that the reader may comprehend them at a single glance. He then inserts several cautions which must be diligently observed by students of Steganography; of which:

I. Is: That students of this art should not presume to work in it unless they have first been well instructed in all things and have a mastery of perfect Latin <note>original: "perfectæ Latinitatis"</note>; for if the speech is even slightly forced, suspicion arises because of the difficulty of the material, which is dangerous for the operator. <note>Because the secret messages are hidden within innocent-looking Latin letters, any grammatical error or awkward phrasing might alert a censor that the letter contains a hidden code.</note>

II. Students of the art should carefully observe by which mode they are working, how the letters of the mystic sense are to be constrained into open speech, and how many or which words of the open speech are effective or vacant. <note>"Effective" words contain the code, while "vacant" words are nulls used to pad the sentences.</note>

III. They should understand well the meaning of the conjurations, as the entire force of the operation consists in them as rules; for even the smallest error very often throws the entire operation into confusion.

IV. Students should not use these modes in writing unless the matter is great and difficult, the manifestation of which would cause loss and danger. For to employ these modes in trivial matters would be a waste of labor, and would easily provoke suspicion later in great matters.

V. Since some modes are easier or more difficult than others, the operator ought to know the nature of all of them, lest he sometimes undergo immense labor without necessity.

VI. He should not use this art in the presence of others who are ignorant of it, whether sending letters to a friend or receiving them from him, for it will cause suspicion and danger.

VII. Finally, let the operator assign the proper symbol <note>original: "characterem"</note> to each mode and attach it to the letters; for if he errs in this, either by omitting it or attaching another, his friend will never understand his mind.

### PREFACE.

In *the preceding book, relying on the help of the most high GOD, we have arranged in order thirty-one supreme spirits—the Emperors of our art—along with their Dukes, Counts, and Servants necessary for our work. We compiled these with no small labor <note>original: "non sine magno sudore," literally "not without much sweat"</note>. Although their ministries are more than sufficient for any operator to announce any secret, however hidden it may be, yet lest we should seem to omit anything that could lead to the perfection of this art, we have decided to join the second book to the first. Since, according to the tradition of certain wise men, specific spirits are assigned to the individual hours of the day and night for various operations and diverse, wondrous effects, it pleased us to imitate their order alone, but not their superstition. This is so that we might take from them what serves our purpose without harm to the Christian name. The rest, however, being full of magical arts and contrary to our faith, we pass over with disdain. Therefore, for each of the hours, both of the day and of the night, we propose the principal spirits assigned by the decree of* Solomon, *also known as* Hermes <note>Trithemius refers to the "Solomonic" and "Hermetic" traditions, which were famous medieval and Renaissance collections of occult and magical knowledge. While he uses their names, he is quick to distance himself from "superstition."</note> *in his volume on Magic, as the supreme Emperors of the art with their other officials, for the operation we have set forth—*

...taking up the necessary things, we will proceed and provide both the method and the teaching to all those studious in this art, so that they may reveal the secret and hidden concepts of their minds to their friends at any hour with safer counsel. For any prince presides like a watchman over his spirits—his leaders, counts, and servants—who, when called by us with a legitimate song <note>original: "legitimo carmine." While "carmen" often means a poem or song, in this context it refers to the specific ritualistic or coded formulas used to "summon" the cryptographic system.</note>, come at his command, carry the secrets entrusted to them, and show themselves obedient and ready to us in all things. 

But since I am to mention spirits again, I believe I must preface my words once more: nothing in this art of ours is to be considered frivolous, nothing is contrary to the Gospel tradition or the Catholic faith, and nothing superstitious is taught here at all. For everything we have said in the preceding volume, or are about to say in the following ones, is supported by natural, licit, and honest principles. The mystery is veiled only by unusual systems <note>original: "peregrinis institutionibus," referring to foreign or exotic-looking methods.</note> and words wrapped in the names of spirits; they require an educated reader. We use the service of a "spirit" to veil a secret that would be harmful if made public to the wicked; and so that no one fails due to an error in calculating the time, let it be known that we have adopted the planetary hours for both day and night.

## The Key.

In the preceding book, our *Trithemius* arranged thirty-one modes of Steganography with no small labor <note>original: "non sine magno sudore," literally "not without much sweat."</note>. Through these modes, while the mystic and hidden meanings remain within the natural value and power of the letters, anything can be communicated safely, secretly, and without any suspicion to one who knows the art. He now adds in this present book another 24 modes, in imitation of the 24 hours of the day and night, which are much safer and more secure than the previous ones. The last three of these modes break the hidden meaning into syllables and entire words, and in this way, they include them into an open message without any damage to the grammar or any cause for suspicion. The first 21 modes, however, adapt individual letters to an open narrative (as in the previous book), but they are first cleverly arranged so that no letter represents itself, but takes on an entirely different nature. Since, therefore, as far as our purpose is concerned, there are 22 letters of the alphabet following one another in this natural order:

->a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x z<-

If the alphabet is transposed while this order remains, 21 ordered transpositions will be created, and each letter will correspond with another in order. For example, if *b* is placed under *a*, then *c* under *b*, *d* under *c*, and so on:

->a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x z<-
->b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x z a<-

In an alphabet arranged this way, *b* stands for *a*, *f* stands for *e*, and so on. If I wished to write the word *Petrus*, it would appear in its new clothing as: *Qfusxt*.

The names of the Hours bear an initial letter that, in this transposition of letters, corresponds with **A**; thus, from the initial letters of the Hours, the specific transposition of the alphabet for that hour is immediately known. The name of the first hour has been omitted, but the names of the remaining hours follow in alphabetical order.

->Ceuorym, Danzur, Elechym, Fealech, Genapharym, etc.<-

The logic of the Spirits is the same as in the preceding book. The names of the Leaders <note>original: "Duces." In this system, these are primary keys or variables within the cipher.</note>, however, are borrowed from the alphabet of that Hour over which they preside, and through the correspondence of their initial letters, they allow for an easy explanation. For example, in the hour called *Genapharym*, this is the arrangement of the alphabet:

->a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x z<-
->g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x z a b c d e f<-

Indeed, the names of the spirits in the upper order are: *Arnebiel*, *Gamyel*, *Nedabar*. Here you see that **A** corresponds with **G**, and **G** with **N**. The same logic applies to the rest.

The key for the conjurations <note>The "conjurations" are the encoded messages themselves, which look like magical incantations to the uninitiated.</note> is the same as above, except that the words which were initially empty in the alternation now have value once the valid ones are filled. For example, in the hour of *Ceuorym*:

> Anael otiel aproify rachymas, thulnear layr meuear theor cralnotiel amerfoty mouear phroys lierto mear urnesa elty famelron.

*Which is arranged thus:*
> otiel rachymas layr theor amerfoty phroys mear elty approyfi thulnear meuear cralnotiel mouear lierto urnesa.

### CHAPTER I.

->SAMAEL, THE SUPREME EMPEROR, PRESIDES OVER THE FIRST HOUR OF THE DAY: HE HAS UNDER HIS COMMAND MANY LEADERS, COUNTS, AND SERVANTS, WHOM HE SENDS IN THIS HOUR ONLY WHEN CALLED UPON BY AN OPERATOR SKILLED IN <term>STEGANOGRAPHY</term>.<-

The spirit and emperor of the first hour of the day, which takes its beginning at sunrise, is called **Samael**. He has under his command many leaders, counts, and sub-servants: when called by an operator during this hour specifically, they come through <term>Steganography</term> <note>Literally "hidden writing." Trithemius uses the metaphor of spirits "carrying" a message to describe the process of encryption and decryption.</note> and carry the secret <note>original: "Arcanum."</note> entrusted to them; however, they utterly refuse to come outside of their assigned hour. And note, that the Leaders and the primary princes of Samael are rarely sent by him into the service of this science, for they perform the duty of stirring up the magical and nocturnal illusions of men. The Counts, however, along with their servants, are specifically assigned to the service of this art, and they are more frequently sent even without the presence of the Leaders; they,

Since they are of the highest order among the spirits, they are accustomed to showing themselves somewhat proud and rebellious to those who call upon them; they do not easily obey anyone except those most highly skilled in the art of **Steganography** <note>In this context, the "rebellion" of the spirits represents the difficulty of the cipher; if the practitioner is not precise, the message remains unreadable.</note> without great effort and danger. For they are insolent and very ready to deceive and mock men; they especially ridicule and sneer at those whom they find to be less than expert in the art of Steganography. However, those whom they consider bold, constant, and experienced in the art itself, they revere and fear, and they always most promptly obey their commands with trembling and reverence. Now, therefore, we shall record the names of their companions who are necessary to us for the operations of Steganography in this hour.

Therefore, when you wish to work in the art during the first hour of the day, first write the character of the **rising Lord** <note>original: "Domini ascendentis." In astrological terms, this refers to the planet ruling the current hour or the sign on the horizon.</note> on a small sheet of paper, then that of the Moon, then of all the remaining Planets according to the accustomed order, and finally the character of the astrological sign rising at that same hour. When you have completed this, write that conjuration on the back of the same sheet in silence, remaining still.

->The Key.<-

This first method arranges the alphabet in its natural order, as has been said, such that the second letter becomes the first; thus, for **A** one takes **B**, for **B** one takes **C**, and so on consecutively until the end of the alphabet. Then the letters of the mystical meaning from this new alphabet are transformed into others, and are adapted to the letters according to the modes handed down in the first book. In the present example, all initial letters carry the meaning. The alphabet is indeed arranged thus:

**Power** <note>original: "Potestas." This represents the standard alphabet used for the plaintext.</note>: A b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t v x z.
**Character** <note>original: "Character." This represents the cipher alphabet used for the encoded text.</note>: b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t v x z a.

# BOOK TWO

->The Incantation.<-

**Samael, afluar, onayr, Myscolayr, Madiel, Cuhiel, naniel, Nabruys, fatiel, Atharbiel, nadian, naslo, ranialcoha, Pemarson.** <note>These names function as the phonetic keys for the cipher system described in this section.</note>

->The Key and Meaning.<-

**aFlVaRmYsCoLaYrCuHiElNaBrVySaThArBiElNaSlOoNaYrMaDiElNaNiElSaTiElNaDiAnRaNiAlCoHa.** *Meaning:* For every letter, take the next one after it. <note>original German: "Für iclichen Bustaben so nimb den nesten darnach." This is a direct instruction for a simple substitution cipher where each letter is replaced by its successor in the alphabet.</note>

Once this incantation has been written on a small scroll, as described before, beautifully, clearly, and distinctly; you shall prepare the letters to be sent to the person whom you wish to know the secret. You may shape these in whatever form pleases you, because it does not matter what kind of letters are formed for sending, provided they contain no secret in themselves. Then, once the letters are written, call one or two of the companions according to their order—if you are working many times in this very first hour of the day—and recite the prescribed incantation from that same scroll with the strongest intention, fearing nothing. Once it is rightly completed, the spirits called will immediately appear to you, visible in a familiar form, calm in their usual manner, benevolent, and most ready to meet all the services required. 

When they approach, entrust your secret to the leader among them, saying: *Ameniel*, I command you through the hidden power of this incantation to go as quickly as possible to *Albert Goëler of Ravensburg* <note>Albrecht Göler von Ravensburg (1444–1503), a historical nobleman and bailiff.</note>, the Governor in *Kreuzenach* <note>Modern-day Bad Kreuznach, Germany.</note>, and tell him from me thus or so. After saying these things, add the secret word, which must not be written down, and the spirit will immediately fly away. However, send the letters sealed with the character of **Samael** (as is the custom) by a messenger; these letters should contain no secret and need not fear the gaze of anyone.

->*Let the secret be whatever occurs to you.*<-

Let the secret be great and difficult, whatever occurs at the time, and of such a nature that it should be communicated to no one, nor trusted to letters, nor even to *couriers* <term>Tabellionibus: Originally Roman public scribes, here referring to official messengers or notaries.</term>. For in this art, one must not operate through the spirits of the second volume for small or trivial causes that could otherwise be announced through ordinary letters.

# You shall form the letters concerning these matters as you please.

The Catholic Majesty of the Faith must be firmly preserved by all men; it has promised the happiness of eternal life to those serving Christ. Hold fast to the Christian Catholic Faith, glorify the Almighty, and flee the tumult of vanity. No one of wicked works shall possess the blessed life. Let the faithful man follow Christ along the path of virtues. Integrity is adorned by good works, and the Catholic name is preserved by Christian fidelity; for a wicked man clouds the faith. Christ hates the rash and loves Christians who practice Catholic works and venerate tranquility. <note>original Latin: "Majestas Katholica Fidei..." This entire paragraph is a "decoy" text. # CHAPTER 11.

## THE SECOND HOUR OF THE DAY IS CALLED CEUORYM, WHOSE PRINCE AND SUPREME SPIRIT IS ANAEL, WHO HAS UNDER HIS COMMAND 10 DUKES, COUNTS, CENTURIONS, AND 100 PRESIDENTS; THE NUMBER OF SERVANTS AND SUBSERVANTS IS NOT FIXED.

The presiding ruler and Commander of the second principal hour of the day is called Anael, who has under his command 10 dukes, counts, centurions, and 100 presidents over all his spirits, all assigned to the ministry of this art of Steganography; as for the servants, their exact number is not yet certain to me. Furthermore, the second hour of the day is called *Ceuorym*, in which wonderful operations are performed that are astounding to all men. All the spirits of this Commander are quite benevolent, pleasant, cheerful, and very prompt to obey the one working in this art: provided that he is skilled in the art, strong and constant in spirit, and of good understanding. <note>Trithemius uses the language of "spirits" and "magic" as a metaphor for cryptographic keys and systems. To a casual reader, this looks like a grimoire; to an initiate, it is a technical manual for coded communication.</note>

### CHAPTER III.

### THE HOUR OF WHICH IS CALLED DANZUR, AND ITS SUPREME EMPEROR IS THE SPIRIT VEQUANIEL, WHO HAS UNDER HIS DOMINION 20 DUKES, 200 COUNTS, AND OF SERVANTS THERE IS NO NUMBER.

The third hour of the day is called Danzur; its supreme spirit and emperor is called Vequaniel, who holds under his command 20 dukes and 200 counts, while the number of servants is uncertain. Their duty is general to all things; they are quite prompt and benevolent in everything entrusted to them, being both faithful and reliable. Nor are they unwilling to obey, yet they can by no means be called in public without harm or danger to the caller. For they love secrecy, just as do all the others who preside over the hours and their operations. I do not know the names of them all, but only a few, which—having been revealed by the spirits themselves—have been set down in this table and are sufficient for our purposes.

| Murfiel | Parniel | Serviel | 20 | 20 | 200 | 200 |
| Zœfiel | Comadiel | Furiel | 20 | 20 | 200 | 200 |

In this table, we have named 4 of the dukes, 8 of the counts, and 1,730 of their uncounted servants, who are sufficient for us for all operations of this art in the third hour of the day. Therefore, when you wish to call a spirit in this hour to carry a message <note>original: "pro aliquo numero perferendo," literally "to carry a certain number," likely referring to the numerical shifts in a cipher</note> to a friend, you should use no fewer than at least two dukes, and as many counts,

**Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Arnold Bostius, Carmelite of Ghent, fellow philosopher, greetings and charity.**

## *Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Rutger Vencaius of Sicambria, Canon of the Order of the Holy Father Augustine of the Monastery of Dameten, Greetings.*

->With the help of Christ <note>original: "Xsto", a common Greek-Latin abbreviation for Christo</note>, I have resolved those things which you proposed to me to be solved; whether well, you, who proposed them, shall be the judge. I shall relate to you briefly a stupendous thing that has happened. A certain brother, also a friend and not the least among them, recently reported to me that a youth had been raised from the dead at the invocation of Christ. This youth reported marvelous and horrifying things among the inhabitants of the Underworld, describing the torments of wicked Christians—specifically those who crucified Christ by acting perversely. He said they were especially guilty because, having forgotten the benefit of the most kind redemption, they remained always ungrateful to Christ. He saw those people suffering horrible things who were known to be ungrateful for His benefits by not living well; blinded by sins, they neglected future joys while pursuing the pleasures of the world. Those who were remorseful for their committed negligences cried out most bitterly: "We justly suffer these things, we who were always ungrateful to the Redeemer of the human race; Christians in name, but pagans in action." We wretches always sought earthly consolations: why did we offend Christ? Alas, for us most unhappy mortals! The resurrected youth told us many other things which I am now entirely unable to write, being greatly hindered by heavy business. Therefore, brother, let us zealously imitate the footsteps of Christ, always giving thanks to our most gentle Savior, asking that He may forgive us for the crimes we have committed. Farewell. March 30th <note>original: "3. Calend. April.", the third day before the Kalends of April</note>.<---

When he to whom these letters are sent, being skilled in the art, receives them, he should observe the Lord of the Ascendant <term>Lord of the Ascendant: In astrology, the planet that rules the sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</term>, and the sign of the twelfth house of that same hour. He should write their characters on paper along with the other things required for the operation, and afterward, he should speak the aforementioned conjuration, and upon seeing the spirit, say these words:

### Conjuration 2.

> Camerusin aproysi lierto Thulnear venean maveas fabelron.

---

### The Key and the Meaning.

**aPrOySiThVlNeArMaVeAsLiErToVeNeAn.** *Meaning.* **After one, one is valid.** <note>original: "Post unam valet una." This is the cryptographic rule for this section: to find the hidden message, the reader must skip one letter and take the next.</note>

When these things are said, the sent spirit will approach, and he will reveal the secret entrusted to you faithfully and without danger.

### CHAPTER V.

->THE HOUR OF WHICH IS CALLED FEALECH, AND THE SPIRIT AND SUPREME EMPEROR IS NAMED SASQUIEL, HAVING UNDER HIS COMMAND 10 DUKES, 100 COUNTS, AND A VERY GREAT NUMBER OF SERVANTS.<-

The fifth hour of the day is called Fealech, and its spirit is named Sasquiel, a great and powerful Emperor, who has under his command, among many dukes, 10 specific ones, and 100 counts, along with their servants: these are assigned to the service of various and especially secret arts and this science of ours. And it should be noted that dukes are rarely summoned in the fifth hour for operations of <term>Steganography</term> <note>Steganography: Here, Trithemius refers to his system of "hidden writing" which he presents as a form of angel magic to mask the underlying cryptography.</note>, because they are not always necessary, since the counts, together with the servants assigned to them, are more than sufficient for every operation. If, however, anyone should wish to see any of the dukes or use their power, he may call one, two, or more, and they will come without delay, for they are quite well-disposed and ready to obey those performing the work.

### *A pretext for announcing a secret.*

### *The tenor of the letter at will.*

### *Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to the religious brother Nicolaus Baselius from Durckheim, a Monk of Hirsau, etc.*

Holy Obedience, Good Brother, and Humility you Neglect; Benedict’s Constitutions are Undermined; by the Report of All who have Successively Met, I have Learned that You hold Good Zeal in Hatred, you Scorn the Rule of Religion and Catholic Obedience, and are Occupied with Secular Works and Arts. Good Brother, what are You Doing? You have Troubled Us, and You Envy the Two-tongued Fools; You Love Hatred, Bitterness, Strife, and Contentions; You Hate Goodness; You are Contentious, Proud, Two-tongued, and Foolish—what are You Doing? The Time is at Hand to Quickly and Zealously Correct these Negligences of Yours according to Justice, and unless You Humbly come to Meet us, to Break your Zeal of Bitterness with the Lashes of Humiliations. We are Compelled by our Office to be Zealous against All things You do that are Seditious to the Faith and Catholic Morals. Farewell. From Sponheim, the Calends of April, in the Year 1500. <note>This letter is a "null cipher." The harsh language is a cover; the actual secret message is hidden within the text, often formed by the first letter of each word or every second word.</note>

When he to whom the letter is sent—being skilled in the art—receives it and recognizes the character of Sasquiel, having performed the customary preliminaries, let him speak the aforementioned conjuration, and immediately the sent spirit will appear and show himself visibly. Once he is seen, let him then speak those words.

### CHAPTER VI.

## THE HOUR OF WHICH IS CALLED GENAPHERYM, AND ITS SUPREME SPIRIT AND EMPEROR IS CALLED SANIEL, WHO HAS UNDER HIM 110 DUKES AND COUNTS, WITH MANY SERVANTS.

The sixth hour of the day is called Genapherym, and its angel is **Saniel**, great and powerful in his operations. He holds under his command 10 dukes and 100 counts, with 5550 servants assigned to the ministry of various operations, who are sufficient for us in all things we wish to perform through Steganography in this hour.

The dukes, however, are called upon more rarely, even though they are prompt and very willing to obey our commands, because their counts have been accustomed to carry out most of their duties, as the dukes are often occupied in other magical experiments.

### Subject of the Secret.

Whatever secret you have for anyone skilled in the art of Steganography, you can send it securely through the spirits of Samiel in the sixth hour of the day, because they are generalists for communicating all things and entirely faithful in what is entrusted to them, if you proceed in the proper manner in all things according to our instructions.

### General content of the letter as desired.

> *By praying with the most humble laments, we shall obtain the grace of forgiveness, and with groans, we shall receive freedom from our guilts; men who are diligently repentant will deservedly perceive joy, adorning Catholic piety with works of justice: they will hold the law of kindness, the praise of the Catholic [faith]. ### Argument for the Secret as you wish.

Whatever secret you have for a friend that you wish to be common to no one else, and therefore you believe that neither letters nor couriers should be trusted—because fraud can intervene in both—call as many of the above-mentioned spirits as you wish and commit the secret to the stronger one, fearing nothing, because they are good and faithful in all things.

### The form of the letters is made at your pleasure.

### CHAPTER VIII.

### WHOSE HOUR IS CALLED JAFANYM, AND WHOSE ANGEL IS CALLED OSMADIEL, WHO HAS UNDER HIS COMMAND 10 DUKES, 100 COUNTS, AND AN UNCERTAIN NUMBER OF SERVANTS.

The eighth hour of the day is called Jafanym, and its principal spirit is named Osmadiel, according to the *Picatrix* <note>original: "Picatricem"; a famous medieval grimoire on astrological magic often cited by Trithemius</note> in magical matters. He has under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts, and innumerable servants assigned, not only for the operation of our <term>Steganography</term><note>The art of "hidden writing"; here, it refers to the system of hiding messages within what appear to be magical prayers or incantations</note>, but also for many magical experiments. Solomon the Jew, also known as Hermes <note>original: "Salomon Judæus cognomento Hermes"; Trithemius often conflates biblical and legendary figures to lend authority to the text</note>, says in his book *On the Nature of Spirits*, that all these dukes and counts, who are obedient and subject to the aforementioned Osmadiel, are accustomed to come in various transformations at the will of the practitioner, just as they have been ordered by the practitioner; but now let us list the names of some of them.

Once this conjuration song has been spoken, the summoned spirits will appear, prompt and obedient in all things. You should entrust the Secret to the Duke, not to the count, unless the Duke is absent; for the secret must always be commended to the highest-ranking among those who arrive.

### A method for a secret according to one’s pleasure.

Suppose we have a secret of some kind (which we wish a friend far away to know) and it is of such a nature that we do not wish it to come to the knowledge of anyone else, as can often happen. Therefore, lest the Courier <note>original: "Tabellarius"; a letter-carrier or messenger</note> reveal the Mystery by any chance, or the letters fall into foreign hands, let us work, and through the spirit we shall be secure.

->*Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, sends greetings to Lord Conrad, Abbot of Saint Stephen in Würzburg.*<-

*A Rumor went out concerning the Abbot of Limburg, that he dismissed Brother John of Feilsdorff, a Faithful man and Greatly skilled in Temporal matters, and introduced New monks, pantimoranos <note>original: "pantimoranos"; likely a Greek-derived word meaning "all-wretched" or "unfortunate," used here as a derogatory term for the replacement monks</note>, and Appointed them as his officials. I wonder greatly at this useless Deed; However, when I Recall the custom of the people of Limburg, I do not know What to say. Since they are Ignorant of Temporal matters, they Dismissed a Faithful man because his Deeds Refuted theirs; they who Ought to have given Thanks to our Savior Jesus Christ for the Faithfulness of such a Brother, who could have Relieved their Necessities. Wretches, why do you Repel a good and Necessary helper? What shall I say? I do not praise the Retreat of so Useful a brother, most skilled in Temporal matters, who would have Helped those at Limburg as quickly as possible. I Grieve deeply that the monks of Limburg have been so Foolish as to Dismiss an excellent man And appoint as Stewards monks who are Worth nothing at all in temporal matters. Abbot Macharius, it did not Befit a man to act so. First you praised, Now you have repelled a man Very necessary to you, and second to None. I Confess, if Christ had given him To me, I would now give the Greatest thanks, as befits a Christian, and would take Diligent care that he Never departed; but you Preferred to dismiss a Faithful man, exhausted by the Foolish counsel of the Wicked, lest there seem to be Any hope of Recovery for your abandoned affairs. From Sponheim, April 3, 1500.* <note>In the original Latin, this letter functions as a "null cipher." The actual secret message is hidden in the first or second letters of each word. By translating the text into English prose, the original cipher is broken, but the "cover" story of the letter—a complaint about monastery management—is preserved.</note>

## CHAPTER IX.

### WHOSE HOUR IS CALLED KARRON, AND THE NAME OF ITS ANGEL IS QUABRIEL, HAVING UNDER HIS COMMAND 10 DUKES, 100 COUNTS, AND OF SERVANTS THERE IS NO CERTAIN NUMBER.

The ninth hour of the day is called Karron, and its principal spirit is named Quabriel. He has under his command many and almost innumerable dukes, counts, and servants. From these, 10 dukes and 100 counts have been assigned to the service of this our art of Steganography <term>Steganographia: "Secret Writing," from the Greek words for "hidden" and "writing"</term>. These leaders have many servants assigned to them in ranks: in the first rank there are 10, in the second 20, in the third 30, in the fourth 40, in the fifth 500, in the sixth 600, in the seventh 700, in the eighth 1080, in the ninth 90,000, and in the tenth rank there are 100,000. However, spirits are rarely summoned through all these ranks; even if they are summoned, not all of them, but only some, are accustomed to come with their dukes and counts according to the command of the emperor.

### Let us form letters according to our pleasure.

**Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim of the Order of Saint Benedict, to the religious Father John Hugo, Guardian of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis in Kreuznach, greetings and charity.**

Religious and venerable father, I know that you willingly grant all things desired to friends, therefore I humbly pray that, in view of Catholic piety, you do not take it poorly that your zealous brothers have been detained with us for a longer time with the greatest charity. <note>In Trithemius's system, this letter is a "cover text." The actual secret message is encoded in the letters of the words themselves, often by taking the first or second letter of every word.</note> For it was necessary that they remain at my request; it was a glorious joy for us, as we were all rejoicing without fault. We exulted in the Lord with spiritual joy, offering thanks to God Almighty with good zeal. Our joy was most devout, and our joy was also decorated in every way with the most holy manners: the religious and Catholic brother beautifully adorned our joy with the most holy zeal of discipline. For we exulted without dissolution of mind, always preserving most religiously; he was strenuously devoted to us all, and most similar was divine love and zeal for souls, with which piety he was adorned, shining most holily, he exhibited great fervor for disputing, and was applying vehement labor with the most holy devotion of mind in religion. What, I ask, is more religious than such a gathering? Where Catholic conversation flourishes, where nothing idle is said, nothing wicked is sought, may Jesus Christ the Savior of all make us rejoice in heavenly glory, and may the love of God and fervor recreate all true zealots of truth; the glorious zealots of virtues prefer nothing to the truth; we have rejoiced with holy joy, praying and beseeching that you receive the brothers with a tranquil mind, and lay aside all zeal of bitterness. Farewell. From Sponheim, on the Nones of January <note>January 5th.</note>, in the year of our Lord 1598. <note>Trithemius died in 1516. This date likely refers to the specific printing or transcription of this edition of the *Steganographia*, which was first published posthumously in 1606, though circulated in manuscript long before.</note> Johannes Trithemius, Abbot. <sig>tt.</sig>

When someone skilled in this art receives these letters, or any others marked with the character of Quabriel <note>Quabriel is the "spirit" or governor of this specific cipher method.</note>, having performed the necessary preliminaries, let him say the prescribed conjuration: which having been said, he will soon see the destined spirit, whom when he has seen, let him say these words:

->Conjuration 2.<-

**Mesraym paslotiel vear, Reneam, cralti Thio phroyfyma mear hamorfy.**
<note>To the uninitiated, this looks like a magical incantation. In reality, it is a second layer of ciphered text.</note>

->The Key and the Sense.<-

**pAsLoTiElReNeAmThloMaVeArCrAlTyPhRoIsMeAr.**
**The Sense.** The first is vacant alternately. <note>original: "Alternatim vacat prima." This is the decryption instruction. It tells the reader to discard every other letter to find the hidden message. If we apply this to the string above, skipping the first (lowercase) letter and keeping the second (uppercase), we begin to extract the hidden message.</note>

## CHAPTER X.

->Whose Hour is Called LAMARHON, And Its SUPREME RULER<-
->Is Called The SPIRIT ORIEL, WHO HAS UNDER HIS COMMAND DUKES,<-
->COUNTS AND MANY SERVANTS.<-

The tenth hour of the day is called Lamarhon, and its supreme angel is called Oriel, a great and powerful emperor, who according to Solomon the Jew <note>Solomon the Jew refers to the legendary King Solomon, to whom many medieval and Renaissance magic texts were attributed.</note> has many dukes under his command. Through these spirits, wonderful experiments in magic are performed in the seventh hour of the day <note>original: "horâ diei septimâ". Trithemius often uses the hours of the day to categorize different sets of cryptographic "spirits" or keys.</note>. These ten dukes and counts, who are assigned to the work of Steganography <term>Steganography: From the Greek for "hidden writing"; in this context, it refers to Trithemius's method of hiding secret messages within innocent-sounding prayers or letters to spirits.</term>, maintain their own rankings along with their servants. In the first rank there are 10, in the second 20, in the third 30, in the fourth 40, in the fifth 500, in the sixth 600, in the seventh 700, in the eighth 800, in the ninth 900, and in the tenth 1000. In our operations, however, we are satisfied to take only 10 counts from the first five ranks and exactly five dukes from the last ranks. If anyone delights in knowing the names of more, let him call one of those named in the table and question him; he will hear whatever he wishes, and whatever he desires to know, he shall know perfectly from that spirit.

### Let a letter be formed as desired.

# CHAPTER XI.

## WHOSE HOUR IS CALLED MENELOYM, AND WHOSE SUPREME COMMANDER IS CALLED BARIEL, WHO HAS UNDER HIS DOMINION PRINCES, DUKES, COUNTS, AND MANY SERVANTS.

The eleventh hour of the day is called Meneloym, and its supreme angel and commander is named Bariel. As Hermes the Jew <note>original: *Hermes Judæus*; a legendary figure often associated with early Hermetic and alchemical texts.</note> writes, Bariel has many spirits under his command, through whom wonders are performed during the eleventh hour in various experiments. From among these, many have been assigned to the operation of Steganography <term>Steganography: Literally "hidden writing." Trithemius uses the guise of "angel magic" to encode secret messages.</term> according to their ranks. In the first rank there are 10, in the second 20, in the third 30, in the fourth 40, in the fifth 500, in the sixth 600, in the seventh 700, in the eighth 800, in the ninth 900, and in the tenth 1,000. 

All of these are sent into the service of this art by their turns and ranks. Among them are many dukes and counts with their servants; it is not easy to list all of their names, nor indeed is it necessary. Knowing the names of a few is sufficient, for the practitioner of the art can always learn more names of other spirits from the report of a single spirit. Note that, according to Raziel <note>A reference to the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, a famous medieval grimoire of practical Kabbalah and angelology.</note>, all these spirits shape and transform themselves according to the will of the operator. Thus, in whatever form the operator wishes to see them, let him command it before the conjuration in the manner prescribed by the art, and they will obey most promptly in all things. But let us now set out the names of some which will be sufficient for us.

| R. | | R. | | R. | | R. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Almarizel | Menafiel | Almas | 10 | 10 | 100 | 100 |
| Prasiniel | Demasor | Perman | 10 | 10 | 100 | 100 |
| Chadros | Omary | Comial | 10 | 10 | 100 | 100 |
| Turmiel | Helmas | Temas | 10 | 10 | 100 | 100 |
| Lamiel | Zemoel | Lanifiel | 10 | 10 | 100 | 100 |

Here we now have fifteen of Bariel's spirits named, of whom five are dukes and ten are counts, who command a total of 1,100 servants. These are sufficient for our operations of the eleventh hour of the day in Steganography. Therefore, when you wish to work through these spirits, observe the lord of the ascendant <term>Lord of the Ascendant: In astrology, the planet that rules the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time of the operation.</term> along with the other requirements, according to what we have said in the previous chapters. Write this conjuration along with the others on clean paper, as is the custom in this science.

### Let the secret be as you wish.

It shall be a great mystery and a demanding secret, which would be harmful if made public; for this reason, it is to be committed neither to ordinary letters nor to a notary, but should undergo the ministry of the spirits who preside over the hour in which you are working. Confirm our fragility with the zeal of Your love; save us, sweetest Jesus, and pour the zeal of the Catholic faith into our hearts. Holy is Your zeal; it works a union in the hearts of those seeking You, Christ, most kind Savior.

<header>BOOK SECOND</header>

### *A secret should be whatever appears to us as great and difficult.*

The secret <note>original: "Arcanum"</note>, which we wish to reveal to a friend by means of spirits, may be whatever occurs to us at the time according to the variety of business, provided it is not something trivial or of the sort that can otherwise be safely announced.

*Johannes Trithemius* <note>The author (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and polymath</note> to the holy nuns *on the Mount of Saint Rupert* <note>The Rupertsberg monastery near Bingen, founded by Hildegard of Bingen</note> who adorn the Catholic faith with shining virginity, may they deserve to earn eternal happiness through their continuous and most holy religious zeal. By the mercy of the eternal King’s providence, we send to you a man much expected for some time, of great experience in worldly affairs, born in *Kaunenstat* <note>Johannes von Cannstatt</note>, for a long time the Reverend and zealous Abbot of the monastery of *Vielsdorf*, who has freely resigned that same abbacy. I went to him at the monastery of *Limburg*, as I had promised you, where he was serving Christ with continuous prayers and occupied with the reading of the Holy Scriptures along with the monks of that same monastery. And I asked that he might come down to your convent and take up the care of your temporal affairs, becoming your procurator and cellarer <term>cellarius</term> <note>The official in charge of a monastery's provisions and financial management</note>. The Abbot of *Limburg*, changed in mind by his usual instability, finally agreed to dismiss him. I prayed with the greatest urgency, and could hardly obtain consent from him. At last, by the inspiration of Christ, he consented, though timidly; for he fears to serve nuns, who are very easily changed. He fears not without merit, since, as experience has taught us, sometimes nuns have returned to their stewards a reward for their good deeds that is not praiseworthy. The female mind is suddenly changed by the zeal of bitterness; however, by the grace of Christ, I know that he will be useful to you. He is a Christian, he is a monk, he fears his Savior, and he is of good understanding. Therefore, accustom yourselves to restrain womanly changeability, so that you may remember to be constant, looking up to him with holy honor and sincere charity, setting aside all levity of the female mind; especially since he can, with the help of Christ the Redeemer who guards charity, assist you and recover the fallen state of temporal affairs in your monastery. Farewell, from *Sponheim*, the 17th of the Calends of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

When the person to whom it is sent, being skilled in our art, receives a letter marked with the character of *Tartys* <note>The spirit/angel presiding over this hour and method</note>, let him observe the Lord of the Ascendant <note>A technical astrological term referring to the planet ruling the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the operation</note> and perform each and every thing most diligently that is to be done, and let him add the customary conjuration; and, when he sees that the spirits sent are present, let him say these words to the principal one.

### CHAPTER XV.

->WHOSE HOUR IS CALLED QUABRION, AND ITS SUPREME ANGEL IS NAMED SERQUANICH, HAVING UNDER HIS COMMAND PRINCES, DUKES, COUNTS, AND SERVANTS WITHOUT NUMBER.<-

The third hour of the night is called Quabrion, whose commander and supreme angel is named Serquanich. He has under his command many princes, dukes, and counts, divided through twelve orders with a great and continuous multitude of servants. In the first order there are 10; in the second, 20; in the third, 30; in the fourth, 40; in the fifth, 50; in the sixth, 60; in the seventh, 70; in the eighth, 80; in the ninth, 90; in the tenth, 100; in the eleventh, 1,000; and in the twelfth, 10,000. From these, sufficient dukes, counts, and servants are called and sent from their respective orders by turns for the service of various experiments.

### *The logic of the secret.* <note>original: "Argumentum secreti"</note>

**We desire to advise a friend of an imminent danger, but we fear the danger itself; for if it were noted that we ourselves had advised him, we would be subjected to no less a disadvantage. Therefore, since neither letters nor a messenger can be trusted, we have decided to trust the spirit of the hour.**

...I would not begrudge the Catalogue <note>referring to Trithemius’s own work, the *Catalogus illustrium virorum* or *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*</note>, as the Pompous Evaluator <note>original: "Tumidus pensator," likely a derogatory nickname for his critic Carolus Bovillus</note> falsely claims, disparaging the Catalogue with the most foolish words. He imagined that I failed to mention his people solely out of envy, which is utterly false. Indeed, I wrote concerning the Conception of the most holy Mother of God, and I affirmed that she was always most beautiful and without the stain of original sin. The Pompous Evaluator, wishing to pompously rebuke this, said that the most radiant Virgin was spotted with the guilt of original fault—a claim of the vainest temerity against Catholic observance. It is a reckless thing to wish to defile the most Blessed Virgin. However, the most renowned doctors of Cologne, wishing to uproot the opinion of that insane little friar <note>likely a reference to a member of the Dominican order, who at the time often disputed the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception</note> which is contrary to the truth, compelled him to recant his cited vain fables. They asserted and confirmed that by decree it must be believed that the most blessed Virgin is most pure and at no time (not even for the briefest moment) was subject to original foulness. Because you love the truth, I wished to write these things to you, so that you may avoid those who reproach the most blessed Virgin. Farewell. April 16th, in the year of our Lord 1520.

However, the one receiving the letter, being skilled in this art, should attend to the sign of the principal spirit, so that he may know whom he ought to call upon according to the turns of the hour. Omitting nothing of those things which have been commanded, and having spoken the conjuration, when he sees the spirit present, let him say the following words.

### CHAPTER XVI.

# WHOSE HOUR IS CALLED RAMERZY, AND WHOSE SUPREME ANGEL
# AND EMPEROR IS CALLED JEFISCHA, WHO HAS UNDER HIM MANY
# PRINCES, DUKES, COUNTS, AND SERVANT SPIRITS.

The fourth hour of the night is called Ramerzy, whose angel is named Jefischa. He holds under his command many princes, dukes, counts, and servant spirits, who—much like those we described in the preceding chapter—are distributed by turns and ranks into twelve groups. In the first rank there are ten, in the second 20, in the third 30, in the fourth 40, in the fifth 50, in the sixth 60, in the seventh 70, in the eighth 80, in the ninth 90, in the tenth 100, in the eleventh 1000, and in the twelfth 10000. From these twelve ranks, spirits are sent to us for service in their turns during the operations of the art of Steganography <note>The art of secret writing; Trithemius uses the framework of "angel magic" to disguise sophisticated cryptographic methods</note>. Of these, we shall now name a few.

These princes, according to the saying of Solomon the Philosopher <note>A common medieval reference to King Solomon, who was traditionally credited with the power to command spirits and authoring magical texts</note>, are multiform and take on whatever shapes they are commanded. Therefore, when you wish to work through them in the fourth hour of the night, observe the Lord of the Ascendant <note>original: "Dominum ascendentis," an astrological term for the planet that rules the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time</note> and the entire configuration of the heavens, and do everything according to what we have instructed you, writing everything on a clean slip of paper and writing this conjuration on its back.
