Then, after adding what needs to be added, when you have spoken the conjuration itself in the proper manner, form, and order, the spirits will appear visible in whatever form you commanded, ready and willing for all things.

->*Let the secret be as you please.*<-

Whatever secret happens to occur to you at the time, which you want an absent person to know in this fourth hour of the night, you can safely entrust to the spirits, provided it is such that you cannot safely convey it to them either by letters or by messengers; for those things which we can convey without danger either by letter or by messenger, we ought by no means to convey by the ministry of spirits <note>Trithemius uses the "ministry of spirits" as a metaphor for his cryptographic systems. He warns that using these complex codes for trivial matters is a waste of effort and risks exposing the secret method to discovery.</note>; whoever, moreover, shall attempt to summon spirits for light matters and secrets which can be conveyed without danger by letters or messengers, will undoubtedly receive loss and inconvenience with danger.

->*The content of the letter as you please.*<-

*To the venerable father in Christ, the religious steward of the people of Limburg, the lord* **John Weisdorffen** <note>Johannes Weisdorffen was a contemporary of Trithemius; the use of real names adds to the "mask" of the letter.</note> *so-named, from* **Johannes Ovilis of Sponheim** <note>original: "joannes Ovilis ſpanheimenſis." Trithemius often used "Ovilis" (meaning "of the sheepfold") as a Latinization of his family name, Heidenberg.</note> *humble Abbot, [wishes]* **the joys of heaven.**

*The nuns of* **Saint Rupert** *desire you as their* **Governor** *with* **excessive** *eagerness*, *and they ask you with* **humble** *benevolence*, *that you might undertake the* **government** *of the* **temporal** *affairs of that* **monastery**. *To* **serve** *the devout virgins of* **Christ** *is* **praiseworthy** *and* **meritorious**. *You have a* **good** [man] *over the* **spiritual** *affairs of that* **same** *cloister, a most* **renowned** *visitor,* **embracing you** *with the greatest* **honor**; [he is] **grave** *in character*, **adorned** *with virtues*, **cautious** *in counsel*, **beloved** *by all*, *well-* **famed** *for his* **monastic** **religious** *way of life, and* **noteworthy** *to* **all** *men* (*which* **life** *is deservedly most* **pleasing** *to* **Christ**), *the* **excellent** *Abbot of the* **monastery of Saint John**. *He* **is** *most learned in the* **letters** *of both* **Christians** *and* **Gentiles**, *and most* **studious**, *who* **notably** *exceeds the* **wisdom** *of* **all** *men by far*. *He* **knows** *how to* **rule** *the* **flock** *entrusted to him* **excellently**, *and* **is** *a* **zealous** *guardian of the virgins of* **Christ**, *whose* **cloister** *he* **guards** **most firmly**. *Do not* **fear** *to serve such honorable nuns under* **him**, *who knows how to* **govern** *the spouses of* **Christ** *according to* **monastic** **law** *with the* **best** *discretion: who by* **virtue** *and* **zeal** *for the* **Christian** *faith will* **gladly** *come to your aid in time of* **necessity**. **Since** *you have* **this** *man, so* **distinguished** *and* **kind** *a pastor, as an* **intimate** *friend, I ask that you* **gladly** *take up the* **helm** *of such* **religious** *virgins;* **Christ** *will reward* **your** **labor** *with eternal* **joys**. *May the* **Tutor** *and most* **kind** *rewarder of the* **nuns** **grant** *you to* **be zealous** *for better things with a good* **zeal**. **Farewell**. *From Sponheim, the 13th day before the Calends of May* <note>April 19th</note>, *1500.* ♁♁ <note>The symbol for Earth/Antimony, used here as a closing flourish or sign.</note>

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

### A Method for a Secret that Arises

Whatever secret you may have, which you otherwise cannot safely make known to a friend—whether they are nearby or far away—commit it to the more powerful of the spirits using the rite and form which is appropriate according to this art. Fear nothing, for they are faithful and well-disposed. <note>In the context of this book, "spirits" are not literal ghosts but are metaphors for cryptographic methods or keys. Trithemius uses this "angel magic" terminology to disguise a system of secret writing.</note>

->*Let the letters be formed as desired.*<- <note>This instruction tells the user they can write the following "innocent" text in their own handwriting or style to avoid suspicion.</note>

> The Catholic faith saves no one who despises the fervor of divine love. To believe without having the zeal of divine love contributes nothing at all to the redemption of the soul. However, many people are found now boasting in the Catholic faith, but few possess the works of Christian faith, and an idle faith dies. Many believe, but very few observe the commandments of God. Alas, the zeal of believers is weak—a zeal which even unbelieving men can sometimes possess more strongly. Indeed, many do. The Gentiles and those men who do not believe our Savior was made man, the son of the Almighty, will be tortured by the punishments of hell. However, all those who believe the son of God came into the world and was made man for the zeal of human redemption, but who do not adorn that Christian faith with holy works, will be tortured with even more grievous punishments. Those always involved in sins prefer the honors of the world to eternal beatitude, zealously performing impious actions and staining the purity of faith with wicked morals against the virtue of obedience. But the lovers of God, who have the right zeal of the Christian faith, prefer nothing to God; they imitate Christ, flee from sins, and despise the riches and honors of the world. Now, therefore, attend to these words, you who boast of your faith: love God, and you will have the reward of beatitude by being zealous for justice. If you love the vanities of this age against the honor of God, you will receive the prize of those who are zealous for iniquity: the horrors of hell. Written 15 days before the Calends of May <note>original: "15. Cal. Maji" — this corresponds to April 17th.</note> in the Year of our Lord 1500. <note>original: "M.D. ωω" — the Greek omega characters here likely serve as placeholders or part of a date code common in 15th-century manuscripts.</note>

# BOOK TWO.

*With a broken body, a sad soul, and a marred face, carrying our crimes through the zeal of ineffable charity, you healed our wounds. For our sake, you subjected the blossoming youth of your most noble body to harsh wounds so that you might bring back to life a man dead <note>referring to the spiritual death of humanity</note> through being overcome by excessive love; and wishing most laboriously to die to restore Catholic communion. Therefore, let us Catholics, groaning and praising the memory of the Passion in the Christian manner, piously recollecting, give such thanks as we can to our Redeemer. O most kind Jesus, save me by your accustomed goodness, and I pray, forgive me all my sins: Gladdening me with holy joy, my Redeemer, heal me, sanctify me, O Christ, true light of hearts. I bless you, most powerful Creator of the world, King Christ, Savior, unquenchable light. I pray, purify my soul, Favorer of all things; enlighten me, O Christ, lover of the high glory of those who seek you. Look upon me and grant the joys of eternal blessedness; grant the most fervent fires of your love, O life of Jesus, Savior of the world for all the saints. Most merciful Jesus, through the pain of your blessed and most bitter Passion, grant me the light of understanding, and to pre-taste the rays of light with a humble and pure conscience of your love. Have mercy on me, good Jesus, fountain of clemency, abyss of piety, and fullness of graces, light of the heavenly citizens; infuse into me the most sweet and delightful taste of holy charity. Deliver me, O Searcher of all hearts, and give me joy with purity and exultation in your praises, glorifying you because you have healed me by the pain of your wounds. What shall I return to your charity, my Redeemer, my Quickener? I suffer with you, weeping, and blessing your most happy passion and the holy wounds of your body. Most kind Savior Jesus, I give immortal thanks, asking for the pardon of my crimes. In the year of the Lord 1500, on the 13th of the Kalends of May <note>April 19, 1500</note>, I, Johannes Trithemius <note>original: "ἐγὼ ἰωαννης τριτήμιος"</note>, wrote this prayer. C.*

### CHAPTER XXI.

## WHOSE HOUR IS CALLED ZESCHAR, AND ITS SPIRIT IS CALLED PAMIEL, HAVING MANY PRINCES UNDER HIM.

The ninth hour of the night is called Zeschar, and its supreme angel and Emperor is called Pamiel. Following the manner of those preceding him, he has under his command many other spirits—both good and bad—including princes, dukes, counts, and attendants <term>ministeriales: lower-ranking officials or servants in a courtly structure</term> assigned by their turns and ranks. However, in our operations of Steganography, we do not require all of these, as a few are sufficient for us.

# BOOK TWO.

Here we now have 18 princes from the spirits of <term>Pamiel</term><note>In Trithemius's system, Pamiel is the name of a planetary or hourly spirit governing a specific set of ciphers.</note>, who by their turns are sometimes leaders and sometimes counts. ### *The Conjuration*

->**Pamyel lyraz lafian mavelo breothis Thirmoan erfoti layr pornis Theori moar azas penason.**<-
<note>original: "Pamyel lyraz lafian mavelo breothis Thirmoan erfoti layr pornis Theori moar azas penason." This string of words appears to be gibberish but serves as the ciphertext or key for the following explanation.</note>

### *The Key & Meaning.*

->llrAzMaVeLoThIrMoAnLalrTHeORiAzAsLaFiAnBrEoThIs ErSoTiPoRnIsMoAr. *Meaning.* Now the last letter of the alphabet is the first.<-
<note>The rule "the last letter of the alphabet is the first" indicates a reversal or Atbash-style substitution cipher (where A=Z, B=Y, etc.) is being used to decode the message.</note>

Then, once everything prescribed in the art is completed, say the conjuration itself, taking the greatest care not to omit any of those things required for the perfection of the operation. Once the conjuration has been spoken, the spirits will immediately appear visible in whatever form you commanded them to take; for all those we have named are benevolent, good, prompt, ready to obey the one operating correctly, and faithful in their commissions.

### *The Secret Argument.*

Whenever any secret occurs to us which we cannot otherwise safely make known to a friend, either by letter or by messenger, we first commit it to the spirits appearing to us, and we are secure; the one who is more powerful among the others is distinguished by his clothing and a crown.
<note>This "Secret Argument" explains that the "spirits" are actually the encoded messages themselves. The "spirit with a crown" likely refers to the primary key or the first letter of a sequence.</note>

### CHAPTER XXII.

#### THE HOUR WHICH IS CALLED MALCHO, WHOSE SUPREME ANGELIC EMPEROR IS NAMED JASGUARIM, WHO HAS UNDER HIS COMMAND MANY PRINCES, DUKES, COUNTS, AND SERVANTS.

The tenth hour of the night is called Malcho, and its supreme angelic Emperor is named Jasguarim. He has under his command many princes, dukes, counts, and servants assigned to wonderful and diverse magical operations, just as Solomon, also known as Hermes <note>Trithemius often identifies King Solomon with Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>, testifies in his secret of Magic. Appointed to Steganography <note>Here referring to Trithemius’s system of secret communication through the invocation of spirits.</note> by their turns and ranks are 100 dukes, 100 counts, and many servants, such as:

| R. | | R. | R. | | R. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Lapheriel | Chameray | 30 | 100 | 100 | 300 |
| Emarziel | Hazaniel | 30 | 100 | 100 | 300 |
| Nameroyz | Vraniel | 30 | 100 | 100 | 300 |

However, although there are many dukes and counts appointed for the work of Steganography in the tenth hour of the night, since a few suffice for all our purposes, we have listed three from the dukes and likewise three from the counts by name in this table, adding the number of their servants lawfully distributed by turns and rank. Whoever wishes to know the names of more should call upon one of the aforementioned spirits and question him about each one. When you wish to work through these spirits in the tenth hour of the night, observe and do all that has been commanded, most diligently writing everything on a clean sheet of paper, and on its back, write that conjuration in the manner which has been commanded.

->The Key.<-

Hitherto, both in the first and the present book, we have applied only the individual first letters of certain words to the hidden secret. Now, the method is handed down whereby the entire first syllables of certain words serve the purpose of the secret. This is a general method; to break it down into specialized types (as was done with the letters) is a task of neither little labor nor necessity. The Author provides a single example: where, three empty lines being omitted from the beginning and the end, the first word of the fourth line is irrelevant to the secret, but the first syllable of the second word serves the intended purpose, and so on following that pattern.

...nearly infinite ministerial spirits, yet the chiefs themselves are beyond measure benevolent, cheerful, and pleasant; they delight in conversing with men and are most obedient to those who are well-instructed in the operation of this art. And note, that the number of these chiefs is infinite, because almost the entire air is filled with them and they cannot be counted. Solomon and Hermes <note>A reference to King Solomon and Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founding figures of Western occult and hermetic traditions.</note> say—and we have experienced it ourselves—that among the chiefs, counts, and ministerial spirits of **Dardariel** <note>The spirit governing the eleventh hour of the night.</note>, many are good, useful, and most honorable. These always desire to benefit men, constantly urging them by a certain invisible Mastery toward good, toward honesty, peace, and concord; toward the integrity of faith, the love of God, the observance of His commandments, contempt for the world, the desire for celestial happiness, and toward every good thing.

These are the good and most holy spirits who love, worship, and possess God; they delight in being with holy men and those who fear God, because they are assigned to them as protectors by God, the creator of all things. Conversely, there are enemies <note>referring to fallen or malignant spirits</note> who continually tempt mortals and lie in wait for men; whatever good the holy spirits establish for the honor of God, these others always strive to destroy and revoke. The air is full of these malignant spirits; they run and scurry invisibly among men, always inciting them to evil, and they drag the unwary with them to hell. Through these evil spirits of Dardariel, infinite wicked deeds are performed, not only among Christians but also among the unfaithful. They especially deceive ignorant women <note>original: "mulierculas," a diminutive often used in this period to suggest those perceived as intellectually or spiritually weak</note> who are more prone to malice; whoever wishes to persist in sorcery through them will be powerful in evil above all other sorcerers and worthy of the eternal fire.

We, however, who desire always to teach and work not evil but good according to our strength, let us set down a few chiefs as messengers for us from the good spirits, not the evil ones.

<header>BOOK TWO.</header>

From the good spirits of **Dardariel**, we have therefore named here fourteen chiefs and seven counts, who are sufficient for us for every operation of Steganography for the eleventh hour of the night, along with their many and almost infinite servants. When, therefore, you wish to operate through any one or several of them, perform all things that are prescribed in the art of Steganography, and after you have completed all, recite this conjuration with attention.

### Key.

In the previous chapter [we used] syllables; now we insert whole words of the secret meaning into manifest and unsuspecting letters with such cunning that neither the connection, nor the sense hidden beneath them, can be detected by any reason or probability. This method is also varied by so many differences that it is impossible to examine them all and publish them in writing; for this science is a chaos of infinite depth, which no one can perfectly comprehend. However much you may be learned and experienced in this art, you will nonetheless always have grasped less than that which you do not know. For this profound and most secret art has this property: it easily makes a disciple incomparably more learned—so to speak—than the master, provided he is naturally disposed to proceed and is studious in those things which he perceives in the Cabalistic tradition <note>referring to the "Kabbalah," a Jewish mystical tradition which Trithemius adapted for his systems of cryptography and angel-magic</note>. Therefore, in this chapter, it prescribes one method in which three lines at the beginning and at the end are vacant <note>meaning they contain no hidden data</note>; in the remaining lines, the second and the second-to-last words are the ones that carry the value.

### Conjuration 1.

> Dardariel pirno **Nadeuym** pornis melto , nachir pheon pliros evali estafri **Thyrmauo**,oniel **Maviel** vear Rabi cralnoti vemy **Throe** orbafiel asar **Ravean**, purgiel near jano masiel arlay **Nasevi** myrsos modias merchul, noti penason.

### *The matter to be entrusted.*

All the above-mentioned dukes and counts are good and faithful, harming no one at all who loves God in truth; therefore, entrust to them whatever you wish to announce in the eleventh hour of the night to a friend, whether nearby or far away, hesitating in nothing according to the art.

### *Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Cornelius Gyrardi of Gouda, Canon of Saint Augustine near Leiden, sends greetings.*

*Our Lord Jesus Christ, the most gentle savior of our souls, promised us the happiness of eternal consolation, if we always observe His commandments with a pure heart; you therefore, dearest brother, **GUARD** the commandments of God and of the holy rule **DILIGENTLY**, because unless you have kept **ALL** things inviolate until death **WHICH** almighty God has commanded **TO YOU**: you shall perish by eternal death: for that reason **I HAVE DELIVERED** to you the form **AND** law of religious and holy conversation. **BEWARE** therefore diligently, **LEST** you **GIVE** your heart **TO ANYONE** mortal creature to be possessed through the desire of love; because no one comes to **THOSE** supreme joys, **UNLESS** he who despises the world for God; therefore again **THROUGH** these my **LETTERS** I urge you, as a most dear friend, that you observe for **YOURSELF** my warnings **WHICH** I have made, for I consider myself happy when **I SHALL HAVE WRITTEN** something good **AT THIS** sacred time, especially for the building up of the **WAY** of living well **BY WHICH** you may always be made better; therefore **NOW** again I **WRITE** to you for your own good, because I **FEAR** your danger no less than **MY OWN**, but I pray you always watch so that you may profit daily in the fear of God, **AND** living innocently, harming **NO ONE**, and **ALTOGETHER** persevering in your holy purpose, **DO NOT TRUST** in time, nor fortune, nor age, because they are nothing **UNLESS** they are smoke; in truth **I** love you sincerely in Christ Jesus, praying that **HE HIMSELF** may also ordain that **I MAY BE** beloved to you, and I who am absent from you in body may always be **PRESENT** in spirit; whence, since I have a constant memory of you in my prayers, I vehemently pray that you do not forget me. Farewell. April 20th <note>original: "12. Calend. Maji," the 12th day before the Calends of May</note>, in the year 1509.*

### CHAPTER XXIV.

### THE TWELFTH HOUR IS CALLED XEPHAN, AND ITS ANGEL IS CALLED THE SUPREME RULER SARANDIEL, HAVING UNDER HIM MANY PRINCES, DUKES, COUNTS, AND SERVANTS.

The twelfth hour of the night, which touches the dawn, is called Xephan, and its angel is named Sarandiel. He has under his command many spirits, both good and evil—princes, dukes, counts, and officials—who are assigned to various operations: the good to good deeds, and the evil to evil deeds. These princes (as Hermes the Hebrew <note>original: "Hermes Hebræus"</note>, who is called Solomon, says in the fourth book on the offices of spirits) are often accustomed to appear in that form in which we read the Devil appeared to Eve: having one beautiful head like a virgin’s, with hair hanging down on both sides, but having two serpentine bodies. These they always veil and hide beneath various coverings and foliage lest they be seen. In their faces, however, they are most beautiful, benevolent, and pleasant, and they are most ready and cheerful in performing every obedience for the practitioner.

### *The Arrangement for Announcing the Secret.*

When you see the spirits standing by you in a foreign form, do not be terrified, for they are good and benevolent, harming no one. They almost always hide their monstrous forms—lest they frighten anyone—appearing with most beautiful faces. Commit securely to them whatever you wish a friend to know during the hour of night. <note>Trithemius uses the metaphor of "spirits" to describe the process of sending a message; the "foreign form" refers to the encoded text that looks strange to the uninitiated.</note>

### *Let the letters be formed as you please.*

*O Wretched man and truly miserable, why do you not attend to the instability of all temporal things, and why do you not think that you will die shortly? Remember what the first man **DESERVED**, because he violated the commandment; if only **JUST AS** he desired, **MAY DIE** our soul the death of the righteous, **SO THAT** despising **PRESENT** pleasures and the vain honors of the world, **WE MAY BE** immaculate, guarding **OURSELVES** from every sin; but we do not care **UNTIL** at last we fall into the horrendous **BONDS** of death, to be tortured **FOR** eternity. I judge **THAT** man happy who foresees these things. Therefore, O man, **CAST AWAY** the world, just as **DID** the Son of God, and think how many **EVILS** follow us out of love for it. For it brings **MANY** dangers upon us, and **BECAUSE** it **IS** damnable to its lovers, it is rightly despised. Truly **WORTHY** of eternal **DEATH** is the lover of the world. What does **THIS** miserable world profit you, **O MAN**, which flees while it is loved; passes away while it is present; casts down while it exalts; deceives while it flatters; withers while it flourishes; and when it sends away its lovers, it transmits them to perpetual miseries. In the year 1500, on the 20th of April.* <note>original date: "Anno M. D. 12. Cal. Maji." — The 12th day before the Kalends of May is April 20th.</note>

## CHAPTER XXV.

### IN WHICH WE WILL TEACH THE METHOD AND GENERAL FORM FOR APPROACHING THIS ART OF STEGANOGRAPHY, AND FOR OPERATING WITHIN IT WITHOUT DANGER AND WITH THE GREATEST BENEFIT.

Whoever desires to approach the knowledge of this our secret art; whoever chooses to work through it wonders that are advantageous to many and free from dangers, it is first necessary for him to be adorned with virtues and a clean conscience, and of good will toward God, toward himself, and toward his neighbor. He must not be inclined to harm anyone, nor seek shameful dealings. Then, it is necessary that he be somewhat educated in the liberal arts, and especially in the science of the stars <note>original: "scientia astrorum," referring here to both astronomy and astrology, which were inextricably linked in the Renaissance.</note>, so that he may know the general movements, courses, paths, changes, orders, natures, positions, risings, settings, and effects of the stars, signs, and planets. Without a competent knowledge of these things, no one can have access to the depths of this art.

Consequently, it is necessary that he have a teacher <term>preceptor|A master or expert instructor who guides the student through the complexities of the art.</term> who is perfect and experienced in the art. We believe it is possible for only a few—and those the most learned in many things and skilled in magic—to come to this knowledge without a teacher. Moreover, the teacher must be proven and experienced not only in knowledge, but also faithful, upright, and God-fearing: because the more he lives in good conversation with God,

In Trithemius’s system, these "spirits" are often metaphors for the cryptographic keys and procedures themselves, though they are presented here in the guise of traditional magic to emphasize the weight of the work.</note> obey virtues. Therefore, when anyone is about to approach this art, let the preceptor <note>original: "praeceptor," the teacher or master of the art.</note> take him and lead him into some secret and clean place; let the weather be calm and clear, with the moon in full opposition <note>original: "lunâ in oppositione completa," meaning a full moon.</note> and the sun shining brightly. And let Mercury be in the Ascendant <note>The "Ascendant" is the sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time.</note> conjoined with Venus or Jupiter, if possible; and let Saturn and Mars be far away: for if they, or either of them, should be with the Ascendant, the instruction will not be perfect. > I, [Name], swear and promise by the power of almighty GOD, by the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment, and by the salvation of my soul in the holy catholic faith, to almighty GOD, to the Blessed Virgin, to all the Saints, and to you, [Name], that I will faithfully keep this art of Steganography <note>original: "Steganographiæ." So help me GOD, and so save me at the final judgment.

Then let the preceptor read the following conjuration in the mystical language <note>original: "lingua mystica." This refers to the coded, often nonsensical-sounding Latin or Greek used to mask the actual cryptographic instructions.</note>, and let him interpret it and all the conjurations contained in this work in the presence of the disciple: lest he suspect that anything is diabolical, superstitious, or contrary to GOD, or that a pact with demons is implicitly or explicitly hidden within it in any way.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF STEGANOGRAPHY.

### The Meaning of the General Conjuration.

All the methods of this art can be varied endlessly in every way by rearranging letters and words, and even without any shifting <note>original: "translatione"; here referring to the physical movement or transposition of letters within the cipher text</note> at all, just as it pleases the industrious practitioner who is well-trained and fluent in Latin vocabulary.

Once the master of this art has explained the conjurations of all the spirits <note>Trithemius uses the names of "spirits" or "angels" as metaphors for specific cryptographic keys or algorithms. To an outsider, the text looks like magic; to the initiated, it is mathematics.</note>, their order, and their sequence to his disciple, let him reveal the most hidden secrets of this science. These secrets are neither written down nor should they ever be written. He must forbid the disciple, under a solemn oath, from revealing them to anyone for as long as he lives, except to those who are worthy and sworn into the art; nor should he write them down by any means or for any reason. Then, let him teach him the natures, names, locations, numbers, duties, and properties of all the spirits assigned to this art: how, when, and where one must work through them, and the remaining mysteries that belong to the perfection of this art, which must not be committed to writing.

->PREFACE.<-

After we have completed the first two books of our art with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the souls of the faithful—in which we have described our Steganography <note>The title comes from the Greek words *steganos* (hidden) and *graphein* (to write). While it sounds like magic, Trithemius is describing the science of cryptography.</note> in some fashion—it is necessary for us to join this third book to them, and to couple even more wonderful things to those wonderful inventions already found. I discovered in a certain book by a certain ancient philosopher, who is called Menastor <note>scholars believe "Menastor" may be a pseudonym or a fictional authority created by Trithemius to lend an air of ancient mystery to his cryptographic methods</note>, that it is possible through a certain art to make the concept of our mind known to a friend, no matter how far away they may be, within twenty-four hours, without letters and without a messenger, most perfectly, most fully, and most secretly. Since I was led by a most vehement desire for knowledge, I began to wish to test the truth of these claims, and after much labor, I finally found the science itself proven by experience. 

The secret of this kind of art is very great, and wrapped in such obscurities that it is not easily accessible to anyone; for Menastor involved the mystery in too much obscurity and too few words, and used such efforts to ensure the secret remained hidden that, until now, no one has been found after him who dared to make his discourse clearer by any instruction. I, however, fearing that such a wonderful work might be despised by the unskilled because of its extreme obscurity, or eventually be burned in a fire—since I have long been experienced in it through many trials—[have decided to write] it down in let- <note>The text breaks here mid-word; the Latin "lite-" is completed by the catchword "ris" on the next page, forming "literis," meaning "letters" or "writings."</note>

<summary>This page serves as the formal dedication and preface to the third book of Steganographia, addressed to Prince Philip. Trithemius introduces a method for near-instantaneous long-distance communication without physical messengers, which he claims to have rediscovered from an ancient philosopher.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Trithemius, Prince Philip of the Palatinate, Steganography, Menastor, long-distance communication, cryptography history, secret knowledge</keywords>

...to entrust <note>The Latin text here picks up mid-sentence from the previous page: *commendaris* or *tradideris*, meaning "to entrust" or "to hand over."</note> in more open terms, so that with God’s help it might become accessible to some extent to learned men and those most devoted to the study of magic <term>magic: in the 15th century, "natural magic" referred to the study of the hidden forces of nature and the universe, distinct from forbidden sorcery</term>, and yet remain hidden at all times from the unskilled Rapophagi <note>original: "Rapophagis". Literally "turnip-eaters," this was a favorite derogatory term used by Trithemius to describe the uneducated or those he deemed intellectually unworthy of his secrets.</note>, and in no way known to their dull intellect.

Moreover, Menastor said: there are seven planets, over which seven angels preside, and to them twenty-one spirits are subject, through whom secrets are announced.

# BOOK THREE.

<note>This table concludes the list of spirits and numerical values started on the previous page. These names and numbers serve as the "keys" for the cryptographic system described in this book.</note>

These are the seven Angels of the planets according to the tradition of the ancient sages, each of whom leads the world for three hundred fifty-four years and four months <note>This period—354 years and 4 months—is a "great year" based on the lunar calendar (354 days). Trithemius developed this chronological theory more fully in his work *De Septem Secundeis*.</note> in their proper order. Orifiel is the angel of Saturn, who from the beginning of creation governed the world for 354 years and 4 months; afterwards Venus ruled, then Jupiter, after him Mercury, and then Mars, then the Moon, and finally the Sun. Each is described as having held the Dominion of the World for 354 years and 4 months under their own Angel as written in the common table. 

Thus, the sages say that at the time of the Great Flood, Samael, the angel of Mars, served in the Office of Government; Gabriel, however, the angel of the Moon, ruled at the time of the confusion of tongues <note>The biblical story of the Tower of Babel.</note>; and Michael, the angel of the Sun, ruled at the time of Israel's departure from Egypt. Indeed, if anyone places faith in the aforementioned system, he will be able to easily calculate by himself the changes of times and the governance of the Angels from the origin of the world down to his own age according to the prescribed order. 

We, however, pursuing those things which serve our purpose, do not doubt that there are 21 other spirits subject to the seven aforementioned Angels of the planets—that is, three spirits for each one—according to the instruction of this art of ours, through whom we work the effect of our intention. We shall observe the customary order of the planets, beginning from Saturn, the highest of all, down to the Moon, first describing the operation of each principal Angel, and then those of the subservient spirits, joining the chapters together in order.

### CHAPTER I.

## CONCERNING ORIFIEL, THE FIRST AND HIGHEST ANGEL OF SATURN, AND THE OPERATIONS PERFORMED THROUGH HIM.

Saturn, the highest and loftiest of all the planets, is by nature slow in motion and cold because he is so remote. He is difficult and heavy; from the point of his beginning he moves 650 [units], remaining for 30 months at the point of his first station in any given sign, and moves 626 by his own natural motion. His first and highest angel, according to the opinion of the ancients, is called Orifiel, who has under him three other principal spirits, namely: Sadach, Poniel, and Morifiel, of whom we shall speak in their own place and order. 

Through this Orifiel, the great angel of Saturn, many and diverse operations are performed in <term>Steganographia: Derived from the Greek *steganos* (hidden/covered) and *graphein* (to write), this is the art of hiding a secret message within another text or through seemingly magical means.</term>. Through him, we can make the secret of our mind known to a friend who knows this art, wherever he may be, by means of letters if it pleases, or even without letters, and perform many other wonders which no one else understands who [is not trained] in this our science... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

...if he should be unskilled; Therefore, one wishing to perform any work through this angel in <term>Steganography<note>Original: *Steganographia*. While literally "hidden writing," Trithemius uses it to describe his system of secret communication through the names of planetary spirits.</note></term>, especially on the day of Saturn, and in those matters, businesses, and causes which pertain to Saturn, it is first necessary that you know its various and diverse movements; and first the various [movements]: pure, proper, mixed, direct, retrograde, and confused. And in all these things, it is necessary to know not only the general rules handed down by the astronomers (because although they are extremely helpful to this science of ours, they are nevertheless not entirely sufficient) but also the specific ones. Therefore, as a foundation, having presupposed the tables and rules of the planetary motions—which it is absolutely necessary for one working in this art to know—we have added special rules and tables of <term>point movements<note>Original: *punctualium motuum*. These are numerical values assigned to specific moments in time, used as keys to encode or decode messages.</note></term> through the individual chapters of this work, without the observation of which no one will be able to work in this art. And note, that the day of any planet is divided into four equal parts, the first of which—that is, three <term>unequal hours<note>Unequal hours (also called "temporal hours") are a traditional system where the period of daylight is divided into 12 equal hours regardless of the season. Thus, an "hour" in summer is much longer than an "hour" in winter.</note></term>—the principal angel of that planet holds; and his substitutes follow the remaining three parts in order: For example, on the day of Saturn, Orifiel, its first angel, possesses three unequal hours from sunrise (which are called planetary hours); his first subordinate angel, Sadaël, holds the second three; Poniel, the second, holds the third; and Morifiel, the third angel of Orifiel, holds the fourth three hours. Under the first three hours of the day—of Saturn as well as the other stars—one must work through Orifiel in matters appropriated to Saturn; under the second through Sadaël; under the third through Poniel; and under the final three through Morifiel. All operations receive either a successful or a weak effect according to the movement of Saturn. But now, let us set down the point table.

Once the <term>mean motion</term><note>The average speed at which a planet travels, ignoring the complexities of its actual elliptical orbit.</note> of Saturn for a specific day, degree, and hour is known from the common tables, you should know that first of all, it must be carefully observed whether it is direct, retrograde, pure, proper, mixed, or confused. You will find this in the common tables; for this reason, we have organized the prescribed table in which you can find the starting and ending points of its motion at any hour, with the intervening degrees divided simultaneously into smaller parts. 

Specifically, this is done so that every minute is divided into two, three, or four hourly parts, according to the proportion of the <term>pure or confused motion</term><note>Pure motion refers to a planet acting alone; "confused" or mixed motion refers to a planet's influence being modified by its proximity to other celestial bodies.</note>—that is, by observing the <term>conjunction and separation</term><note>Terms for when planets appear to meet in the sky or move apart.</note> of other planets. For it is impossible for you to achieve the effect of this art either through the stars or through the <term>spirits of the stars</term><note>Trithemius claims his ciphers are sent via planetary spirits, a controversial idea that led to accusations of magic, though many scholars believe the "spirits" were themselves part of the code.</note> unless you have identified and most diligently observed the exact motion. You must know how to precisely arrange your operations according to the specific qualities of the planets: for in different degrees, signs, days, hours, minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths, the effects of the planets vary in different ways with regard to this science. In every single degree, we have observed and found 25 different changes, from which and

It seemed necessary to us to divide any given degree into an equal number of principal parts. However, this division does not take place through all degrees, but only in those in which the stars conducive to this art of ours arise. It is through these stars that the operation is performed for signaling anything we wish to those who are absent, by the <term>ministry of spirits</term><note>While Trithemius speaks of spirits, he is often describing a method of encoding information within a text that appears to be about summoning spirits.</note> and without the use of letters <note>original: "sine literis" — this refers to a method where the secret message is not written in plain text but is encoded through mathematical or astrological variables.</note>, just as we shall explain. Thus, the first table of the division of the degrees of Saturn's motion, which we have placed before this, serves the first quarter of the day or night perpetually in those matters pertaining to the operation of Saturn and his <term>princes</term><note>In the context of the Steganographia, "princes" refers to the primary spirits or entities associated with a specific planet.</note>; the second table serves the second three hours, the third table the third, and the fourth table the fourth. Next, we have added the order of points for the motion of Saturn itself in the <term>ascendant</term><note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note>, specifically when it is in one of the first four signs—which are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer. We will also arrange a subsequent table for the remaining eight signs.

# ON THE VARIOUS MOTION OF THE PLANETS, AND THE INTERPRETATION OF THE TABLES.

Although in the present chapter we must provide a special treatise concerning the motions of **Saturn** and its spirits, and the operations in **Steganography** <note>In this context, Trithemius uses "Steganography" to refer to his system of "hidden writing" disguised as planetary magic.</note> performed through them, the studious reader should nonetheless be warned to remember what we say in this very chapter for those that follow, lest we be forced to repeat what has been aptly stated once in every single chapter. There are indeed various motions for each of the planets, and they are divided most subtly into all sorts of others. The **pure and proper motion** <note>original: "motus purus et proprius"</note> is manifold, and is varied by various subtle divisions: direct, retrograde, mixed, and confused. These are varied by almost as many points as they are pulled apart from the beginning of their motion in the circle. What shall I say of the conjunction of these planets with one another? For as **Ptolemy** says in his <term>Centiloquium</term> <note>original: "gentiloquio." The Centiloquium is a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>, there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions among these planets: namely, 21 binary, 35 ternary, 35 quaternary, 21 quinary, 7 senary, and one septenary <note>These represent the mathematical combinations of the seven traditional planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) taken in groups of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or all 7.</note>. We shall speak of these in their proper place. Regarding the other motions, however, although we cannot give a certain limit because of the infinite diversity—not knowing the daily increasing or decreasing points by which they are varied—we have nonetheless found, as far as we have been able to observe, more than 300,000 divisions. In these, all operations of this art often vary in their effect. Unless one is highly experienced in all these matters and perfectly understands the mean motions of these planets, and then the most minute <term>punctual divisions</term> [precise numerical units] which come from fourths, thirds, seconds, minutes, and unequal degrees most subtly divided, he will easily fall into true errors and will hardly escape grave danger.

Therefore, for the perfect instruction of this science, we have arranged three tables. In the first of these, we have reduced the motion of **Saturn**—according to the four parts of both day and night, namely the proper and pure motion—to a <term>root</term> [a base number for calculation] and have arranged it to the true point of any <term>ascending sign</term> [the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon]. Beginning from the first degree of **Aries** at point 641, ♈︎ ♉︎ ♊︎ and ♋︎ <note>The symbols for Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer.</note>, we have encompassed the entire Zodiac in the second table. Then, in that same second table, we have arranged the motion of **Saturn** in each of the twelve signs for all quarters of the day and night. We have digested this into such small details that at any hour, the degree of the ascendant in which **Saturn** happens to be—

Saturn itself, once known, can clearly reveal its own **point-based root** <note>original: "radix ipsius punctualis." In Trithemius's system, "points" often refer to specific numerical values or positions in a cipher key.</note>; however, once the calculation of someone's table is finished—and I do not know if our age can ever fully attain this—the table must be started again from the very beginning. In the third table, we have reduced the **sevenfold conjunction** of Saturn with the other planets (which is unique) to the proportion of a point; through this, all one hundred and twenty conjunctions are easily reduced to a point. In the same table, the **pure motion** of all the planets is recognized through the point-based division of any beginning, progression, and distance from the point in any motion, provided that the **mean motion** <term>mean motion: the average or uniform motion of a planet, as opposed to its apparent or "true" motion which varies</term> is first perfectly grasped. For without the knowledge of the mean motion, it is impossible for anyone to be able to approach the practice of this science. Furthermore, even if you understand both the mean and true motion perfectly, it will profit you nothing toward the knowledge of this science unless you understand the three prescribed tables for all the points of division in the motions of the planets—taken equally from unequal degrees—down to the individual minutes in their entirety. But now, let us proceed to the operation.

When all these things we have said (and what we are about to say with the **help of God** <note>original: "auxiliante DEO"</note>) are known and perfectly understood, and when you wish to operate in this most profound speculation: first, you must know the rising, the exaltation, and the setting of all the stars of the **eighth sphere** <note>In the Ptolemaic universe, the eighth sphere is the firmament containing the fixed stars, located beyond the seven spheres of the planets.</note>, through which the operation is performed, and how far each is distant from another. There are, moreover, stars through which we work to announce any secret to one who is absent—without words, without writing, and without a human messenger—numbering seven hundred in total. We have described their names, locations, rising, setting, elevations, distances, approaches, and retreats in a special book, which would be too tedious for the student to repeat here by inserting them again. # CONCERNING THE FIRST ANGEL OF SATURN, WHO IS THE CHIEF, AND IS CALLED ORIFIEL, WHO OBSERVES THE FIRST QUARTER OF SATURN.

**T**he first and chief angel of Saturn, as we have said in the preceding pages, is called **Orifiel**. He, along with the other angels of the planets, rules the world in his proper order for 354 years and four months. He holds the first part both in the day and in the night. Through him, the operation is performed from sunrise during the day and from sunset at night, up to the third hour inclusively, in all matters that pertain to Saturn and in his day and night, as we have stated. 

Therefore, when you wish to announce <note>original: "nunciare." In the context of Trithemius's Steganography, this refers to the occult transmission of messages to a distant person.</note> something to an absent person during the first quarter of Saturn without words and without letters, then no other spirit of Saturn must be called by you than **Orifiel**, because through him you will be able to announce all things most perfectly. 

First, consider in which zodiacal sign this Saturn is located, and in what degree, and whether it is **direct** <term>Direct: The standard forward motion of a planet through the zodiac.</term> or **retrograde** <term>Retrograde: When a planet appears to move backward in the sky, often interpreted as a time of weakened or inverted influence.</term>, and with which planets it forms a **conjunction** <term>Conjunction: An astrological aspect where two planets are in the same degree of the zodiac, combining their powers.</term>. 

Let us set an example of the first: Behold, Saturn is now in the 25th degree of Taurus on the 28th day of the month of April in the present year, which is 1500 AD. Now, therefore, let us multiply 25 by 25, which makes 600 <note>original: "ducamus 25 per 25, & fiunt 600." Mathematically 25 x 25 is 625; the author may be rounding or using a specific numerological reduction common in Renaissance magic.</note>. Let us divide these by four equal quarters, and 150 will remain for each quarter. Let us complete all the degrees of Saturn in the sign of Taurus, which will be 30. Let us multiply another 30 by 25 in total, and they become 750. Let us discard four superfluous degrees from the middle of the third quarter, and 650 will remain. Let us now take the point of Saturn's motion from the table for the present day and hour, and we will be able to know what the rising, elevation, and setting of the Angel **Orifiel** is, with Saturn in the first quarter. Once these are known, our operation will be easy.

The second angel of Saturn is called Sadael, who is established as the first under Orifiel in order, and he holds the second portion after his prince, both in the day and in the night, in the works and times of Saturn. # JOANNES TRITHEMIUS,
## FIRST ABBOT OF SPONHEIM AND LATER OF SAINT JAMES IN WÜRZBURG,
# STEGANOGRAPHY ILLUSTRATED.

---

### PREFACE.

We saw in *Steganography Defended*, how *Trithemius*, through his incomparable sharp-wittedness of mind, conceived—among other things—a most subtle work of <term>Steganography<note>From the Greek 'steganos' (hidden/covered) and 'graphein' (to write); the art of secret communication. To contemporaries, it often looked like magic.</note></term> of wonderful invention, and intended to bring it forth into the world. We saw from the *Chronicle of Sponheim* <note>Latin: "Chronicon Spanheimense." A history of the monastery written by Trithemius himself.</note> how in the year 1499 he wrote a letter containing the material and arrangement of this future work to *Arnold Bostius*, a Carmelite in **Ghent**; and, since it had happened in the meantime that *Bostius* himself had departed this life without *Trithemius* knowing, how that letter was opened and read by the Prior of the Convent in **Ghent**. 

It was spread abroad as if it were a miracle, and in a short time published throughout all **France** and **Germany** before many Princes and most learned men, copied out, and read with the greatest admiration of all. Regarded as a new and unheard-of miracle, it excited various judgments in the minds of men: some proclaimed *Trithemius* a divine man, others a most learned one, and others a magician and necromancer. 

We saw from the preface to <term>Polygraphia<note>Trithemius's later, more technical work on cryptography, written to prove his methods were linguistic rather than demonic.</note></term> how in the year 1500 he began to write the eight books of mysteries in *Steganography*. However, while he was continuing his work on the third book of that same project, it happened that **Carolus Bovillus**, a **Picard** <note>Charles de Bovelles (1479–1567), a French philosopher and mathematician.</note> by nation, having traveled through the upper regions of **Alsace**, came to *Trithemius* at **Sponheim** for the sake of hospitality, planning to return to **France** via **Trier**. Having been received with every kindness, and having looked over—among other things shown to him—the aforementioned work of *Steganography* (which was not yet finished), he read it only in passing, his mind occupied with other things. Nor did he take care to understand the manner in which it was to be understood; and so, after returning to **France**, he returned evil for

<header>PREFACE.</header>

*...returned for good, and having been asked by Germain de Ganay (who was later Bishop of Orleans) what he had found at Trithemius’s place, he wrote back falsehoods instead of truths, and lies in exchange for kindnesses. Writing letters to the aforementioned most learned man, he filled them with falsity, lies, insults, and many affronts; making mention of the Steganography—which he did not understand—he proclaimed Trithemius to be devoted to wicked arts, a magician, and a necromancer, doing so falsely, deceitfully, and most injuriously with rash presumption.* 

*We saw, finally, how these very insults and blasphemies of Bovillus <note>Charles de Bovelles (1479–1567), a French philosopher who visited Trithemius and later denounced him as a sorcerer.</note> (which I report with sorrow) were the reason why the admirable work of Steganography was not completed by the Author, but lies hidden forever, buried together with his most subtle inventions within the friend of Trithemius. It is a matter certainly to be deplored by the entire Republic of Letters <note>The long-distance community of intellectuals in late medieval and early modern Europe.</note>, by all schools of Steganographers, by the greatest Kings, Princes, and military Leaders, and others who use messengers as carriers of secrets—the more so because the most subtle minds of the world were frustrated and eluded in finding and solving those things which Trithemius proposed and promised.* 

*For until now, there have not been wanting most sagacious and studious men who, in scrutinizing the mysteries of nature, avoided no honorable and possible labor—and what did they profess? Some, since they could not grasp Trithemius, did not blush to carp at him, and turning to insults, they cried out that he had rashly boasted of an impossible thing. Others, after long and fruitless speculation, concluded that many things found in the context of the words by which Trithemius proposed his inventions were utterly contradictory and impossible, and that some ill-considered assertion lay hidden there. Others, by selling and substituting cheap and common arts for the inventions of Trithemius, mocked them as if they were for children; they judged it was not necessary for Trithemius to boast of that secret with such pompous, high-sounding words <term>ampullis<note>Literally "jars" or "bottles," a Latin idiom for bombastic or inflated language.</note></term>, since the secret had already become cheap through almost daily use and is open even to children. Finally, others frankly confessed their ignorance.* 

*But the opinion of all these people displeases me. For the things Trithemius promised are not impossible, nor do they suffer from ambiguity or contradiction in their words, nor are they common so as to be open to children, nor finally are they so hidden that they have not been known and discovered by others as well. Therefore, to that end, I judged this part of the edition necessary, and I have called it **Steganography Unlocked** <note>Latin: "Steganographiam Referatam." This title indicates that the author intends to explain or provide a key to Trithemius’s puzzles.</note>, not because I consider myself of such learning that I might be able to illustrate the writings or inventions of that most excellent man, but because while until now they have suffered no small amount of damage, suspicion, and [perceived] impossibility from the suspected obscurity of Steganography, I am bringing them out into the light once again...*

...for him, and I will subject [the work] to a new examination by Steganographers <note>The term "Steganographer" here refers to those who study the art of secret writing or "covered writing."</note>; I promise only this: whether I provide more, the reader shall judge. I had recently decided to treat this truly difficult and profound material with a bit more accuracy and to adorn it with the proper luster; however, it seemed that a longer time was required for that end—both to bring the material itself to maturity and because the writer is endowed with no skill or elegance in writing. Furthermore, a *Synopsis* was recently published, somewhat hastily and exceeding its set limits, which might make everyone's minds certain about the publication of this work. Therefore, I judged it necessary to treat this material in a simple style, following the manner of the other parts, trusting in the kindness of the benevolent reader, and thus satisfy the common expectation and recent promises.

### CHAPTER I.

## A COMPENDIUM OF UNIVERSAL STEGANOGRAPHY IS PRESENTED.

We read that many wise Kings and Princes of old devised various and manifold ways by which they might safely entrust the secrets of their counsel—and whatever mystery occurred that required secret confidence—to their messengers to be sent to remote places. This was done so that the messengers might be fit for carrying the messages through, and secure from every incursion of the wicked, lest either the simplicity of the Cabalists <note>original: *cabalisticorum*; here referring to those who seek hidden or mystical meanings in texts.</note> should lay bare the mystery, or the innate curiosity of the simpletons <note>original: *baucceorum*; a derogatory term for those who are foolish or meddlesome.</note> should bring harm to matters of state. The great Roman Caesar Augustus, desiring to use the service of messengers in difficult and dark matters, changed the "breath of the conceived voice" <note>Referring to the spoken or written word.</note> from clear into opaque; he made the resistant barbarism of that voice suitable at his command through the beautiful invention of an "orchestral transposition" <term>metathesis: the transposition of letters or sounds, likely referring to the "Caesar Cipher" where letters are shifted.</term>. 

That Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the prince of mathematicians, established a white bird suitable to his purposes, naked about the head and feet, and attached it around a rod <note>original: *bactro*</note> cut into the shape of a square <note>original: *tetragoni*</note>. Having organized his servants in due proportion, he entrusted the work to this winged instrument. When this was duly completed, he released with his own hand the one he had attached; once he had allowed it to fly away, suddenly a great separation occurred among the household members, and there soon arose a wandering monster of a twisted, formerly monk-like image <note>This appears to be an allegorical or legendary description of a mechanical automaton or a complex cipher device attributed to Archimedes.</note>, in whose appearance no one could think what it was. Nor did the dissension of the "owls" <note>original: *bubonum*; likely referring to the confused scholars or onlookers who "hoot" in disagreement.</note> rest, until...

...until the image of the master had skillfully bound the magpie <note>original: *picam*; possibly referring to a specific bird, but in cryptographic contexts, it often refers to a particular arrangement of type or a "pie" of jumbled characters.</note> within a similar square. Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator, employing both genius and art, transformed the subtle details of phrasing into signs. He substituted his own diligent shorthand <note>original: *thelamatos sui philergiam*; "thelamatos" likely refers to Tironian notes, an ancient Roman shorthand system, while "philergia" means a love of work or diligence.</note> or unique characters for common phrasing. 

Pharamond also, the 43rd king after Marcomer and a most powerful ruler of the Franks in Germany, ensured that all things might be done safely by binding foreign details to his secrets. Clodius "the Long-Haired" also, the son of Pharamond, imitated his father by shrouding the mysteries of his counsel in unique and foreign marks. Charlemagne, the 63rd king of the Franks after Marcomer, bound "owls" <note>original: *bubones*; in the context of Johannes Trithemius’s steganography, "owls" are a technical term for specific cryptographic methods or symbols, often framed as the names of spirits who "carry" the message.</note> to many and various details; by his art, he assigned individual "owls" to each of the kingdom's governors. 

The Northmen, having emerged from the borders of Gothia, summoned "owls" from Greece and prepared a safe hiding place for their secrets. There were those who could discern small details through visible "accidents" <term>accidents: in classical philosophy, these are non-essential qualities of a thing, such as its color, position, or size, which can be changed without changing the thing's nature.</term>; by their wisdom, night was turned into day, and light shone in the darkness without the need for the "owls'" assistance. 

Others, however, multiplying these details through a regulated division after the manner of barbarians, subverted the patterns of nature. They hid the movements <note>original: *orchemata*; from the Greek for "dances" or "rhythms."</note> of nascent things in the shadows of darkness, and when a secret counsel required it, they provided a Cabala <note>A system of secret or mystical interpretation, here used to mean a hidden code.</note> to those far away through lattice-screens <term>diapyramata: likely referring to "grille ciphers," where a card with holes is placed over a text to reveal a hidden message while the rest remains nonsensical.</term>. 

There were even those whom celestial harmony taught to compose foreign voices, which served a dual purpose for those who understood: while one use suspended the literal meaning, the other raised the mind into the heavens. Many have attempted to seek light in the shadows without light, yet they were entirely unable to do so, because the fire lies buried in the ashes. Some practiced painters of masks <note>original: *larvarum*; can mean masks, ghosts, or specters.</note> distinguished a single wind into two points; one of these, the "light-hater" <note>original: *misophos*; though the Greek roots literally mean "light-hater," the text paradoxically states he "hates darkness and loves light."</note>, hates darkness, loves the light, and guards the secret with an "owl." 

Again, as Bede <note>Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), an English monk and scholar known for his works on time-keeping and finger-counting codes.</note> testifies, there were some whose purpose, moving toward broader things, bound the wind (which is invisible to the eyes) to visible objects. They compelled many plants, as well as stones and shrubs—which lack voices—to speak with a human tongue. Why should I mention brute animals, when all things obey Art? 

And who could describe all the secret writing methods of the ancients? But even the modern world, though it has far surpassed the most ingenious inventions of the ancients, has reached such a level of subtlety that it can place and hide the very shadow of night under the light of day. This is done so that neither the night prejudices the day, nor the day raises suspicion of the night. Indeed, some of those who laid the foundations of this primary art, at that time of year when the day naturally exceeds the night, so diminished the night...

<header>STEGANOGRAPHY</header>

...immediately beneath the degrees of the day, so that with the naked eye only the degrees of the day were visible, but with a steganographic telescope <note>original: *telescopio steganographico*; in the 17th century, this often referred to a specialized viewing device or a metaphorical "lens" (a key or grid) used to reveal hidden layers of text.</note> a full minute of the night could be detected under each degree of the day. Others met with success during the equinoxes themselves, when night is equal to day, and hid the whole night under the whole day <note>In the context of this work, "Day" typically represents the overt, public message, while "Night" represents the hidden, secret message.</note>; thus, they concealed individual degrees of the night under individual degrees of the day in a wonderful proportion. Finally, others around the winter solstice, when the night exceeds the day by as much as the day exceeds the night in summer, concealed individual degrees of the night under individual minutes of the day by an admirable and almost incomprehensible invention. But even this admirable invention is varied by so many differences and extended by so many enlargements that there is no one in the world who could enumerate all the species of such a great mystery. And hence I might seem strange to some, because in the recently published synopsis I promised to exhibit the inventions of almost all steganographers in a compendium; but to such a person, when the occasion arises, I think I must respond: that it is indeed very difficult, or even hardly possible, to enumerate every person's familiar ways of writing in secret; however, it is not impossible to exhibit those which have been published by steganographic writers up to now, encompassed under certain rules and divisions—which was and is my intention in the present chapter, toward which I hasten. However, it must first be noted that I have taken "Steganography" in a general sense, which also includes "Steganology," although otherwise they are specifically distinguished from one another, as we will see shortly.

## § 1. It encompasses Steganology in a compendium.

Although Steganology <term>Steganology: from the Greek *steganos* (hidden) and *logos* (word/speech); here used to mean secret signaling or speaking in person, as opposed to writing.</term> differs and is distinguished from Steganography <term>Steganography: from the Greek *steganos* (hidden) and *graphein* (to write); the art of secret writing.</term> by its very name due to the diversity of both the word and its meaning, yet because everyone does not always agree on where particular methods should be categorized, I establish and follow this distinction in this treatise: all those methods by which something is sent to an absent person, whether it be a piece of writing or something serving the function of writing, are ascribed to **Steganography**; but when nothing is sent to an absent person, but instead something occurs in the presence of the one announcing it <note>This refers to manual signals, gestures, or spoken codes used between two people in the same room.</note>, from which the other gains knowledge of the secret, it belongs to **Steganology**. Moreover, both Steganology and Steganography can branch off into various lower species through multiple divisions, taking the difference from the reason...

<header>ILLUSTRATED.</header>

...as much by suspicion and ease of use as by time, place, convenience, and utility. I have set those aside, and in <term>Steganology</term><note>The general study or science of secret communication.</note> I establish the <term>specific difference</term><note>A logical term referring to the essential characteristic that distinguishes one category from another.</note> according to the ratio of distance, which I assign in three parts: first, "presence," which the natural human voice, when naturally uttered, can reach and be perceived; second, "medium distance," through which human sight and hearing act naturally and distinctly; and finally, "maximum distance," which is beyond the limits of said senses—for example, at 5, 10, 100, or 1000 miles and more. The divisions of <term>Steganography</term><note>The art of secret writing specifically, as opposed to the broader science of secret communication.</note> itself, however, I base on the nature of the writing.

First, therefore, we can communicate secret concepts to those present, or in the "presence of the mind." I. By the human voice naturally uttered, and in this way: 1. By a language entirely unknown and fictional, which the correspondents have adopted at their pleasure. This mode of speaking, though it is very difficult, is nonetheless entirely secure. A new language can be devised in which individual words correspond to words of a common language, or where an entire word represents only a single letter. I remember that I once adopted a language of the former kind; those of the latter kind are what Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot and polymath, famous for his pioneering works on cryptography and steganography.</note> teaches in the 3rd and 4th books of his *Polygraphia*. Although the method in Book 3 is very difficult and not recommended for speech, the method in Book 4 is pleasant and easy. 2. By a certain foreign language, provided it is unknown to those from whom the mystery must remain hidden—such as using Spanish in Germany, German in Spain, English in France, etc. But one must act cautiously in this, for besides the fact that different languages are in use in many places, such speech generates suspicion and is sometimes forbidden. 3. By a common and familiar language, but one so deformed by the transposition of syllables that it is judged to be entirely foreign. This is the kind used by Trithemius in his *Polygraphia* in these words: <note>Trithemius’s original Latin in this quote is intentionally scrambled through syllable shifting to demonstrate the method.</note> *Furthermore, his writing is done on paper or without paper with light and pen, receipts, and other various things; letters are likewise written and hidden in various ways and places, such as under floorboards, in a sunroom, in a bed in any place, in windows, in a cup, in a staff, in the ground, in hairs, and in almost infinite other similar things.* <note>original: "Ejus autem scriptura fit in charta vel sine charta cum nemilua & cala, raphocam, lapolce, aliisque rebus diversis; scribuntur item literæ ac variis modis absconduntur & locis, ut sub race tabulata, sub rosirila cubior in leopi, in necoflas, in ceocali, locubat, in ratera, in lispilia, & aliis similibus penè infinitis." Note how "nemilua" is "lumine" (light) and "cala" is "calamo" (pen) scrambled.</note> 4. A common language can also take on such novelty through the transposition, mutation, addition, and repetition of certain letters that it can neither be easily recognized by anyone, nor can the hidden secret be detected. Such modes are recounted by Janus Hercules de Sunde <note>A pseudonym for the German cryptographer Johann Balthasar Friderici (1639–1704).</note> in the first book of his *Steganography*, and others, from which I provide the following examples. By transposition: *In the month of May* <note>original: "Im maice", a transposition of "In maio".</note>

*geo mesper & maavi xe ouq rpiinum ide. &c.* <note>Scrambled Latin: "ego semper amavi te ex quo primum die"</note> which denotes: *My friend, I have always loved you, from the first day.* Likewise: *Morturiunt pantes risce- tur nadiculus mus &c.* <note>A corruption of Horace's "Parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus."</note> which signifies: *The mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born.* By mutation: *fio naulvurg io finen barteo odes bofinen andreo &c.* <note>original German: "Ein Maulwurf in einem Garten / oder an einem andern"</note> which sounds like: *A mole in a garden / or in another [place] &c.* By addition: *Itluwen itmem irrmem engen aspurgstren jehenzen* <note>original German: "Wiltu mit mir gen Straßburg ziehen"</note> which is the same as: *Will you go with me to Strasbourg?* By repetition—for example, if one were saying "fabricator" <note>builder or maker</note>, it would be said: *fababribicabatobor*; or: "My father is not at home": *Pabateber mebeubus nobon ebest dobomibi.*

5. A language can be employed such as that which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the abbot who wrote the first major works on cryptography.</note> uses in the conjurations of his *Steganographia*, where only every other letter is significant, while the rest are chosen at will. This is a very secure way of speaking, as it went undetected for such a long time, and it is easy for both the speaker and the listener—for example: *intermio nec feti dromeis.* That is: *nemo est domi* <note>no one is at home</note>. 

6. One can generally use a common language, but when a word occurs that must be hidden, express it in another language. This is how the Hebrews among us speak to one another when they mix Hebrew terms into German speech. Such also is the language the Italians call *Calman* <note>likely "Gergo," a type of slang</note> and we call *Rothwelsch* <note>A secret jargon or "thieves' cant" used by travelers and the underworld in early modern Germany.</note>. An example of this is provided by *Hercules à Sunde* <note>A pseudonym for a 17th-century writer on cryptography.</note> in *The Bearded Dialogue* between a soldier from Leming, his "Krönerin" <note>likely a term for a camp-follower or wife</note>, a tinsmith, a kettle-maker, and a tavern host who cheats at dice.

7. One can speak in a common language through enigmas, figures, and metaphors, so that it is not understood by everyone. I provide examples from *Hercules à Sunde*. Thus the Italians say: *Baldezza de patrone capello de matto* <note>original: "The master’s boldness is the fool’s hat"</note>, when they want to say that "too much familiarity breeds contempt." So too it could be said with the ancient Rabbis: *Isteri bilgina kisch kisch karie* <note>original: "A single coin in a jar makes a loud noise"</note>, meaning to signify that someone has stolen an art from another and is boasting of it as his own.

8. Finally, a secret meaning can be so interspersed and hidden within common language that there is no break in the sense nor suspicion of the subject matter. A beautiful example is provided by *Hercules à Sunde*, and from him by Father Schott <note>Caspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and mathematician who published works on ciphers.</note>, where the word following any noun of a living creature or its pronoun is the significant word. Indeed, multiple meanings can be made and distinctly pronounced, being effective from the beginning or end of all words. 

**Example.** 
N. is a good man. His will is like my will. Nothing is so dear to me as this. I will stand by him in good fortune and bad. He is desired for us. Let it happen that

<page-num>321</page-num>
# ILLUSTRATA. #

...evil or good toward [someone]. Such a friend is to be highly valued. <note>original German: "böses oder gutes Zu. Ein solcher Freund ist hoch zu Schätzen." This completes a thought from the previous page about loyal friends and secret-keeping.</note>

II. Something can be signaled to another person in a low voice, specifically:

1. By whispering into the ear of another, which should be hidden from those standing nearby; however, this method is crude, indecorous, and dangerous, and therefore should be avoided. Therefore, matters will be handled better and more securely using acoustic instruments <note>Devices designed to amplify or direct sound.</note> or techniques derived from them, which may be seen in the works of writers who specialize in this subject; I will provide a few methods from Father Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and mathematician famous for his works on "natural magic" and acoustics.</note>.

2. Thus, something can be communicated quietly to another if the speaker moves their mouth to one end of a beam—even a very long one—lying on the ground or, better yet, placed on supports, and speaks softly so that none of the bystanders perceive it, while the other person applies their ear to the opposite end.

3. If the speaker applies their mouth to one part of a polished circular surface, and the other person applies their ear to the part diametrically or nearly diametrically opposite: then, whatever the speaker says in the lowest whisper, the other will hear most distinctly, even if those standing by are talking among themselves, singing, or making all sorts of shouting and noise. The same thing also occurs in any rounded, concave, and polished structures, such as a certain round hall in the Heidelberg Castle <note>original: "arce Heidelbergiensi." This likely refers to the "Whispering Gallery" effect found in many circular architectural spaces.</note>.

4. If the walkways of long houses or halls are chosen, where a similarly polished vault is placed over two sides and parallel polished walls. If one person applies their mouth to one wall and the other applies their ear to the other wall, and they speak softly, they will hear each other.

5. Through open channels—that is, those like a concave semi-cylinder or a hollowed prism—for through these channels, whatever has been whispered into one end is carried to the other.

6. Through closed channels and covered aqueducts <note>original: "aquaeductus"</note>. The Overseers of the Roman aqueducts noted that the voices of people speaking in them could be heard at a distance of five hundred feet as if they were right there.

7. Through machines and acoustic instruments, which Father Schott described in great number throughout the second treatise of his *Acoustic Magic* <note>original: "Magia Phonotectica."</note>.

8. Through "speaking statues," which the same Father Schott described in great number and with no less ingenuity throughout the third treatise of the same *Magic*.

III. We can reveal the thoughts of our mind through various signs chosen at will; such a method is as follows:

Secondly, when something must be announced at a certain distance, we shall achieve it: I. **By various musical instruments** such as the lute, the flute, the trumpet, and similar ones, according to the distance. This can be done in two ways: 1. So that the notes on the musical scale, according to their different positions and properties, take on the duty of letters, and then a letter of the alphabet is understood when the note representing it is expressed on the instrument. See an example in Father Schott and Hercules à Sunde, but this method is very difficult and should only be put into practice by musicians; therefore, the following operation will be easier and more pleasant. 2. If, instead of individual letters of the alphabet, one, two, or three entire melodies <note>original: "cantilenae."</note> are substituted. This method will indeed be very slow, but it is nevertheless most secure and should therefore be practiced only as circumstances require. Thus, by means of a sweet flute, for example, we could signal anything to a friend sitting in prison, or to a sweetheart <note>original: "amasiae."</note> kept within domestic walls; likewise, a trumpeter in a military camp or anywhere else can announce all secrets to one who knows the art, over a fairly large distance in a short time. II. Several different musical instruments can be taken at once, and secrets can be announced through their sounds—even if the sounds are not specifically determined in relation to each other. However, the more instruments there are, the more efficient the matter becomes; for instance, if there were 24 instruments, each one could represent one letter when played once. If there were 12, each could be played once for the first twelve letters of the alphabet, and twice...
