## §. 2. *A Compendium of Steganography is Presented.*

I said above that all those methods of secret writing by which something is sent to an absent person ought to be referred to as Steganography; therefore, before all else, let us establish messengers, for without them this operation will not achieve its effect. I. Now, the name and duty of "messenger" belongs to man and almost man alone. We must choose the most faithful for carrying secrets, unless we wish to undergo danger; but who is of such sharp wit or prudence that he can search the hearts of men? Indeed, human faith is very unstable and gold blinds many; therefore, remedies must be used. Father Schott provides us with such things where he prescribes **sleep-inducing medicines** <note>original: "medicamenta soporifera"</note> by which sleep is brought upon messengers, and thus the secret is hidden according to whim and necessity. But even messengers themselves sometimes suffer suspicion or do not have free passage; therefore, messengers free from all suspicion must be chosen. Such are II. **Beggars** <note>original: "mendici"</note>, whom the Fathers of the **Council of Ephesus** <note>A major church council held in 431 AD.</note> who condemned **Nestorius** <note>The Archbishop of Constantinople who was declared a heretic for his views on the nature of Christ; his supporters blocked communication between the Council and the Emperor.</note> are said to have used. For when they wanted their sentence to be known in Constantinople, and all the gates and roads were infested by the friends of Nestorius, they gave letters hidden inside **reeds** <note>original: "calamos"; hollow walking sticks or writing quills</note> to beggars [traveling] to Constanti-

VII. Today, they also enclose letters within a **lead ball** <note>a bullet</note> and send them to the intended location via a musket or cannon. Not every method suits every situation; a choice must be made according to the circumstances.

Hitherto we have established faithful, swift, and suspicion-free messengers; now let us devise the letters to be entrusted to them. II. **Silk ribbons** <note>original: "ligulæ sericæ"</note> of various kinds and colors provide the same; they can be assigned the power of letters and joined and sent in an easy and pleasant composition to express a secret meaning.

...as Father Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and mathematician</note> relates in the cited place, section 2. **XIII.** Letters are hidden inside an egg by the following practice: A letter written on paper is cut into long strips, each containing one line of the letter. These strips are marked on the back with letters or numbers to preserve their order, then pushed one by one into a fresh egg through tiny slits of sufficient capacity made in the shell. The egg, with the slits closed up, is then sent to the recipient, either mixed with other eggs or by some other means that will not arouse suspicion. But the same thing can be achieved by another method: An egg is immersed in sharp vinegar for three, four, or more hours; when the shell has softened, the shell is opened with the edge of a knife and the egg is emptied. The paper containing the secret is pushed through the slit, and then the cut is plugged with a mixture of lime and gum. The egg is then soaked in cold water to be softened <note>The author likely means "to be tempered" or "steeped"</note>, by which the shell is restored to its original hardness.

**XIV.** A letter containing a secret can also be cut into long strips, and those strips hidden within the braids <note>original: "plegmata" — plaited or braided hair</note> or folded hair of women or men, or even horses, and so sent to the recipient.

**XV.** Finally, a letter can also lie hidden inside sweets <note>original: "bellaria" — desserts, dainties, or confectionery</note>, an example of which Father Schott tells in the cited place, chapter 4, section 8, concerning the woman **Polycrata** <note>A historical or legendary figure who allegedly smuggled a message in a cake to her brothers during a siege</note>.

Thirdly, a secret can be sent to a recipient through **open letters**—that is, letters that are not physically hidden, but which are written with **invisible characters**. These are characters that remain hidden as they are written and can only be made legible by one who knows the art, either by heat, by dusting them with powder, by immersion in water or a similar liquid, or by other means. Such writing is done on parchment, paper, cloth, eggshells, stone, crystal, etc. Therefore:

1. Invisible writing can be made that is only rendered legible again by fire: 
   1. If one writes with the juice expressed from apples, pears, peaches, grapes, lemons <note>original: "malis citreis"</note>, and similar fruits; for as the letters are written they remain hidden, but they "revive" once they are moved near a fire. 
   2. Writing done with milk performs the same way, whether it is the milk of animals or of plants, such as spurge <note>original: "tithymali"</note>, fig trees, etc. 
   3. Similar writing is made with water in which vitriol <note>Sulfate minerals used in inks</note>, alum, sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride</note>, lime, cream of tartar, camphor, or similar substances have been dissolved or tossed; for it will remain hidden and be summoned back by fire. 
   4. we will achieve the same effect if sulfur is mixed with a little salt of wine <note>original: "salis vino" — likely potassium tartrate or a similar chemical derivative</note>, and this is strained and used in place of ink. 
   5. The juice of onions and garlic has the same power: namely, that letters written with it first vanish, and are afterwards brought back by fire.

6. Juice squeezed from onions, mixed with salt and urine, at first keeps written letters hidden; later, when brought near a fire, it makes them turn black and legible.

**II.** Invisible writing can also be created that is made legible by water or another liquid. 

1. If writing is done on paper with water in which <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: *vitriolum seu calchantum* — likely iron(II) sulfate</note> has been dissolved and finely ground <term>nutgall</term> <note>original: *galla* — oak galls, which contain tannic acid</note> powder has been added, the writing will vanish at once. It will be restored when cold water is splashed on it, making the letters appear even whiter than the paper itself. 

2. Similarly, a pleasant spectacle is provided if finely ground <term>alum</term> <note>a mineral salt often used in dyeing and tanning</note> is dissolved in water, and that water is used to write on thick paper, linen, or white parchment. 

3. If vitriol is finely ground and dissolved in cold water, and writing is done with it on paper, the letters vanish immediately. They will return if half an ounce of pulverized nutgalls is cast into a quarter-measure of common water, mixed well, strained through a linen cloth, and the written letter is passed through this water several times; for the letters will then turn black. 

4. A similar thing happens if you write letters on paper with lemon juice, for once they are thoroughly dried, they disappear. However, if you place <term>litharge</term> <note>original: *lythargirium* — lead(II) oxide</note> into an earthenware vessel with vinegar, boil it down, strain the decoction, and immerse the writing in this liquid, it will immediately be rendered white and legible. 

5. Egg white, tempered and beaten for writing, renders the script entirely illegible; it will not appear unless it is placed in cold water. 

6. If you write on a stone with goat fat, you yourself will no longer recognize or detect your own writing at once, unless you immerse the stone in vinegar. This causes the letters to return to view, appearing as if they are raised above the stone. 

7. Writing can also be made with a "double ink," one visible and one invisible. The visible ink is for matters that fear no one’s gaze, while the invisible is for a secret concept, which must remain hidden from everyone except those who know the art. It will remain hidden unless the visible writing is erased by a certain operation, at which point the invisible writing is revived. Father Schott provides the method for this from **Porta** <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian polymath known for his work on cryptography</note>.

**III.** Inconspicuous writing can be made that is read by sprinkling it with fine powder. This can be done with 1. wine, vinegar, urine, fat, tallow, or other greases, gum, animal milk, or the "milk" of herbs or leaves, such as that of the fig tree or <term>spurge</term> <note>original: *Tithymali* — plants of the genus Euphorbia, known for their milky, irritating sap</note>. For if you make letters with one of these materials prepared for writing—either on paper or on some part of the body, such as the hand, arm, or forehead—and allow it to dry, not a single trace of the writing will appear. However, the letters will return if you use charcoal ground into powder, or

However, it is not possible to bring all the inventions of everyone here, nor does it serve our purpose, since anyone can fashion a new alphabet for himself as he pleases. Trithemius records several in Book 6 of his *Polygraphia*, where he brings forward the alphabets of the Normans and the ancient Franks, as well as one found in the *Codex of Hunibald*, and those of Pharamund, Honorius (surnamed the Theban), Cicero, and others. Sunde has similar examples, where he places three Cabalistic alphabets, the first of which is called the *celestial script*; the second, the *angelic script*; the third, the *Passing the River script* <note>original: *scriptura transitus flavii* — likely a variation of *Transitus Fluvii*, an occult alphabet derived from the Hebrew alphabet</note>, etc. But in this kind of writing, one must proceed cautiously, for not only are many people found who can open such writings with easy and brief study, but rules for reading them and finding the hidden secret exist everywhere among various authors.

Therefore, multiple characters can be substituted for a single letter, especially for vowels; or, two words can be joined together, or certain letters of one word can be attached to the letters of another word through various changes or transpositions to make the writing more difficult to decipher. Furthermore, according to **Trithemius** in his *Polygraphia*, **M. T. Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator. He was traditionally credited with the invention of the first Latin shorthand system, the "Tironian notes."</note> substituted a single character for any Latin word and arranged such a great abundance of these marks in a dictionary with the corresponding words placed below them that they are entirely sufficient for writing whatever you wish in the Latin language. Trithemius asserts that he once saw an entire Latin <term>psalter</term> <note>a book containing the Book of Psalms</note> beautifully written in such marks or characters in the library of the Great Church of **Strasbourg** <note>original: *Argentinensis*</note>; because the person in charge was ignorant of such things, he had placed a title on the outside: *Psalter in the Armenian language* <note>original: *Psalterium in Armenica lingua*</note>.

II. Numbers can also be substituted in place of letters through various combinations and variations, and thus transmitted to a partner who knows the system. However, so that such letters may arouse less suspicion, the numbers can be placed and used in the likeness of a common or astronomical calculation. But since even this is not always safe, we may use a most ingenious trick which **Father Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who published extensively on cryptography and linguistics.</note> invented, and which **Father Schott** <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a student of Kircher who recorded many of his inventions.</note> reviews and refines in his entire *Steganographic School* <note>original: *Schola Steganographica*</note>. It consists primarily of this: in a letter written back about any matter at all—one that fears no inspection—the individual characters of any language or idiom are counted from the beginning. When one reaches the letter where the number to be signified ends, a mark is made, either visible or invisible (though intended to appear at the right time). For the second number, as many letters are likewise counted starting from this mark as the units the number contains, and a mark is made again; this is continued until all the numbers to be communicated are inserted into the letter.

III. Even simple dots, not formed into characters or letters, serve the purpose. However, their various positions, combinations, and distances must create enough differences to correspond to the necessary letters of the alphabet. **Hercules à Sunde** <note>A pseudonym for Daniel Schwenter (1585–1636), a German mathematician and linguist.</note> describes such methods in Book 5, Chapters 3, 10, and 12, and he makes use of a triangle, a single line, or the radius of a circle.

IV. The common letters themselves also provide a safe refuge for secrets when they change their power so that they take on an entirely different nature through an ordered or disordered transposition of the alphabet. The entire fifth book of Trithemius's *Polygraphia* pertains to this; but also, through the various combinations of a few letters, it will be possible...

But I will also show examples in the following chapter where it is not the initial letters, but the second, the last, or the second-to-last letters of certain words that serve the secret. The open speech is then constructed so that, by counting the letters of the letter from the beginning, the first letter of the secret falls on the spot where the first chosen number ends; the second letter of the secret falls on the spot where the second chosen number ends (counting from the first letter), and so on. The same logic applies to syllables, although the method of operation is a little more difficult. The most pleasant operation of all is to insert entire words of the secret into the "patent" <note>open or visible</note> letters; for besides being the most secure, it is also established with the greatest ease. However, I would not want this to be understood so generally for all modes of this operation; for certainly Trithemius’s method in Book 2, chapters 23 and 24 of his *Steganography* is not so easy, nor is that one which Hercules de Sunde describes and values so highly in chapter 9, book 5 of his *Steganographia Aucta*.

If indeed it should happen that I enter into a dispute with learned men who are practiced in the writing of letters, I could demonstrate the entire proof in the course of a single day; for I am certain that such men would overcome every difficulty in a very short time and would, in the future, write with the greatest ease and pleasure.

## § 2. Containing the expansion of the first book of Steganography.

Although the *Steganography* of Trithemius can be extended and amplified in almost innumerable ways, and it would be a labor of nearly unnecessary effort to list them all, I nevertheless thought I would be doing something worthwhile if I added a few general rules. By these, the approach to this art might be made much easier and more pleasant for beginners, and a way might be shown for devisting others that are far more subtle.

First, therefore, Trithemius treats all words as meaningful. This method admits no other expansion than the general and most useful one for this entire book: that which is done through the <term>transposition of letters</term> <note>original: "transpositionem literarum." A transposition cipher where the letters of the secret message are rearranged according to a specific rule or key.</note>. In this case, all letters retain their natural value, but change their position so that, for example, what was first becomes third or fourth, and so on. Such a transposition can be done first in individual secret words separately (as in Chapter 21), or with all words taken together (as is done in Chapters 24, 27, 28, 29, 30, and 31), where the secret is distributed into certain parts according to the number of letters. From these individual divisions, the first letters are taken first, then the second, then the third, and so on. 

**Example:** Let this sentence be divided: *Omnes consiliari sunt contra te, res est perdita* <note>Translation: "All the advisors are against you, the matter is lost."</note>; into six parts, and it will stand thus: *Omnesco nšiliar iišuntc ontrate rešeštp erdita*. If now, from each part...

After a certain secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> has been transposed in this way, it can then be inserted into open speech through all the modes of this book, so that either all letters are significant or alternating, as it pleases the practitioner. Look at the example.

->Letter.<-

From your last letter sent to me from Cologne, I learned with no little joy that the status of your condition has been changed, and that you are now in possession of a well-known office; for I recently doubted whether this matter would succeed according to your wish, and therefore I moved every stone <note>The Latin idiom *omnem lapidem movi* means to leave no stone unturned or to try every possible means.</note>. Therefore, I rejoice greatly that you have been so provided for that for your whole life you will be illustrious in honors and abundant in riches; and you have also obtained the best opportunity for excellently benefiting your friends and kinsmen, and, on the contrary, for adding a sting to the envy of your enemies. Farewell.

Secondly, Trithemius places only alternating words as meaningful <note>original: "significativas"</note>, so that the vacant and idle words vary with the valid ones in an alternating position. The number of both can be chosen at will; the Author <note>Referring to Johannes Trithemius.</note> only goes up to five. Furthermore, he concludes the individual words of the secret with certain words of the open speech and separates them from one another. This method can be very conveniently varied if an unequal number of valid and vacant words is chosen in the aforementioned alternation, just as the Author did in chapters 17, 18, 19, and 20; or, while the number of valid words remains the same throughout, the number of vacant words can ascend and descend, as in chapters 15 and 16, or vice versa. The matter will be made clear by an example.

->Letter.<-

I have received your last letter of August 26, and have learned from it with great joy how your old and closest friends are all of the mind to send you to Ingolstadt, Vienna, Prague, or Louvain, or some other German university that has the Catholic exercise of religion. To go to France at present is unsafe and still very dangerous; in England it is not at all advisable: therefore, I do not only not discourage you from the intended journey, but rather I wish you much luck and prosperity in it.

# STEGANOGRAPHY

<page-num>338</page-num>

Thirdly: In Chapter 14, Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German abbot and polymath, often considered the father of modern cryptography.</note> presents a method where a whole secret word <note>original: "integra dictio arcani"</note> is placed between two empty or "filler" words in the open speech. This method can be varied according to the first rule through the transposition of letters; or simply by inverting any word so that the last letter becomes the first, the second-to-last becomes the second, and so on. Furthermore, each secret word can be followed by as many filler words, and separated from the next, as the number of letters it contains. For example:

->*A Letter.*<-

I have had to hear, not without weariness, the report quite often, the copy of which you recently sent me, which is altogether ridiculous; for besides the fact that it is clearly contrary to the truth, it is also full of such immature wit and tasteless metaphors that it ought to move the reader to laughter. Therefore, hereafter you ought to take care to complete such a hidden work with greater sharpness; for you know, and by reason of your duty you ought to know, that immense care must be applied to reports, which surely you have not provided.

Fourthly: Trithemius in Chapters 16 and 17 proposes a method in which both the valid <note>meaningful</note> and the empty <note>null</note> words ascend from one to eight and then descend again. That is, first one empty word is placed, then one valid word, then two empty and two valid, then three, and so on up to eight. This method can also be varied: 1. Either by only descending or only ascending. 2. By having only the valid words (or vice-versa) descend or ascend. 3. By making the very patterns of ascent or descent themselves ascend or descend. The matter will be understood by an example.

->*A Letter.*<-

I do not fully understand your letter from yesterday, in which you intend to maintain a negative opinion; for you do not sufficiently declare from where that experience you describe results, nor do you provide its physical reasoning. It is beyond doubt, as you say, that the soul of man is threefold: rational, sensitive, and vegetative <note>The "triple soul" is a concept from Aristotelian philosophy: the vegetative soul (growth), the sensitive soul (perception/movement), and the rational soul (thought), unique to humans.</note>; and that the sensitive soul contains the whole perfection of the vegetative, just as the rational soul virtually and eminently holds the sensitive. Truly, however, you do not correctly indicate what that "prime mover" of good action might be, or from where that motion results.

Fifthly: Trithemius places some entirely idle lines at the beginning and end, which he does (besides other uses) so that the letter may become more fluid, and therefore generate all the less suspic-

**Sixth:** Just as Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot whose works on "Steganographia" mixed cryptography with occult terminology.</note> has until now throughout the entire first book used the first letters of certain words to carry the secret meaning, so by a general expansion, the **second letters** can be taken. One must then seek words suitable to the intended message whose second letters express the hidden sense <note>original: "sensum arcanum"</note>. 

Example:

->*A Letter*<-

Therefore, continue that love, affection, and kindness which you have always shown toward me, and strive to recommend me to the stated condition or a similar one; you will find me mindful of your favors and always grateful, and I shall never do anything else sooner than to repay it in turn toward you with reciprocal good affection. Farewell.*

**Eighth.** Finally, from all these general rules—whether the first, the second, the last, or even the second-to-last <note>original: "penultimæ"</note> letters of certain words are the significant ones—infinite combinations can be created, more than a page could hold. I provide one example:

->A Letter<-

I admire the mercy of our prince and the justice which he shows to all his subjects. Certainly no one departs without consolation who enjoys the sight of him; he draws the minds of everyone to himself by a certain sympathy <note>original: "sympathia"</note>. He tempers his majesty with a reverent sweetness, and punishes wicked excesses with a moderate severity of speech, while he heaps rewards upon those who deserve them. Under such a prince, our Archbishopric <note>original: "Archiepiscopatus"</note>, which was nearly cast down for several years, shall rise again and receive its ancient splendor and dignity. The greatest thanks, therefore, must be given to Almighty GOD that we have received him in this troubled time. Farewell.

## §. 1. Examination of the Second Book of Stegano-
## graphy.

If the arguments regarding the security, ease, and other requirements of steganography <term>steganography<gloss>the practice of concealing a secret message within an ordinary-looking text</gloss></term> in the first book, as brought forward above, contain any strength or probability, they will certainly receive their full completion here in this demonstration. For whatever you might say of the first book, it can be said much more forcefully and excellently regarding the steganographic methods of this book; especially when the controversy concerns security. Indeed, the methods in this book are so secure and safe, and so remote from all danger, that what Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and pioneer in the field of cryptography</note> suggests in his letters to Arnold Bostius <note>a Carmelite monk and close correspondent of Trithemius</note> is entirely true. Furthermore, they are no less easy and free from suspicion; which I can show in no better way than by presenting a few examples suited to the purpose.

### *First Letter.*

Although I have learned with the greatest grief of heart that your only brother has paid the debt of nature <note>original: "naturæ debitum solvisse"—a common Latin idiom for dying</note>, nevertheless, because the same messenger informed me of your inheritance, that sorrow conceived from the beginning of the letter was so tempered toward the end that I am in doubt whether grief or joy occupies the greater part of my soul. I grieve indeed most greatly, and I grieve deeply, that I have been deprived of such a singular friend; but because I recognize this was done by the immutable divine decree <note>original: "numinis decreto"</note>, and I see that nothing will be reversed by my grief, why should I not rather rejoice with you? Meanwhile, I shall not forget your brother in my prayers to GOD for his happy resurrection. Farewell.

### *Second Letter.*

Noble time passes inadvertently; it is necessary to be zealous for the security of eternal rest. Let us rise, therefore, and lift our minds in devotion and humility to GOD, and daily wash away our heavy sins with many tears—those sins by which we offend the divine majesty while seeking the favor of the world. Behold, now the desired time for us to mourn is at hand; without delay, let us clean our consciences from the dark shadows of worldly pleasures. Let us detest and leave behind the dangerous vanities of this perverse age, and fleeing the cursed sluggishness of this laziness, let us constantly hold fast to the burning Zeal for the Catholic religion and Holiness. Farewell.

### Third Letter.

In response to your latest letter of the 6th of this month, I immediately and eagerly sought an audience with His Electoral Grace <note>original: "Churfürstliche Gnaden" — a title for one of the high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire who possessed the right to elect the Emperor.</note>; however, because he was holding a meeting of the Privy Council, I was not able to gain admittance as I had hoped, and I have had to wait until tomorrow. At that time, I shall not fail to petition again. Likewise, I have already visited His Excellency our Lord Chancellor to further the progress of this matter, as well as most of the gentlemen of the Government Council. In the meantime, you should be diligently concerned that the still-required known document is sent with the next post, along with the bond for the 400 Imperial Thalers <term>Reichsthaler<gloss>a standard silver coin used throughout the Holy Roman Empire</gloss></term> which I delivered to you only a few days ago, so that in the main matter everything necessary may be ready and no delays may occur.

### Fourth Letter.

I recently scanned through all your books, yet I could not find the known conjurations of the spirits of Synesius <note>original: "Sinesii" — likely referring to Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher to whom various magical and alchemical works were later attributed</note>, nor the books of the more occult philosophy of Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim (1486–1535), a famous theologian and occult writer whose work 'De Occulta Philosophia' was highly influential</note>, although I searched through everything most diligently. Therefore, I confidently ask you that, if you hold the aforementioned treatises in secret, you transmit them to me for re-reading; I firmly promise their return, for I only desire to refute such vain doctrine, or if it be natural, to turn myself with all fervor to its explanation. Farewell.

### Fifth Letter.

I recently possessed a complete celestial globe, well-arranged for the zenith <note>the highest point in the sky directly above a specific location</note> of that region, and I sent it back to Heidelberg, from where I had received it. Truly, I have seen nothing better or more useful for students until now, for it represents the daily revolutions of the wandering stars <note>original: "stellarum errantium" — the planets, which appear to move against the backdrop of the stars</note> and the entire structure of the firmament of fixed stars <note>original: "stellarum fixarum"</note>, which moves so slowly that it almost seems to stand still and appear at rest; nevertheless, this motion can be observed very well here and easily calculated on the horizon, showing how much it recedes toward the east every day. You will hardly believe my words at first, but see to it that you see that globe yourself; you will have great consolation when you see with your own eyes how the entire world is displayed in a brief compendium.

# § 2. Elaboration on the Second Book of Steganography.

Three general steganographic methods are proposed in this book: The **first**, spanning the first 21 chapters, teaches how to compose letters in the same manner as the first book, such that the initial letters of specific words represent individual letters of the secret message in a fixed order—though these are first transformed through a varied **metathesis** <note>original: "metathesin" — a Greek term for the transposition or rearrangement of letters in an alphabet.</note> of the natural alphabet. The **second** method places letters where the initial syllables of specific words represent entire syllables of the secret message. Finally, the **third** method inserts whole words of the secret meaning into the open, visible speech. The expansion of all these methods will be neither unpleasant nor difficult. Therefore:

**First:** Because Trithemius, in this book, uses only three variations for determining the "meaningful" words (that is, those whose initial letters carry the code)—either making all words meaningful (as in chapters 1, 5, 6, and 20), or alternating words (as in chapters 2, 4, 7 through 19, and 21), or alternating two meaningful words with two "null" words (as in chapter 3)—we can easily borrow other variations from the entire first book. For example: 1. By the number of alternating words, such as alternating three meaningful with three null, or four with four. 2. By the logic of how individual secret words are concluded. 3. By the logic of the beginning—such as starting the secret sense from the end, from the start, or after skipping a certain number of lines. 4. By the logic of the arrangement of the letters of the mystical sense. The prudent reader will achieve all of these more easily through their own study than through long descriptions. Behold an example:

->*An Example Letter.*<-

You could have recently argued against your adversary using the second law of the *Codex* regarding general amnesty <note>original: "Ex lege secunda C. de generali abolitione" — a reference to the Code of Justinian, a fundamental work of Roman Law, specifically the section concerning the pardoning of crimes.</note>; however, you did not understand that law well, and thus you yielded a glorious triumph to your opposing party along with a good portion of your assets. You will eventually become wise through your own misfortune, and you will learn what the ignorance of the later books of law brings, especially since you were a candidate for the law and could have achieved your degree. You would have become an Advocate of the High Court <term>Dicasterii<gloss>A "Dicastery" was a term used for a high judicial or administrative court.</gloss></term>, who ought to apply the laws of the entire body of justice well, without any disregard for the titles of the law. Therefore, work hard so that you may be a little more cautious in the future and do not overlook any laws or headings. Farewell.

**Second:** We can also expand this book through the same methods of expansion used in the first book, which I hinted at or demonstrated in the previous chapter. These methods are truly infinite, easy, and pleasant. They will render a letter so secure from any interference by examiners that no one in the entire world would be able to detect the hidden secret by any natural power, unless they heard it from the writer or were themselves masters of the art. Take this example:

### *Letter.*

> From your letters I have understood abundantly that my father is held by a heavy infirmity, and will hardly rise from it unless the omnipotent Physician raises him with His blessing—which could not happen without a miracle. Truly, you have filled my soul with heavy sadness, and shortly, due to such bitter grief, I would have wasted away just as much. For during these greatest feasts of the whole year, I have been unable to set a foot out of bed for two days. Six days ago I began to resume my step somewhat, and to walk about the house plainly like a newborn infant on the shortest journeys; indeed, I am asthmatic, and can hardly draw breath. Therefore, you will fill my absence with your own fervor, and you will love my father as if he were your own; I promise to do the same for you in turn. Farewell.

**Third:** Just as Trithemius uses an ordered and natural series of the letters of the alphabet to form the transposition <note>original: "metathesi" — the Greek term for rearranging the order of letters</note> and transformation of letters, we could instead use a series that is transposed and scrambled. For example:

And this method will be even more intricate and secure, and it can be used in other cases as well, as all steganographers agree with me. Here are two examples:

### *Letter 1.*

> Until now, I have truly been able to find no one who could ever defend this subtle question well and prudently according to my wish. For certainly it consists of subtle material not known to everyone; hence Caraffa <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary scholar or a member of the influential Carafa family used in this sample text.</note> showed his genius while he successfully defended that question. I would never have solved it in this way or by this logic, so much is it beyond the usual Authors and even against the common opinion. He himself, meanwhile, was alone able to show us the explanation and solution through such a long disputation by bringing forward various Authors who supported this opinion. Hence Caraffa obtained great praise; [he will] easily [attain] the Doctoral Degree...

### Letter 2.

I received your Lordship’s last letters dated October 6th most favorably on the 7th of this month. **Third:** In the expansion <note>original: "ampliatione" — the process of making a cipher more complex</note> of the second part—which adapts the whole syllables of the secret meaning <note>original: "arcani sensus"</note> to the open speech—I find nothing new to bring forward. He will observe various differences himself, whether by reason of the order of the significant words compared to the nulls <note>original: "vacantibus" — filler words that carry no hidden message</note>, or by reason of the termination and conclusion, or by reason of the beginning, or by reason of the transposition of the secret syllables, or by reason of the first, second, last, or other syllables in the words serving the purpose, or finally by reason of alternating one mode with another. **Fourth:** Because Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Benedictine abbot and author of this work</note> inserted entire words of the secret message into the open text, this can be expanded with easy and manifold variation. For:
1. Just as he inserted words there in a specific relation to individual lines of the letter—by taking the second and second-to-last words—so from the beginning of the letter, having counted all the words, one can take the fifth, tenth, fifteenth, and so on, proceeding by fives; or the sixth, twelfth, etc., proceeding by sixes.
2. Certain numbers can be taken that demonstrate the placement of the meaningful words, just as the people of Brescia <note>original: "Brixienses" — likely referring to a specific school of cryptographers or a known system used in that Italian city</note> used for letters. For example: 7, 11, 3, 8, 13, 5, 2, 6, etc. But more on this expansion will be found in the penultimate chapter of this part.

### *Example.*

We expected the arrival of the Prince Elector of Trier <note>one of the most powerful rulers in the Empire; the "open" message uses his arrival as an excuse for the writer's actions</note> yesterday, but he is only coming tomorrow, and thus I could not obtain permission for my wish to come to you to celebrate Carnival <note>original: "Bacchanalia"</note>. I could indeed be away for a little while around the sixth hour, but what does it profit me to spend half an hour on pleasure unless I may join it with the entire night? It is said, moreover, that the aforementioned most high Elector is coming with three hundred men, and thus all soldiers have been ordered to be under arms. Farewell, and do not be unmindful of me amidst your joys.

## CHAPTER IV.

### AN INVESTIGATION INTO THE METHOD OF COMMUNICATING SECRETS THROUGH FIRE AT ANY DISTANCE WITHOUT WORDS, WRITINGS, OR SIGNS.

What I have presented with great effort in the last two chapters will hardly win the applause of the most learned steganographers <note>practitioners of secret writing</note> of this time, for these methods are neither new nor previously unknown or unheard of. Many steganographers—among them Hercules à Sunde <note>a pseudonym for the 17th-century cryptographic author Johann Balthasar Friderici</note>—have long since brought to light similar and equally subtle inventions. Indeed, the inventions of the Brixians <note>referring to scholars from Brescia, Italy, likely Giambattista della Porta and his circle</note> are even more subtle, although they are simultaneously more difficult in practice. Therefore, those methods were only to be touched upon in passing, lest a sense of weariness be created in minds already kindled toward a deeper knowledge of this science. However, the matters to be treated next depart a little further from the common artifice of steganographers and are not so obvious; they have so twisted the wits of even the most learned men that they eventually either confessed their ignorance or turned to insults. Here, primarily, the artifice of writing by means of fire presents itself, which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the monk and polymath whose works on codes were often accused of being magical or demonic</note> proposes in these words in a letter to Arnold Bostius <note>a Carmelite monk and close friend of Trithemius</note>:

> *The second book contains many more wonderful things; specifically, by means of fire in this art, I can make the concept of my mind known to anyone who understands my art—without words, without writings, and without signs—through any messenger. If that messenger is captured on the way, and even if he is interrogated through the harshest tortures, he can confess nothing about my message because he is entirely unaware of it. Whatever may happen, my message will always remain hidden, and not even all the men of the entire world, if they were gathered together at once, could investigate it by natural power. Furthermore, I can even do this without a messenger, whenever I wish.*

It could certainly seem like a paradox that fire—that most manifest element of the universe—could be employed for the service of this most occult and secret art. After all, due to its most intense and highly active qualities, fire can neither be hidden nor confined by any art. Therefore, it is a question worthy of steganographers: how this could be done naturally and without superstition, and how Trithemius knew it and promised he would provide it. To be sure, there have been most learned men up to this point—such as Father Athanasius Kircher, Father Caspar Schott, Giambattista della Porta, Cornelius Agrippa, and others—who have treated this question from its foundations and illustrated it with such ingenious inventions that it seems nothing can be added to them. However, since these matters pertain entirely to this place and to the defense of Trithemius, it is neces—

multifariously <note>original: "farium," likely completing "multifariam" from the previous page</note> I judged it necessary to repeat it with the rest in my own thin style for the completion of my defense. But here, on the very threshold, a grave question occurs: whether the cited promise of Trithemius does not contain certain contradictions and impossibilities? For Father Athanasius Kircher <note>a famous 17th-century Jesuit polymath and scholar of many sciences</note> thinks it impossible for anything to be signified to those who are absent through fire without a sign, since fire itself is a kind of sign. Therefore, although something can be signified to an absent person through fire without letters or writing, he asserts that it can by no means be done without signs that are equivalent to letters and writing. From this he infers that an ill-considered assertion of great magnitude lies hidden in this promise of Trithemius. 

He also thinks it no less impossible for something to be signified to those far away through fire *by means of any messenger*; for he says that if it is by fire, how can it be by messenger or courier, since manifestations made by fire have no need for a messenger? But to this objection I lead the response along with Father Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a physicist and mathematician who published many of Kircher's ideas</note>, that Trithemius was not speaking about just any signs—as if he were saying that something could be announced to someone absent without any sign at all—but only without *apparent* signs: those that are new, extraordinary, inducing suspicion, and by which men before him used to converse or correspond in writing. For he was a Philosopher; he knew that nothing can be indicated to another, whether present or absent, without signs. Indeed, the voice, writing, and gestures are the natural signs of our concepts, without which no one can manifest his mind to another; nor are we Angels, that we might speak angelically, though even that does not happen without signs. Now to the question itself.

### §. 1. The Opinion of Father Kircher is Examined.

Father Schott reports in his *Schola Steganographica* <note>original: "sch. steg.," a reference to Schott's 1665 manual on secret writing</note>, class 7, question 7, that he saw for a span of many years in Sicily, all around the maritime regions, towers or watchtowers frequently arranged in high places, and in each of them watchmen lived permanently at the public expense of the kingdom. Whenever one of these observes ships approaching from afar on the sea, he gives a signal with smoke by day and fire by night, by which signal he alerts the nearest watchman. Seeing this signal, the second gives another signal for the third, then the third for the fourth, and the fourth for the fifth, so that within a quarter of an hour <note>fifteen minutes</note> all the coastal cities are warned of the ships sighted and the number of ships. He thinks, therefore, consequently: if in this manner frequent towers were arranged throughout any kingdom, however large, from which—

That the described device is done through signs is manifest and assumed by Father Kircher's own confession; but it also cannot be done by a messenger, for how could anyone send fire by a messenger? Fire can indeed be signaled to one who is absent, but can it be sent to any distance, to a hundred miles or more? And finally, such a transmission of fire would truly be a new, ridiculous, and inconvenient method of writing, when many and infinite other methods would carry the secret more easily and secretly.

### §. 2. Father Schott’s Opinion is Proposed.

I brought forward earlier in Chapter 1—and they are found everywhere among the Steganographers, and especially in Giambattista della Porta <note>a famous Italian polymath and pioneer in cryptography</note> and Father Schott, scattered throughout the entire 8th class of steganographic schools—various devices for writing secretly by which writing can be done using juices. These, once dried, hide away and do not return until the paper is moved near a fire; and that writing can be done on paper, parchment, an egg, cloth, etc. Thus Father Schott thinks the device for writing through such juices or liquids is the very device of Trithemius; for, he says, let it be written on blank paper or in the spaces between two lines written with ink...

on blank [paper] <note>original: "vacuis mentis," likely a corruption of "vacua membrana" or similar, referring to blank sheets</note> whatever secret [is written] with such a juice, the letters do not appear unless the paper is moved toward a fire. Let the paper be handed to any messenger and sent to anyone, however distant, who is aware of this same art of writing. In this case, the messenger does not know the secret contained in the paper and therefore cannot reveal it; nor do any letters or traces of the same secret appear on the paper, so it remains unknown even to someone intercepting the letters. However, as soon as the distant recipient applies the received letters to the fire, the secret becomes known to him through the fire, but without words or signs made by the writer through fire or impressed upon the paper. **Note.** It is well known that there are many qualities of fire, and among them light and heat hold the primary place. Each of these is active and can produce wonderful effects both in Physics and in Steganography <term>Steganographia<gloss>the art of hidden writing or cryptography</gloss></term>. Therefore, to solve this question, we must first see through which of these two qualities of fire the effect promised by Trithemius can be achieved. For if you say this effect is produced through **light**, Father Schott's opinion immediately collapses of its own accord; but if through **heat**, the opinion of Father Kircher and many followers will rest on no foundation. Let us see first, therefore, whether we can achieve anything through light. Now, light can operate in three ways: either on the part of the sender, or on the part of the receiver, or in the medium between them. If the light is only on the part of the sender, it will be the method reported by Father Kircher and already refuted; if the light is only on the part of the receiver, it will be a method of writing letters that do not appear except by the introduction of fire or light, such as Father Schott reports in Class 8, Chapter 6, Paragraph 4. And this way of writing can be defended no less than the one reported by Father Schott, and thus it will undergo the same examination. If the light is in the medium, it will be the method of Cornelius Agrippa or Giambattista della Porta, which I shall discuss in the following paragraph and easily refute, since it cannot be done through a messenger. Now let us see what we can achieve through heat; but the operation of heat is far different from that of light. For if it is on the part of the sender, it cannot act over any great distance, and thus it is easily excluded—unless someone wishes to use fire to heat the writer's liquid and evade the solution of the question by mockery, or use "strong water" <term>aquam fortem<gloss>nitric acid, often used in early chemistry and for invisible inks</gloss></term> or the "fire of separation" <note>a chemical process used to separate precious metals</note> and write with that liquid, as will be said in Number 2. Nor can heat in the medium achieve an effect so distant that it acts on both sides. Therefore, only on the part of the receiver, as reported by Father Schott, could heat display the effect of Steganography—but is it Trithemius's?

I state firstly: The method of writing by means of juices and liquids satisfies the promises of Trithemius, and I show this through an enumeration of its parts.

1. *In such a manner, we can send word to any distance, up to a hundred miles or more*; for such letters can be sent throughout the whole world no less than other common and ordinary ones. Nor need it be feared that through such a long journey, changes in the air, or other accidents, the power of such juices might perish, preventing the hidden writing from "reviving" <note>This refers to the chemical reaction where the heat of a fire makes the invisible ink appear.</note>, or that the writing might in any way reveal itself and thus disclose the secret; for daily experience stands against this.

2. *Such writing is done without words*; for the secret is entrusted to the paper, not to the messenger. Therefore, there is no need for spoken words, and consequently, nothing is to be feared from the unfaithfulness of a messenger.

3. *This writing is done without signs, without scripts*; if it were done through signs, those signs would be the writing itself which contains the secret. But the writing does not appear, nor does it show even a trace or indication to those looking at it; therefore, it is done without signs. But is it "without scripts"? This is a little more difficult to explain, but I think this is also satisfied if it is said that Trithemius was speaking of *visible* scripts <note>original: "scriptis apparentibus"</note>, to distinguish it from other methods where, otherwise and without this distinction, Trithemius's promise would have applied. For certainly all the other things said about this method could have applied to common writing using fabricated alphabets <note>This refers to substitution ciphers or "fake" letters that look like a strange language.</note> written with standard ink.

4. *The writing is done through any messenger whatsoever*; he says this to exclude other methods where the secret is entrusted to messengers in some way. Thus, this method does not require a messenger who is a participant in the secret for any reason. Instead, one can entrust the letters to be carried by anyone—even one who is mute and can neither speak nor express his will through signs—or even by pigeons, dogs, war machines <term>tormentis bellicis<gloss>literally "engines of war," likely referring to messages hidden inside projectiles shot from catapults or early cannons</gloss></term>, etc. And hence, if the messenger is captured on the road and interrogated even through the harshest tortures, he will be able to confess nothing about the message, because he knows nothing and possesses nothing but the letters that are privy to the secret.

5. *The message will always remain hidden, nor could all the men of the whole world, if they were gathered together, track it down by natural power*. Here Father Schott <note>Kaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit scientist who sought to explain "magical" effects through physics.</note> thinks that Trithemius added this either because the method was unknown to others in his time, or because Trithemius believed it was unknown and had first occurred to his own mind. Indeed, however these things may be, Trithemius could have hidden the secret by writing with that juice of his in such various ways that, even if the letter were held to the fire by someone other than the intended recipient, and the characters appea-

**I state secondly:** The method reported by Father Kaspar Schott seems to be the very device used by Trithemius himself. I gather this from Trithemius’s own words in his *Explanation of Polygraphy* <note>The "Polygraphia" (1518) was Trithemius's more "respectable" book on cryptography, published after the "Steganographia" caused a scandal.</note>, where, after he had introduced three types of invisible characters, he added:

1. <term>Dormaticum</term> <note>Derived from the Latin "dorsum" (back).</note>, which is done on the backs of messengers using a certain artificial writing that is only visible through the washing of a specific liquid. 

2. <term>Hyphasmaticum</term> <note>From the Greek "hyphasma" (textile/fabric).</note>, by which one writes on cloth with certain substances; once dried, it cannot be seen at all, until it is seen when moistened in cold water. 

3. <term>Aleoticum</term>, the writing of which is done on paper or without paper, using <term>nemilua</term> and <term>cala</term>, along with <term>raphocam</term>, <term>lapolce</term> <note>These strange terms—nemilua, cala, etc.—are likely Atbash-style ciphers or scrambled names for chemical ingredients like alum, vinegar, or onion juice.</note> and other various things. 

After suggesting these, he adds: *But because none of these serve our current purpose, it is therefore proper that we hasten to those things which reason demands.* Likewise, a little later: *Finally, so that you may announce the secret of your mind to one who is absent without letters, even without the knowledge of the person performing the duty of messenger, it remains ascribed to the inventions of Steganography.* It clearly appears, therefore, that Trithemius wished to include in his *Steganography*, among other things, the <term>aleoticic</term> style of writing, which contains the methods of making writing with certain juices and liquids that lie hidden when dried and return when moved near fire; nor does it appear under what title he could have better categorized it than under the device of "writing through fire," especially since I have shown that the method of writing with these juices matches Trithemius’s promises.

### §. 3. The Opinions of Others are Examined.

Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath, physician, and occult writer.</note> provides another device for announcing something by fire, or rather by light, in the first book, chapter 6 of his *Occult Philosophy*, where he says: *There is also another even more admirable trick: where one might place images painted with a certain skill, or written letters, against the rays of the full moon on a clear night. Their likenesses, multiplied in the air and carried upward, are reflected back along with the moon's rays. Another person, aware of the matter, can see, read, and recognize them from a great distance upon the very disk or circle of the moon. This device is extremely useful for announcing secrets to besieged towns and cities; it was once practiced by Pythagoras, and today it is not unknown to some others, as well as to myself.*

Likewise, in his critique or retraction concerning Magic, in the chapter on illusions, he writes: *But we read that the most learned Pythagoras also occasionally performed this ridiculous feat: whatever he pleased, he would write in blood on a mirror. When this was turned toward the orb of the full moon, he would show the things inscribed on the moon's disk to someone standing behind him.*

Giambattista della Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar and pioneer in optics and cryptography.</note> hints at the same device in book 17 of his *Natural Magic*, chapter 17: *We have said and observed this so that we might use this skill in great and marvelous matters, and especially for inscribing letters upon the disk of the moon. And because we said it is easy to send things even to infinity, they are easily sent as far as the moon, especially since they are aided by its own light.*

**I say:** The method of signaling through such mirrors is clearly not the Trithemian method. For:
1. Trithemius’s method must be performed "by fire," but here there is no fire, for neither the moon nor its rays can properly be called fire. 
2. Trithemius’s method must be possible "without signs and without writing"; this certainly does not happen in the aforementioned mirror methods, as is plain to all. 
3. Trithemius’s method must be able to be carried out through a messenger; but how would Agrippa or Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar famous for his work on optics and natural magic.</note> achieve that with a mirror? 

By this same reasoning, I also state that Trithemius’s secret cannot be displayed through other **catoptric** operations <term>Catoptric: The branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light by mirrors.</term>. Through the help of a flat steel mirror or a large glass lens, any figures, letters, or entire theatrical representations can be projected into a distant, darkened place. This can be done not only by the light of the sun during the day, but even by the light of a candle by night or day, as the praised Father Schott proves in many ways in his *Catoptric Magic*.

### §. 4. The Opinion is Proposed which Cornelius Agrippa Boasts to be Trithemian.

In Book 1, Chapter 6 of his *Occult Philosophy*, Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath and occult writer.</note> uses a new and unheard-of way of reasoning to elevate the nature of the air to such a point of perfection. He claims the air impresses these upon the senses of men and animals according to the receiver’s disposition, until they are carried to the **phantasm** <note>The mental image or the faculty of the mind that processes sensory data.</note> and the soul. Thus, through the mediation of the air, someone could announce a concept of their mind to another at a very great distance in a very short time. For he says:

> For the very images of things, although they are carried by their own nature to the senses of men and animals, can nevertheless acquire some impression from the heavens while they are in the air. From this—combined with the aptitude and disposition of the receiver—they may be carried more to the sense of one person than another. And hence it is possible, naturally and far from all superstition, with no other spirit mediating, for one man to communicate to another at any distance, however long or even un-

### CHAPTER V.

### INVESTIGATING THE METHOD OF INDICATING ONE'S WILL TO A PERSON SITTING IN PRISON, EVEN IF FAR DISTANT, NO MATTER HOW CLOSELY THEY ARE GUARDED, EVEN IF THEY SAT THREE MILES UNDERGROUND.

**Father Schott** <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and mathematician who published and commented on Trithemius’s work.</note> believed that this concept of **Trithemius**, by which he thought the things he described could be done, was merely a fantastical concept, since it cannot happen by natural means. He argued that in this matter **Trithemius** was deceived, acting just as **Alchemists** are prone to do. They claim their "Philosopher’s Stone" possesses such power that it can heal all incurable diseases, almost raise the dead, change old age into the bloom of youth, and prolong life to three hundred years or more. With it, they promise the world mountains of gold and inexhaustible treasures of wealth, yet they are so far from achieving these things that for many centuries not a single person has been found who succeeded—unless, perhaps, someone was instructed by the master Devil, the craftsman of all lies, who could verify the kind of secrets they foolishly promise. Truly, however, I would prefer to confess my own ignorance along with **Father Schott** rather than doubt the faith of **Trithemius**, a most religious, learned, and prudent man; but the final judgment shall be given at the end.

### §. 1. An investigation into the principle of discovering the art of writing to one sitting in prison.

I stated above in Chapter 1 that *Steganography* in a general sense is twofold, containing within itself two species: *Steganography* <note>original: "Steganographiam in specie," referring here to secret writing.</note> in the specific sense and *Steganology* <note>original: "Steganologiam," referring to secret communication via speech or signals.</note>. I distinguished these species from one another such that *Steganography* contains those modes of writing occultly by which letters, or something in the place of letters, are sent to an absent person; whereas *Steganology* concerns those methods where nothing is sent to the absent person, but something is done by the messenger through which the recipient gains knowledge of the secret. We must therefore see through which species of *Steganography* **Trithemius’s** art is performed. If **Trithemius** intended to show this through *Steganography*, the matter seems straightforward, and we need not labor long over his intention. For it could plausibly be said that **Trithemius** understood and wished to suggest those modes of secret signaling by which a letter is so concealed and hidden by the messenger or carrier that it cannot be found. I have reported many such methods above, and they are found everywhere in the works of **Steganographers**, and especially in **Father Schott**, Book 8, Chapters 2, 3, and 4, and elsewhere at length. I draw the conjecture for this opinion from the very words of **Trithemius** in his *Explanation of the Prologue to Polygraphia*, where, after recounting the ways of hiding letters, he adds that they belong to *Steganography*. For he says: *Letters are likewise written and hidden in various ways...*

### §. 3. A method is proposed for signaling through the reciprocal grafting of blood or flesh.

Hercules de Sunde <note>A pseudonym for the German polymath Daniel Schwenter (1585–1636), who wrote extensively on mathematical recreations and secret signaling.</note> proposes this method in the cited place: Mars, about to depart from Mercury to a distance of 100 or 1,000 miles, intends to signal certain specific things at that distance in a single moment; for example: *I am well*, *I am at death's door*, *Come to us by post*, *One of your friends is dead*, or something similar. Before Mars departs, he opens a small wound in his arm or a similar fleshy place with a bloodletting lancet <note>original: *phlebotomica lanceola*</note> or another instrument, which he washes well with blood and allows to dry. Then Mercury slightly wounds himself in the finger or arm, draws a few drops of blood, and drips them into Mars’s wound; once this is done, the wound is closed with a plaster and healed. In a similar way, Mars gives a few drops of blood to Mercury, and then the device will be perfected. 

When Mars wishes to signal to Mercury (or vice versa) the first of the aforementioned messages they agreed upon, he pricks the site of his wound with a needle, and Mercury will immediately feel it and understand it to be the first message. If he pricks it twice, it will be the second; if thrice, the third, and so on. The entire logic and method of this trick consists in Mercury feeling the prick of Mars at such a great distance, and vice versa. He confirms this opinion with the following story: In Italy, he says, there are found skillful surgeons—or rather, most excellent "Nose-makers" <term>Rhinurgi</term> <note>original: *Rhinurgi*; early plastic surgeons who specialized in rhinoplasty, specifically the "Italian method" of grafting skin from the arm to reconstruct a nose.</note>, as Father Schott calls them—who reconstruct a mutilated or decayed nose using the flesh from another living man’s arm, or from another very fleshy place. 

However, Father Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit scientist and student of Athanasius Kircher.</note>, as established above, argues that this steganography via the grafting <note>original: *insitionem*</note> of flesh or blood is by no means natural. That is, it is not at all natural for the pricking of a needle into the flesh of one person here to be followed immediately by the sensation of a prick in the flesh of another person located at any distance. Rather, he argues that if such an effect ever follows, it occurs only by the work of an evil spirit <term>cacodæmon</term> <note>original: *cacodæmone*; a "bad spirit" or demon. In the 17th century, if a physical phenomenon lacked a mechanical explanation, it was often attributed to demonic interference.</note>. He is led to this conclusion because no reasons occur to him or are suggested that prove it to be natural; for Janus Hercules himself, in the cited place, adds that he has learned from experience...

## §. 4. An examination of the steganographic device involving the distillation of blood.

Lest this device come to the knowledge of just any peasant or lazy commoner, Hercules de Sunde <note>A pseudonym for Daniel Schwenter (1585–1636), a German polymath who wrote about "mathematical recreations."</note> proposes it in the aforementioned book using steganographic writing <note>Secret writing or cryptography.</note> through the transposition of letters; he advises that he who would share in the secret must strive to solve it according to the rules that follow.

It consists mainly of this: in the month of August, blood is drawn from a vein (for example, in the arm) of two friends who intend to correspond secretly. The blood is mixed and distilled, and from it an oil is made. Each friend then anoints the arm from which the blood was taken with this oil. Then, using a bloodletting lancet <note>original: *lanceola phlebotomica*</note>, one pricks his arm, just as in the previous device, and the other will feel the same puncture. Truly, dear reader, before you place your faith in these words, investigate its natural reasoning for a moment, and you will find it is of no better quality than the previous one. The "sympathetic ointment" of Giambattista della Porta <note>An Italian polymath (1535–1615) famous for his work on "Natural Magic."</note> meets with the same judgment, as related by Father Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and student of Athanasius Kircher.</note> in Book 7, Section 13, § 2, note 2.

### CHAPTER VI.

## AN EXAMINATION OF THE ART BY WHICH AN UNEDUCATED MAN, KNOWING ONLY HIS MOTHER TONGUE AND NEVER HAVING KNOWN A WORD OF THE LATIN LANGUAGE, IS TAUGHT IN TWO HOURS TO WRITE, READ, AND UNDERSTAND LATIN.

It would certainly be most desirable—truly most desirable—if Charles de Bovelles <note>A French scholar (1479–1567) who visited the occultist-abbot Johannes Trithemius and later accused him of practicing demonic magic.</note>, that rash and most unjust slanderer of Trithemius, had either never come to Sponheim or had never set eyes on the beginning of the *Steganographia*. Then this invention would have received its completion, and these admirable discoveries would have come to light, rather than remaining hidden from us forever, buried in the mind of Trithemius, as we have no other way of discovering it. For...

Truly, anyone might grasp this art at first glance, which he proposes in a letter to Arnold Bostius <note>Arnold Bostius (1445–1499) was a Carmelite monk and a close friend of Trithemius; their correspondence is a major source for early cryptographic history.</note> in this way: *It is wonderful, I admit, but hear more wonderful things; the third book teaches an art through which I can teach an unlearned man who knows only his mother tongue—who never knew a word of the Latin language—to write, read, and understand Latin elegantly and eloquently enough within two hours, as much as he wishes, so that whoever sees his letters will praise the words and understand them as composed in Latin.* But if anyone considers it more deeply, he will not wonder, nor think it ridiculous, what Trithemius says in these words regarding the author of this invention in his letters to Arnold Bostius: *If you ask from where these things come to me, which no one else knows, listen: I did not learn these from a man, nor through a man, but through revelation—I know not whose; for when, once during the present year, I was thinking what new thing I could find that might lie hidden from all, I began to wonder if I could devise those marvelous things I have mentioned. When, after long fantasy, I utterly despaired as if of an impossible thing, I lay down to sleep that night, mocking my own foolishness for attempting to seek the impossible. That same night, something stood by me, saying: "The things you have thought are not in vain, O Trithemius, although they are impossible for you—things which neither you nor another with you can find." And I said to it, "If they are possible, tell me, I pray, how they may be done." And opening its mouth, it taught me about each thing in order, showing how what I had thought about in vain for many days could easily be done."* Whether one calls this a Good Angel <note>original: "Agathangelum"</note>, or an Evil Spirit <note>original: "cacodæmonem"</note>, or an illusion of a preoccupied imagination, they will yet confess with me that this invention belongs to a creator more than human, or at least incomparable. Indeed, Father Athanasius Kircher <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit polymath who studied Trithemius’s work extensively.</note> eventually came along and showed this device of Trithemius to the world—not so much by his own invention, but by such a new illustration of it that he himself seems to carry the name of the author; however, he does not attribute this to himself, but returns all the glory of the invention to Trithemius and his *Polygraphia*.

In an Eastern city <note>likely referring to Würzburg in Franconia, where Trithemius served as Abbot of the Monastery of St. James</note>, where he was then Abbot at the Monastery of St. James the Apostle, he wrote another *Steganography* <note>the art of hidden writing</note>. However, due to the fear inspired by the previous title—which was already hated everywhere—he named it *Polygraphia* <note>literally "many-writing," a more neutral term for cryptography</note>. He divided this work into six books. In the first two, he handed down a skill by which you may make the secret of your mind known safely, secretly, and without any suspicion from any onlookers to one who knows the art. This can be done as widely as necessary, at any distance of places, through regulated speech. Regarding the first book, Trithemius himself speaks in this preface:

In the first book of this our *Polygraphia*, we have distributed the words of the Latin language, as many as are seen, by placing them through the order of our ternary <note>a system based on sets of three</note>. By the use and ministry of these words, all Princes throughout the world will find a safe service for any secrets, which will remain perpetually hidden without danger to the mystery, without a mark, and without the suspicion of blockheads <note>original: "bacuceorum," a derogatory term Trithemius used for those he considered fools or uninitiated</note>. It is established that this path is safe for "owls" <note>original: "bubonibus"; Trithemius uses the owl as a symbol for initiates who can see what is hidden in the dark</note> and shall never be violated by the investigation of anyone. The knowledge of the hidden matter is granted to only two people, if the binary is skillfully reduced to a monad <note>philosophical terms for "two" and "one," suggesting the two correspondents acting as a single mind</note>. Furthermore, these are paraphrases composed in the manner of someone either advising or petitioning, which can be varied for every kind of visible subject matter. We have proposed the letters of the Latin alphabet in order for each word with this consideration: so that the operator has an easy method for his purpose, and the respondent is relieved of excessive labor in the reading. That is: we have distributed the words of the Latin speech, over 9,000 in number, under nearly 400 alphabets in such a series that if only one word is taken after another from each alphabet, from the beginning to the end, they will coherently form a fitting Latin sentence. Indeed, the method of writing will be very convenient, as each individual word represents a letter placed at its head. For if, as we have said, you take one word from the first alphabet, and one from those following in a line, until the period or the end of the book, a Latin and sufficiently fitting discourse will arise for you.

Let us take a case: suppose a wicked man seeks to be promoted by you to some friend of yours. You, however, in order to cut off his opportunistic prayers without promoting an unworthy person, decide to write more secretly to your friend so that the requester does not understand. *Beware of this man, for he is a thief and the worst of villains, but be silent, I pray.* <note>The secret message being hidden</note>. Go to the first alphabet and write the word *Conditor* <note>Founder/Creator</note>, which signifies C. In the second, *Clemens* <note>Merciful</note>, which denotes A. In the third, *Decernens* <note>Decreeing</note>, which represents V. In the fourth, *Mundana* <note>Worldly</note>, which represents E.

In each of these alphabets, the reader will discover that all the words are synonyms or near-synonyms. Thus, if a person selects one word from each list at random, they will always find the resulting sense to be harmonious and written in perfectly correct Latin. Therefore, to communicate any secret message <term>arcanum; a hidden or secret matter</term>, a word should be taken from the first alphabet corresponding to the first letter of the secret; from the second alphabet, the word corresponding to the second letter of the secret, and so on.

For example: Suppose the secret message to be sent is *Come quickly* <note>original: "Veni cito"</note>. From the first alphabet, the word *Author* <note>representing 'V'</note> is taken. From the second, *Great* <note>representing 'e'</note>, and so following the sequence, the resulting "open" or visible text will be: *The Great Author, establishing angelic things, may He grant to those who seek it an inestimable clarity.* However, the hidden intention will be: *Come quickly.*

In the second book of *Polygraphia*, nothing new is composed that differs from the first, except that the paraphrases of a single day are varied. For this reason, we advise that whatever we said must be observed in the first book must also be maintained in this one; for the symbols of both books are arranged in the same order according to the path of light, and the meaning of the paraphrases is only changed where necessary. Furthermore, these two books of our *Polygraphia* serve the promised operation sufficiently. Through them, you will not only be able to write and communicate whatever you wish to your friends at any time with the greatest safety and security, but also—and we believe this has never been heard of before—to make a person who is entirely ignorant of the Latin language a participant and scholar in this art, provided they simply know how to form letters.

### §. 2. Addition of Father Kircher and Father Schott.
<note>Athanasius Kircher and Gaspar Schott were 17th-century Jesuit scholars who expanded upon Trithemius's work, often defending it against accusations of magic by highlighting its mathematical and linguistic ingenuity.</note>

Although Trithemius proposes many wonderful uses for this invention in both the *Polygraphia* and its "key," he also hints at expansions and faithfully hands down the precautions to be observed in its operation.

**1.** How, by the service of this work, you may teach a man ignorant of the Latin tongue in a short space of time—provided he only knows how to read and write letters—to write everything in his mother tongue but expressed in the Latin tongue, as you wish, either elegantly or harmoniously. Thus, he may conceal and hide all the secret mysteries of his will, and safely, secretly, and without suspicion communicate this art as widely as he pleases to one who understands it.

**2.** How, by the expansion of the likeness of the matter received, all these things can be extended into any language whatsoever, once the teacher has reduced the <term>binary to unity; a cryptic reference to simplifying the two-part substitution system into a single operation</term>.

3. How, by the imitation of similarity, we can communicate the art of our invention to one who knows any secrets of the mind as abundantly, manifoldly, and widely as you wish, in various ways that no one else can know or notice. A manifold "speech without voice" is provided here, through which we can most fully indicate all the conceptions of our mind, however difficult, to those who know the art—safely, securely, and most broadly, with all suspicion removed. This wonderful invention has innumerable applications and is capable of containing all mysteries.

4. If you wish this industrious method to remain perpetually secret and hidden, you should learn how to rewrite the *Polygraphia* <term>Polygraphia; literally "many-writing," the title of Trithemius’s work on cryptography</term> anew, but in such a way that you do not place the letters of the alphabet before the words; then, no one will easily suspect the logic of the secret. However, to ensure no difficulty occurs for the writer or the reader of the mystery, one must learn how the letters of the alphabet should be written on a small slip <term>schedula; a small leaf or slip of paper used for notes</term> in an order corresponding to the words, and how that mobile slip should be adapted to the headings of the columns. One must also learn how the letters can be engraved on a copper plate so that they may be moved from one sequence to another.

5. How Kings and Princes—who have many deputies in various locations to whom it is not safe to write using a single type of hidden narrative—might have a unique, secret way of writing for each individual. They ought to change the order of words as many times as they wish to have separate modes of communication. In this way, the rulers themselves hold the keys to everyone’s method of writing, yet none of their subjects can understand the method used by another. Indeed, the variable ways of writing more secretly through this art are infinite.

6. How, within this very invention of *Polygraphia*, there lie hidden certain things far better than those already described. For instance: how you can instruct someone ignorant of the Latin language in a few days—if not hours—so that he knows how to write, read, speak, and understand Latin. This is not meant in a universal sense, but in a specific way, so that he may handle whatever necessary matters arise in his business. Likewise, you can learn how to make all the conceptions of your mind known to a distant friend who knows the art, without using writing and using an ignorant messenger, securely and most secretly. This can even be done at times without any messenger at all, naturally and without any suspicion, danger, or fear.
