...Saints, on Nations, on Cosmography <note>The science of mapping the general features of the universe, including both heaven and earth.</note>, on Astronomy, and the seven **liberal arts**, and even on all those things which are in common use among men, and concerning the universal world of both visible and invisible things.

8. And finally, how whatever is visible and placed within the circle of the universe provides a ready support for the service of this new art: air and fire, water and earth, springs and rivers, trees and orchards, flowers and grasses, words and names, <term>accident and substance</term> <note>These are Aristotelian philosophical terms: "substance" is what a thing is in its essence, while "accidents" are its external properties, like color or weight.</note>, stones and sand, dung and manure, things and terms, the honorable and the modest, wood and metals, hard and liquid, things existing and non-existing, histories and fables, beasts and brutes, men and cattle—every single thing and all things together, which either speech can express or the soul can imagine, provide the widest possible field for **Polygraphy** <note>original: "Polygraphiæ"; Trithemius's term for his cryptographic system, literally meaning "many-writing."</note>. They promise that this art, as far as it can be established for mortals, will be expanded unto infinity.

In truth, however, Trithemius did not explicitly provide all of this in the *Polygraphia* itself, but left it to the wit of the reader. Indeed, as he himself says, a prudent reader—given his outstanding intellect—can easily find greater and more polished things from these small and not-quite-perfectly refined inventions, if he is diligent. A studious posterity will easily provide both: adding luster to the material and sufficient progress to the form. 

The first inventor of any art transmits the greater part to those who come after, because since the beginnings of an art are difficult and unfamiliar, no subtle invention is found to be perfect from the start. It was enough for him to have discovered the principles of the art and to have handed down a method of writing in symbols—rough and intentionally shaped—for there was neither time nor reason to form those inventions more elegantly. He did this lest "honey create vomit for the nauseous," or "truth produce hatred for the indignant" <note>This is a proverbial way of saying that too much information at once can be overwhelming or provoke a backlash from those not ready for it.</note>. 

Therefore, the frequently praised **Father Athanasius Kircher** <note>A 17th-century Jesuit polymath famous for his massive works on everything from linguistics to volcanoes.</note> followed in the footsteps of Trithemius. He brought this subtle invention to such perfection through his many refinements and expansions that it now seems to be complete, lacking nothing further. This can be seen briefly from the work of **Father Schott** <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a student of Kircher who popularized many of his teacher's ideas.</note>.

**First:** Since it is not always proper or secure to use prayer-like formulas in writing (which Trithemius uses), it is better to use speech in the manner of a letter written about any subject whatsoever. Father Athanasius Kircher, with the shrewdness of intellect in which he excels, commands in the *New Polygraphia* <note>original: "Polygraphia nova"</note> that new paraphrases—following one another in a continuous progression in the light of day—be established under this or a similar concept of a letter. He himself uses this example:

> I received your letter, my dearest Anthony, which your courier delivered to me; and as soon as I perceived your wish, I desired to obey you. For at your command, I immediately took care that one hundred pounds be given from the treasury to Simon, your dearest friend. I pray that you look upon this affection of mine, for I desire nothing else but that I may be able to honor you with this most humble service of mine. If you wish anything else, command and I shall obey, as one who feels himself bound by your distinguished integrity. Farewell, dearest friend. Given at Rome, on the first day of January in the Year of Christ 1660.

**Second:** From this letter, he takes 40 words—although even more could be taken, or the letter’s meaning and subject matter could be made larger and fuller—then, by varying each word twenty-four times, he applies them to the same number of letters of the alphabet. In this way, he established forty polygraphic <note>A "polygraphic table" in this context is a lookup table where each letter of the alphabet corresponds to a specific word or phrase used to disguise a secret message.</note> tables for the use explained thus far.

**Third:** In order to verify what Trithemius says—that by expanding the similarity of the subject matter, all these things can be extended into any language—he varied and extended these Latin polygraphic tables (which were originally of only one language) into four other languages: namely German, Italian, French, and Spanish. Although Father Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit scientist who published and expanded upon the secret works of Athanasius Kircher.</note> in his *Schola Steganographica* provides only four, which can be seen there, I judged it superfluous to fill this page with them. Let it please you to accept at least one example in all the languages. Suppose, for example, a secret message must be sent: *Go quickly.* <note>original: "Abi cito."</note> In Latin, the message would be reported thus: *I have received your bond, most excellent Lawrence, which Andrew, your close friend, showed me.* <note>original Latin: "Accepi Syngrapham tuam, Excellentissime Laurenti, quam mihi monstravit Andreas, intimus tuus." Note how the innocent sentence about a bond hides the secret command.</note> In German, it would be: **I have received your signature, excellent Lawrence, which Andrew your secret friend showed to me.** <note>original German: "Ich hab empfangen deine Unterschreibung/fürtrefflicher Lorenz/welche mir gezeigt Andreas dein geheimer Freund."</note> In Italian: *I have received your note, most excellent Lorenzo, which Andrew your intimate friend has shown me.* <note>original Italian: "Ho ricevuto il vostro viglietto, Eccellentissimo Lorenzo, il quale m’ha mostrato Andrea vostro intimo."</note> Finally, in French: *I have received your note, very excellent Lawrence, which Andrew, your intimate friend, has shown me.* <note>original French: "J’ay receu vostre billet, tres excellent Lorent, que m’a monstré André, vostre intime."</note>

**Fourth:** He constructed a <term>Glottotactic</term> <note>From the Greek roots for "tongue" (language) and "arrangement." Finally, the chest will be of such height that it can contain a tablet having 24 spaces...

### §. 3. An examination of whether the craft passed down thus far satisfies the promises of Trithemius.

Whoever weighs the *Polygraphy* <note>Trithemius's *Polygraphia* (1518) was the first printed book on cryptography.</note> of both Trithemius and Father Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who expanded these methods.</note>, as well as Classes 1 and 2 of Father Schott’s *Steganographic School*, will undoubtedly agree with me and assert that the invention explained thus far performs most perfectly what Trithemius promises in his *Polygraphy*: namely, how you may make known the secret of your mind safely, securely, and without any suspicion from any observers, to one who knows the industry of the art, as widely as necessary at any distance, regulated by speech.

Nor should it trouble you that a multitude of words in the open sense contains a brief meaning in the hidden sense; for you should know that this method is to be employed only in great and difficult matters. And truly, who is so lazy that he would not undertake the labor of filling a page of paper for the sake of gaining a city or a fortress—which might otherwise be bought with the blood of many thousands? Neither are all people so lazy or idle that such a subtle and pleasant labor would displease them. One might advise those "sleepyheads" <note>original: "dormilionibus"</note> that they should busy themselves finding a way for us to communicate the secrets of the mind while sleeping.

Furthermore, it is no objection that this mode of writing can now hardly be free from suspicion, since the craft is now known to almost everyone and the polygraphic tables are available everywhere. Father Schott responds first: this craft is exceedingly ingenious; Trithemius cast its first seeds, Father Kircher cultivated them, and learned men perfect them daily, since it is easy to add to things already invented. Therefore, although it might perhaps be conceded that after the publication of the *Polygraphy* of Trithemius and even of Kircher, it is scarcely safe enough to use those specific letter-writing models—even if they are varied, changed, and so arranged that the latent secret cannot be found by any natural subtlety—especially since, as I have already suggested above and as Father Schott also asserts, Trithemius's invention by means of a form...

# EXPLAINED
### Aaa 2

...of a prayer <note>original: "precatoriæ"</note> is neither becoming nor beyond suspicion, nor is it suitable for every rank of person or correspondent. Furthermore, the Kircherian tables <note>The systems designed by Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680) used grids of words to hide secret messages within seemingly mundane text.</note> themselves suffer from defects: not all the word choices are true synonyms, they do not maintain proper grammatical connection in terms of gender and number, and the proper names cannot be applied to just anyone—especially among well-known persons. We must see, then, if other tables can be made from these same ones that are more elegant, without being forced, and beyond the suspicion of any observers.

Let us take several tables and reform them, so that the reader, for his own private correspondence, may be able to reform the subsequent tables in a similar way through this easy craft.

1. From the first table, more appropriate words suited to the purpose can be taken, for example, the following eight: *I received, I found, I attained, I held, I obtained, I received, I perceived, I took up.* <note>original: "Accepi, nactus sum, adeptus sum, tenui, obtinui, recepi, percepi, suscepi"</note> However, so that they may be varied twenty-four times <note>To correspond with the 24 letters of the Latin alphabet used in ciphers of this era.</note>, adverbs can be placed before or after them, such as: *excellently, correctly, well,* etc. Or only six, five, or four words might be taken, and by placing adverbs before or after them, 24 variations can be made. For an example, let 4 words be taken here: *I received, I obtained, I found, I attained,* for the first 4 letters, **a, b, c, d**. Let *excellently* <note>original: "optimè"</note> be placed before these for the next 4: **e, f, g, h**. For the next 4, **i, k, l, m**, let *excellently* be placed after. For **n, o, p, q**, let *correctly* <note>original: "rectè"</note> be placed before; for **r, s, t, u**, let *correctly* be placed after. For the remaining **x, y, z, w**, let *well* <note>original: "bene"</note> be placed before.

2. In the second table, these words, *your letters* <note>original: "literas tuas"</note>, varied through transposition <note>term: transposition (the process of changing the order of words in a sentence to encode different letters while keeping the meaning the same)</note>, will stand for the first letters **a, b**. These three words—*your last letters* <note>original: "postremas tuas literas"</note>—since they can change their position six times, will stand for the next six: **c, d, e, f, g, h**. Again, these three—*your latest letters* <note>original: "ultimas tuas literas"</note>—arranged in the same way for the six letters **i, k, l, m, n, o**. Likewise, these three—*your previous letters* <note>original: "posteriores tuas literas"</note>—for **p, q, r, s, t, u**. And finally, these three—*your reply letters* <note>original: "responsorias literas tuas"</note>—for **x, y, z, w**.

3. The third and fourth tables can be omitted entirely, as even at first glance they show suspicion, forced phrasing, or affectation; the same applies to the sixth table which follows.

4. The word *which* <note>original: "quas"</note> remains throughout. Then, for the first 12 letters, **a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m**, let *to me* <note>original: "mihi"</note> be placed before the following 12 synonyms: *delivered, bore, brought, reported, sent, transmitted, presented, gave, carried, brought over, rendered, returned.* <note>original: "tradidit, tulit, attulit, detulit, misit, transmisit, exhibuit, dedit, portavit, adportavit, reddidit, retulit"</note> For the following **n, o, p, q, r, s, t, u, x, y, z, w**...

5. For these six words: *servant, slave, host, friend, intimate, messenger* <note>original: "famulus, servus, hospes, amicus, intimus, nuncius"</note>. For the letters **a, b, c, d, e, f**, let the word **your** <note>original: "tuus"</note> be placed before them. For **g, h, i, k, l, m**, let **your** be placed after them. For **n, o, p, q, r, s, t**, let **my** <note>original: "meus"</note> be placed before them. For **t, u, x, y, z, w**, let **my** be placed after them.

6. For the first twelve letters **a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m**, use these twelve words: *I perceived, I understood, I learned, I grasped, I penetrated, I weighed, I saw, I read, I read through, I examined, I knew, I recognized* <note>original: "perspexi, percepi, cognovi, intellexi, penetravi, expendi, vidi, legi, perlegi, examinavi, novi, agnovi"</note>. Place **your** after them for **s, t, u, x, y, z, w**.

8. For the first six letters **a, b, c, d, e, f**, let these three words be transposed six times: *I wished to please you* <note>original: "tibi gratificari volui"</note>. For **g, h, i, k, l, m**, let these three be transposed: *I wished to agree with you* <note>original: "tibi condescendere volui"</note>. For **n, o, p, q, r, s**, let these be transposed: *I wished to satisfy you* <note>original: "tibi satisfacere volui"</note>. For the last letters **t, u, x, y, z, w**, these six: *I wished to assent to you* <note>original: "tibi annuere volui"</note>.

For **g, h, i**, place **for truly** <note>original: "etenim"</note> before them. For **k, l, m**, place **for** <note>original: "enim"</note> after them. For **n, o, p**, insert **for indeed** in the middle. For **q, r, s**, insert **for truly** in the middle. For **t, u, x**, insert **for** in the middle. For **y, z, w**, place **for truly** after them.

Let these nine tables suffice for the studious reader, who will very easily supply the rest by his own ingenuity; nevertheless, it was pleasing to add an example, so that it might appear how fluid and elegant a letter may be constructed from these tables. Suppose, for example, the message to be sent is: *I flee to you* <note>original: "Fugio ad te"</note>. It would come out in the "paraphrase of the day" like this: *I have excellently obtained your latest letters, which your host delivered to me, and as soon as I perceived your will, I wished to please you, for for your sake as quickly as possible, etc.* <note>The seemingly normal words "excellently obtained," "your host," "perceived your will," "wished to please you," and "for your sake" each correspond to a letter in the hidden message "Fugio ad te."</note> Again, if another example is given: *flee quickly* <note>original: "cito fuge"</note>. *I have found your last letters, which my servant delivered to me, and as soon as I weighed your spirit, I wished to agree with you: for indeed by your favor, etc.* Let us now clothe these same examples from the **Glottotactics** <term>Glottotactica: A method of secret writing using natural language, described by Gaspar Schott.</term> of Father Schott, even omitting tables 3, 4, and 6. **Response II.** Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German abbot and polymath, often considered the father of modern cryptography.</note> and Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680) was a Jesuit scholar who published extensively on "steganography" or hidden writing.</note> only handed down the method of this art and showed the practice through tables published for the public. However, they did not intend for anyone to use those exact same tables. Instead, one should manufacture their own similar correspondences according to the condition and social status of the people writing. I shall show such examples to you, curious reader, which I have designed for use between a master and a servant, or if one wishes to write to a lord to whom one gives the title of grace, in German: **Grace** <note>original German: "Gnaden"</note>.

### §. 4. Whether this Artifice is the very one that Trithemius knew and promised.

Consequently, Father Kircher and Father Schott <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680) and Gaspar Schott (1608–1666) were famous Jesuit polymaths who attempted to decode and defend Trithemius’s controversial work on cryptography.</note> believe that this artifice is the very one that Trithemius once knew and promised in his letters to Arnold Bostius <note>Arnold Bostius was a monk and friend of Trithemius; their correspondence about secret writing sparked centuries of debate over whether Trithemius was practicing magic or math.</note>. They are moved by these primary reasons: 1. Because the said artifice performs exactly what he promised, as we have seen; it is a Trithemian invention and truly wonderful, deserving of such a splendid preface, yet it escaped the comprehension of even the most learned men. Thus, it is probable that Trithemius inserted it into his *Polygraphia* along with many things he had promised in his *Steganographia*, because he intended to suppress that work and deprive it of light <note>Trithemius faced accusations of demonic magic regarding his *Steganographia* and sought to publish a "safer" version of his cryptographic methods in his *Polygraphia*.</note>, so that such a subtle and beneficial invention would not remain buried in darkness. 2. Because in many places in the *Polygraphia*, where he explains its uses and the precautions to be observed in operation, Trithemius says in express words that the invention lies hidden beneath the principles handed down in the *Polygraphia*—for example, on page 61: 

> *Fourteenth, it should be known that in this very invention of our Polygraphia, there lie hidden certain things far better than those prescribed: namely, how you can inform one ignorant of the Latin speech in a few days—I might even say hours—so that he knows how to write, read, speak, and understand Latin, etc.* <note>original: "Quarto decimo sciendum, quod in hac ipsa inventione Polygraphiæ nostræ adhuc latent quædam præscriptis longè meliora, videlicet quomodo latini sermonis ignarum in paucis diebus ne dicam horis, informare poteris, ut sciat latinè scribere, legere, loqui & intelligere &c."</note>

However, Trithemius's own words in the *Polygraphia* on page 38 prevent me from subscribing to this opinion so quickly: 

> *The third utility, however, is that you will teach one unskilled in the Roman tongue not only to write and read what we promise in a few hours, but also to understand it, if you prudently apply the gift of your office—which we have decided should be reserved, not without reasonable cause.* <note>original: "Tertia vero utilitas, quod Romani sermonis imperitum, non solum in paucis horis docebis quod pollicemur scribere ac legere, sed etiam intelligere, si prudenter munus officii adhibueris, quod non sine rationabili causa nos duximus reservandum."</note>

From this it clearly appears that Trithemius neither handed down nor wished to hand down this invention of his in the *Polygraphia*. Nor do the arguments brought forward above carry any weight. The first is not convincing because it is uncertain and merely a conjecture supported by no foundation. The second argument actually confirms my own opinion, as he says that "certain things far better than those prescribed lie hidden" in the invention of the *Polygraphia*; for if they lie hidden, they are certainly not expressly...

### § 5. Whether the Kircherian invention, refined by Father Schott, satisfies the promises of Trithemius.

Father Kircher, by the wondrous sharp-wittedness in which he excels, found a most ingenious method—impenetrable to the common human mind—by which one can announce the secret concepts of the mind to another through any language of the whole world, even an unknown one and one which a person has not even heard of by reputation. He himself delivers that discovery in his *New Polygraphia*, treatise 3, chapter 5, where he proposes it thus: *How, by the aid of this artifice, anyone can write through letters in whatever language, even those of which he is unskilled and which he has not even perceived by reputation; indeed, using any foreign characters, such as Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Chinese, and finally any other kind of characters for revealing hidden senses of the soul to another, using no transmission of numbers.* <note>original: "Quomodo hujus artificii ope, per epistolas quacunque lingua... nulla numerorum transmissione, uti possit." This was a bold claim: sending a secret message in Chinese without actually sending a list of numbers.</note> Father Schott also delivers this same thing in his *Steganographic School*, classes 3, 4, and 5.

It consists principally in this: he converts the letters of the secret to be announced into numbers in various and most subtle ways—using a numerical abacus <term>abacus numeralis: a grid or table used to convert letters into digit coordinates</term>, an uncut cryptographic table, or the same table cut into various columns, through smaller tablets, or by a simple or double steganographic wheel <term>rotula steganographica: a cipher disk used for encryption</term>. This is done through a varied and manifold combination with or without a key. Then, by a new artifice, he subtly includes those numbers within letters written in any language of the entire world: namely, he begins to count the individual letters of a letter written in any language from a natural or assumed beginning. When he reaches that letter where the first number of the secret to be announced ends, he places a mark or fixes a visible or invisible dot. From this letter, excluding it, he again begins to count letters until he comes to the letter where the second number of the secret ends, and again he fixes a dot, and so on consequently, until all the numbers are dotted.

Take an example: I wish to announce to someone: *beware of him whom you do not know.*

All these letters, by his invention and method, are transformed into numbers in this way: 20. 6. 5. 9. 3. 8. 6. 9. 12. 13. 10. 22. 9. 7. 16. 13. 24. 13. 14. 16. 8.
I wish to include them in a letter; I take any letters whatsoever—for example, Latin ones—which begin: *I want you to know very much that I am angry with you, who would not...* etc. I count the letters from the beginning until I reach the twentieth, which is **S**, and I fix a point <note>A small dot placed beneath the letter.</note> there; from this one, I count the following letters until the sixth, which is **S**, and again I fix a point; from that one again, I count the rest until I reach the fifth, which is **i**, and again I fix a point; the same reasoning applies to the rest. ## CHAPTER VII.

# INVESTIGATING TRITHEMIUS’S <term>STEGANOLOGY</term><note>The study or theory of secret communication.</note> WITHOUT WORDS, WITHOUT GESTURES, WHILE SPEAKING, PREACHING, PLAYING THE ORGAN, OR SINGING, WITHOUT HINDRANCE TO ANY OTHER ACTION.

Persisting in the arrangement of *Steganographia* according to the letters written to Arnold Bostius <note>A Carmelite monk and friend of Trithemius to whom he revealed his secret inventions in a famous letter in 1499.</note>, I have thus far briefly examined three books and the inventions promised in them. Now follows the <term>Steganology</term>, which he promised in that same place in the fourth book and proposed as follows: *“The fourth book contains many stupendous experiments, but purely natural ones: namely, I can indicate my mind to one who knows my art while eating, or sitting with others, without words, and without gestures; I can do so as widely as I wish even while speaking, preaching, playing the organ, or singing, without hindrance to any other action whatsoever. Thus, by preaching good and holy things, I may indicate to anyone who knows [the art]—and as widely as I wish—whatever I want, without words, without signs, and without gestures, even with my eyes closed. And the fourth book will contain many other secrets which are not to be brought forth into public.”*

These things are marvelous, I confess, if they are consistent with both truth and nature; for it seems impossible to many to be able to signify anything to another without gestures, words, signs, and so on. And for this reason, Father Kircher thinks that the said words should be taken not in a collective sense, but in a "disjunctive" sense <note>Kircher argues that Trithemius means he can use *either* words *or* signs, but not necessarily nothing at all.</note>. He believes Trithemius means nothing else than that we can indicate the secrets of the mind to another sometimes by gestures without words, sometimes by words without gestures, sometimes by both words and gestures without signs, and sometimes by signs alone without gestures or words.

However, Father <term>Schott</term><note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a student of Kircher who also wrote extensively on cryptography and magic.</note> more correctly thinks that Trithemius’s words are <term>equivocal</term><note>Having double meanings.</note> and entirely true in a certain sense; therefore, they should be understood exactly as they sound, even if it is not clear what Trithemius's specific art was. Trithemius’s words can be saved <note>Proven true or logical.</note> in two ways. First, if we interpret them in this sense with Father Schott: *“I can, while eating, sitting, or speaking with others, preaching, playing the organ, singing, etc., indicate my mind to another who knows the art and is present, without signs, gestures, or words that are distinct from the aforementioned actions. Thus, from those very signs, gestures, and words with which I perform those actions, another person who is present and either seeing or hearing them may understand my mind.”*

However, an objection is raised against this interpretation: that Trithemius mentions <term>Dactylogy</term><note>The art of communicating using finger signs or a manual alphabet.</note> in his *Stegano...*

...if he had wished to write about the art of secret communication; for he says the following in his *Exposition on the Prologue of Polygraphia*: 
*“This monk <term>Bede</term><note>referring to Bede the Venerable (c. 672–735), an English monk whose works on time and finger-counting were often cited by early cryptographers.</note> reviewed many and various ways of writing and signaling secretly in his little book on the inventions of the ancients; by these means, they safely sent their secrets to friends and spoke without a voice to those present. We have long ago assigned a proper place for these difficult matters in the <term>Steganographia</term>, which we do not yet intend to publish.”* If, therefore, <term>Trithemius</term> wished to write about finger-talking in the *Steganographia*, how could he have shown it without signs, or what actions could he have employed by which the method of speaking through the fingers would have been indistinguishable? Secondly, the words of Trithemius can be interpreted in such a way that they are understood to be placed only to distinguish them from the ancient ways of secret speaking, which were done through words, nods, and signs that were suspicious and apparent. Thus, Trithemius may have known and promised methods of speaking *without words*—that is, so that the secret speech occurs without spoken words, though not necessarily without any expression—and *without nods and signs*—meaning those signs which are recognizable as signals in themselves, rather than actions which are used incidentally to signify something, while being naturally intended for another purpose or being common traits of human behavior. Whatever explanation you accept, I hasten to the matter itself.

When about to speak a certain secret to a friend, one inserts the individual words of the secret into a prior open narrative, in any way and order, without any regard for specific words of the narrative. It is agreed upon with the friend that those words of this narrative are the meaningful ones for which the speaker gives some sign. However, such a sign—a nod, a gesture, a movement of the hands, etc.—must be indistinguishable from the ordinary actions of people speaking, so that it gives no indication of the hidden matter nor arouses suspicion; this is to be left to the ingenuity of the <term>Steganologist</term> <note>A practitioner of steganography, the art of hiding a message within a non-secret medium.</note>. He is a brave man <note>The second secret word is "man" (man).</note>, he loves you, and will with all possibility assist you, also upon request advance enough money, therefore when you do not know what you should start <note>The final secret word is "catch/start" (fangen).</note>.**

Behold the narrative: while speaking it, the person gives a sign at the word **"go"** with a gesture of the hand—for example, by touching it to the chest or the knee—and does the same at the word **"man,"** and so on consecutively.

...I distinguish by name and power: for example, A is Genesis; B, Exodus; C, Leviticus; D, Numbers; E, Deuteronomy; F, Joshua; G, Judges; H, Ruth; I, the first book of Kings <note>In the Vulgate tradition used here, 1 and 2 Kings refer to 1 and 2 Samuel, while 3 and 4 Kings refer to the books known today as 1 and 2 Kings.</note>; K, the 2nd book of Kings; L, the 3rd book of Kings; M, the 4th book of Kings; N, 1 Chronicles; O, 2 Chronicles; P, Tobit; Q, Judith; R, Esther; S, Job; T, Psalms; V, Proverbs; X, Ecclesiastes; Y, Song of Songs; Z, Wisdom; W, Ecclesiasticus <note>A book of the Apocrypha, also known as Sirach.</note>. The remaining letters are rarely in use, except for Z, for which we shall place the second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians, so that the first Epistle stands for F <note>The author is adjusting the New Testament list to ensure every letter of the alphabet has a corresponding book for encryption.</note>. We could manufacture a third and fourth alphabet from the Prophets, the Holy Fathers, and the Historians, which is left to the ingenuity of the reader.

Therefore, when a preacher is about to announce some secret, he cites a text, or at least names a book of Holy Scripture (or of the Holy Fathers and others) which has been assigned to that letter of the alphabet which he intends to signify, using whichever alphabet he pleases. For example: a preacher knows from a secret council that a friend is to be captured; he wishes to indicate this with these words: "today you will be captured" <note>original Latin: "hodie capieris"</note>. 
1. First, he takes a text from H, which is Ruth, or Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, whichever suits the matter better <note>The letter 'H' is the first letter of 'Hodie' (Today).</note>. 
2. Second, from O: the 2nd book of Chronicles, or Paul’s Epistle to Titus <note>The letter 'O' is the second letter of 'Hodie'.</note>. 
3. Third, from the book of Numbers (D), or the Gospel according to John. 
4. Fourth, from the 1st book of Kings (I), or Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians. 
5. Fifth, from Deuteronomy (E), or the Acts of the Apostles. 
Under these texts, the word "today" <note>original: "hodie"</note> will be understood; the same method applies to the remaining words.

### §. 2. Steganology while playing the organ.

The material of this section was introduced previously in the *Compendium of Universal Steganography*, where I displayed various modes through which—by the help of music or musical instruments—anything can be indicated to another most secretly. ## CHAPTER VIII.

### PRESENTS THE STEGANOGRAPHIC METHOD BY WHICH ONE WHOLE WORD REPRESENTS ANOTHER WORD.

What *Trithemius* promised in his letters to *Arnold Bostius* <note>Arnold Bostius (1445–1499) was a Carmelite monk and a friend of Trithemius; their correspondence is a primary source for early cryptographic history.</note> regarding the four books of *Steganography*, I have examined thus far with the greatest and most forced brevity. Now remain the other things which he promises here and there in the *Polygraphia*, and among them first that wonderful and incomprehensible artifice of writing by which one word represents another entire word of any kind. This is proposed by *Trithemius* in these words:

*We shall therefore give, in the four following books, easier ways of writing; though they are not entirely free from the suspicion of those who look upon them, for the reason that they are alien to the understanding of most people. In the Steganography, however, there are more abundant methods of writing most secretly and without any suspicion, where a word does not represent a letter, but every word represents another whole word suitable to the mystery.* <note>original: "Dabimus ergo in quatuor sequentibus libris faciliores quidem scribendi modos... ubi non dictio literam, sed quæque aliam integram ad mysterium convenientem repræsentat dictionem."</note>

Let us provide an example of this matter, as if you wished to forewarn a friend about some imminent danger, under a narrative of words such as this: *Melancius, Tiberius, John, and Peter, servants of the Count of Asoro, have conspired for your death, and on the fourth day after Lawrence* <note>Referring to the Feast of Saint Lawrence, August 10th.</note> *at night they will surround your house; see to what you should do.*

The *Steganography* cloaks this secret in such a way: *I pray you, dearest friend, that you send me ten florins by the bearer of these presents, because they are very necessary to me for the construction of a certain building; I will faithfully restore them to you.*

Who would believe this secret, or suspect it to be hidden in the prescribed speech? Let us also place the same message under another narrative: *Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who willed to become man, to suffer and die for us, have mercy on me, an unworthy sinner, now and in the terrible hour of my death.*

Behold, you now have one hidden thought of your heart veiled by a double narrative within the limits of *Steganography* in a speech brief but faithful, which the whole world could not even suspect, nor, if it searched for a hundred years, find in any way, even if all the learned men were to meet. Finally, the aforementioned *Steganography* teaches how to hide this same secret thought of your heart not only in one or two prescribed narratives, but in almost infinite ways, and to announce it to whomever you wish most safely, most secretly, and most securely. All methods of this kind of invention can also be changed through <term>metathesis</term> <note>From the Greek for "transposition"; here referring to the rearranging or substitution of elements in a code.</note> in infinite turns, and everything can be written and announced through them. Behold the artifice proposed in the simplest words, which Steganogra-

This was a problem proposed by Father Kircher that seemed highly paradoxical, unless he was laboring under an ambiguity.

## §. 1. The method of Father Kircher is proposed and examined.

When about to describe his method, Father Kircher introduces it as follows:

> *I proceed at last to that great and wonderful secret of writing, which Trithemius described with such magnificent, bombastic words, and which he thought should be protected from the access of ungrateful men with such thorns of speech and metaphors; in the discovery of which the industry of so many most ingenious men has until now exhausted itself.* <note>original: "Procedo tandem ad magnum illud & mirabile scribendi secretum... in quo reperiundo tot hucusque ingeniosissimorum hominum desudavit industria."</note>

Briefly, it is this: With the help of a <term>steganographic chest</term> <note>Kircher's "Arca Steganographica" was a physical wooden box containing slats or "tables" used to automate the encryption process.</note> and whole steganographic tables—or, more pleasantly and ingeniously, with tables divided into various columns—he converts each letter of the secret message into numbers through various arrangements and combinations with each letter of a sentence chosen as a key. He then hides these numbers within letters, in the manner described above in the last section of Chapter 6. The "artifice," and that in which the whole subtlety and impenetrability consists, is that once a combination of a certain key-letter and a certain secret-letter is set, only one and the same number can ever result; yet, one and the same number can result from several different combinations. ### §. 2. The Author’s first device is proposed.

Having refuted Kircher’s device, I will propose another. It is similar to his in that it shows letters corresponding to and represented by other letters, but it is most similar to Trithemian Steganography in that it commands concealment according to the manner of Trithemius’s first book. It is as follows: Let two concentric <term>volvelles</term> <note>Small rotating paper disks often found in early modern books for calculation or cryptography.</note> be made of different sizes, namely one larger than the other. Let the smaller be fixed above the larger at the same center so that it can easily be rotated in any direction. Let the edge of each be divided into as many equal spaces as the letters you intend to use for your work—for example, 22, as Trithemius used. In these spaces, let the 22 letters of the alphabet be inscribed: **A b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x z**. Thus, the instrument will be complete.

Now for the operation: I wish to notify a friend, for example, **Beware of Frederick** <note>original: "Cave à Friderico"</note>. However, I have previously agreed with the friend on a certain sentence to be used as a key, for example: *Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, etc.* <note>original: "Gloria Patri & Filio & Spiritui Sancto &c."</note> This sentence must be both known by heart and used everywhere as a rule...

| *Key* | G | l | o | r | i | a | P | a | t | r | i | e | t | f |
| *Secret* | c | a | v | e | a | f | r | i | d | e | r | i | c | o |
| *Letters* | t | n | g | l | p | f | c | i | h | l | i | e | g | i |

<note>The "Key" is the phrase *Gloria Patri et f* ("Glory to the Father and..."). The "Secret" message is *Cave a Friderico* ("Beware of Frederick"). The "Letters" are the resulting ciphertext.</note>

Once the letters have been transformed in this way, one could insert them into a letter—following the method of the first book of <term>Steganography</term> <note>Referring to Trithemius’s *Steganographia*, which hides messages within seemingly innocent text.</note> or my own expansions—to be sent securely to a friend without fear. Here is an example, where alternative words are used to hide the letters.

->*The Letter*<-

From your last letters, I have read in many words the weight of your affairs; would that I could help with such happy advice. May your integrity be most joyfully crowned with the honors you are due. Meanwhile, I will take care of what you desire, wishing to please you in all things. Farewell.

<note>The recipient would extract the specific letters (t, n, g, l, etc.) from the words of this "innocent" letter to reconstruct the ciphered "Letters" from the table above, then use the cipher wheels to decode them.</note>

->*Corollary*<-

I. What I have demonstrated through these disks could just as easily have been shown through a <term>numerical abacus</term> <note>A mathematical grid or table used for calculating substitutions.</note>, if letters were placed in the position of numbers, or through the cut and uncut steganographic tables of Father <term>Kircher</term>. Truly, however, the use of these disks is much more concise and pleasant regarding the expansion of the code.

II. Just as it is not necessary for Kircher's key to contain exactly as many letters as the secret, so also this key can overflow, as in the example; or it can fall short, and when it is finished, be repeated. Furthermore, anything can be used as a key: a person's proper name, a title, or even the beginning of the letter itself.

III. Just as I said that when a certain letter of the secret is placed over a certain letter of the key, one must notice which letter of the upper disk corresponds with the **A** on the lower disk; so too another letter of the lower alphabet could be chosen...

# STEGANOGRAPHY

the letters of the upper alphabet are to be noted. This is done by positioning the combination of the letters of the **key** and the **secret message**; however, more can be added subsequently as far as expansions are concerned.

### Expansion I: In which two keys can be assumed.

That two keys can be assumed for hiding any secret message, or even several in succession—so that letters transformed by the first key are transformed again by another key—is neither a matter of great skill, nor of necessity, nor is it my intention. What I intend is that two keys be used simultaneously for this purpose, which is done as follows: Let the first key be *Glory to the Father and the Son* <note>original Latin: "Gloria Patri & Filio"</note>. Let the second key be *Glory be to the Trinity* <note>original Latin: "Sit Trinitati gloria"</note>. Let the secret message be the same as above: *Beware of Frederick* <note>original Latin: "Cave à Friderico"</note>. 

Now, on the lower <term>disk</term> <note>original: "rotula"; the outer part of the cipher wheel</note>, look for the first letter of the first key, which is **G**, and move the first letter of the secret message, which is **C**, to it. Then, in this adjusted position, look on the lower rim for the first letter of the second key, which is **S**, and observe which letter of the upper disk corresponds to it; you will note that letter down. Perform the same operation for the rest. Behold the letters that result:

| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Key 1** | G | l | o | r | i | a | P | a | t | r | i | e | t | f |
| **Secret** | C | a | v | e | a | f | r | i | d | e | r | i | c | o |
| **Key 2** | S | i | t | t | r | i | n | i | t | a | t | i | g | l |
| **Letters** | O | x | c | g | i | o | p | r | d | l | e | n | n | t |

From this, it can be clearly gathered how a single letter could be assumed in place of any key; for what is done more easily by this method using several letters can also be done using one.

### Expansion II: In which the same letter is read in different ways according to different keys.

I do not wish to be understood here as if I wanted to transform two secrets into other letters through two keys and insert both into an open speech so that some letters serve one secret and others serve the other; for that would be to expand the books of <term>Steganography</term> <note>Likely referring to Johannes Trithemius’s famous 1499 work on cryptography and spirits</note> or to deceive by ambiguity. 

Therefore, I shall hand down a device by which the same letters of the same epistle, when combined with different keys, exhibit a different secret message. I shall do it in this way: let there be two keys, a first and a second; likewise, let there be two secret messages, a first and a second. Let the first secret be changed into other letters through a combination with its own key, and let these letters be saved as a new key for the second secret. Again, let the second secret be changed into other letters through a combination with its own key—namely the second one—and let these be saved as a new key for the first secret message. Then let these two new keys also be combined with each other, and by the described device, indeed

# EXPLAINED.

indeed, so that one part acts as a secret and the other as a key, they are transformed into new letters which are then inserted into ordinary correspondence. The result is that the person to whom the first secret is to be announced, if he combines these letters of the letter with the new key of the second person, will find his own new key; by applying this to the first and true key, he will become a participant in the hidden message. The same logic applies to the second person.

**Expansion III:** That the same letter <note>original: "epistola"; referring here to the physical message or dispatch</note> can be understood in the same way according to different keys. This is, as it were, an expansion of the previous method; for if, just as there were two keys there, here the same hidden meaning <note>original: "sensus arcanus"</note> is combined with different keys, and the operation is carried out in the prescribed manner, we will achieve this effect no less than the other. This expansion is primarily for the purpose of being able to correspond secretly with two people using the same or different letters, yet neither can discover the key of the other, even though they can extract the same secret from the same letters.

**Expansion IV:** Whereby the same letter is read in different ways according to the same key; that is, so that two secret meanings can be hidden in the same letter under the same key. This is, as it were, the reverse of the preceding expansion, and therefore its operation must be established in the same way: namely, that the same key is first combined with two secrets, and the letters resulting from those two combinations are again combined with each other, and the letters resulting from that are inserted into the speech <note>original: "orationi"; the "cover" text of the message</note>.

->§. 2. The second artifice of the Author is presented.<-

Finally, with God's help, I have been led to that point where I may reveal, in the designated order, that wonderful artifice of writing so far only desired, believed by so many to be impossible, and attempted by the greatest **steganographers** <note>practitioners of "hidden writing" or cryptography</note>; and thus I may satisfy my promises and restrain the envy of my rivals. I would certainly have incurred the mark of an impostor if, after the recently published synopsis, I had not had the opportunity to make public this invention, which has until now escaped the subtlety of all steganographers. *For who could conceive of a way of writing in which, instead of a key phrase, individual words represent individual letters, syllables, and words of the secret message to be sent? Likewise, that individual syllables represent individual letters, syllables, and words of the secret; likewise, that individual letters represent individual letters, syllables, and words of the secret; and finally, that a single letter, syllable, or word assumed in place of a key represents each and every letter, syllable,*

the words of the secret? Therefore, so that I may study brevity and not be delayed too long in the defense of my honor, here briefly is this artifice—indeed, the final and most incomprehensible one—in which a single letter, taken in place of a key, represents each and every word of the secret, from which the prudent reader will easily discover the rest and greater things. Let the letter **E** be taken as the key. Let the secret to be announced be, for example: *Tomorrow I will be with the soldier before the gate of the citadel.* <note>original Latin: "Cras ero cum milite ante portam arcis."</note> I compose letters <note>original: "literas"; meaning the outer cover letter or dispatch</note> that are not at all suspicious, and I insert the words of the aforementioned secret into them, so that they have no obvious connection among themselves and cannot move suspicion in any way, yet they maintain a fluid connection with the rest of the words of the letter. For example, let these be the letters:

### *Letter.*

Because General Montecuccoli <note>Raimondo Montecuccoli (1609–1680) was a celebrated Italian professional soldier and military theorist who served the Holy Roman Empire.</note> has directed his journey here, I have it in my orders to go out to meet him tomorrow; I will, however, be proceeding *with all the nobility of this place and many a soldier.* Our Prince will receive him *before the new gate*, and *splendidly*, for it has been decided that twenty cannons shall be fired three times from the *rampart of the citadel*.

Now, from the beginning, I count the words of this letter, and I note at which number the words serving the secret fall. I find them arranged thus: 12, 4, 3, 7, 5, 2, 13. <note>These numbers represent the intervals between the hidden words. For example, "cras" (tomorrow) is the 12th word; counting 4 more words leads to the next secret word, and so on.</note> Having set these down, I begin another period or continue, or I form a postscript, where—having counted the words from the beginning in a similar way—the words falling on these specific numbers must begin with **E**, namely, that letter which was taken as the key.

### *Continuation.*

I hope, however, that he has not undertaken that journey here in vain, but **From** <note>original: "Ex"</note> a reasonable cause, for this place **Is** <note>original: "Est"</note> plainly **Outside** <note>original: "Extra"</note> the way; I omen that this **Is** <note>original: "Esse"</note> a sign of peace to be concluded shortly, especially since **Also** <note>original: "Etiam"</note> from elsewhere a proof of **His** <note>original: "Ejus"</note> was assured to me; whatever the case may be, shortly his whole intention **Will be** <note>original: "Erit"</note> in the proof. <note>original: "in probabulo"; a phrase suggesting the matter will soon be tested or made clear.</note> Farewell.

I believe you see, and most clearly see, curious reader, how one single letter represents whole words; from which you can easily gather how the same letter might represent syllables and letters, which I show with two examples.

### *Letter 1.*

Because General Montecuccoli has directed his journey here to Vienna, I have it in my orders to go out to meet him; I will, however, be with the nobility

You shall come therefore to us; Peter will offer you his house, which you shall inhabit as your own. Therefore, consider what you should do.

## CHAPTER IX.

### IT WILL EXPLAIN ALL THE REMAINING THINGS WHICH TRITHEMIUS PROMISED HE WOULD WRITE IN HIS STEGANOGRAPHY.

I have reserved for the present chapter those things which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Benedictine abbot whose works on cryptography were often accused of being magical or demonic.</note> indeed promised he would write in his *Steganography*, but which until now had not achieved light from the *Steganography Illustrated* <note>original: "Steganographia Illustrata"; likely referring to the title of this current commentary or edition.</note>: Among which, first, were <term>Arthrologia</term> <note>From the Greek 'arthron' (joint); a method of signaling using the joints or knuckles.</note> and <term>Dactylogia</term> <note>From the Greek 'daktylos' (finger); finger-spelling or signing.</note>: by the use of these, one person reveals to another most securely whatever secret he wishes, which no one else sitting nearby will notice, and much less understand. Second, a triple kind of secret writing with invisible characters: the first of which is called <term>Dormaticum</term> <note>Likely derived from 'derma' (skin); though the text says "dorso" (back), it refers to writing on the body.</note>, by which a certain artificial writing is made on the back of messengers, which no one is able to penetrate who does not know the secret of the art. The second is called <term>Hyphasmaticum</term> <note>From the Greek 'hyphasma' (textile/fabric).</note>, by which one writes on cloth with certain substances, which when dried cannot be seen at all, until it is perceived when moistened in cold water. Truly, since I have already hinted at all these things in the appropriate place above, and they exist everywhere in the works of other Steganographers <term>Steganographers: Writers who study the art of hiding messages in plain sight.</term> most extensively and learnedly, and especially in Father Caspar Schott’s *Schola Steganographica* <note>original: "sch. steg. cl. 7. erot. 8. 9. 10." refers to the classification and sections in Schott's 1665 handbook on cryptography.</note>, I did not wish to "pour water into the Rhine" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to do something redundant or unnecessary.</note>, but I hasten immediately to the artifice by which everything contained in this universe can serve Steganography, which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and pioneer of early modern cryptography.</note> proposes thus:

Lest I explain this with a long and tedious circumlocution of words, I wished only to add a few examples, from which the reader may easily grasp the matter itself and the method.

### Example 1.

A grammarian has secret business with another grammarian, and so that these things remain secret, they form an Alphabet for themselves from Grammar. For example: for the first five letters of the alphabet, they place the five cases of the singular number of the first or second declension, but the vocative <note>The vocative is the case used for direct address, such as "O Friend."</note> is omitted everywhere. For the second 5 letters, they take the plural cases of the same declensions. For the third five, the singular cases of the third and remaining declensions. For the fourth 5, the plural cases of these declensions. For the last 4 letters (w, x, y, z), four vocatives can be placed. With these established, he forms the letter so that all the substantives <note>Nouns.</note> are in that case in order which the logic of the secret letters requires. Suppose the message to be announced is: *unless you come, I perish* <note>original: "nisi venias pereo".</note>; such letters are formed:

## STEGANOGRAPHY ILLUSTRATED.

I. CHAP. *It presents in a summary almost all the inventions of the Steganographers.*
II. *It examines and expands upon the first book of the Steganography.*
III. *It examines and expands upon the second book of the Steganography.*
IV. *It investigates the method of communicating secrets by fire at any distance whatever, without words, without writing, and without signs, through any messenger.*
V. *It investigates the method of indicating one's will to someone sitting in prison, even at a great distance, however much they are guarded, even if they were sitting three miles underground.*
VI. *It examines the art through which an uneducated man, who never knew a word of the Latin language, is taught in two hours to read, write, and understand Latin.* <note>original: "homo idiota". In this context, it refers to a "layperson" or someone lacking formal academic training.</note>
VII. *It investigates Trithemius's <term>Steganology</term> <note>From the Greek 'steganos' (secret) and 'logos' (speech); the art of secret communication through spoken word or performance.</note> without words, without gestures, while speaking, preaching, playing the organ, or singing, without hindrance to any action whatsoever.*
VIII. *It presents a steganographic method by which one whole word represents any other word.*
IX. *It explains all the remaining things which Trithemius promised here and there in the "Steganographia" that he would write.*

<note>This table is a mathematical implementation of a polyalphabetic cipher. To use it, a sender would pick a keyword and a plaintext letter. By finding the intersection of the keyword's letter (lateral) and the plaintext letter (frontal), they would receive a number. This converted text into a numerical code that appeared meaningless without the specific "abacus" and key.</note>
